items.title: Paver Patio Cost: DIY vs Pro Breakdown and Worked Example
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A DIY 12 × 12 ft paver patio costs roughly $965 in materials and tool rental, about $6.70 per square foot, using the example prices in this guide. Professional installation costs more because it adds labor, excavation and overhead. Your own prices will differ by region, so check local quotes.

If you're pricing a paver patio, you'll find wildly different numbers online. The reason is simple: cost depends on paver choice, base depth, how much soil has to be dug out and hauled, and whether you or a crew do the work. Instead of quoting a number you can't check, this guide shows how to build your own estimate line by line.

The worked example uses clearly labeled assumed prices for a 12 × 12 ft patio. Swap in prices from your local supplier, or let the paver patio calculator handle the quantities.

Key takeaways
  • Example DIY total: about $965 for 144 sq ft, or $6.70 per sq ft, with pavers at $3 per sq ft.
  • Biggest line items: pavers (about half) and base gravel (about a fifth) in this example.
  • The hidden cost: digging and hauling roughly 4.2 cubic yards of soil for a 12 × 12 ft patio.
  • Quote check: ask pros to list base depth, paver product, edge restraint and excavation separately.
  • Prices vary: every price here is an example, not a quote.

How much does a paver patio cost to build yourself?

A DIY patio is mostly material cost plus a day or two of tool rental. This worked example uses the quantities from our paver patio calculator for a 12 × 12 ft patio (144 sq ft) with a 6 inch base, plus 10% extra pavers. All prices below are assumptions for illustration.

ItemQuantityAssumed priceCost
Pavers (144 sq ft + 10%)158.4 sq ft$3.00 per sq ft$475
Crushed stone base (6 in, +20% for compaction)4.5 tons$40 per ton$179
Bedding sand (1 in)0.62 tons$40 per ton$25
Edge restraint48 ft$2.00 per ft$96
Polymeric jointing sand2 bags$30 per bag$60
Geotextile fabric (optional)158 sq ft$0.25 per sq ft$40
Plate compactor rental1 day$90 per day$90
Totalabout $965

That works out to $6.70 per square foot. It leaves out delivery fees, a wet saw rental if you have many cuts, spikes for the edge restraint and any disposal charge for the dirt you dig out, so allow some margin.

🧮

Put your own prices into the estimate. The paver patio calculator gives the pavers, stone and sand for your exact size, and the gravel calculator converts yards to tons.

How much does a professional paver patio cost?

A contractor's price covers everything above plus labor, equipment, excavation and haul-away, overhead and profit. Quotes vary widely by region, patio size, design complexity and the paver you pick, and they change with the season and local demand, so there is no single figure that fits everyone.

The reliable way to compare is per square foot, with the scope spelled out. As a purely hypothetical illustration, a quote of $18 per square foot for 144 sq ft would be $2,592, nearly three times the DIY material cost in the example. That gap pays for crew labor, equipment and a workmanship guarantee. It isn't automatically a rip-off, and the cheapest quote isn't automatically the best.

What to make every contractor itemize

  • Base depth and material: 4 inches versus 6 inches of compacted stone is a big quality difference.
  • The paver product: brand, size, thickness and cost per square foot.
  • Excavation and disposal: whether hauling away roughly 4 cubic yards of soil is included.
  • Edge restraint and jointing sand type.
  • Drainage and slope work, if the yard is uneven or wet.
  • Warranty terms, in writing.

What makes a paver patio cost more or less?

FactorEffect on cost
Paver type (basic concrete vs. premium or natural stone)Largest swing in materials; natural stone can cost several times basic concrete
Patio sizeLarger patios cost more total but less per square foot, since fixed costs spread out
Pattern and shapeCurves, herringbone and borders add cuts, waste and labor
Base depthA 6 in base uses 50% more stone than a 4 in base
Site conditionsSlopes, tree roots, poor drainage and tight access add excavation and labor
Soil removalDig depth of 9 3/8 in on a 144 sq ft patio means about 4.2 cubic yards to move
Region and seasonLabor and material rates differ across the country

Is DIY or professional installation cheaper?

DIY is cheaper in cash, but only if you value your time at close to nothing and own or can rent the tools. A first-time 12 × 12 ft patio takes most people a long weekend or two, because digging, hauling and compacting are hard work.

DIYProfessional
Cash costMaterials + rentalsMaterials + labor + overhead
Time2–4 days of work for a small patio, more for a first attemptOften 1–3 days of crew time
Skill neededBasic, with careful compaction and levelingIncluded
Physical effortHigh (moving several tons of stone and sand)None for you
WarrantyNone, except on materialsOften offered

A common middle path: hire a pro for excavation and base, then lay the pavers yourself, or the reverse. The base is the part most likely to fail and the heaviest to move, so paying for it is where hiring pays off most.

How can you lower the cost of a paver patio?

  1. Size it to the paver. A patio that's a multiple of the paver dimensions needs few cuts. A 12 × 12 ft patio in 12 × 12 in pavers needs exactly 144 and almost no waste.
  2. Choose a simple pattern. Running bond wastes less than herringbone at 45°.
  3. Compare bulk to bagged materials. Buying stone and sand by the ton from a landscape yard is usually much cheaper per pound than bagged material, though delivery adds a fee.
  4. Reuse excavated soil. Spread it to fix low spots in the lawn or use it in a raised bed, if it's good soil, to avoid disposal fees.
  5. Get three itemized quotes. Prices for the same scope can differ a lot between contractors.
Don't cut costs on the base. Thinner base, skipped compaction or no edge restraint all save money on day one and cost far more when the patio sinks. Save on the paver choice or the pattern instead.

When does a paver patio cost more than you expect?

Surprises usually come from the site, not the pavers. Roots, rock or buried debris slow digging. Clay soil that holds water may call for a deeper base. A steep yard may need a small retaining wall, and a long carry from the driveway to the backyard adds labor if you're paying a crew or wheeling stone yourself.

Delivery is the other common add-on. Bulk stone and sand arrive by truck and are dumped in one pile, often on your driveway, and many suppliers charge a separate delivery fee. A tarp, plywood to protect the driveway and a plan for moving 5 tons of material in a day or two are part of the real project cost. Build 10–15% contingency into the budget so a surprise doesn't stall the job halfway.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a 12x12 paver patio cost?

With the example prices in this guide, a DIY 12 × 12 ft patio is about $965 in materials and rental. A professional installation will cost more because it includes labor, excavation and overhead; get itemized local quotes.

Is a paver patio cheaper than concrete?

It depends on the finish. Basic poured concrete is often cheaper to install than pavers, but pavers can be repaired by lifting individual units and are less likely to crack as a single slab.

How much do pavers cost per square foot?

Pavers alone range from basic concrete at a few dollars per square foot to premium or natural stone at several times that. This guide's example uses $3 per square foot; check your local supplier.

What is the cheapest way to build a patio?

A small, rectangular patio of basic concrete pavers in a simple pattern, built yourself on a well-drained site, is typically the lowest-cost paver option. Gravel patios cost less still but are a different surface.

Does the cost include digging out the soil?

The DIY table doesn't include a soil disposal fee, although it assumes you do the digging. A 12 × 12 ft patio excavated 9 3/8 in deep produces about 4.2 cubic yards of soil, so ask whether contractors include haul-away.

The bottom line

A small DIY paver patio can come in under $1,000 in materials and rental at the example prices, with the paver choice and base depth driving most of the cost. Itemize every quote, never skimp on the base and check the quantities with the paver patio calculator before you buy.

Related tools: Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Installation and base guidance from the Interlocking Concrete Pavement Institute (ICPI) and paver manufacturers' instructions. All prices in this article are assumed examples for illustration, not quotes or averages; get current prices from local suppliers and licensed contractors. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Paver Base Depth: How Much Gravel and Sand Under Pavers
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

For a typical patio, lay 4–6 inches of compacted gravel base topped with 1 inch of bedding sand. Use 6 inches or more for driveways, soft or clay soil, and freeze-thaw climates. A 12 × 12 ft patio with a 6 inch base needs about 3.2 cubic yards (4.5 tons) of crushed stone and 0.6 tons of sand.

The base is the part of a paver patio nobody sees and the part that decides whether it lasts. Pavers don't fail on their own; they sink, tilt and heave when the base underneath was too thin, too wet or not compacted. Get the depth right and a patio stays flat for decades.

Below you'll find the recommended depth for each use, how much gravel and sand to order by patio size, and how deep to dig. For your own dimensions, the paver patio calculator returns the quantities directly.

Key takeaways
  • Walkways and patios: 4–6 in of compacted crushed stone; add depth on clay soil or in cold climates.
  • Driveways: 8–12 in of base, since they carry vehicle loads.
  • Bedding sand: 1 in, screeded and never compacted before the pavers go on.
  • Dig depth: base + 1 in sand + paver thickness. A 6 in base with 2 3/8 in pavers means digging about 9 3/8 in.
  • Order extra: loose stone compacts by roughly 20%, so buy about 1.2 times the finished volume.

How deep should a paver base be?

Paver base depth depends on what the surface carries and what's underneath it. The ranges below reflect typical guidance from the paver industry. Always follow the installation instructions for the product you use, and check any local frost or soil conditions.

UseCompacted gravel baseBedding sand
Walkway or garden path4 in1 in
Patio on firm, well-drained soil4–6 in1 in
Patio on clay, soft soil or in a freeze-thaw climate6–8 in1 in
Driveway or parking pad8–12 in1 in

If soil is very soft or stays wet, a thicker base won't help on its own. Fix drainage first, and consider asking a local landscape supplier or a contractor about a geotextile layer between soil and gravel.

What kind of gravel goes under pavers?

Use an angular, crushed aggregate that locks together when compacted, sold under names like "crushed stone," "road base," "dense-graded aggregate" or "3/4 inch minus." The fine particles mixed in among the larger pieces are what make it compact into a solid layer.

Avoid rounded pea gravel or river rock for a base. The pieces roll over each other and never lock, so the surface keeps shifting. Ask your supplier for the material they recommend for paver bases in your region, since names vary.

How much sand goes under pavers?

Bedding sand is a thin, even leveling layer, about 1 inch thick. It's not the structure; the gravel is. Use coarse, washed concrete sand rather than fine play sand or stone dust, which hold water and drain poorly.

Screed the sand flat, then lay the pavers on top without walking on the sand. Joint sand, which is swept into the gaps afterward, is a separate (and much smaller) quantity.

How much gravel and sand do you need for a patio?

Volume is area × depth. Convert to cubic yards by multiplying square feet by depth in inches and dividing by 324. Crushed stone weighs about 1.4 tons per cubic yard, and the table adds 20% to the base because loose stone compacts to roughly 80% of its loose volume. These figures are planning estimates; your supplier's stone may weigh a bit more or less.

Patio sizeBase depthGravel (cu yd, +20%)Gravel (tons)Sand at 1 in (cu yd · tons)
100 sq ft4 in1.482.10.31 · 0.43
100 sq ft6 in2.223.10.31 · 0.43
144 sq ft (12 × 12 ft)4 in2.133.00.44 · 0.62
144 sq ft (12 × 12 ft)6 in3.204.50.44 · 0.62
200 sq ft4 in2.964.10.62 · 0.86
200 sq ft6 in4.446.20.62 · 0.86
300 sq ft6 in6.679.30.93 · 1.3
300 sq ft8 in8.8912.40.93 · 1.3
🧮

Not sure about tons versus yards for your patio? Open the paver patio calculator for pavers, base and sand together, or the topsoil and gravel calculator to convert any volume to tons.

How deep do you dig for a paver patio?

Dig deep enough for the base, the sand and the paver itself, so the finished surface ends up where you want it, usually 1 inch or so above surrounding soil in your lawn so water runs off.

Dig depth = base depth + 1 in sand + paver thickness. Typical residential pavers are about 2 3/8 inches (60 mm) thick, so:

  • 4 in base: 4 + 1 + 2.375 = 7 3/8 in
  • 6 in base: 6 + 1 + 2.375 = 9 3/8 in
  • 8 in base: 8 + 1 + 2.375 = 11 3/8 in

Excavate 6–12 inches beyond the patio edge on each side so the base extends under the edge restraint. For a 12 × 12 ft patio dug 9 3/8 inches deep, expect about 4.2 cubic yards of soil to move or haul away.

How do you build the base, step by step?

  1. Call 811 first. Utility locates are free in the US and required before digging in most states.
  2. Mark and excavate. Stake the outline, run string lines and dig to your calculated depth, sloping the subgrade about 1/4 inch per foot away from the house.
  3. Compact the soil. Run a plate compactor over the bare subgrade until it feels firm, and replace any soft spots with gravel.
  4. Add gravel in 2–3 inch layers (lifts). Spread, wet lightly and compact each lift before adding the next. Compacting a single deep layer leaves loose stone underneath.
  5. Check the slope. Use a level and string line to confirm the base slopes the way you intended before any sand goes down.
  6. Screed the bedding sand. Lay two parallel pipes on the base, fill between them with 1 inch of sand and drag a straight board across. Pull the pipes out and fill the grooves.
  7. Lay pavers and edge them. Install the edge restraint, compact the pavers, sweep in joint sand and compact again.
Don't use the sand as a thick leveling fix. Sand layers deeper than about 1 inch settle unevenly and show up as dips. If the base is uneven, correct it with gravel and recompact, not with extra sand.

What are the most common paver base mistakes?

  1. Skipping the plate compactor. Hand tamping can't compact a gravel base to the density a paver surface needs. Rent a plate compactor for a day.
  2. Using the wrong material. Pea gravel, stone dust alone or topsoil can't be compacted into a stable layer.
  3. Building too shallow for the climate. A 4 inch base on clay soil in a freeze-thaw region invites heaving. Go deeper where winters are cold or soil is soft.
  4. No slope. A perfectly flat patio holds water. Aim for about 1/4 inch of fall per foot, directed away from buildings.
  5. No edge restraint. Without it, the paver edges spread and the joints open up.

Frequently asked questions

Can I put pavers directly on dirt?

You can, but it isn't recommended. Pavers on bare soil sink, shift and fill with weeds within a season or two, because soil doesn't drain or support a load the way compacted gravel does.

Is 4 inches of gravel enough for a paver patio?

Four inches is generally acceptable for walkways and patios on firm, well-drained soil in mild climates. On clay, soft ground or in cold-winter regions, 6 inches or more is safer.

Do I need landscape fabric under a paver base?

Fabric isn't needed over firm soil. A geotextile layer between soil and gravel can help over soft, clay-heavy soil by keeping the layers from mixing. Don't put fabric between the base and the bedding sand.

How many tons of gravel do I need for a 10x10 paver patio?

For a 100 sq ft patio, a 4 inch base needs about 2.1 tons and a 6 inch base about 3.1 tons, including a 20% allowance for compaction. Ask your supplier whether they sell by the ton or the yard.

Can I use stone dust instead of sand under pavers?

Coarse concrete sand is the standard bedding layer because it drains well. Stone dust holds water, packs hard and can cause pavers to settle unevenly, so most installers avoid it for bedding.

The bottom line

Plan on 4–6 inches of compacted crushed stone and 1 inch of coarse bedding sand for a patio, and go deeper on soft soil, in cold climates or for driveways. Dig to base + sand + paver thickness, compact in lifts and order about 20% more stone than the finished volume. The paver patio calculator turns your dimensions into exact quantities.

Related tools: Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Soil Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Base and bedding guidance from the Interlocking Concrete Pavement Institute (ICPI) and paver manufacturers' installation instructions. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; crushed stone is estimated at about 1.4 tons per cubic yard, which varies with the material and moisture. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Landscape Edging Ideas: Materials Compared by Cost and Effort
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The cheapest landscape edging is a spade-cut trench; the most durable are steel, brick, stone and concrete; plastic sits between for cost and ease. Pick by how long you want it to last and how much effort you'll put in. Dig the trench 4–6 inches deep, and set rigid edging so it holds in your mulch depth.

Good edging does three jobs at once. It keeps mulch and gravel inside the bed, keeps lawn grass from creeping in and gives the yard a finished look that's out of proportion to what it costs.

This guide compares the main materials by cost, effort and where they work best, then shows how to install them and how much mulch the bed inside needs. To size the fill, use the mulch calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Free option: a spade-cut trench costs nothing but needs re-cutting once or twice a year.
  • Lasts longest: steel, brick, stone and concrete; plastic is the shortest-lived and cheapest.
  • Height: the edging should be at least as tall as your mulch layer so mulch doesn't spill over.
  • Curves: steel, plastic and small pavers follow curves; large blocks and poured concrete suit straight or gentle lines.
  • Mowing: set edging flush with or slightly below the lawn to run a mower wheel along it.

What are the best landscape edging ideas?

Here are the six options most homeowners choose from. Costs are rough example ranges for materials only, with a typical retail spread; they vary a lot by region, brand and style, so check your local prices.

Edging typeExample cost per ftExample cost for 100 ftEffortDurabilityBest for
Spade-cut trench$0$0Low to start; re-cut yearlyNeeds upkeepInformal beds, tight budgets
Plastic (roll or sections)$1–$3$100–$300LowShort; can heave and crackQuick, temporary fixes
Steel or aluminum strip$2–$6$200–$600MediumLongCrisp, modern lines and curves
Brick or pavers on end$3–$8$300–$800Medium to highLongTraditional look; follows curves
Natural stone or block$4–$12$400–$1,200HighVery longRaised borders and cottage styles
Poured concrete curbingOften quoted installed, so ask for quotesGet quotesUsually hired outVery longLong, straight or gently curved runs

What is the cheapest way to edge a garden bed?

A spade-cut edge costs nothing. With a flat-bladed spade, cut a clean line along the bed and dig a V-shaped trench about 4–6 inches deep. Pull the sod out of the bed side, angle the lawn wall at roughly 45 degrees and fill the trench with mulch.

The trade-off is upkeep. Grass roots creep back, so plan to re-cut the edge once or twice a growing season. Spade-cut edging works best for informal beds and for people who like the soft, natural look.

Which edging lasts the longest?

Hard materials that don't rot or flex last the longest. Steel and aluminum resist heaving and bend into curves, but sharp tops can be a hazard, so choose rolled or capped tops where kids play. Brick, pavers and stone can last decades if set on a compacted base. Poured concrete lasts longest but is hard to change later.

Plastic and thin wood timbers are the least durable. Plastic can bow in heat and break from mower strikes, and untreated wood rots when it's in constant contact with soil.

Which edging is best for curves?

  • Steel and aluminum strips: bend by hand into gentle curves, held by stakes.
  • Plastic edging: flexible, but kinks on tight curves and needs frequent stakes.
  • Bricks or small pavers: follow tight curves because each unit is small.
  • Large stone blocks and poured concrete: best on straight lines or sweeping, gentle curves.
🧮

Edging is only half the bed. Use the mulch calculator to work out the cubic yards and bags for the area inside, including odd shapes and rings around trees.

How do you install landscape edging?

  1. Mark the line. Lay a garden hose or rope along the curve and adjust it until it looks right from the street and from windows. Spray-paint the line.
  2. Cut or dig a trench. For rigid edging, dig a trench the width of the product and deep enough that the top sits where you want it, usually flush with the lawn or 1/2 inch above it.
  3. Set the edging. Place it in the trench, check the height along its length with a string line and backfill with soil, tamping as you go.
  4. Secure it. Drive stakes or spikes for metal and plastic. Set brick and stone in a base of compacted gravel or sand for stability.
  5. Add mulch. Fill the bed to 2–3 inches, leaving a few inches of bare soil around any trunk.

How tall should landscape edging be?

For holding in mulch, the top of the edging should rise at least as high as the mulch, so it contains a 3 inch layer without it spilling over. Most beds use edging that stands 2–4 inches above grade; steel strips are often 4–5 inches tall with 1–2 inches showing and the rest buried.

If you want to mow right up to the bed, set the top of the edge flush with the lawn or just below it. A raised edge needs separate string-trimming along it.

How much mulch does an edged bed need?

A bed with 100 ft of edging that's 4 ft wide is 400 sq ft. At 3 inches deep, that needs 400 × 3 ÷ 324 = 3.7 cubic yards, or about 50 bags of 2 cu ft. Measure inside the edging and use the mulch calculator for odd shapes.

Check before you dig. Call 811 before digging deeper than a few inches, and avoid trenching near tree roots. Cutting large roots near a trunk can damage or destabilize the tree, so route edging around them.

What are the most common edging mistakes?

  1. Setting it too low. Mulch spills over a 1 inch lip as soon as it rains.
  2. Skipping the base for brick and stone. Unsupported units tilt and sink after the first winter.
  3. Tight curves in stiff material. Plastic kinks and large blocks gap; choose a flexible or small-unit edge instead.
  4. Unfinished joins. Gaps at metal and plastic joints let grass roots through.
  5. No edge along walkways. Without a border, mulch and soil spread onto paths and drives.

Which edging suits which yard?

Match the material to the style of the house and the way you maintain the yard. A cottage-style border of mixed perennials looks right with a spade-cut edge or low stone. A modern front yard with ornamental grasses and gravel suits thin steel. A formal brick walk calls for matching brick or paver edging.

  • Mowing along it: choose flush edging, such as a mowing strip of pavers, so wheels roll over it.
  • Pets and kids: avoid sharp, thin metal tops; choose rolled-edge metal, brick or stone.
  • Rocky or rooty soil: a spade-cut edge or surface-laid stone is easier than trenching for steel.
  • Slopes: heavier stone or brick edging holds mulch back better than light plastic.

When in doubt, start with a spade-cut edge for a season. You'll learn where mulch tends to spill and where the lawn creeps in, then choose a permanent edging for those spots.

Frequently asked questions

What is the easiest landscape edging to install?

A spade-cut trench is the easiest: you only need a flat spade. Among products, roll-out plastic edging is the quickest to install, though it doesn't last as long as steel or stone.

How deep should you bury landscape edging?

Bury rigid edging so only 1–2 inches show above ground, with the rest below, so it stays put and resists heaving. For a spade-cut trench, dig a V-shape 4–6 inches deep.

Does steel edging rust?

Plain steel will rust, and some people like the rusty look. Galvanized or powder-coated steel and aluminum resist rust for much longer, so choose those if you want a clean finish.

Should I put landscape fabric under edging?

You don't need fabric under the edging itself. Brick and stone edging benefits from a compacted gravel or sand base for stability instead.

Can I use landscape edging to separate gravel from lawn?

Yes. Steel and aluminum edging give a clean, long-lasting boundary because they hold gravel in and keep grass roots out, and they bend well around curves.

The bottom line

Choose edging by lifespan and effort: a free spade-cut trench for informal beds, steel or aluminum for crisp lines, brick or stone for a traditional look and concrete for permanent runs. Set it at least as tall as your mulch and use the mulch calculator to fill the bed.

Related tools: Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Soil Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Bed-edging and mulch-depth guidance from US university extension services, including University of Maryland Extension and Penn State Extension; tree-root protection guidance from the International Society of Arboriculture. Costs shown are rough example ranges, not quotes; check current local prices. Volume conversion: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Laminate vs Vinyl Plank Flooring: Which Is Better for You?
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Choose vinyl plank (LVP) for kitchens, bathrooms, basements and rooms with pets or spills, since it's waterproof. Choose laminate for dry living areas where you want a harder, more wood-like surface. Both are floating floors you can install yourself. The deciding factors are moisture, noise and how you'll use the room.

These two floors look alike in the store and behave differently once they're down. Laminate has a wood-fiber core under a printed photographic layer. Vinyl plank is plastic all the way through, so it doesn't mind water the way a fiberboard core does. That one difference decides most of the choices below.

Whichever you pick, you'll need to know how much to buy. Use the flooring calculator to turn your room measurements into boxes before you compare prices.

Key takeaways
  • Water: vinyl plank is waterproof; laminate is water-resistant at best and swells if water reaches the core.
  • Feel: laminate is harder and more rigid, vinyl is softer and slightly warmer underfoot.
  • Wear: check the laminate AC rating (AC3 and up for homes) and the vinyl wear layer in mils.
  • Install: both float over a flat subfloor with a small expansion gap at the walls.
  • Price: both span a wide range, from budget to premium, so compare actual products.

What is the difference between laminate and vinyl plank?

Laminate is made of layers: a clear wear layer on top, a photographic image of wood or stone, a high-density fiberboard (HDF) core and a backing. It's a wood-based product with a protective surface.

Vinyl plank (luxury vinyl plank, or LVP) is built from layers of PVC. Many current products have a rigid core, often labeled SPC (stone plastic composite) or WPC (wood plastic composite), while older flexible vinyl is thinner and bends more. Neither core type is wood fiberboard.

Laminate vs vinyl plank: side-by-side comparison

FeatureLaminateVinyl plank (LVP)
CoreHigh-density fiberboard (wood-based)PVC; rigid SPC/WPC or flexible
WaterResistant to surface spills; swells if water gets into seams or edgesWaterproof core; seams can still let water reach the subfloor
HardnessHard and rigid, can feel more like woodSlightly softer and quieter underfoot
Scratch/dentSurface is hard and scratch-resistant; chips can show white edgesResists dents less; wear layer thickness matters
Typical thicknessAbout 6–12 mmAbout 4–8 mm, sometimes with an attached pad
Wear ratingAC (abrasion class) rating, AC3 and above for most homesWear layer in mils; thicker is more durable
TemperatureStable; expands and contracts with humidityCan expand and contract with temperature swings
RepairReplace damaged planks if they click apartReplace damaged planks, easier with some locking systems
Best roomsLiving rooms, bedrooms, dry hallwaysKitchens, baths, basements, mudrooms, laundry

Which is better for water, kitchens and bathrooms?

Vinyl plank is the safer pick for wet rooms. A fiberboard core absorbs water at the edges and seams, then swells and ruins the plank, which doesn't flatten again once it dries. Many laminates now have water-resistant coatings, but their guarantees usually cover only short-term spills that you wipe up promptly.

Waterproof vinyl isn't a flood solution either. Water that gets through the joints can still reach the subfloor and grow mold. Fix leaks quickly, keep the expansion gap sealed according to the manufacturer's instructions where required and read the warranty for water limits before you buy.

Which wears better with kids and pets?

Laminate has a hard, abrasion-resistant surface, rated AC1 to AC5 under European-style classes. AC3 is the usual choice for homes, and AC4 or AC5 for busy spaces. It resists scratches from pet claws but can chip.

Vinyl plank wear layers are measured in mils (thousandths of an inch). Many residential products have wear layers in the range of roughly 6–20 mil, and thicker is generally better for busy households with pets. A thicker vinyl wear layer resists scuffs, but heavy furniture or sharp objects can dent it.

How do laminate and vinyl plank compare on cost?

Both come in budget, mid-range and premium versions, and the ranges overlap so much that cost alone rarely settles the question. Material prices per square foot differ by brand, thickness and wear layer, and installed price depends on your region.

To compare fairly, price the material per square foot after your waste factor, add underlayment if the product doesn't include it, and count trim, transition strips and removal of the old floor. The flooring calculator helps you compare boxes and cost between products.

🧮

Deciding between two products? Use the flooring calculator to work out how many boxes of each you'd need for your room, including waste.

How hard is it to install each one?

Both are click-lock floating floors you can install yourself over a clean, flat subfloor. You won't need nails or glue for most products, just a saw, a tapping block and a few spacers.

  1. Check the subfloor. Most manufacturers ask for flatness within about 3/16 inch over 10 feet. Vinyl, being thinner, can telegraph bumps and dips more than laminate.
  2. Acclimate the planks. Leave the unopened boxes in the room for the period listed in the instructions, usually around 48 hours, so they adjust to room conditions.
  3. Leave an expansion gap. Keep a gap, commonly about 1/4–1/2 inch, around the room's edges so the floor can move. Baseboards or trim cover it.
  4. Stagger the seams. Offset end joints by at least the distance in the instructions, often 6 inches or more.
  5. Cut with the right tool. Laminate dulls blades faster and needs a fine-tooth saw; vinyl can often be scored and snapped.

Always follow the manufacturer's installation instructions, since gaps, underlayment and acclimation rules differ by product and affect the warranty.

Which should you choose?

  • Choose vinyl plank for kitchens, bathrooms, basements, laundry rooms, mudrooms and homes with pets or small children.
  • Choose laminate for dry living areas and bedrooms where you want a harder, more wood-like feel, as long as the room isn't prone to spills or humidity.
  • Choose vinyl when you can't be sure the subfloor will stay dry, such as over a concrete slab.
  • Choose laminate when you want a stiff floor that doesn't flex over minor subfloor flaws.
Whichever you choose, don't skip the subfloor prep. Floating floors telegraph every dip and bump, and the locking edges can break if the floor flexes. Level high spots, fill low spots and fix moisture problems before the first plank goes down.

How do laminate and vinyl compare for sound and comfort?

Floating floors can sound hollow when walked on, and the type of underlayment makes a big difference. Laminate tends to be a bit louder because the fiberboard core is rigid and transmits impact noise, so a quality underlayment helps in upstairs rooms. Vinyl plank, especially with an attached pad, is typically quieter and slightly softer underfoot.

Temperature is another comfort factor. Vinyl can feel cooler over a concrete slab, and some rigid-core vinyl products have limits on indoor temperature swings, such as in sunrooms with large south-facing windows. Laminate is generally stable in temperature but reacts more to humidity. Read the manufacturer's limits for your room before buying.

If you're torn, bring home large samples of both and look at them in your own room's light. Drop a little water on each, scratch them with a key and step on them barefoot. Ten minutes with samples settles more questions than a spec sheet.

Frequently asked questions

Is vinyl plank more durable than laminate?

It depends on the use. Vinyl handles moisture better and tolerates impacts that would chip laminate, while laminate resists scratches better. For wet areas vinyl is more durable; for dry rooms they're close.

Can you put laminate in a bathroom?

It isn't recommended. Water that reaches the fiberboard core at seams or edges can make it swell permanently. Waterproof vinyl plank or tile is the safer choice for bathrooms.

Does vinyl plank flooring need underlayment?

Many products have an attached pad, and adding another layer can void the warranty. Check the instructions; laminate often needs a separate underlayment unless a pad is attached.

What does the AC rating on laminate mean?

AC stands for abrasion class, a scale from AC1 to AC5 that rates how well the surface resists wear. For homes, AC3 is a typical minimum, while AC4 and AC5 are for heavier traffic.

How thick should the wear layer on vinyl plank be?

Many residential products fall in the 6–20 mil range. A thicker layer lasts longer, so look for 12 mil or higher in busy homes or with pets, and check the manufacturer's residential warranty.

The bottom line

Pick vinyl plank where water is a factor and laminate for dry rooms where a harder feel matters. Prepare the subfloor carefully, follow the manufacturer's gap and acclimation rules and buy from one lot. The flooring calculator will tell you how many boxes you need before you commit.

Related tools: Paver Patio Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Product construction and installation guidance from flooring manufacturers' published instructions, the National Wood Flooring Association (NWFA) and the Resilient Floor Covering Institute (RFCI) for resilient floors. Always follow the instructions and warranty for the specific product. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Level Ground for a Patio or Shed Base (Step by Step)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To level ground for a patio or shed base, stake out the area, run level string lines, cut the high spots and fill the low ones with compacted gravel. Patios should slope about 1/4 inch per foot away from the house, so a 10 ft patio drops 2.5 inches. A shed pad should be level, on 4–6 inches of compacted gravel.

Almost no backyard is flat. A patio or shed set on uneven ground will rock, crack or collect water, and once it's built, the only fix is to tear it up. A few hours with stakes and string at the start saves that.

This guide shows how to find out how far off level you are, how to cut and fill without causing settling, and how much gravel the base needs. For quantities, use the topsoil and gravel calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Patio slope: 1/4 inch of fall per foot, away from buildings (a 12 ft run drops 3 in).
  • Shed pad: as level as you can get it, with a 4–6 inch compacted gravel base extending about a foot past the footprint.
  • Cut rather than fill: dig down into firm soil on the high side where you can; fill settles.
  • Compact in lifts: spread fill in layers of about 4 inches and tamp each one.
  • Quantity: a 10 × 12 ft shed pad at 6 inches deep needs about 3.7 tons of crushed stone.

How do you check whether your ground is level?

Don't trust your eyes. A yard that looks flat can have a 6 inch drop across 12 feet. Use one of these methods.

  • String and line level: drive a stake at each end of the site, tie a mason string at the height of the highest ground and hang a line level on it. Pull it taut and measure from the string down to the ground at several points.
  • Straight board and level: lay a long straight 2 × 4 on the ground, set a 4 ft level on top and shim until the bubble centers. The gap under the board shows the dip.
  • Water level or laser level: faster across big areas. Rental stores and hardware stores carry rotary and line lasers.

Measure at the corners and the middle, write the numbers down and you have a map of the high and low spots.

How much slope should a patio have?

A patio needs a slight slope so rain runs off instead of pooling or heading toward the foundation. The usual rule is about 1/4 inch of fall per foot (roughly 2%), sloping away from the house. Shed pads and the areas beneath them should be as close to level as you can manage, since the shed floor must sit flat.

Patio depth away from houseTotal drop at 1/4 in per ft
8 ft2 in
10 ft2.5 in
12 ft3 in
16 ft4 in
20 ft5 in

To set the slope, put the string line at the finished height along the house side, then lower it at the far end by the drop in the table. Dig or fill to match that sloped line.

How do you level ground, step by step?

  1. Call 811. Have utilities marked before digging. It's free in the US.
  2. Outline the site. Stake the corners, 6–12 inches wider than the finished patio or shed footprint, and run string.
  3. Set the finished height. Choose the top of the finished surface, mark it on the stakes and run level or sloped string lines at that height.
  4. Remove sod and topsoil. Strip the grass and the soft top 3–4 inches, since organic soil settles and holds water.
  5. Cut the high side. Dig down to the required depth, measuring from the string. Work down to firm soil, not loose fill.
  6. Fill the low side with gravel. Add crushed stone in layers of about 4 inches and compact each with a hand tamper or plate compactor. Don't fill with topsoil, which keeps settling.
  7. Screed the surface. Lay two parallel pipes at the right height, fill between them and drag a straight board across to smooth the base. Compact again.
  8. Recheck. Measure from the strings and use the level. Fix any hump or dip now, because it won't be fixable later.
🧮

Know the size and depth of your pad? The topsoil and gravel calculator converts it into cubic yards, tons and bag counts, with a waste allowance.

How much gravel do you need to level a base?

Use area × depth ÷ 324 for cubic yards (area in sq ft, depth in inches). Loose stone compacts by roughly 20%, so the table multiplies by 1.2, and weight uses a planning figure of 1.4 tons per cubic yard.

Pad sizeDepthCompacted cu ydOrder (cu yd, +20%)Order (tons)
8 × 8 ft4 in0.790.951.3
10 × 10 ft4 in1.231.482.1
10 × 12 ft6 in2.222.673.7
12 × 16 ft6 in3.564.276.0

If you must fill more than 4–6 inches over a large area, ask a local landscape supplier or a contractor to confirm the material and how to compact it.

Patio vs shed base: what's different?

Patio baseShed base
SlopeAbout 1/4 in per ft away from houseAs level as possible
Base depth4–6 in compacted gravel plus 1 in bedding sand for pavers4–6 in compacted gravel; some builders add a timber frame
SizePatio footprint plus edgingAbout 1 ft past the shed on every side
Key checkDrainage away from foundationDiagonal measurements equal, floor flat
RulesCheck local codes for setbacksCheck permits and the shed maker's base specs

For shed pads, check that the two diagonals measure the same, which proves the frame is square, and follow the manufacturer's base instructions to keep the warranty valid.

What if the slope is steep?

If the ground drops more than about a foot across the site, filling the low side gets expensive and unstable. Consider cutting a terrace into the hill and holding the uphill side with a small retaining wall, or choosing a smaller or elevated deck instead. Taller walls and big grade changes can require permits or an engineer, so check local rules.

Don't level with loose topsoil. Topsoil and fill dirt settle over the first year or two, leaving dips and tilted pavers. Use compacted crushed stone for any fill under a patio or shed.

What are the most common leveling mistakes?

  1. Leveling by eye. Always use a string line and level, and recheck after each step.
  2. Making the patio perfectly flat. It needs about 1/4 inch per foot of fall away from the house.
  3. Leaving organic soil. Roots and topsoil rot and settle, so strip them before building up.
  4. Compacting one thick layer. Do it in lifts of about 4 inches.
  5. Forgetting drainage. Pools of water near the foundation or under the pad cause the problems you were trying to avoid.

What tools make leveling easier?

You can level a small site with basic tools, and a few rentals make bigger jobs faster. Here's a practical kit.

  • Flat spade and a square-point shovel for cutting and moving soil.
  • Mason string, stakes and a line level to set the finished height.
  • A 4 ft level and a long straight 2 × 4 for checking and screeding.
  • Hand tamper for small pads; a plate compactor, rented by the day, for anything bigger.
  • Wheelbarrow and rake to move and spread gravel evenly.
  • Marking paint or flags to show the high and low spots you measured.

Mark every spot where you measured and write the depth of cut or fill beside it. Working from a simple map prevents over-digging, which is the most common reason a base ends up needing extra gravel.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best way to level a yard for a shed?

Stake the footprint, strip the sod, cut the high side down and fill the low side with compacted crushed stone. Finish with a screeded 4–6 inch gravel pad about a foot larger than the shed.

Can I level ground with sand?

Sand works only as a thin 1 inch bedding layer under pavers. As the main fill it washes out and shifts, so use compacted crushed stone for anything thicker.

How do I level ground without a laser level?

Use stakes, mason string and a line level, or a long straight board with a 4 ft level on top. Both are accurate enough for a patio or shed base.

Should a patio be perfectly level?

No. A patio should slope about 1/4 inch per foot away from the house so water drains. A shed pad, which has to support a floor, should be level.

How far past the shed should the gravel pad extend?

About 6–12 inches on each side keeps water from pooling at the edges and gives you room to work. Always check your shed maker's instructions for base size.

The bottom line

Stake and string the site, cut the high side, fill the low with compacted crushed stone in lifts and slope patios 1/4 inch per foot away from the house. Aim for a flat, 4–6 inch gravel pad under a shed. Get your quantities from the topsoil and gravel calculator before you order.

Related tools: Paver Patio Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Site-preparation and base guidance from the Interlocking Concrete Pavement Institute (ICPI), US university extension services and shed manufacturers' published base instructions; utility locating from the national 811 "Call Before You Dig" program. Volume conversion: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; crushed stone is estimated at about 1.4 tons per cubic yard. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Build a Gravel Path: Materials, Depth and Steps
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To build a gravel path, dig about 5 inches deep, lay landscape fabric, add 3 inches of compacted crushed stone and finish with 2 inches of gravel topping, held in by edging. A path 3 ft wide and 30 ft long (90 sq ft) takes about 1.4 tons of base stone and 0.8 tons of topping, around 2.2 tons in all.

A gravel path is one of the cheapest, most forgiving hardscape projects. It drains water, it isn't hard to curve around trees and beds, and you can finish it in a weekend with a shovel, a wheelbarrow and a hand tamper.

The difference between a path that stays crisp for years and one that turns into a weedy mud strip is the layers underneath. This guide gives the depths, the materials, a quantity chart and the steps. For your own length and width, use the topsoil and gravel calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Width: 3 ft for one person, 4 ft so two can walk side by side, 5 ft for a wheelbarrow.
  • Layers: 3 in compacted base + 2 in topping, so dig 5 in.
  • Material: angular crushed stone for the base and topping; rounded pea gravel shifts underfoot.
  • Edging: required on both sides, or the gravel migrates into the lawn and beds.
  • Quantity: a 3 × 30 ft path needs about 1.0 cu yd of base (loose) and 0.6 cu yd of topping.

What materials do you need for a gravel path?

  • Crushed stone for the base: 3/4 inch angular stone, sometimes sold as "3/4 minus" or road base, which includes fine particles that lock together when compacted.
  • Gravel for the top layer: 3/8 to 3/4 inch crushed stone in the color you like. Small, angular stone is more comfortable and stays put better than large rounded pieces.
  • Landscape fabric (woven or non-woven), to keep soil and weeds from mixing into the stone.
  • Edging: steel, aluminum, plastic, brick or stone. See our mulch and edging planning tool for length estimates around beds.
  • Tools: flat spade, rake, wheelbarrow, hand tamper (or a rented plate compactor for long paths), a level and string line.

How deep should a gravel path be?

A footpath that only carries foot traffic does well with 3 inches of compacted base and 1–2 inches of topping, so you dig roughly 4–5 inches. If the soil is clay or stays wet, go deeper on the base, up to 4–6 inches, so water can drain through. Paths that carry carts or light vehicles need a much thicker base, which is a different project.

LayerDepthPurpose
Topping (small crushed stone)1–2 inThe walking surface and the color
Compacted base (3/4 in crushed stone)3 in (4–6 in on clay or wet soil)Strength and drainage
Landscape fabricUnder the baseStops weeds and soil mixing into the stone
Compacted subgradeDig 4–5 in deep (more for deeper base)Firm foundation

How much gravel do you need for a path?

Volume = length × width × depth. This chart uses a path 3 ft wide, a 3 inch base and a 2 inch topping. Loose base stone is increased by 20% because it compacts, and weights use about 1.4 tons per cubic yard, a common planning figure that varies by material.

Path length (3 ft wide)AreaBase, loose cu ydBase, tonsTopping cu ydTopping, tons
20 ft60 sq ft0.670.90.370.5
30 ft90 sq ft1.001.40.560.8
50 ft150 sq ft1.672.30.931.3
100 ft300 sq ft3.334.71.852.6

A 4 ft wide path needs one-third more of everything; a 2 ft wide path needs one-third less.

🧮

Enter your path's length, width and depth in the topsoil and gravel calculator to get cubic yards, tons and a bag-versus-bulk comparison for your own project.

How do you build a gravel path, step by step?

Step 1: Call 811 and mark the route

In the US, call 811 a few days before you dig so utility lines can be marked for free. Then lay a garden hose or rope along the route and adjust the curves until it looks right from the house and from the path's far end.

Step 2: Excavate 5 inches

Cut along the marked line with a flat spade and remove the sod and soil to a depth of about 5 inches (more if you're using a deeper base). Keep the bottom level across the width, and slope it very slightly so water runs off: about 1/8 to 1/4 inch per foot across the path, or along it, toward a lower area.

Step 3: Compact the soil and install the edging

Tamp the bare soil until it's firm. Install the edging along both sides with the top at your finished gravel level, 1/2 inch or so below the lawn if the path is next to turf so the mower can pass.

Step 4: Lay landscape fabric

Roll the fabric over the soil, overlapping seams by about 6 inches and tucking the edges against the edging. With a 3 ft path, a 30 ft run needs about 99 sq ft with a 10% allowance.

Step 5: Add and compact the base

Spread 3 inches of crushed stone in two lifts, wetting lightly and tamping each one until it's firm and doesn't shift underfoot. A hand tamper works for short runs; rent a plate compactor for anything over about 30 ft.

Step 6: Add the topping

Rake 1–2 inches of topping gravel over the base to the finished level. Light compaction with the tamper settles it. Gravel is meant to move a little, so keep a bucket of spare stone to top up the low spots.

Gravel path edging and weeds: what actually works?

Edging does two jobs: it holds the gravel in and keeps lawn and bed edges out. Steel and aluminum give crisp lines and flex around curves. Brick or stone looks traditional and lasts. Plastic is the cheapest and the first to heave or bow.

No fabric is weed-proof forever, because wind-blown seeds sprout in the gravel itself. Pull seedlings when they're small, rake the topping every season or two and don't put soil or mulch on the path. A shallow layer of coarse stone (1–2 inches) stays drier and grows fewer weeds than a deep one.

Skip the pea gravel for a walking surface. Rounded stones act like ball bearings: they roll underfoot, migrate off the path and make wheelbarrows and strollers hard to push. Angular crushed stone locks together and stays put.

What are the most common gravel path mistakes?

  1. No base. Gravel poured straight on soil sinks within a season and mixes with the dirt.
  2. No edging. The gravel creeps into the lawn and the mower throws stones.
  3. Flat grade in a wet spot. Water pools and the base turns soft. Give it a slight slope or add drainage.
  4. Too deep a topping. More than 2 inches of loose stone is tiring to walk on.
  5. Underordering. Loose stone compacts. Order about 20% extra for the base layer.

How much does a gravel path cost to build?

Material cost depends on your local stone prices, so plug your own numbers into the quantities above. Using assumed example prices of $40 per ton for the base stone and $55 per ton for decorative topping, a 3 × 30 ft path needs 1.4 tons of base ($56) and 0.8 tons of topping ($44), about $100 in stone. Fabric for 99 sq ft at $0.25 per sq ft adds about $25, and 60 ft of edging at $2 to $6 per foot adds $120 to $360.

These are example prices, not quotes. Delivery fees, tool rental and disposal of the soil you dig out (about 1.4 cubic yards for this path) come on top. Even so, a gravel path usually costs far less per square foot than pavers or concrete.

Frequently asked questions

How wide should a garden gravel path be?

Three feet suits one person, four feet allows two people to walk together and five feet fits a wheelbarrow comfortably. Narrower than 2 feet feels cramped.

Do you need landscape fabric under a gravel path?

It's recommended. Fabric keeps the base stone from sinking into the soil and slows weeds from below, though weeds can still sprout from seeds that land in the gravel.

What is the best gravel for a walking path?

Angular crushed stone in small sizes, around 3/8 to 3/4 inch. It compacts and locks together, so it's more stable underfoot than round pea gravel.

How much does a ton of gravel cover on a path?

A ton of gravel is about 0.7 cubic yards, which covers roughly 115 sq ft at 2 inches deep. That is based on the planning figure of 1.4 tons per cubic yard, so confirm weight with your supplier.

How do you keep a gravel path from washing out on a slope?

Use a thicker, well-compacted base, choose angular stone, and add cross-slope or small check dams. Very steep paths need steps or a different surface.

The bottom line

Dig about 5 inches, lay fabric, compact 3 inches of crushed stone, finish with 1–2 inches of topping and edge both sides. Order about 2.2 tons for a 3 × 30 ft path and use the topsoil and gravel calculator to size your own.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Soil Calculator · Paver Patio Calculator

Sources: Path-base and drainage guidance based on general extension and landscape-industry practice, including state university extension services and the Interlocking Concrete Pavement Institute for compacted aggregate bases. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; crushed stone is estimated at about 1.4 tons per cubic yard. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How Much Topsoil Do I Need? Chart by Depth and Square Feet
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

One cubic yard of topsoil covers 108 square feet at 3 inches deep. To find your amount, multiply the area in square feet by the depth in inches and divide by 324. A 1,000 sq ft lawn at 4 inches needs 12.3 cubic yards, so order about 14 yards with a 10% allowance for settling.

Topsoil is sold by the cubic yard, weighed by the ton or bagged by the cubic foot, and none of those match how you measure a yard. The fix is one formula and a depth that suits the job, because a new lawn and a leveled low spot need very different amounts.

This guide gives the formula, a chart for common lawn and garden sizes, the right depth for each use and how to buy. For your own measurements, use the topsoil and gravel calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: square feet × depth (in) ÷ 324 = cubic yards.
  • Coverage: 1 cubic yard = 324 sq ft at 1 in, 162 at 2 in, 108 at 3 in, 81 at 4 in, 54 at 6 in.
  • Depth: 4–6 inches for a new lawn or bed, 1/2 inch or less at a time for leveling, 1/4–1/2 inch for top-dressing.
  • Extra: order 10–15% more for settling and uneven ground.
  • Weight: a cubic yard is roughly 1–1.3 tons, so check your truck's payload.

How do you calculate how much topsoil you need?

Topsoil follows the same volume math as mulch: area × depth, converted to cubic yards. Four steps cover it.

Step 1: Measure the area in square feet

Multiply length × width in feet. For circles, use 3.14 × radius squared, and split irregular areas into rectangles and circles.

Step 2: Choose the depth for your job

See the depth table below. If you're adding to existing soil, measure what's already there.

Step 3: Multiply and divide by 324

Square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards. The 324 is 12 inches per foot × 27 cubic feet per yard.

Example: 1,000 sq ft × 4 in ÷ 324 = 12.35 cubic yards.

Step 4: Add 10–15% and round up

Loose topsoil compacts as it's spread and settles after watering, and ground is never perfectly flat. 12.35 × 1.10 = 13.6, so order about 14 cubic yards.

🧮

Have several areas or odd shapes? Use the topsoil and gravel calculator to add them all up and convert yards to tons, bags and cost.

How much does a cubic yard of topsoil cover?

Depth1 cubic yard covers1 cubic foot covers
1/2 inch648 sq ft24 sq ft
1 inch324 sq ft12 sq ft
2 inches162 sq ft6 sq ft
3 inches108 sq ft4 sq ft
4 inches81 sq ft3 sq ft
6 inches54 sq ft2 sq ft

How many yards of topsoil for common areas?

These are cubic yards before any settling allowance.

Area1/2 in (leveling)1 in4 in (new bed or lawn)6 in (new lawn, poor soil)
500 sq ft0.81.56.29.3
1,000 sq ft1.53.112.318.5
2,000 sq ft3.16.224.737.0
5,000 sq ft7.715.461.792.6

How deep should topsoil be?

Depth depends on the job and on how good the soil underneath is. These are typical ranges; if your project is large, check with your local extension office for your soil and grass.

UseTypical topsoil depth
New lawn on compacted or subsoil-only ground4–6 in, blended into the top layer if possible
New flower or shrub bed4–6 in
Vegetable garden on poor ground6–8 in of good soil, often mixed with compost
Filling low spots in an existing lawnUp to 1/2 in at a time, repeating once grass grows through
Top-dressing a lawn1/4–1/2 in
Filling around a foundation or raising a bedAs needed, graded away from the house

How many cubic yards for a lawn or a garden bed?

For a new lawn of 5,000 sq ft at 4 inches, that's 61.7 cubic yards (about 68 with 10% extra), which is a large delivery, so confirm access and a place to dump the load. For a garden bed 4 × 25 ft (100 sq ft) at 6 inches, it's 100 × 6 ÷ 324 = 1.85 cubic yards, about 2 with extra.

When leveling small low spots, it's more efficient to calculate just the dip rather than the whole lawn. A 100 sq ft dip filled 1/2 inch deep needs only 0.15 cubic yards, about 4 cubic feet.

How much does topsoil weigh?

A cubic yard of topsoil weighs roughly 2,000–2,600 lb (about 1–1.3 tons), depending on moisture, sand content and organic matter. Wet topsoil is much heavier than dry. A full-size pickup can legally carry about a cubic yard or two of topsoil before it hits payload limits, so for bigger orders, have it delivered.

Ask your supplier for their own weight per yard if you're buying by the ton, because it varies by pit and by season.

Bagged or bulk topsoil: how do you buy it?

Bagged topsoil, sold by the cubic foot (0.75 and 1 cu ft bags are common), makes sense for small jobs. A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, so it equals 27 bags of 1 cu ft or 36 bags of 0.75 cu ft. Bulk topsoil, delivered by the yard, is nearly always the better buy past a couple of yards. Check bag sizes carefully when comparing price per cubic foot.

What to ask a topsoil supplier

  • Is it screened? Screened topsoil has been sifted to remove rocks, roots and large clods.
  • What's in it? Ask about organic matter and the source. Avoid soil with a strong chemical smell or lots of debris.
  • Does it contain weed seed or clay? Cheap fill dirt often does.
  • How is it sold? By the cubic yard or by the ton, and the weight per yard.
Test unfamiliar soil before a big order. Ask for a small sample or buy a few bags first, and send a sample to your state's soil-testing lab through your county extension office if you plan to grow food. A load of poor soil is expensive to remove.

What mistakes lead to ordering the wrong amount?

  1. Forgetting to subtract. Don't count patios or sheds in your measurement, but do count steps and dips.
  2. Burying grass under thick fill. More than about an inch of soil over turf can smother it; for large raises, strip the turf first.
  3. Mixing up units. Cubic yards, cubic feet and tons are different; use consistent units.
  4. Skipping settling. Fresh topsoil sinks. Order 10–15% more.
  5. Grading toward the house. Slope fill away from foundations so water drains away.

Where does topsoil go wrong, and what are the alternatives?

Topsoil isn't always the best fill. Under a patio or shed, use compacted gravel instead, because soil settles. For a vegetable bed, a mix of topsoil and compost generally grows better than topsoil alone, since topsoil by itself can be dense and low in organic matter. For leveling, compost-and-sand blends are often used to top-dress established lawns without smothering the grass.

If you only need a modest amount, compare delivered bulk with bagged by cubic foot, and consider whether you can improve the soil you already have with compost. Adding 1–2 inches of compost and mixing it into the top 6 inches is often cheaper than replacing the soil, and it improves structure at the same time.

Frequently asked questions

How many cubic yards of topsoil do I need for 1,000 square feet?

At 4 inches deep you need 12.3 cubic yards, and with 10% extra order about 14. At 1 inch deep it's 3.1 cubic yards, and at 6 inches it's 18.5 cubic yards.

How many bags of topsoil are in a cubic yard?

A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, so it equals 27 bags of 1 cu ft or 36 bags of 0.75 cu ft. Check the bag size on the label before comparing prices.

How much does a cubic yard of topsoil weigh?

About 2,000–2,600 lb, or roughly 1–1.3 tons, depending on moisture and the mix. Ask your supplier for their exact weight per yard.

How deep should topsoil be for a new lawn?

Aim for 4–6 inches of topsoil, ideally tilled into the layer beneath so there's no sharp boundary. If the existing soil is already decent, a thinner layer can be enough.

What is screened topsoil?

It's topsoil sifted through a mesh to remove rocks, roots and big clumps, leaving a finer, more even material that's easier to spread and better for lawns and beds.

The bottom line

Multiply square feet by depth in inches and divide by 324 to get cubic yards, then add 10–15% for settling. Use 4–6 inches for new lawns and beds and only 1/2 inch at a time for leveling. The topsoil and gravel calculator converts the result to tons, bags and cost.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Lawn and bed soil-depth guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and Oregon State University Extension; soil testing through state land-grant university labs. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Weights are typical estimates and vary by moisture and soil type. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How Much Flooring Do I Need? Square Footage and Waste Factor
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To find how much flooring you need, multiply room length × width to get square feet, then add 5–10% for waste (10–15% for diagonal or herringbone). A 12 × 15 ft room is 180 sq ft, so buy about 198 sq ft at 10% waste. Divide by the coverage per box, usually around 20 sq ft, and round up.

Flooring is sold in full boxes, can't be returned once it's opened in many stores and often changes color between production lots. A good measurement is what keeps you from a half-finished room and a hunt for a matching box.

This guide shows the formula, a waste-factor chart, box counts for common room sizes, and how to handle closets, L-shaped rooms and stairs. For several rooms at once, use the flooring calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: length × width × (1 + waste %) ÷ box coverage = boxes to buy, rounded up.
  • Waste: 5–10% for straight layouts, 10–15% for diagonal or herringbone, and more for tricky rooms.
  • Boxes: a 12 × 15 ft room needs 10 boxes at 20 sq ft each with 5–10% waste; 11 with 15%.
  • Same lot: buy all boxes together and check the lot number so colors match.
  • Keep a spare: save at least one unopened box for future repairs.

How do you calculate how much flooring you need?

You only need a tape measure, a notepad and about ten minutes. Here are the steps.

Step 1: Measure each room's length and width

Measure wall to wall at the widest points, in feet and inches. Convert inches to decimals by dividing by 12: 10 ft 6 in is 10.5 ft. For a plain rectangle, length × width gives square feet. A 12 ft × 15 ft room is 180 sq ft.

Step 2: Add spaces that need flooring

Measure closets, alcoves, hall sections and doorways separately, then add them to the total. A 3 × 4 ft closet adds 12 sq ft, which takes the room above to 192 sq ft.

Step 3: Subtract only permanent fixtures

Kitchen islands and built-in cabinets don't need flooring under them. Furniture, appliances you'll replace and removable fixtures do. Many installers don't subtract small areas at all, since leftover material is useful for cuts.

Step 4: Add the waste factor

Multiply the area by 1.05 to 1.15 depending on the layout (see the next section). For 192 sq ft at 10%: 192 × 1.10 = 211.2 sq ft.

Step 5: Divide by the coverage per box and round up

The box label shows square feet per carton. At 20 sq ft per box, 211.2 ÷ 20 = 10.56, so buy 11 boxes.

🧮

Measuring several rooms with different box sizes? Try the flooring calculator. Add each room, choose a waste factor and get the number of boxes to buy.

How much waste factor should you add for flooring?

Waste covers cuts at walls and doorways, damaged or defective planks and the occasional mistake. The right percentage depends on the layout and the room's shape, so the numbers below are ranges, not rules; your installer or the manufacturer may recommend a specific figure.

SituationTypical waste factor
Simple rectangular room, planks laid straight, experienced installer5%
Typical DIY job, standard rectangular room7–10%
Rooms with many corners, closets, doorways or an L shape10%
Diagonal layouts10–15%
Herringbone or chevron15% or more
Long, narrow planks in a small, cut-up room10–15%

How many boxes of flooring for common room sizes?

This chart assumes boxes cover 20 sq ft each, which is common for laminate and vinyl plank (check yours). Counts are rounded up.

Room sizeAreaArea + 7%Boxes at 5%Boxes at 10%Boxes at 15%
10 × 10 ft100 sq ft107 sq ft666
10 × 12 ft120 sq ft128 sq ft777
12 × 12 ft144 sq ft154 sq ft889
12 × 15 ft180 sq ft193 sq ft101011
15 × 20 ft300 sq ft321 sq ft161718
20 × 25 ft500 sq ft535 sq ft272829

If your boxes cover a different area, divide the adjusted square footage by your own coverage instead. Boxes of 24 sq ft would reduce the 12 × 15 ft count at 10% from 10 to 9.

How do you measure an L-shaped or irregular room?

Break any odd room into rectangles, measure each one, then add the areas together.

  • L-shaped room: split it into two rectangles. A 12 × 10 ft main space plus an 8 × 6 ft nook is 120 + 48 = 168 sq ft.
  • Bay window or alcove: measure its width and depth as a rectangle and add it.
  • Room with a diagonal wall: measure the full rectangle, then subtract half the area of the cut-off triangle.
  • Open floor plan: decide where the flooring will end, usually at a doorway or threshold, and measure each zone separately.

How much flooring do you need for stairs?

Stairs are measured by the step, not square feet. Each step has a tread (the flat part) and a riser (the vertical part). Measure the tread depth and width plus the riser height, then add the two for each step. Stair-nosing pieces are sold separately by length.

For a quick estimate, multiply the number of steps by the width of the staircase times roughly 1.5 ft to cover tread and riser, then add 10–15% because stair cuts waste more. Most stair covers are sold as pre-cut treads, so check your product's packaging instead of relying on a general rule.

What mistakes lead to buying the wrong amount?

Check the box size before you pay. Square feet per carton varies by brand and product, from under 15 to more than 25. Compare price per square foot, not price per box, and recalculate the box count for the product you actually choose.
  1. Forgetting the closets and hallways. Adjacent spaces often add up to a full extra box or two.
  2. Using too little waste for the layout. A diagonal pattern needs about twice the allowance of a straight one.
  3. Measuring only the middle of the room. Walls aren't always square. Take the longest length and widest width.
  4. Mixing lots. Production lots can vary in color. Buy everything at once and check the lot numbers.
  5. Buying exactly what you need. One unopened leftover box saves you from sourcing a discontinued product when a plank is damaged later.

Do you need underlayment, trim and extras?

Flooring boxes are only part of the order. Many floating floors need underlayment unless a pad is attached, which is sold in rolls by the square foot, so buy the same area as the floor plus a few percent. Transition strips are needed at doorways and where the floor meets carpet or tile, and quarter-round or baseboard covers the expansion gap at the walls.

Measure the linear feet of wall for trim and the number of doorways for transitions. A 12 × 15 ft room has 54 ft of perimeter, minus doorway openings. Moisture barrier is needed over concrete slabs for many products. Check the installation instructions for the product you choose, since requirements differ and affect the warranty.

Frequently asked questions

How much flooring do I need for a 12x12 room?

A 12 × 12 ft room is 144 sq ft. With 10% waste, buy about 158 sq ft, which is 8 boxes at 20 sq ft each. For diagonal or herringbone layouts with 15% waste, plan on 166 sq ft or 9 boxes.

How many square feet is a typical box of flooring?

It varies by product, but many laminate and vinyl plank cartons cover roughly 18–25 sq ft. The label lists the exact coverage, so use that figure rather than an average.

Should I subtract closets and cabinets from the flooring total?

Add closets, since they need flooring. Don't subtract fixed cabinets or a kitchen island unless the area is large, and treat the leftover as extra cutting material.

Do I need to buy extra flooring for future repairs?

Yes, if possible. Keeping one or two unopened boxes from the same lot lets you replace a damaged plank later even if the style is discontinued.

How do I convert square feet to square yards for flooring?

Divide square feet by 9. A 180 sq ft room is 20 square yards. Carpet is often priced per square yard, while plank flooring is sold by the square foot.

The bottom line

Measure each space, add them together, then add 5–10% for straight layouts or 10–15% for diagonal ones, and divide by the box coverage. Round up, buy from a single lot and keep a spare box. The flooring calculator does the multi-room math instantly.

Related tools: Paver Patio Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Waste-factor and layout guidance reflects published installation instructions from flooring manufacturers and the National Wood Flooring Association (NWFA) for wood products; always follow the instructions for the product you buy. Area conversions: 1 square yard = 9 square feet. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How Many Pavers Do I Need? Formula, Chart and Examples
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To work out how many pavers you need, divide your patio's area by the area of one paver, then add 10% for cuts and breakage. A 12 × 16 ft patio (192 sq ft) in 6 × 9 inch pavers needs 512 whole pavers, so order about 564. Pavers measuring 12 × 12 inches need 1 per square foot.

Ordering pavers is a one-shot decision. Run short and the next pallet may come from a different batch with a slightly different color, which shows in a finished patio. Order far too many and you're paying for stone you'll stack behind the shed.

This guide gives you the formula, a pavers-per-square-foot chart for the common sizes, worked examples for rectangles and curves, and the right amount of waste for each pattern. If you'd rather not do the math, the free paver patio calculator works out pavers, base gravel and sand together.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: patio area (sq ft) ÷ one paver's area (sq ft) × 1.10 = pavers to order.
  • Per square foot: 4 × 8 in = 4.5 · 6 × 6 in = 4 · 6 × 9 in = 2.67 · 12 × 12 in = 1 · 16 × 16 in = 0.56 · 12 × 24 in = 0.5.
  • Waste: about 5–10% for straight patterns, 10–15% for diagonal, herringbone or curved edges.
  • Joints: the 1/8 to 3/8 inch joints shift your count by only a few percent; the waste allowance covers it.
  • Same batch: buy everything in one order so colors match, plus a few spares for future repairs.

How do you calculate how many pavers you need?

The method is the same for any paver shape: find the patio's area, find one paver's area, divide, then add waste. It takes four steps.

Step 1: Measure the patio area

For a rectangle, multiply length × width in feet. A patio 12 ft by 16 ft is 192 sq ft. For other shapes, split the patio into rectangles, circles and triangles, work out each, and add them together.

Step 2: Work out the area of one paver

Multiply the paver's length by its width in inches, then divide by 144 (the number of square inches in a square foot). A 6 × 9 inch paver is 54 sq in ÷ 144 = 0.375 sq ft.

Step 3: Divide and round up

Patio area ÷ paver area gives the number of whole pavers. For the example, 192 ÷ 0.375 = 512 pavers.

Step 4: Add the waste allowance

Multiply by 1.10 for a 10% allowance and round up: 512 × 1.10 = 563.2, so order 564. With a simple running-bond pattern and few cuts, 5% (538 pavers) can be enough.

🧮

Want pavers, gravel base and bedding sand in one result? Use the paver patio calculator. Enter your patio size and paver dimensions and it gives you counts and material quantities.

How many pavers are in a square foot?

This chart shows pavers per square foot for the sizes sold at most US home centers. Sizes are nominal: real pavers are often a fraction of an inch smaller or larger, so check the dimensions on the product sheet.

Paver size (in)Area of one paverPavers per sq ftPavers per 100 sq ft
4 × 80.222 sq ft4.5450
6 × 60.25 sq ft4400
6 × 90.375 sq ft2.67267
12 × 121 sq ft1100
16 × 161.78 sq ft0.5656
12 × 242 sq ft0.550

How many pavers for common patio sizes?

These counts include a 10% allowance for cuts and breakage, rounded up.

Patio area4 × 8 in6 × 6 in6 × 9 in12 × 12 in16 × 16 in12 × 24 in
100 sq ft4964412941116256
144 sq ft (12 × 12 ft)7136344231599080
200 sq ft991881587221124111
300 sq ft1,4851,320880330186165
400 sq ft1,9811,7611,174441248221

How much waste should you allow for?

The waste allowance depends on the pattern and the shape of the patio, because every pattern that doesn't line up with your edges creates cut pieces. Most of those offcuts end up in the bin.

Pattern or shapeTypical allowanceWhy
Stack bond or running bond, rectangular patio sized to the pavers5%Few or no cuts; only breakage
Running bond, patio not a multiple of paver size10%Cuts along two edges
Basket weave or herringbone (90°)10%Edge cuts on all sides
Herringbone at 45°, diagonal layouts12–15%Triangular cuts along every edge
Curves, circles, many corners15%Lots of small cut pieces

Because most of the waste is edge cuts, a patio sized to a whole number of pavers wastes very little. A 12 × 12 ft patio in 12 × 12 inch pavers needs exactly 144, with no cutting at all.

What about the joints between pavers?

Pavers are laid with narrow joints, usually 1/8 to 3/8 inch depending on the product, and filled with jointing sand. Joints make each paver effectively a little larger than its face, so the true count for a given area can be a few percent lower than the simple formula says.

The 10% allowance more than absorbs that difference, so there's no need to adjust for it. Your measurements, cuts and any broken pieces matter far more than a 1/8 inch joint.

How to calculate pavers for a circular or curved patio

For a round patio, area = 3.14 × radius squared. A circle 10 ft across has a 5 ft radius, so 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 sq ft. With 12 × 12 inch pavers and a 15% allowance, that's 78.5 × 1.15 = 90.3, so order 91.

For a patio with one curved side, work out the full rectangle and then subtract roughly half the area of the curve you remove. Add the 15% allowance regardless, because curved edges are where most cuts happen. Smaller pavers such as 4 × 8 or 6 × 6 follow curves with less waste than big square slabs.

Common mistakes when ordering pavers

Don't order by area alone. Pavers are sold both by the piece and by the square foot or pallet, and the coverage printed on a pallet is for the face area only. Always confirm whether the quote is per paver or per square foot before you compare prices.
  1. Forgetting the border. A soldier-course border in a contrasting paver counts as its own area. Subtract it from the field, then calculate it separately by length.
  2. Using nominal sizes without checking. A "12 × 12" paver may measure 11 3/4 inches. On a big patio that's a few extra pavers.
  3. Skipping the spares. Keep 5–10 extras from the same batch. Matching a color years later is often impossible.
  4. Mixing pallets. Pavers vary slightly between production runs. Lay from several pallets at once so any shade differences blend instead of forming patches.
  5. Ordering before the base is planned. The paver thickness drives your excavation depth. Decide on the product first, then dig.

Frequently asked questions

How many 12x12 pavers do I need for a 10x10 patio?

A 10 × 10 ft patio is 100 sq ft, which takes 100 whole 12 × 12 inch pavers. With a 10% allowance, order 110. If the patio size matches the paver size and you use a straight pattern, 105 is usually enough.

How many 6x9 pavers cover 100 square feet?

It takes about 267 pavers of 6 × 9 inches to cover 100 sq ft with no waste. Adding 10% for cuts and breakage brings the order to 294.

How many pavers are on a pallet?

It depends on the product, so read the label or ask the supplier. Pallets are usually sold by their coverage in square feet, and the number of pieces on them changes with the paver's size and thickness.

Do I need extra pavers for cuts?

Yes. Add 5–10% for straight layouts and 10–15% for diagonal, herringbone or curved patios. Offcuts are only reusable if they happen to fit another edge.

How many pavers do I need for a walkway 3 feet wide?

Each foot of a 3 ft wide walkway is 3 sq ft. With 12 × 12 inch pavers, that's 3 pavers per foot of path, so a 20 ft walkway needs 60 plus about 10% extra, which is 66.

The bottom line

Divide your patio's area by the area of one paver, add 5–15% depending on the pattern, and round up. Order everything from one batch and keep a few spares. When you want pavers, base gravel and sand worked out together, the paver patio calculator does it in one step.

Related tools: Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Paver layout and installation guidance from the Interlocking Concrete Pavement Institute (ICPI) and from paver manufacturers' published installation instructions. Paver sizes shown are common nominal sizes; always confirm the dimensions of the product you buy. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Drip Irrigation for Raised Beds: Simple Setup and Run Times
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A 4 × 8 ft raised bed needs about 20 gallons of water a week for 1 inch of watering. With three drip lines and a 0.6 gph emitter every 12 inches, that takes about 83 minutes a week, split into 2–3 sessions. Connect a timer, filter and pressure regulator at the spigot, then run tubing along the bed.

Hand-watering raised beds works until you go on vacation or a heat wave hits. Drip irrigation puts the water at the roots, a little at a time, on a schedule. It wastes less water, keeps leaves dry (which helps with fungal disease) and takes about an afternoon to install.

This guide shows the parts you need, a simple layout for a 4 × 8 bed, a run-time chart by emitter size and the mistakes that cause clogs and dry spots. For other bed sizes, the irrigation runtime calculator works out minutes from your flow rate.

Key takeaways
  • Water need: 1 inch of water over 1 sq ft is 0.623 gallons, so a 4 × 8 bed (32 sq ft) needs 19.9 gallons per inch.
  • Layout: three lines per 4 ft bed, with emitters every 12 inches.
  • Run time: about 83 minutes per week with 0.6 gph emitters, 50 minutes with 1 gph emitters.
  • Parts at the spigot: timer, filter, pressure regulator, then tubing.
