  • Adjust: add water in heat, with sandy soil or for seedlings, and cut back after rain.

How much water does a raised bed need?

Most vegetable gardens need about 1 inch of water per week from rain and irrigation combined, which is the figure most US extension services give, more in hot, windy weather or sandy soil. One inch of water on one square foot is 0.623 gallons, so:

4 × 8 ft bed: 32 sq ft × 0.623 = 19.9 gallons per week for 1 inch.

Bed sizeAreaGallons for 1 inGallons for 1.5 in (hot spell)
4 × 4 ft16 sq ft10.015.0
4 × 8 ft32 sq ft19.929.9
4 × 12 ft48 sq ft29.944.9

What parts do you need for drip irrigation in a raised bed?

A basic kit has these parts, connected in this order from the hose bib.

  1. Timer: a battery hose-end timer is enough for one zone.
  2. Backflow preventer: required in many areas; ask your local water utility or check the kit.
  3. Filter: a 150–200 mesh filter stops grit that blocks emitters.
  4. Pressure regulator: drip lines are designed for low pressure, commonly around 25 psi.
  5. Mainline tubing: 1/2 inch poly tubing from the spigot to the beds.
  6. Drip lines or emitter tubing: 1/4 inch lines with inline emitters, or 1/2 inch tubing with built-in emitters spaced 12 inches apart.
  7. Connectors, stakes and end caps: to hold lines in place and close the ends.

How do you set up drip irrigation in a raised bed?

Step 1: Plan the lines

In a 4 ft wide bed, run three lines along the length, spaced about 16 inches apart and 8 inches from each side. For a 4 × 8 bed that's three 8 ft lines, or one long line looped back and forth. Emitters every 12 inches give each plant a water source within a few inches.

Step 2: Connect the spigot assembly

Thread the timer onto the spigot, then the backflow preventer if needed, then the filter, then the pressure regulator. Attach the 1/2 inch mainline to the regulator outlet.

Step 3: Run the mainline to the bed

Lay the tubing in the sun for a few minutes so it softens and uncoils. Run it to the bed edge and add a tee or a manifold for each bed.

Step 4: Lay out and stake the drip lines

Connect each drip line to the mainline with a fitting and stake it every 2–3 feet. Close the far end with an end cap or a figure-8 end clamp.

Step 5: Flush, test and check coverage

Open the ends briefly to flush dirt, then close them and run the system. Walk the bed: every emitter should drip steadily, with no leaks at connections. Dig a small hole after a run to see how far the water spreads sideways and down; this is your real coverage.

How long should you run drip irrigation on a raised bed?

Run time = gallons needed ÷ total flow in gallons per hour × 60. The table uses the 4 × 8 bed with 24 emitters (three 8 ft lines with 8 emitters each) and about 20 gallons per week, or 1 inch.

Emitter flowTotal flow (24 emitters)Rate appliedMinutes for 1 inWeekly schedule
0.5 gph12 gph0.60 in/hr100 min3 × 33 min
0.6 gph14.4 gph0.72 in/hr83 min3 × 28 min
1.0 gph24 gph1.20 in/hr50 min2 × 25 min

The run times stay about the same for other bed sizes if you keep the same layout, because a layout with the same emitter density per square foot gives the same inches per hour. A 4 × 4 bed with three 4 ft lines also takes about 83 minutes a week at 0.6 gph.

🧮

Using a different emitter or bed layout? Open the irrigation runtime calculator, enter your flow rate and area, and get minutes per session.

How often should you water raised beds with drip?

Split the weekly total into two or three sessions so water soaks deeper and plants don't sit wet. Raised bed soil drains faster than ground soil, so sandy mixes may need shorter, more frequent runs.

  • Seedlings and new transplants: short runs every day or two until roots establish, then switch to longer, less frequent runs.
  • Established vegetables in warm weather: 2–3 deeper sessions per week.
  • Heat waves: raise the total toward 1.5 inches, spread over more days.
  • After heavy rain: skip a session. A rain gauge or a timer with a rain sensor saves water.

Check with a finger or trowel. If the top 2 inches are dry, water; if soggy, wait. Mulching the bed with straw or shredded leaves slows evaporation.

How many beds can one spigot run?

A 4 × 8 bed with 24 emitters at 0.6 gph uses only 14.4 gallons per hour, or 0.24 gallons per minute. A typical hose spigot delivers several gallons per minute, so one spigot can feed many beds. Eight such beds use about 1.9 gpm. Still, check the maximum tubing run length in your kit's instructions, since long runs of 1/2 inch tubing lose pressure and the far beds get less.

Don't skip the filter and regulator. Drip emitters have tiny openings that clog with grit, and full house pressure can pop fittings and split tubing. Both parts are cheap and are the two most common reasons beginner systems fail.

What are the most common drip irrigation mistakes?

  1. Lines too far from the plants. Emitters should be within a few inches of each root zone; in sandy soil, water spreads down more than sideways.
  2. Running too long, too rarely. Long, infrequent runs can waste water below the roots in sandy soil.
  3. Burying lines under mulch and forgetting them. Check emitters monthly for clogs and leaks.
  4. Mixing flow rates on one line. Emitters of different sizes make dry and wet patches. Use one flow rate per zone.
  5. Leaving it on in winter. Drain or disconnect the system before freezing weather, since water in tubing and fittings can crack them.

Frequently asked questions

How many drip lines do I need for a 4-foot-wide raised bed?

Three lines spaced about 16 inches apart covers most vegetable beds evenly. A narrower 2–3 ft bed can use two lines.

Is drip irrigation better than a sprinkler for a vegetable garden?

Usually yes. Drip puts water at the roots, wastes less to evaporation and keeps foliage dry, which helps reduce leaf diseases. Sprinklers still suit lawns and seed beds that need an even surface mist.

What psi should a drip irrigation system run at?

Most drip systems are designed for low pressure, commonly around 10–30 psi, and a regulator set near 25 psi is typical. Check your tubing and emitter specs for the exact range.

Can I use a soaker hose instead of drip tubing in a raised bed?

Yes, soaker hoses work in a small bed and are simpler to install. Their output is less even over long runs and they clog and wear sooner than emitter-based drip tubing.

How do I know if my drip system is watering deep enough?

After a run, dig a small hole near an emitter. The soil should be moist 6–8 inches down for most vegetables. If it's dry below 3 inches, increase the run time; if it's wet beyond the root zone, shorten it.

The bottom line

A 4 × 8 raised bed needs about 20 gallons a week. With three lines and 0.6 gph emitters every 12 inches, that's roughly 83 minutes, split into 2–3 runs. Add a timer, filter and regulator, check for clogs monthly and adjust for weather. The irrigation runtime calculator sets run times for any bed.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Vegetable watering guidance of about 1 inch per week and drip-system design from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension and Colorado State University Extension, and from drip-irrigation manufacturers' installation guides. Conversion: 1 inch of water over 1 square foot = 0.623 gallons. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Watermelon: Dates by Zone and Soil Temp
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant watermelon 2–3 weeks after your average last frost, when the soil is at least 70°F and nights stay above 55°F. Most varieties need 80–100 days, so gardeners in zones 3–5 should start seeds indoors and transplant. Southern zones can direct sow in March or April.

Watermelon is the most heat-hungry crop in the vegetable garden. It needs a long, warm season, and it will sulk for weeks in cold soil. The goal is to give seedlings a head start where summers are short and to plant at the right moment where they are long.

This guide covers the soil-temperature rule, dates for USDA zones 3–10 and the tricks that make a northern watermelon crop possible. To get dates for your town, look up your frost dates by ZIP code, then find your exact dates with the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Soil temperature: 70°F minimum for transplanting or sowing; 80–95°F is ideal for germination.
  • Timing: transplant 2–3 weeks after the last frost; direct sow 3–4 weeks after.
  • Season length: standard varieties need 80–100+ days; icebox types ripen in about 70–80.
  • Cold zones (3–5): start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting and warm the soil with black plastic.
  • Spacing: 2–3 ft apart in rows 6–8 ft apart, or one hill every 4–6 ft.

What soil temperature does watermelon need?

Watermelon germinates best at 80–95°F and will barely sprout below about 65°F. Seedlings stop growing in cold soil, and chilled roots can stunt a plant for the whole season. Use a soil thermometer pushed 2–4 inches deep.

Soil temperatureWhat to expect
Below 65°FSeed rots or stalls; transplants stunted
65–70°FSlow germination; wait if you can
70–80°FGood conditions for transplants and direct sowing
80–95°FFast, reliable germination in 3–5 days

When should you plant watermelon by USDA zone?

These dates are computed from typical average last and first frost dates for each zone. Indoor seeds start in the week before the last frost; transplants go out 2–3 weeks after; direct seed goes in 3–4 weeks after. They are estimates for a representative location, and elevation and microclimate can shift them by a couple of weeks.

USDA zoneTypical last frostStart indoorsTransplant outdoorsDirect sow
3May 25May 18 – May 25Jun 8 – Jun 15Not recommended
4May 15May 8 – May 15May 29 – Jun 5Jun 5 – Jun 12 (short types)
5May 5Apr 28 – May 5May 19 – May 26May 26 – Jun 2
6Apr 25Apr 18 – Apr 25May 9 – May 16May 16 – May 23
7Apr 15Apr 8 – Apr 15Apr 29 – May 6May 6 – May 13
8Mar 25Mar 18 – Mar 25Apr 8 – Apr 15Apr 15 – Apr 22
9Feb 15Feb 8 – Feb 15Mar 1 – Mar 8Mar 8 – Mar 15
10Jan 31Jan 24 – Jan 31Feb 14 – Feb 21Feb 21 – Feb 28

If your last frost is two weeks later than the typical date for your zone, move the whole row two weeks later. Always confirm with the thermometer before planting.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get a watermelon schedule based on your own last and first frost.

Is your growing season long enough for watermelon?

Count the days from your planned transplant date to your average first fall frost. The table shows what is left, after the planting dates above.

USDA zoneDays from transplant to first frostLatest transplant date for an 85-day melonWhat it means
3about 99Jun 12Only short-season types; very little margin
4about 124Jun 27Use 70–85 day varieties
5about 144Jul 7Most varieties work
6about 164Jul 17All varieties
7about 186Jul 29All varieties
8about 221Aug 12All; second crop possible
9about 275Aug 28All; plant spring or late summer
10about 309Sep 16All; avoid peak summer heat at flowering

The "latest transplant" column is the first fall frost minus 95 days (an 85-day variety plus 10 days of buffer). In zone 3 it falls only a few days after the earliest sensible transplant, so there is no room for a cold snap or a slow start.

How do you grow watermelon in a short northern summer?

Gardeners in zones 3–5 can succeed, but they need to stack the odds:

  • Pick short-season varieties. Look for icebox types that mature in 70–85 days instead of 90–100.
  • Start seed indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting, in 3–4 inch pots, on a warm spot with strong light.
  • Warm the soil. Lay black plastic mulch 1–2 weeks before planting. It can raise soil temperature by several degrees.
  • Add row cover over transplants until flowers open, then remove it so bees can pollinate.
  • Choose the warmest site: south-facing, with shelter from cold wind.

How do you plant watermelon step by step?

  1. Prepare a sunny bed. Watermelon needs at least 8 hours of full sun and well-drained soil with a pH of about 6.0–6.8. Mix in 2–3 inches of compost.
  2. Warm the soil with black plastic in cool regions.
  3. Harden off seedlings for 5–7 days if you started them indoors.
  4. Plant when soil reaches 70°F. Set transplants at the same depth as in the pot, 2–3 feet apart in rows 6–8 feet apart.
  5. For direct sowing, plant 3–4 seeds per hill, 1 inch deep, then thin to the best 2 plants.
  6. Water deeply once or twice a week, about 1–2 inches in total, and mulch with straw once the soil is warm.

A single row 20 feet long at 3-foot spacing holds 7 plants, and each vine needs roughly 16–24 square feet to sprawl. That is why watermelon suits a large bed or a trellis with slings more than a small raised bed.

How do you know when watermelon is ripe?

Count days from planting, then look for physical signs: the curly tendril closest to the fruit turns brown and dry, the underside spot (field spot) changes from white to creamy yellow, and the rind loses its shine. A ripe melon also sounds dull when tapped, though that clue is less reliable. Most varieties are ready 35–45 days after the female flowers are pollinated.

Don't rush the planting date. A watermelon transplant set into 60°F soil often sits motionless for weeks and can end up behind seed planted a month later. If a cold snap is coming after you plant, cover plants overnight with row cover or buckets.

5 mistakes that cost you a watermelon harvest

  1. Planting on the calendar, not the thermometer. Cold soil stunts the whole plant.
  2. Choosing a long-season variety in a short climate. A 100-day melon in zone 3 may never ripen.
  3. Crowding vines. Poor airflow invites disease, and plants compete for water.
  4. Keeping row cover on through bloom. Bees must reach the flowers for fruit to form.
  5. Overwatering near harvest. Heavy watering late can dilute sweetness and split fruit; ease off once melons reach full size.

Frequently asked questions

Can you grow watermelon in zone 3 or 4?

Yes, with effort. Choose icebox varieties that mature in 70–80 days, start seeds indoors, use black plastic mulch and transplant 2–3 weeks after the last frost. Expect smaller fruit than in the South.

How long does watermelon take to grow?

Standard watermelons need 80–100 days from planting to harvest, while small icebox types often ripen in about 70–80 days. Cool summers add a week or more.

How far apart should watermelon be planted?

Plant watermelon 2–3 feet apart in rows 6–8 feet apart. In hills, space hills 4–6 feet apart with two plants per hill.

Is it too late to plant watermelon in July?

In zones 6 and warmer, a transplant in early July can still ripen before frost if the variety is 85 days or less. In zones 3–5 it is usually too late.

Do watermelon seeds need to be soaked before planting?

It is not required. Soaking for 4–8 hours can speed germination in warm soil, but in cold soil it raises the risk of rot, so only soak if you are planting right away into soil above 70°F.

The bottom line

Plant watermelon 2–3 weeks after your last frost, when the soil is 70°F or warmer. In zones 3–5, start seeds indoors, use black plastic and pick a variety that ripens in 70–85 days. Look up your frost dates by ZIP code and use the planting calendar to set your own schedule.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator

Sources: Watermelon growing guidance from US university extension services, including Clemson Cooperative Extension, Penn State Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; frost-date averages from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Dates in the tables are computed estimates from typical zone frost dates, not forecasts. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Tomatoes: Dates by Zone and Last Frost
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant tomato transplants outdoors 1–2 weeks after your average last spring frost, when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is at least 60°F. Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before that date. Most gardeners in zones 5–7 plant between late April and mid-May.

Tomatoes are the crop gardeners most often put out too soon. The plants look ready in April, the garden center is full of them, and then one cold night turns the leaves black. The good news is that the right date comes from one number: your average last frost.

This guide gives you tomato-specific dates for USDA zones 3 through 10, the soil temperature that really matters, and how to handle fall crops in the South. To get dates for your exact location, find your frost dates by ZIP code, then drop them into the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Transplant date: 1–2 weeks after the average last frost, never before nighttime lows hold above 50°F.
  • Soil temperature: at least 60°F at 4 inches deep; 70–85°F is ideal for root growth.
  • Seed starting: 6–8 weeks before the last frost date, indoors under lights.
  • Direct sowing: only works in long, warm seasons (zones 8–10); elsewhere use transplants.
  • Harvest: about 60–85 days from transplanting for most varieties; 55–60 days for the earliest types.

When is the best time to plant tomatoes?

Tomatoes are frost-tender and heat-loving. A light frost at 32°F kills the plant outright, and even temperatures in the 40s stunt growth and cause leaves to turn purple. For this reason the standard extension advice is to wait until 1–2 weeks after the average last spring frost.

The "average" last frost date means there is still about a 50% chance of a later frost in some years. Waiting the extra week or two covers that risk and gives the soil time to warm. If you plant earlier, be ready to cover plants overnight with row cover, buckets or frost cloth.

What soil and air temperature do tomatoes need?

Calendar dates are a shortcut. The plant cares about temperature, and you can check it directly.

ConditionWhat happens
Below 32°FPlants killed by frost
Nights under 50°FGrowth stalls; leaves may turn purple from poor phosphorus uptake
Soil under 60°FRoots grow slowly; transplants sit and stay small
Soil 70–85°FBest root growth and nutrient uptake
Daytime above 85–90°F with nights above 75°FBlossoms drop and fruit set falls sharply

Push a soil thermometer 4 inches into the bed in the morning. If it reads under 60°F, wait a few days or warm the soil with black plastic mulch for one to two weeks before planting.

What are the tomato planting dates by USDA zone?

The dates below are computed from typical average last-frost dates for each zone: seeds are started 6–8 weeks before, and transplants go out 1–2 weeks after. They are estimates for a representative location. Your own last frost can differ by several weeks depending on elevation, city heat islands and microclimate, so shift the whole row by the same number of days.

USDA zoneTypical last frostStart seeds indoorsTransplant outdoors
3May 25Mar 30 – Apr 13Jun 1 – Jun 8
4May 15Mar 20 – Apr 3May 22 – May 29
5May 5Mar 10 – Mar 24May 12 – May 19
6Apr 25Feb 28 – Mar 14May 2 – May 9
7Apr 15Feb 18 – Mar 4Apr 22 – Apr 29
8Mar 25Jan 28 – Feb 11Apr 1 – Apr 8
9Feb 15Dec 21 – Jan 4Feb 22 – Mar 1
10Jan 31Dec 6 – Dec 20Feb 7 – Feb 14
🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get tomato start and transplant dates built from your own frost dates.

Can you plant tomatoes in fall in warm climates?

In zones 9 and 10, summer heat is the problem rather than frost. When daytime highs stay above 90°F, tomatoes drop blossoms and fruit set stops. Southern gardeners often get two seasons: an early spring crop planted from mid-February to March, and a fall crop planted in late summer so fruit sets as nights cool. For the fall crop, count back roughly 90–100 days from your first fall frost (December 1 in zone 9, December 20 in zone 10) to a planting date in late August or early September, and give seedlings afternoon shade while they establish.

In the rest of the country, frost ends the season well before a second crop could ripen, so one planting in spring is the rule.

Should you start tomatoes from seed or buy transplants?

Both work, but the timing is different.

  • Seed indoors: sow 6–8 weeks before the last frost in a warm spot (70–80°F) under lights. Older, bigger plants than 8 weeks tend to get leggy and root-bound.
  • Buy transplants: look for stocky plants about 6–10 inches tall with dark green leaves, and no flowers or fruit yet. Do not buy the biggest plant in the flat.
  • Direct sow outdoors: tomato seed needs soil of at least 60°F to germinate well and a long season. This works in zones 9–10 but is risky elsewhere, as it adds three to four weeks to the wait for fruit.

Tomato varieties differ in how long they take to ripen. Short-season types such as many cherry tomatoes and early slicers can ripen in 55–70 days from transplanting. Large beefsteak and heirloom types usually need 80–90 days or more. In zones 3–4, choose short-season varieties so fruit ripens before fall frost.

How do you plant tomato transplants step by step?

  1. Harden off the plants. For 7–10 days, set them outdoors in shade for a few hours, then lengthen the time and sunlight each day.
  2. Prepare the bed. Pick a spot with 6–8 hours of full sun and well-drained soil. Mix in 2–3 inches of compost.
  3. Dig the hole deep. Tomatoes grow roots along buried stem, so plant them deeper than they were in the pot.
  4. Remove the lowest leaves and bury the stem up to the first set of true leaves. For a leggy plant, lay the stem sideways in a shallow trench and bend the top upward.
  5. Space plants 18–24 inches apart for staked or caged plants, and 24–36 inches for sprawling types. Use the plant spacing calculator to plan the bed.
  6. Water deeply at planting, then add 2–3 inches of straw or other mulch once the soil is warm.
  7. Add a cage or stake at planting time, so you do not damage roots later.

Which tomato planting mistakes should you avoid?

Do not plant on the first warm weekend. A stretch of 75°F days in March or April is common, and a freeze often follows. Check the 10-day forecast for lows under 40°F before planting.
  1. Planting before the soil is 60°F. Cold soil slows roots even if the air feels warm.
  2. Skipping hardening off. Indoor-grown plants get sunburned and wind-damaged in a single day outside.
  3. Buying plants already in bloom. They stop growing to make fruit. Pinch off early flowers so the plant builds roots first.
  4. Planting too shallow. Roots on buried stem make the plant sturdier and more drought tolerant.
  5. Crowding plants. Poor airflow increases leaf diseases such as early blight and septoria leaf spot.
  6. Planting in the same spot every year. Rotate away from tomatoes, peppers, potatoes and eggplant for about three years to reduce soilborne disease.

How can you plant tomatoes earlier safely?

If you want fruit a little sooner, you can plant up to two weeks before the last frost, but only with protection. Warm the soil first with black plastic or clear plastic for 1–2 weeks. Use wall-of-water sleeves, cloches or a low tunnel, and keep row cover on hand for nights forecast under 40°F. Choose early varieties. Expect some risk: cold weather can delay plants more than it helps them, and a patient planting often catches up with an early one.

Frequently asked questions

What month should I plant tomatoes?

It depends on zone: April or May for most of the country, late May to June in zones 3–4, and February or March in zones 8–10. The rule is 1–2 weeks after your last spring frost.

Is it too late to plant tomatoes in July?

Not in warm climates. Count 60–90 days to harvest from planting and make sure that lands before your first fall frost. In zones 5–6 a July planting of a short-season variety can still work, but zones 3–4 are usually too late.

How cold is too cold for tomato transplants?

Anything near 32°F kills them, and nights below about 50°F stall growth. Cover plants whenever lows are forecast under 40°F.

How many weeks before the last frost should I start tomato seeds?

Six to eight weeks. Starting earlier produces tall, root-bound seedlings that struggle after transplanting.

How long do tomatoes take to ripen after planting?

Most varieties ripen 60–85 days after transplanting. Early cherry types can take about 55–65 days, while large heirlooms may need 90 days or more.

The bottom line

Plant tomato transplants 1–2 weeks after your average last frost, once soil is at least 60°F and nights stay above 50°F. Start seeds 6–8 weeks earlier, and shift the dates in the table to match your own frost dates. The planting calendar turns your ZIP code into exact tomato dates in seconds.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Tomato planting guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and University of Maryland Extension; frost-date statistics from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals; USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. Dates in the table are estimates computed from typical frost dates by zone; confirm yours locally. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Strawberries: Spring vs Fall Dates by Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant strawberries in early spring, as soon as the soil can be worked, roughly 4–6 weeks before your last frost in zones 3–7. In zones 8–10, plant in fall (about October to November) and grow them as a cool-season crop. Dormant bare-root plants go in first; potted plants can follow later.

Strawberries are forgiving about the exact day but not about the season. Plant too late in spring and the crowns face summer heat before their roots are established. Plant too early in fall in a cold climate and frost heaving can push them out of the ground. Matching the planting window to your climate is most of the battle.

This guide gives spring and fall planting dates for USDA zones 3–10, explains how June-bearing, everbearing and day-neutral types differ, and walks through planting bare-root crowns. To pin down your own dates, check your frost dates by ZIP code, then find your exact window in the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Cold zones (3–7): plant in spring, from about 5 weeks before to the day of your average last frost, once soil is workable.
  • Warm zones (8–10): plant in fall; summer heat makes spring-planted crowns struggle.
  • Depth: the crown (where the leaves meet the roots) must sit exactly level with the soil surface.
  • Spacing: 12–24 in apart depending on growing system; a 4×8 ft bed on a 12-inch grid holds 32 plants.
  • First year: pinch off flowers on June-bearing plants; this builds a stronger plant and bigger crops the following year.

What is the best time of year to plant strawberries?

For most of the country the answer is early spring. Strawberries are cool-season perennials that root best in cool, moist soil, and they need the whole growing season to build crowns that will bear well. Bare-root plants are shipped dormant in late winter and early spring for this reason, and they should go into the ground within a few days of arriving.

The exception is the Deep South, the Gulf Coast, southern California and similar mild-winter areas. There, plants set out in fall grow through the mild winter and fruit in late winter and spring before summer heat arrives, and many gardeners treat them as annuals. Extension guidance for the Southeast and Southwest generally follows this fall pattern.

Fall planting in cold climates is possible with potted plants set out very early (late summer), but most northern extension services favor spring because winter heaving and cold injury threaten young plants.

When should you plant strawberries in each USDA zone?

The dates below are computed from typical average last and first frost dates for each zone, then offset: spring planting runs from 5 weeks before to the day of the last frost; fall planting runs from 8 to 5 weeks before the first frost. They are estimates for a representative location; your elevation and microclimate can shift them by a couple of weeks.

USDA zoneTypical last frostSpring plantingFall plantingBest season
3May 25Apr 20 – May 25Jul 21 – Aug 11 (potted only)Spring
4May 15Apr 10 – May 15Aug 5 – Aug 26 (potted only)Spring
5May 5Mar 31 – May 5Aug 15 – Sep 5 (potted only)Spring
6Apr 25Mar 21 – Apr 25Aug 25 – Sep 15Spring
7Apr 15Mar 11 – Apr 15Sep 6 – Sep 27Spring (fall also works)
8Mar 25Feb 18 – Mar 25Sep 20 – Oct 11Fall or late winter
9Feb 15Jan 11 – Feb 15Oct 6 – Oct 27Fall
10Jan 31Dec 27 – Jan 31Oct 25 – Nov 15Fall

In zones 9 and 10 the "spring" column only works for early-winter planting of transplants; most growers there set out fall transplants and harvest through late winter and spring. Dates also shift with actual weather: wait for soil that crumbles in your hand rather than forming a muddy ball.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get your last-frost-based strawberry window.

Do June-bearing, everbearing and day-neutral strawberries need different timing?

The planting window is similar, but the type you choose changes what you do afterward and when you harvest.

TypeWhen it fruitsTypical spacingFirst-year flowers
June-bearingOne large crop over about 2–3 weeks in late spring or early summer18–24 in in rows 3–4 ft apart (matted row)Pinch off all of them
EverbearingTwo to three smaller flushes: early summer, late summer, fall12 in apart (hill system)Pinch off until about early July
Day-neutralSteady production from early summer until frost8–12 in apart (hill system)Pinch off until about early July

Spacing varies by source and system, so treat the table as a range and check the tag that comes with your plants. June-bearing plants send out many runners, which fill in a row (the matted-row system). Everbearing and day-neutral types make fewer runners and do well in tight beds, containers and raised beds.

How do you plant bare-root strawberries step by step?

  1. Prepare the bed ahead of time. Choose a spot with 6–8 hours of full sun and well-drained soil. Strawberries prefer a slightly acidic soil pH of about 5.8–6.5. Work in 2–3 inches of compost.
  2. Avoid recent tomato, pepper, potato and eggplant beds. These crops can leave behind verticillium wilt in the soil, which attacks strawberries. Wait a few years or choose another bed.
  3. Unpack and soak. Soak bare-root plants in a bucket of lukewarm water for 20 minutes to an hour, no longer. Trim any roots longer than about 8 inches.
  4. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out fanned downward rather than curled up in a "J".
  5. Set the crown level with the soil surface. The crown is the thick base where the leaves emerge. Roots covered by soil, crown fully visible.
  6. Firm the soil and water well to settle it around the roots.
  7. Mulch lightly with 1–2 inches of straw once plants are growing, keeping the crowns clear.

A 4 × 8 ft raised bed (32 sq ft) planted on a 12-inch grid holds 32 plants. A 100-foot matted row planted 18 inches apart holds about 67 plants.

Crown depth makes or breaks the plant. If the crown is buried, it rots. If it sits above the soil with roots exposed, the roots dry out. Get it level with the soil surface, and recheck after the first heavy rain, which can settle the soil.

What if you plant strawberries at the wrong time?

Strawberries are tough, but timing mistakes reduce yields. Planting in late spring or summer in a hot climate leaves plants with a weak root system just as heat and drought hit. If you must plant late, choose potted plants, shade them for the first week and water deeply.

Planting too early in fall in a cold zone means plants grow lots of top growth that freezes. Planting too late in fall gives roots no time to establish before the ground freezes, and heaving can lift them. A 2–3 inch layer of straw after the ground freezes helps in cold areas; remove it gradually in spring as growth resumes.

A late frost after spring planting is less of a worry for dormant plants, but open blossoms are tender. If a frost or freeze is forecast when plants are in bloom, cover them overnight with a frost blanket or row cover.

What are the most common strawberry planting mistakes?

  1. Burying the crown. This is the number-one cause of failed transplants.
  2. Letting bare roots dry out. Keep them moist and covered from unpacking to planting.
  3. Letting first-year plants fruit. Early fruiting drains the plant. Remove flowers on June-bearing plants the first season; on everbearing and day-neutral types, remove flowers until about early July.
  4. Planting too thick. Crowded plants get gray mold and leaf spot because air cannot move through them.
  5. Using a bed with heavy weed pressure. Strawberries are poor competitors. Clear perennial weeds first, because pulling them later disturbs the shallow roots.

Frequently asked questions

Can you plant strawberries in summer?

You can, but it is the hardest season. Heat and dry spells stress young plants, so use potted plants, water deeply, and provide afternoon shade for the first week or two. Fall or spring planting is more reliable.

How long until new strawberry plants produce fruit?

June-bearing plants usually give their first real harvest the spring after planting, about a year later. Everbearing and day-neutral plants set in spring can produce a modest crop in late summer or fall of the same year if early flowers were removed.

Should you pinch off strawberry blossoms the first year?

Yes for June-bearing types: remove all flowers in year one so the plant puts energy into roots and runners. For everbearing and day-neutral types, pinch flowers until about early July, then let them fruit.

How deep should bare-root strawberries be planted?

Plant them so the roots are fully covered and the crown sits level with the soil surface. The crown is the thick base from which the leaves grow, and it must never be buried.

How far apart should you plant strawberries?

Space June-bearing plants 18–24 inches apart in rows 3–4 feet apart if you want a matted row. Space everbearing and day-neutral plants 8–12 inches apart in a hill system or raised bed.

Will a spring frost kill strawberry blossoms?

Open blossoms and young fruit are damaged by temperatures around freezing, though dormant plants and leaves tolerate cold well. Cover plants with a row cover or frost blanket the night a frost is forecast and uncover them in the morning.

The bottom line

Plant strawberries in early spring in zones 3–7, from about 5 weeks before your last frost until the frost date itself, and in fall in zones 8–10. Set the crown level with the soil, space plants by type, and pinch off first-year flowers where advised. To find the dates for your exact location, use the free planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Strawberry planting guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and the University of Florida IFAS Extension; frost data based on NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals, with frost dates by ZIP code. Dates in the table are estimates computed from typical zone frost dates. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Pumpkins for a Halloween Harvest (By Zone)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To harvest pumpkins by Halloween, plant them between late May and early July, depending on your climate and the variety's days to maturity. Count back 90–120 days from October 31, and sow only after frost has passed and soil is at least 70°F. A 100-day pumpkin sown around July 9 is ready on time in the warm South.

Pumpkins ask for two things you cannot hurry: warm soil to sprout and a long stretch of heat to ripen. Sow too early and the fruit is ripe in August, then sits in the sun and rots before Halloween. Sow too late and frost kills the vines with green pumpkins still on them.

This guide shows how to count back from Halloween, gives sowing dates for USDA zones 3–10, and explains how to match the variety to your season. Look up your frost dates by ZIP code and use the planting calendar for your exact dates.

Key takeaways
  • Count-back rule: sow date = October 31 minus days to maturity. A 100-day pumpkin: July 23; add a 2-week buffer and aim for around July 9.
  • Soil temperature: pumpkin seeds sprout best in soil at or above 70°F; wait until at least 65°F.
  • Frost: pumpkin vines are frost-tender, so sow about 2 weeks after your last frost.
  • Cold zones (3–5): frost limits you; choose 85–95-day varieties and sow in late May to mid June.
  • Maturity ranges: mini and pie types roughly 90–105 days; large field pumpkins 110–120+ days.

How do you count back from Halloween to find your pumpkin planting date?

Start with October 31 and subtract your variety's days to maturity, found on the seed packet or plant tag. Days to maturity count from sowing for direct-seeded plants. Then subtract about 14 more days as a cushion so the pumpkins are ripe, hardened and ready before Halloween rather than just barely turning orange.

Type of pumpkinTypical days to maturityLatest sow date (Oct 31 minus days)Sow by, with 2-week buffer
Mini pumpkinsabout 90Aug 2Jul 19
Pie / sugar pumpkinsabout 100Jul 23Jul 9
Standard jack-o'-lantern typesabout 110Jul 13Jun 29
Large and giant typesabout 120Jul 3Jun 19

Days to maturity vary by variety, so read your own packet. Those are the dates when frost is not a problem. In cooler climates the first frost, not Halloween, sets your latest sow date, as the next section shows.

When should you plant pumpkins in each USDA zone?

These dates are computed from typical average frost dates for each zone. The earliest safe sowing is 2 weeks after the last frost. The latest sowing for a 100-day pumpkin is the earlier of two dates: 100 days before the first fall frost, or 100 days before Halloween (July 23).

USDA zoneLast / first frostEarliest sowLatest sow (100-day)Ready if sown earliest
3May 25 / Sep 15Jun 8Jun 7 (too short: use 90-day or start indoors)Sep 6–16
4May 15 / Sep 30May 29Jun 22Sep 6
5May 5 / Oct 10May 19Jul 2Aug 27
6Apr 25 / Oct 20May 9Jul 12Aug 17
7Apr 15 / Nov 1Apr 29Jul 23Aug 7
8Mar 25 / Nov 15Apr 8Jul 23Jul 17
9Feb 15 / Dec 1Mar 1Jul 23Jun 9
10Jan 31 / Dec 20Feb 14Jul 23May 25

How to read this table. In zones 4–6 your window is wide, so sow in late May to mid June and pumpkins are ready by September to early October. In zones 7–10, sowing at the earliest date gives pumpkins in early summer, which is too soon for Halloween. For a fresh Halloween pumpkin there, wait and sow in late June to July (see the first table). In zone 3, the season is so short that you should choose an early variety (about 90 days) and start seeds indoors 3 weeks before the transplant date.

In zones 9–10, midsummer heat can stop fruit set; sow in the shade of late afternoon or choose heat-tolerant varieties.

🧮

Not sure where you land? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get your frost-based pumpkin sowing window.

What soil temperature do pumpkins need?

Pumpkin seeds rot rather than sprout in cold, wet soil. Extension guidance generally says to wait until the soil reaches at least 65°F, with 70°F or warmer ideal. Check with a soil thermometer pushed 2 inches deep, in the morning, for three days in a row. Air temperatures should stay above 50°F at night.

Black plastic mulch laid over the bed for a week or two before sowing can warm soil in cool springs, which helps in zones 3–5.

Should you start pumpkins indoors or sow them directly?

In most climates, direct sowing is best because pumpkins dislike having their roots disturbed. In short-season zones (3–4), start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before transplanting, ideally in biodegradable pots that can go straight into the ground, and harden plants off for a few days first.

Zone 3 example: transplant date is two weeks after last frost (June 8), so start seeds around May 18 (3 weeks earlier). That gains about three weeks of growing time compared with sowing outside.

How do you plant pumpkins step by step?

  1. Choose a sunny, roomy spot. Pumpkins need 6–8 hours of sun and plenty of space. Vining types can cover 50–100 square feet or more per plant.
  2. Prepare rich soil. Pumpkins are heavy feeders. Mix in several inches of compost; a pH of about 6.0–6.8 is ideal.
  3. Make hills or rows. Build low mounds about 4–6 feet apart (up to 8 feet for large vines) with rows 8–10 feet apart. Mounds warm faster and drain well.
  4. Sow 4–5 seeds per hill, 1 inch deep. Keep the soil evenly moist until they sprout in 5–10 days.
  5. Thin to the 2 strongest plants per hill once they have a couple of true leaves, cutting the extras at the soil line rather than pulling them.
  6. Mulch and water deeply. Give about 1–2 inches of water per week, applied at the base to keep leaves dry.
Do not sow on the calendar alone. A warm April followed by a cold snap kills seedlings fast. If frost threatens after sprouting, cover young plants overnight with a bucket, row cover or frost blanket.

How do you know when pumpkins are ready to harvest?

Harvest when the rind is hard enough that you cannot dent it with a fingernail, the color is deep and even, and the stem is turning brown and woody. The vine often starts to die back. Cut the stem leaving 3–4 inches attached, and never carry a pumpkin by its stem.

Harvest before a hard freeze. Light frost kills leaves but usually not the fruit; a hard freeze can damage it. For storage, many extension sources recommend curing for about 10 days at 80–85°F, then keeping pumpkins in a cool, dry place around 50–55°F.

What are the most common pumpkin timing mistakes?

  1. Sowing in cold soil. Seeds rot before germinating; wait for 65–70°F.
  2. Sowing too early for Halloween. A pumpkin ripe in August may rot or soften by late October. Delay sowing in warm zones.
  3. Choosing a long-season variety in a short-season zone. A 120-day pumpkin in zone 3 will not ripen. Pick by days to maturity first, looks second.
  4. Crowding vines. Too little space means disease, because powdery mildew spreads in humid, crowded foliage.
  5. Skipping pollinators. Plants make male flowers first and female flowers days later. Do not worry if early flowers do not set fruit; avoid spraying insecticides while flowers are open.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does it take to grow a pumpkin?

Most pumpkins take about 90–120 days from sowing to harvest, with mini and pie types at the shorter end and large field and giant types at the longer end. Check your seed packet for the exact days to maturity.

Is July too late to plant pumpkins?

Not in warm climates. In zones 7–10, planting a 90–100-day variety in early to mid July gives ripe pumpkins by Halloween. In zones 3–5, July is too late because frost arrives before the fruit matures.

How many pumpkins does one plant produce?

It depends on the variety. Small and pie types often set several fruits per vine, while large types are usually best at one to three. Thinning extra fruit helps the remaining pumpkins grow larger.

Do pumpkins need full sun?

Yes. Pumpkins need at least 6–8 hours of direct sun daily for good growth and fruit set. Shade slows ripening and encourages mildew.

How far apart should pumpkin hills be?

Space hills 4–6 feet apart for most varieties and up to 8 feet for large vining types. Keep rows 8–10 feet apart, and allow 2 plants per hill after thinning.

Can you grow pumpkins in a raised bed or container?

Mini and bush varieties can grow in a large raised bed or a 20-gallon or larger container if you train vines onto a trellis. Full-size vining pumpkins need much more ground space than most raised beds offer.

The bottom line

Take October 31, subtract your pumpkin's days to maturity (90–120), then add a two-week cushion. Sow only after the last frost has passed and the soil is at least 70°F, and in zones 3–5 let the first fall frost, not Halloween, set your deadline. For dates tailored to your ZIP code, use the free planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Pumpkin growing and timing guidance from US university extension services, including University of Illinois Extension, Penn State Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; frost data based on NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals, with frost dates by ZIP code. Dates in the tables are estimates computed from typical zone frost dates; days to maturity vary by variety. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Potatoes: Soil Temperature and Dates by Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant potatoes 2–4 weeks before your average last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked and has warmed to 45–50°F. That means March in the South, mid-April in zones 5–6 and late April to mid-May in zones 3–4. Seed pieces tolerate cool soil but not wet, frozen ground.

Potatoes are one of the few vegetables you should plant before the last frost. They are a cool-season crop: tubers form best when soil is 60–70°F, and heat above about 80°F slows them badly. Planting early lets the crop bulk up before summer.

Below you will find potato-specific dates for USDA zones 3–10, the soil temperature to look for, and the planting depth and hilling steps. Look up your frost dates by ZIP code, then use the planting calendar to turn them into a date for your garden.

Key takeaways
  • Plant date: 2–4 weeks before the average last frost.
  • Soil temperature: at least 45°F (many extension guides say 40°F minimum) and not waterlogged.
  • Seed pieces: use certified seed potatoes, cut into 1.5–2 oz chunks with 1–2 eyes each.
  • Depth and spacing: 3–4 inches deep, 10–12 inches apart, rows 30–36 inches apart.
  • Harvest: new potatoes at about 60–70 days, mature potatoes at 90–120 days.

When is the best time to plant potatoes?

The standard recommendation from extension services is to plant two to four weeks before the average last frost, when soil has dried enough to dig without clumping and has reached 45–50°F. Seed pieces sit quietly in cool soil for two to four weeks while sprouts develop, and shoots usually emerge after the hardest freezes are past.

Potato foliage is frost-tender. If shoots emerge and a frost is forecast, cover them with loose soil or row cover. Plants usually regrow from a light frost, though growth is delayed.

What soil temperature do potatoes need?

Soil temperatureWhat it means for potatoes
Below 40°FSeed pieces sit idle and can rot in cold, wet soil
45–50°FGood planting range; sprouts begin to grow
60–70°FBest range for tuber formation
Above 80°FTuber growth slows or stops; yields fall

Take a morning reading 4 inches deep. If the soil is soggy, wait. A handful that crumbles when squeezed is ready; a handful that stays in a ball is too wet.

How do you prepare the soil before planting potatoes?

Potatoes want loose, well-drained soil so tubers can swell without deforming. Work the bed 8–10 inches deep as soon as it is workable, and mix in 2 inches of finished compost. Heavy clay benefits from extra organic matter or a raised bed; soggy ground is the most common cause of rot.

Keep soil pH in the range of 5.0–6.5. Higher pH favors common scab, which makes rough, corky patches on the skin. Do not lime the bed just before planting unless a soil test says you need it, and avoid fresh manure for the same reason. A soil test through your county extension office costs little and tells you exactly what to add.

Potatoes are also heavy feeders. Many extension guides suggest a balanced fertilizer worked in at planting, then a light side-dressing when plants are about 6 inches tall. Follow the product label for rates, and keep fertilizer from touching the seed pieces directly.

What are the potato planting dates by USDA zone?

These dates are computed from typical average last-frost dates for each zone, planting 2–4 weeks before. They are estimates; adjust by the same number of days if your frost date is earlier or later.

USDA zoneTypical last frostPlant potatoesNew potatoes ready (about 10 weeks)*
3May 25Apr 27 – May 11from mid-July
4May 15Apr 17 – May 1from early July
5May 5Apr 7 – Apr 21from late June
6Apr 25Mar 28 – Apr 11from mid-June
7Apr 15Mar 18 – Apr 1from early June
8Mar 25Feb 25 – Mar 11from mid-May
9Feb 15Jan 18 – Feb 1from early April
10Jan 31Jan 3 – Jan 17from late March

*Counted from the middle of the planting window plus about 10 weeks. Mature, storage-quality potatoes need 90–120 days from planting and are ready once the foliage dies back.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get a potato planting window built from your own frost dates.

Can you plant potatoes in fall?

In zones 9–10 a fall crop is possible. Plant in late summer so tubers form as temperatures drop below 80°F, and harvest before a hard freeze or into winter, depending on the area. Check local extension recommendations for exact dates, because summer heat can rot seed pieces. In colder zones, potatoes are a spring-planted crop only.

What are seed potatoes, and can you plant grocery store potatoes?

Seed potatoes are tubers certified to be free of common diseases. Garden centers sell them in spring, usually as whole small potatoes or larger ones to cut. Grocery store potatoes are risky: they are often treated to stop sprouting and can carry diseases such as late blight or viruses. Buy certified seed for the best results.

Potatoes come in early (about 70–90 days), mid-season (about 90–110 days) and late (about 110–135 days) types. Early varieties suit short-season zones 3–4 and hot-summer areas. Late varieties yield more where seasons are long and store longest.

How do you plant potatoes step by step?

  1. Chit the seed (optional). Set seed potatoes in a bright, cool (60°F) spot for 2–3 weeks until stubby sprouts form.
  2. Cut large tubers into pieces of 1.5–2 oz (about egg-sized) with at least one or two eyes. Let cut pieces cure for 1–2 days so the surface dries.
  3. Prepare the bed. Choose full sun and loose, well-drained soil with a pH near 5.0–6.5. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages scab.
  4. Dig a trench 4 inches deep. Place pieces cut side down, eyes up, 10–12 inches apart, in rows 30–36 inches apart.
  5. Cover with 3–4 inches of soil. Water in once, then hold off until shoots appear unless the soil is dry.
  6. Hill the plants. When shoots are 6–8 inches tall, mound soil around them, leaving the top few leaves exposed. Repeat once or twice.

A 4 × 8 ft raised bed fits 2 rows of 8 plants (rows 2 ft apart, plants 12 inches apart), or 16 plants; denser raised-bed spacing of about 9 inches fits roughly 20. Try the plant spacing calculator to plan your bed.

Why does hilling matter for potatoes?

Tubers form above the seed piece, and any exposed to light turn green. That green skin contains solanine, which tastes bitter and can make you sick, so cut away green parts and never eat them. Hilling covers the new tubers with dark soil, supports the plants and encourages more yield. Straw mulch piled 6–8 inches deep works as an alternative to soil hills.

Which potato planting mistakes should you avoid?

Do not plant into wet, cold soil. Cut seed pieces rot quickly when soil is saturated and cold. If you cannot squeeze a handful of soil apart easily, wait a few days.
  1. Planting whole or cut pieces from the grocery store. Disease risk is much higher than with certified seed.
  2. Cutting seed too small. Pieces under 1 ounce lack the energy for strong sprouts.
  3. Planting too late. Tubers stop forming when soil stays above 80°F, so late plantings in hot zones give small yields.
  4. Skipping hills. Exposed tubers turn green and bitter.
  5. Overwatering after planting. Wait until sprouts emerge unless the soil is very dry.
  6. Repeating the crop in the same bed. Rotate away from potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and eggplant for about three years.

Frequently asked questions

Can you plant potatoes too early?

Yes, if the soil is frozen or waterlogged. Seed pieces tolerate cool soil at 40–45°F for a few weeks, but cold, wet ground can cause rot. Wait until the soil can be worked and crumbles in your hand.

Do potatoes need to be planted on Good Friday?

No. Good Friday is a folk tradition and has no scientific basis. Soil temperature and your last frost date are the reliable signals.

How long do potatoes take to grow?

Early varieties give small new potatoes in about 60–70 days and full size in 70–90 days. Late varieties take 110–135 days. Mature potatoes are ready when the foliage yellows and dies back.

Should I let cut seed potatoes dry before planting?

Yes. Leave cut pieces in a cool, humid spot for 1–2 days so the cut surface heals. This helps prevent rot in the soil.

How deep should seed potatoes be planted?

Plant seed pieces 3–4 inches deep, then hill soil around the growing stems as plants reach 6–8 inches tall.

The bottom line

Plant potatoes 2–4 weeks before your average last frost, when the soil is 45–50°F and crumbly rather than soggy. Use certified seed, plant 3–4 inches deep and hill as the plants grow. Use the planting calendar to turn your ZIP code into a planting window.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Potato planting guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension and Oregon State University Extension; frost-date statistics from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals; USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. Dates in the table are estimates computed from typical frost dates by zone; confirm yours locally. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Onions: Sets, Seeds and Day Length by Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant onion sets and transplants 2–4 weeks before your last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. Start onion seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before that date. In zones 8–10, plant in fall instead. Choose short-, intermediate- or long-day varieties to match your latitude.

Onions behave differently from most vegetables: they are cold-tolerant, they size up according to day length, and a badly timed start can leave you with thin bulbs or flower stalks. Get the timing and the variety right and onions are one of the easiest crops in the garden.

Below you'll find the right planting window for sets, transplants and seed, a dates table for USDA zones 3–10, and a clear way to pick the right day-length type. To get dates for your exact location, use the planting calendar and enter your ZIP code, or look up your frost dates by ZIP code first.

Key takeaways
  • Spring planting: sets and transplants go in 2–4 weeks before the last frost; onion tops tolerate frost down to roughly 20–25°F once established.
  • Seed: start indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost (soil germinates at about 50–85°F).
  • Day length matters more than zone: short-day types in the South, long-day types in the North, intermediate in between.
  • Fall planting works in zones 8–10 with short-day varieties, for harvest the following spring.
  • Depth and spacing: 1 inch deep, 4 inches apart; bulbs are ready when about half the tops have fallen over.

When is the best time to plant onions?

The short answer is early. Onions are a cool-season crop that grows roots and leaves in cool weather, then forms a bulb as days lengthen and temperatures rise. Every leaf you grow before bulbing starts becomes one ring of the finished onion, so a big, healthy top in spring means a big bulb in summer. That is why extension services advise getting onions into the ground as soon as the soil can be worked, even 4 weeks before your last frost.

Established onion plants are tougher than they look. Their leaves handle light frosts and freezes into the low 20s°F. What they dislike is a long stretch of cold followed by warmth, which can trigger bolting (more on that below), and ground that is still waterlogged and frozen.

Should you plant onion sets, transplants or seeds?

You can start onions three ways, and each has its own timing and trade-offs.

MethodWhen to startDays to harvest (approx.)Pros and cons
Sets (small dormant bulbs)2–4 weeks before last frostAbout 90–100 days from planting; green onions in 3–4 weeksEasiest and fastest; few variety choices; more prone to bolting and often store less well
Transplants (bundled seedlings)2–4 weeks before last frostAbout 100–120 daysGood size and storage; more variety choice than sets; ordered by mail or bought at garden centers
SeedIndoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–4 weeks before last frostAbout 100–120 days after transplantingCheapest and the widest variety choice (including sweet and storage types); needs the most work

For a first-time grower, sets are the simplest, and transplants give larger bulbs. If you want a specific variety that suits your day length, growing from seed is the way to get it.

What are the onion planting dates by USDA zone?

These windows are computed from typical average last spring frost dates for each zone. Sets and transplants go in from 4 weeks before to the last frost date; seed starts indoors 10–12 weeks before it. In zones 8–10 the fall window is calculated from 30 days before to 15 days after the typical first fall frost. They are estimates for a representative location, so shift them if your frost dates differ (see your frost dates by ZIP code).

USDA zoneTypical last frostStart seed indoorsPlant sets / transplantsFall planting
3May 25Mar 2 – Mar 16Apr 27 – May 25Not recommended
4May 15Feb 20 – Mar 6Apr 17 – May 15Not recommended
5May 5Feb 10 – Feb 24Apr 7 – May 5Not recommended
6Apr 25Jan 31 – Feb 14Mar 28 – Apr 25Not recommended
7Apr 15Jan 21 – Feb 4Mar 18 – Apr 15Not recommended
8Mar 25Dec 31 – Jan 14Feb 25 – Mar 25Oct 16 – Nov 30
9Feb 15Nov 23 – Dec 7Jan 18 – Feb 15Nov 1 – Dec 16
10Jan 31Nov 8 – Nov 22Jan 3 – Jan 31Nov 20 – Jan 4

In the coldest zones the soil often thaws after the start of the window, so plant on the first workable day. In zones 9 and 10, fall is the main season because spring warmth arrives before onions can size up; the spring dates there are a fallback for short-day types.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get your onion planting window from your own last frost date.

Short-day, intermediate-day or long-day onions: which should you plant?

Onions begin forming bulbs when the daylight reaches a certain number of hours. Plant the wrong type for your latitude and you'll get one of two problems: a short-day onion in the North makes a bulb too early, when the plant is still small, and a long-day onion in the South never gets enough daylight to bulb at all.

TypeBulbs when days reachBest region (approx.)Typical traits
Short-day10–12 hoursSouth of about 35°N (Gulf Coast, Southwest, Florida, southern California)Mild, sweet, shorter storage; plant in fall or winter
Intermediate-day12–14 hoursRoughly 32–42°N (middle band of the country)The most flexible; fine in much of the Midwest, mid-Atlantic and lower Northwest
Long-day14–16 hoursNorth of about 36–40°N (northern states and Canada border)Pungent, store well; plant in spring

The bands overlap, and seed companies label varieties slightly differently, so always follow the day-length description on the packet or catalog. Intermediate-day varieties are the forgiving choice if you live near a boundary, such as Kentucky, Missouri or northern Texas.

Can you plant onions in the fall?

Yes, in the South. In zones 8–10, short-day onions planted in autumn spend winter growing roots and leaves, then bulb in spring as days lengthen. Plant transplants or small sets from about a month before to two weeks after your first fall frost (see the table). The plants should have time to reach about pencil thickness without getting so big that a cold snap triggers flowering.

Further north, fall planting only works for green (bunching) onions or special overwintering types, and results vary. Most gardeners in zones 3–7 will do better with spring planting.

How do you plant onions step by step?

  1. Prepare the bed. Pick a sunny site with loose, well-drained soil that has a pH of about 6.0–7.0. Work in 2 inches of compost. Onions have shallow roots, so keep the top 6 inches loose and weed-free.
  2. Mark the rows. Space rows 12–18 inches apart. In a raised bed, use a grid of 4 inches. A 4 × 8 ft bed (32 sq ft) at 4-inch spacing holds 32 × 9 = 288 plants.
  3. Plant at the right depth. Set sets pointed end up about 1 inch deep, with the tip just showing. Plant transplants 1 inch deep, no deeper, and spread the roots out.
  4. Space them. Plant 4 inches apart for full-size bulbs. If you want green onions too, plant sets 1–2 inches apart and pull every other one as scallions.
  5. Water in well and keep the soil evenly moist, about 1 inch of water per week.
  6. Mulch lightly with 1–2 inches of straw or shredded leaves once plants are established, to hold moisture and suppress weeds.

Starting seed? Sow about 1/4 inch deep in a tray, keep the soil at 65–75°F, and expect sprouts in 7–10 days. Trim the tops to 3–4 inches if they flop over, which encourages stocky seedlings.

Why do onions bolt, and how does planting time affect it?

Bolting means the plant sends up a flower stalk instead of swelling a bulb. A bolted onion can still be eaten, but the center turns hard and it won't store. The most common trigger is a prolonged cool spell (roughly two weeks below 50°F) after the plant has grown beyond pencil thickness, which fools it into thinking winter has passed.

  • Don't plant too early in a cold zone if you are using large transplants or sets bigger than a dime.
  • Pick small sets. Sets about 1/2 inch across (smaller than a quarter) bolt less than big ones.
  • Choose the right day-length variety. The wrong type makes small, early bulbs or no bulbs.
  • Cover plants during a hard freeze that arrives after growth is established.
Mistakes that ruin an onion crop: planting too deep (bulbs will not swell when buried), crowding plants closer than 3 inches, letting weeds compete (onion roots are weak), heavy nitrogen late in the season (it gives thick necks that rot in storage), and picking a long-day variety in the Deep South.

When are onions ready to harvest?

Onions are ready when the tops yellow and about half to three-quarters of them fall over, usually 100–120 days after planting transplants. Stop watering as the tops fall, pull the bulbs on a dry day, and cure them in a warm, shaded, airy spot for 2–3 weeks until the necks are dry. Then store them cool and dry.

Frequently asked questions

Can you plant onion sets in the fall?

In zones 8–10, yes. Plant short-day onion sets or transplants from about a month before to two weeks after the first fall frost and harvest the following spring. In colder zones, fall-planted sets mostly produce green onions.

How deep do you plant onion sets?

Plant sets about 1 inch deep with the pointed end up so the tip is just visible. Planting deeper than 2 inches slows growth and gives smaller, elongated bulbs.

Why do my onions go to flower?

Bolting usually follows a cold spell after the plant has grown larger than a pencil. Use small sets, avoid planting too early in cold zones and pick a day-length variety suited to your latitude.

Is it too late to plant onions in May?

In zones 3–5, May is still on time for sets and transplants. In zones 6 and warmer, onions planted in May often make small bulbs because heat arrives before they have grown enough leaves; use them for green onions instead.

How far apart should you plant onions?

Plant onions 4 inches apart in rows 12–18 inches apart for full-size bulbs. For green onions, 1–2 inches apart is fine.

What soil temperature do onion seeds need to germinate?

Onion seed germinates in soil from about 50°F to 85°F, fastest at 65–75°F. Starting seeds in a warm room indoors is more reliable than sowing into cold spring soil.

The bottom line

Plant onion sets and transplants 2–4 weeks before your last spring frost, start seed indoors 10–12 weeks ahead and, in zones 8–10, plant short-day types in fall. Match the variety to your day length and keep them 1 inch deep and 4 inches apart. To get dates for your own ZIP code, use the free planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Onion planting, day-length and bolting guidance from US university extension services, including Cornell Cooperative Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; frost dates are estimates informed by NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Zone dates here are computed from typical frost dates and are approximate. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Green Beans: Dates and Succession Sowing
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant green beans 1–2 weeks after your last spring frost, when the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Sow seed directly in the garden, 1 inch deep, because beans resent transplanting. Bush beans are ready in about 50–60 days; sow again every 2–3 weeks for a steady harvest until about 8–10 weeks before fall frost.

Beans are one of the easiest vegetables to grow, but they punish impatience. Seed sown into cold, wet soil rots instead of sprouting, and a late frost kills seedlings outright. Planting on the right date, not the earliest possible one, is most of the battle.

This guide gives the soil temperature rule, planting dates for USDA zones 3–10, the difference between bush and pole timing, and how to sow in succession so you aren't buried in beans for one week and empty-handed the next. To find dates for your exact location, check your frost dates by ZIP code and then use the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • When: 1–2 weeks after the average last frost, never into soil below 60°F.
  • Method: direct sow only, 1 inch deep, 2–4 inches apart (thin to 3–4 inches).
  • Timing: bush beans take about 50–60 days; pole beans take about 60–70 days.
  • Succession: sow bush beans every 2–3 weeks; stop 8–10 weeks before the first fall frost.
  • Frost: beans are tender. A light frost kills the leaves, so they should never go out early.

What soil temperature do green beans need?

Green beans need soil of at least 60°F at planting depth, and germinate fastest at roughly 70–80°F. Below 60°F, seed can sit for weeks and rot, especially in heavy, wet ground. The seed leaf is also fragile, so cold snaps after sprouting set plants back hard.

Soil temperature (2 in deep)What to expect
Under 55°FSeed rots; do not plant
55–60°FVery slow and patchy germination
60–65°FAcceptable; sprouts in 10–14 days
70–80°FIdeal; sprouts in about 6–10 days
Over 90°FFlowers drop and pods fail to set

A soil thermometer costs only a few dollars. Check the soil at about 8 a.m. for three mornings in a row; if it's 60°F or higher, you're clear to plant. In cold-slow spots, covering a bed with clear plastic for a week warms it a few degrees.

When should you plant green beans by USDA zone?

Dates below come from typical average last and first frost dates for each zone, with spring sowing set at 7–14 days after the last frost. They are estimates for a representative location. Your own frost dates may vary by weeks with elevation and microclimate, so shift the table by the same number of days.

USDA zoneTypical last frostSpring sowing windowTypical first fall frostLast fall sowing (bush)
3May 25Jun 1 – Jun 8Sep 15Jul 7 – Jul 21
4May 15May 22 – May 29Sep 30Jul 22 – Aug 5
5May 5May 12 – May 19Oct 10Aug 1 – Aug 15
6Apr 25May 2 – May 9Oct 20Aug 11 – Aug 25
7Apr 15Apr 22 – Apr 29Nov 1Aug 23 – Sep 6
8Mar 25Apr 1 – Apr 8Nov 15Sep 6 – Sep 20
9Feb 15Feb 22 – Mar 1Dec 1Sep 22 – Oct 6
10Jan 31Feb 7 – Feb 14Dec 20Oct 11 – Oct 25

In zones 9 and 10, beans are a cool-weather crop that must finish before summer heat above about 90°F stops pod set. Sow in late winter for a spring crop and again in early fall for a winter harvest. Fall sowing in the table is the last safe date for bush beans; pole beans need about two more weeks of runway.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get bean sowing dates based on your own frost dates.

Should you start green beans indoors?

No. Beans have a taproot-like root system that hates disturbance, and they grow so fast from seed that starting indoors saves little time. Direct sowing gives sturdier plants. The only exception is a short-season zone 3 or 4 garden where you want a head start, in which case sow into peat-free biodegradable pots only 2 weeks before transplanting and handle the roots gently.

If you want an early crop, protect the planting with a floating row cover instead. It adds a few degrees of frost protection and keeps soil warmer.

When do bush beans and pole beans differ?

Both types are planted at the same time in spring, but they differ in how long they take and how long they produce.

TraitBush beansPole beans
Days to harvestAbout 50–60About 60–70
Harvest period2–3 weeks per planting6–8 weeks or more
Height1–2 ft, no support6–10 ft, needs trellis
Spacing2–4 in apart, rows 18–24 in4–6 in apart at base of support
Succession sowingEvery 2–3 weeksUsually one or two sowings
Last fall sowingAbout 8–10 weeks before frostAbout 10–12 weeks before frost

How do you plant green beans step by step?

  1. Pick a sunny spot. Beans need at least 6–8 hours of direct sun and well-drained soil.
  2. Skip heavy nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen. Mix in a little compost, but avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces leaves instead of pods.
  3. Check the soil temperature. Wait for 60°F or more.
  4. Sow seeds 1 inch deep, 2–4 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart (1.5 inches deep in sandy soil). For pole beans, plant 4–6 seeds around each support.
  5. Water once after planting, then keep soil lightly moist. Soggy soil rots seed.
  6. Thin to 3–4 inches once seedlings have their first true leaves. Snip rather than pull, to protect neighbors.
  7. Mulch with straw once plants are about 4 inches tall.

How do you sow green beans in succession?

A single bush bean planting yields heavily for only two to three weeks. To harvest all summer, plant a new short row every 2–3 weeks from your first sowing date until the cutoff date for your zone. The cutoff is roughly 8–10 weeks before the first fall frost (bush beans need about 55–60 days plus a few weeks of picking).

For example, in zone 6 the first sowing falls around May 2. Planting every 3 weeks gives sowings on about May 2, May 23, Jun 13, Jul 4 and Jul 25, with the last one safe through about Aug 25. That's five harvest waves from a small footprint.

Beans are also useful for filling space after early crops. Once spring peas or lettuce are finished, bush beans can follow in the same bed. They enrich the soil as they grow.

What are the most common green bean planting mistakes?

Planting too early is the top mistake. One cold, wet week can rot every seed in the row, and a single frost kills seedlings that have already sprouted. If a late frost is forecast after you have planted, cover the row overnight with a sheet or row cover.
  1. Planting in cold soil. Wait for 60°F, even if the calendar says go.
  2. Seed too deep. Beyond 1.5 inches, the seedling struggles to push up, especially in clay.
  3. Overwatering after sowing. Water once, then let the top inch dry.
  4. Too much nitrogen. You'll get lush vines and few beans.
  5. Skipping succession sowing. One planting means one big flush, then little else.
  6. Working wet foliage. Picking or weeding while leaves are wet can spread bean rust and other diseases between plants.

Frequently asked questions

How late can you plant green beans?

Bush green beans can be sown until roughly 8–10 weeks before your first fall frost, because they need about 50–60 days to produce. In zone 6, that means late August; in zone 4, early August.

Can I soak bean seeds before planting?

It is best not to. Bean seed soaked for more than a few hours can crack and rot, and soaked seed is especially prone to damage in cool soil. Plant dry seed into moist, warm soil instead.

How long do green beans take to sprout?

Green beans usually sprout in 6–10 days in 70–80°F soil. In cooler soil near 60°F, expect closer to 10–14 days.

How many bean plants do I need per person?

For fresh eating, about 10–15 bush bean plants per person is a common planning figure. For freezing or canning, double it. Sowing in succession smooths the supply.

Do green beans come back every year?

No. Green beans are annuals, so they finish after one season and must be reseeded each year. Rotate them to a different bed every year or two to cut down on soil-borne disease.

Can green beans grow in partial shade?

They tolerate light shade but produce best with 6–8 hours of direct sun. In hot southern gardens, afternoon shade can help keep flowers from dropping in summer heat.

The bottom line

Wait until 1–2 weeks after your last frost and 60°F soil, sow beans straight into the garden 1 inch deep, and keep sowing every 2–3 weeks until about 8–10 weeks before your first fall frost. To get dates tailored to your ZIP code, open the planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Snap bean planting and spacing guidance from US university extension services, including Clemson Cooperative Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and the University of Georgia Cooperative Extension; frost date concepts from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals and the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. Dates in this article are computed from representative frost dates and are estimates only. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Cucumbers: Soil Temperature and Dates by Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Plant cucumbers 1–2 weeks after your average last frost, once the soil is at least 65°F (70°F is ideal) and nights stay above 50°F. For most of the US that means late April to early June. Warm Southern zones can sow again in late summer for a fall crop.

Cucumbers are among the most frost-tender vegetables in the garden. A single night near 32°F kills the vines, and cold, wet soil rots seed before it sprouts. Planting a week too early costs you more than planting a week late, because cucumbers sown into warm soil catch up fast.

This guide gives you soil-temperature rules, a dates table for USDA zones 3–10, and a plan for succession sowing. To get dates for your own town, check your frost dates by ZIP code, then find your exact dates with the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Frost: cucumbers have no frost tolerance. Wait until 1–2 weeks after the last spring frost.
  • Soil: seed germinates slowly below 60°F; aim for 70°F or warmer, with 65°F as a practical minimum.
  • Method: direct sow is best. Start indoors only 3 weeks ahead, in peat-free pots that won't disturb roots.
  • Timing to harvest: most slicers take 50–70 days from sowing; pickling types are often 50–55.
  • Succession: sow a second batch 3 weeks later, and in zones 7–10 a fall crop 10–12 weeks before first frost.

What soil temperature do cucumbers need?

Cucumbers are a warm-season crop from tropical roots. Extension guidance generally puts the germination minimum near 60°F, with fast, reliable sprouting at 70–95°F. Seed in 55°F soil can sit for weeks and rot. The table below shows what to expect.

Soil temperatureWhat happens to cucumber seed
Below 55°FSeed rots or does not sprout; seedlings stall
55–60°FVery slow, uneven germination
65–70°FGood germination in roughly 7–10 days
75–90°FFastest sprouting, often in 3–5 days

Check with a soil thermometer pushed 2 inches deep, at mid-morning, for three days in a row. Air temperature alone misleads you, because soil warms more slowly than the air, especially after a wet spring.

When should you plant cucumbers by USDA zone?

These dates are computed from typical average last and first frost dates for each zone. Spring sowing is 7–14 days after the last frost. The late-sowing column is 70–84 days before the first fall frost, which leaves time for a 50–70 day crop to mature. They are estimates for a representative location; elevation and microclimate can shift them by a couple of weeks.

USDA zoneTypical last frostSpring sowingSecond sowingLate sowing (fall crop)
3May 25Jun 1 – Jun 8Jun 22Jun 23 – Jul 7 (short-season types)
4May 15May 22 – May 29Jun 12Jul 8 – Jul 22
5May 5May 12 – May 19Jun 2Jul 18 – Aug 1
6Apr 25May 2 – May 9May 23Jul 28 – Aug 11
7Apr 15Apr 22 – Apr 29May 13Aug 9 – Aug 23
8Mar 25Apr 1 – Apr 8Apr 22Aug 23 – Sep 6
9Feb 15Feb 22 – Mar 1Mar 15Sep 8 – Sep 22
10Jan 31Feb 7 – Feb 14Feb 28Sep 27 – Oct 11

If your own last frost is two weeks later than the typical date for your zone, move every date in that row two weeks later. In zones 9 and 10, check the soil thermometer rather than the calendar, because cool spells in February can still stall seed. In zones 3 and 4 the growing season is short, so the "late sowing" is really a second chance, not a separate fall crop.

🧮

Want dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get cucumber sowing dates based on your own last and first frost.

Should you start cucumbers indoors or sow them outside?

Direct sowing wins for most gardeners. Cucumbers dislike root disturbance, and seed sown into warm soil often overtakes transplants within weeks. Start indoors only if your season is short (zones 3–5) or you want a head start.

  • Direct sow: best from zone 5 south. Seed goes in 1 inch deep, once the soil is 65°F or warmer.
  • Start indoors: sow 3 weeks before your planned transplant date, in 3-inch pots filled with seed-starting mix. Older seedlings with root-bound roots establish poorly.
  • Harden off: give seedlings 5–7 days of gradual outdoor exposure before planting.

For zone 3, a seed-start date of about May 11 (3 weeks before the June 1 outdoor date) lets you transplant on schedule; for zone 5, about April 21 for May 12 planting.

How do you plant cucumbers step by step?

  1. Pick a sunny spot. Cucumbers need at least 6–8 hours of direct sun and a bed that drains well.
  2. Enrich the soil. Mix in 2–3 inches of compost. Cucumbers are heavy feeders, and ideal soil pH is about 6.0–7.0.
  3. Wait for warmth. Confirm the soil is at least 65°F and the 10-day forecast has no nights below 50°F.
  4. Sow seed 1 inch deep. Plant 2–3 seeds per spot. For vining types on a trellis, space spots 12 inches apart; for sprawling hills, 3 feet apart.
  5. Water gently. Keep the soil evenly moist until sprouts appear in about a week.
  6. Thin to the strongest seedling per spot by snipping the extras at the soil line.
  7. Mulch with 2 inches of straw once plants are established and the soil is warm.

A 4 × 8 ft bed (32 sq ft) with a trellis along one long side can hold about 8 vines at 12 inches apart along the 8 ft length, leaving the other rows free for other crops.

How do you plant cucumbers in succession?

Cucumber vines produce heavily for four to six weeks and then slow down, often from disease or bitter fruit in summer heat. Sowing a second batch about 3 weeks after the first spreads the harvest.
