Zone 6 gardeners, for example, can sow on May 2 and again on May 23, then pull the first planting when production fades.

Count back from your first fall frost to set a last sowing date. A 60-day variety planted 70 days before frost leaves 10 days of buffer for slow growth as days shorten. This is why zone 7 can sow as late as the third week of August, while zone 5 should be done by the first of August.

Can you grow cucumbers as a fall crop?

In zones 7–10 the answer is yes. Late summer soil is warm and seed sprouts in 3–4 days. The challenge is heat stress and pests, so water deeply and choose disease-resistant varieties. In zones 9 and 10, fall cucumbers sown in mid-September often produce until the first cool nights in December. Fall crops usually need less trellis support because vines are smaller.

Frost warning: if frost is forecast after seedlings emerge, cover plants with a floating row cover or an upturned bucket overnight. Even light frost damages cucumber leaves, and a hard freeze kills vines outright. Remove the cover each morning once temperatures rise.

5 mistakes that hurt your cucumber crop

  1. Planting before the soil warms. The seed rots. Use a thermometer, not the calendar.
  2. Letting the bed dry out. Irregular watering causes bitter, misshapen fruit. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week, more in heat.
  3. Skipping the trellis. Climbing vines hold fruit off the ground, improve airflow and make picking easier.
  4. Letting cucumbers overripen. Pick often. Fruit left on the vine tells the plant to stop producing.
  5. Planting in the same spot every year. Rotate away from cucumbers, squash and melons for 2–3 years to reduce soil-borne disease.

Frequently asked questions

How long do cucumbers take to grow from seed?

Most cucumbers produce fruit 50–70 days after sowing. Pickling types are often ready in 50–55 days, while larger slicers and specialty types can take 60–70 days. Cooler weather adds days.

Is it too late to plant cucumbers in July?

It depends on your zone. In zones 6–10 July sowing works well for a late harvest, because a 55-day variety will mature before frost. In zones 3–4, July is the last practical month and only for fast pickling types.

Can I plant cucumber seeds directly in the ground in April?

Only in zones 7 and warmer, and only after the soil reaches 65°F. In zones 3–6, April soil is usually too cold, and seed will rot in the ground.

Should I soak cucumber seeds before planting?

It is not necessary. Soaking for a few hours can speed sprouting slightly, but in cool, wet soil it can encourage rot, so plant dry seed into warm, moist soil.

How many cucumber plants do I need per person?

Two to three healthy vines per person is enough for fresh eating. Plan on 5–8 vines per household if you also want to make pickles.

The bottom line

Wait until 1–2 weeks after the last frost and until the soil is 65–70°F, then sow cucumber seed 1 inch deep. Add a second sowing 3 weeks later, and in warm zones a fall crop 10–12 weeks before the first frost. To turn this into a date for your town, look up your frost dates by ZIP code and use the planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator

Sources: Cucumber growing guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and the University of Maryland Extension; frost-date averages from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Dates in the table are computed estimates from typical zone frost dates, not forecasts. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Carrots: Spring and Fall Sowing Dates by Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Sow carrots outdoors 2–3 weeks before your last spring frost, once the soil is at least 50°F (ideal 55–75°F). Sow again for fall about 10–12 weeks before your first fall frost. Seeds take 1–3 weeks to sprout, and most varieties are ready 60–80 days later.

Carrots are easy to grow and fussy to start. The seeds are tiny, slow to sprout and picky about soil, so a few days of timing can decide whether you get a full row or a bare strip. Planting too early in cold soil or too late in summer heat are the two most common ways to lose a carrot crop.

This guide gives you the soil-temperature rule, a spring and fall sowing table for USDA zones 3–10, and what to do after sowing. For dates matched to your own ZIP code, use the planting calendar or look up your frost dates by ZIP code.

Key takeaways
  • Spring sowing: 2–3 weeks before the last frost, with soil at 50°F or warmer.
  • Germination: works in soil from about 45°F to 85°F, but it is fastest at 70–75°F and can take 1–3 weeks.
  • Fall sowing: 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost; fall carrots are often sweeter.
  • Depth and spacing: sow 1/4–1/2 inch deep, then thin to 2–3 inches apart.
  • Maturity: most varieties take 60–80 days; some storage types take longer.

When is the best time to plant carrots in spring?

Carrot seedlings and young plants tolerate light frost, so you don't need to wait until the danger of frost has passed. Extension guidance is generally to sow 2–3 weeks before the average last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked and has begun to warm. That puts the carrots in early so they mature before summer heat, which makes roots tough and strong-flavored.

Seeds will germinate in soil as cool as about 45°F, but very slowly, and many gardeners treat 50°F as the practical minimum. At 50°F expect close to three weeks; at 70–75°F, about one to two weeks. A cheap soil thermometer pushed 2 inches into the bed removes the guesswork.

You can keep sowing through spring. Make a new sowing every 2–3 weeks, called succession sowing, until about 10–12 weeks before the weather turns hot (daytime highs regularly above 85°F). That spreads out the harvest instead of giving you 100 carrots on one weekend.

What are the carrot sowing dates by USDA zone?

The spring window below runs from 3 weeks before to 2 weeks after the typical last frost date; sow earlier in the window when the soil is workable, later if the spring is cold. The fall window is 10–12 weeks before the typical first fall frost. These are estimates for a representative location, so shift them if your own frost dates differ.

USDA zoneTypical last frostSpring sowingTypical first frostFall sowing
3May 25May 4 – Jun 8Sep 15Jun 23 – Jul 7
4May 15Apr 24 – May 29Sep 30Jul 8 – Jul 22
5May 5Apr 14 – May 19Oct 10Jul 18 – Aug 1
6Apr 25Apr 4 – May 9Oct 20Jul 28 – Aug 11
7Apr 15Mar 25 – Apr 29Nov 1Aug 9 – Aug 23
8Mar 25Mar 4 – Apr 8Nov 15Aug 23 – Sep 6
9Feb 15Jan 25 – Mar 1Dec 1Sep 8 – Sep 22
10Jan 31Jan 10 – Feb 14Dec 20Sep 27 – Oct 11

In zones 9 and 10, carrots are mainly a cool-season crop: sow from fall through winter and avoid summer, when soil temperatures stay above the 85°F germination limit. Further north, late sowings in the fall window can be harvested after frost, which only improves flavor.

🧮

Want sowing dates for your exact location? Use the planting calendar, enter your ZIP code and get spring and fall carrot dates from your own frost dates.

What soil temperature do carrots need to germinate?

Soil temperatureWhat to expect
Below 45°FSeeds sit dormant or rot; wait
45–50°FPossible, but very slow (about 3 weeks or more)
55–75°FBest range; sprouts in roughly 1–2 weeks
75–85°FFast but only if the bed stays moist; crusting is a risk
Above 85°FPoor, patchy germination; wait for fall

The challenge in late spring and summer is not the temperature itself but the surface drying out, because carrot seeds sit in the top half inch of soil.

When should you plant carrots for a fall harvest?

Count back from your first fall frost: most carrots need 60–80 days to mature, and growth slows as days shorten and soil cools, so add a few weeks. That is why the rule is 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost. Carrots do not mind a frost, and cold converts starch to sugar, so frosted carrots taste noticeably sweeter. In zones 6 and colder, a thick layer of straw mulch lets you keep harvesting well into winter.

The difficulty is that fall sowing often falls in the hottest weeks of summer. Keep the seedbed cool and damp by covering it with a board or burlap until sprouts appear, then remove it right away. Shade cloth also helps.

How do you plant carrots step by step?

  1. Prepare deep, loose soil. Loosen the bed 10–12 inches deep and remove stones, sticks and clods, which cause forked or stubby roots. A sandy loam is ideal; heavy clay should be amended with compost.
  2. Skip fresh manure and high-nitrogen fertilizer. Too much nitrogen gives lush tops and hairy, forked roots.
  3. Sow thinly. Scatter seed in a shallow furrow 1/4–1/2 inch deep, in rows 12 inches apart, or broadcast in a raised bed. Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.
  4. Keep the surface moist. Water gently every day or two (not heavy blasts) until seedlings are up, which can take up to three weeks in cool soil.
  5. Thin the seedlings. When they are 2 inches tall, thin to 1–2 inches apart, then thin again to 2–3 inches when the roots are about finger-width. Pinch rather than pull, since pulling can damage neighbors and the scent of crushed carrot tops attracts carrot rust flies.
  6. Water evenly at about 1 inch per week and mulch lightly once plants are 3–4 inches tall.
Why carrots fail to come up: sowing into soil colder than 50°F, letting the surface crust or dry out before the seedlings emerge, sowing too deep (more than 1/2 inch), and old seed. Carrot seed is only reliably viable for about 1–3 years, so replace any packet that has been in a hot garage.

What are the common carrot planting mistakes?

  1. Sowing too thick and never thinning. Crowded carrots stay skinny and twisted.
  2. Planting in rocky or compacted soil. The root forks around anything it hits.
  3. Planting in summer heat. Roots are woody and bitter when matured in hot weather; time them for spring or fall.
  4. Inconsistent watering. Dry spells followed by a soak make roots split.
  5. Leaving shoulders exposed. Soil or mulch around the root tops prevents green, bitter shoulders.

How long do carrots take to grow?

Days to maturity are counted from sowing and vary a lot by type:

TypeApprox. days to harvestBest use
Baby and round types50–60Shallow or clay soil, containers
Nantes and Chantenay65–75Fresh eating; Chantenay suits heavy soil
Imperator (long, tapered)75–85Deep, loose soil only
Storage types85–100+Fall sowing for winter storage

Check the seed packet for the exact number, and pull a test carrot to check the size. A spring sowing on the zone 6 date of April 25 (the typical last frost) is ready from roughly early July with a 70-day variety.

Frequently asked questions

Why aren't my carrot seeds germinating?

The usual causes are cold soil (below 50°F), a surface that dried out, seed sown too deep or old seed. Keep the top half inch evenly damp and be patient; cool soil can take three weeks.

How long does it take carrots to sprout?

Carrots sprout in about 1–3 weeks: roughly 7–14 days in 70–75°F soil, and up to three weeks at 50°F. They are one of the slowest vegetables to emerge.

Can carrots survive a frost after planting?

Yes. Carrot seedlings tolerate light frost, and mature roots handle freezes into the low 20s°F, especially under mulch. That is why you can sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost.

Should you soak carrot seeds before sowing?

Soaking is optional. A 12–24 hour soak in water can speed up sprouting a little, but the seeds must not dry out afterwards, so it only helps if you can keep the bed moist.

Can you plant carrots in summer?

Only for a fall harvest, and only if the seedbed is kept cool and damp. Sow 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost; in zones 9–10, wait until fall because summer soil is too hot.

How far apart should carrots be planted?

Thin carrots to 2–3 inches apart, or 1–2 inches for baby carrots. Rows go 12 inches apart.

The bottom line

Sow carrots 2–3 weeks before your last spring frost in soil that has reached about 50°F, keep the seedbed moist until they sprout in 1–3 weeks, thin to 2–3 inches, and sow again 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost. For dates tailored to your ZIP code, use the free planting calendar.

Related tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator

Sources: Carrot planting, germination and thinning guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension, Oregon State University Extension and Cornell Cooperative Extension; frost dates are estimates informed by NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Zone dates here are computed from typical frost dates and are approximate. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How Much Gravel Do I Need? Tons, Yards and Bags Explained
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

One cubic yard of gravel covers 108 square feet at 3 inches deep and weighs about 1.4 tons. To find your amount, multiply length × width in feet, multiply by the depth in inches, divide by 324 to get cubic yards, then multiply by 1.4 for tons. Add about 10% for compaction.

Gravel is sold three ways: by the ton, by the cubic yard and in bags. That makes ordering confusing, and mistakes are costly. A single cubic yard weighs well over a ton, so ordering the wrong unit can leave you short or paying delivery on a pile you never needed.

This guide gives you the formula, a coverage chart by depth, a tons and bags table, the right depth for paths, driveways and drainage, and a bulk-versus-bag comparison. If you would rather skip the math, the topsoil and gravel calculator converts everything between square feet, yards and tons.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: square feet × depth (in) ÷ 324 = cubic yards.
  • Weight: gravel weighs about 1.2–1.5 tons per cubic yard; use 1.4 for a safe estimate.
  • Coverage: 1 cubic yard covers 162 sq ft at 2 in, 108 at 3 in, 81 at 4 in and 54 at 6 in.
  • Depth: 2–3 in for paths, 4–6 in for driveways, and a thicker bed for drainage trenches.
  • Order 10% extra: loose gravel compacts once it is raked and driven on.

How do you calculate how much gravel you need?

The method is the same for any shape: find the area, multiply by depth and convert to the unit your supplier sells. Here is the process in four steps.

Step 1: Measure the area in square feet

For a rectangle, multiply length × width. A path 3 ft wide and 30 ft long is 90 sq ft. For a circle, use 3.14 × radius². For irregular shapes, split the area into rectangles and add them up.

Step 2: Choose your depth in inches

Depth depends on use. See the depth chart below for the usual range for each project.

Step 3: Convert to cubic yards

Multiply square feet by depth in inches, then divide by 324.

Example: 90 sq ft × 3 in ÷ 324 = 0.83 cubic yards.

Step 4: Convert to tons and add the extra

Multiply cubic yards by 1.4 for tons. Then add 10% for compaction.

Example: 0.83 × 1.4 = 1.17 tons. With 10% extra, order about 1.3 tons (0.92 cubic yards).

🧮

Working with several areas or switching between units? Use the topsoil and gravel calculator. Enter the dimensions and get cubic yards, tons and cost.

Gravel coverage chart: how far does a cubic yard go?

Use this chart to size a bulk order. Tons assume 1.4 tons per cubic yard.

Depth1 cubic yard covers1 ton covers (at 1.4 t/yd)
1 inch324 sq ft231 sq ft
2 inches162 sq ft116 sq ft
3 inches108 sq ft77 sq ft
4 inches81 sq ft58 sq ft
6 inches54 sq ft39 sq ft

How many tons and bags of gravel do I need?

This table shows common project sizes, including 10% for compaction. Bags are 0.5 cu ft (typical for bagged landscape gravel; check your bag size, since 0.5 cu ft is common but not universal).

ProjectCubic yardsWith 10% extraTons (1.4 t/yd)0.5 cu ft bags (no extra)
100 sq ft at 2 in0.620.680.9534
200 sq ft at 3 in1.852.042.85100
400 sq ft at 4 in4.945.437.60267
300 sq ft at 6 in5.566.118.56300
1,000 sq ft at 4 in12.3513.5819.01667

The bags column shows why bags only make sense for small jobs: it takes 54 half-cubic-foot bags to make one cubic yard.

How deep should gravel be for each project?

Depth is a function of what will happen on top of the gravel. Foot traffic needs far less than vehicles.

ProjectTypical depthCommon stone
Garden path / mulch substitute2–3 inPea gravel or 3/8 in crushed stone
Patio or walkway (decorative)2–3 in over a compacted baseFines-binding crushed stone
Driveway4–6 in (more over soft soil)Crushed stone, 3/4 in
Base under pavers4–6 in compacted (more in cold or wet climates)Crushed, angular base stone
Drainage trench / French drainFills the trench, often 12 in or moreWashed 3/4 to 1.5 in stone
Around foundation / drip line2–3 inWashed river rock

Round, smooth stone such as pea gravel rolls underfoot and shifts, so it is a poor choice for a driveway. Angular crushed stone locks together and compacts firmly.

Compacted base matters more than top depth. A driveway built with 6 inches of gravel directly on soft topsoil will rut. Dig out soft soil, compact the subgrade and consider landscape fabric under the stone for a stable surface.

How much gravel do I need for a driveway or French drain?

Two examples show how quickly quantities grow on bigger projects.

  • Driveway: 12 ft wide × 40 ft long = 480 sq ft. At 4 inches deep that is 480 × 4 ÷ 324 = 5.93 cubic yards, or about 8.3 tons. With 10% extra, order about 6.5 cubic yards (9.1 tons).
  • French drain: a trench 1 ft wide × 2 ft deep × 50 ft long holds 100 cubic feet, which is 3.7 cubic yards. Order about 4.1 cubic yards with 10% extra, then subtract any volume the pipe takes up.

For a driveway, build up in layers: larger base stone first, then a smaller top layer, compacting each one. Local suppliers can recommend the right mix for your soil.

Is bagged or bulk gravel cheaper?

Bulk gravel is almost always cheaper per ton or yard, but delivery fees mean bags can win for tiny jobs. Using purely example prices of $5 per 0.5 cu ft bag, $55 per ton in bulk and a $75 delivery fee:

  • One cubic yard in bags: 54 bags × $5 = $270
  • One cubic yard in bulk: 1.4 tons × $55 + $75 = $152

Even for one yard, bulk wins in this example, and the gap grows with volume. Bags make sense only for jobs under about a quarter of a yard, or when you cannot take a delivery. Check local prices, which vary widely by stone type and region.

Will it fit in my truck?

Two cubic yards of gravel weigh about 2.8 tons, which is more than the payload of many half-ton pickups. Trucks are often rated around 1,500–2,000 lb of payload. Fill the bed only part-way, or have it delivered.

5 gravel mistakes that waste money

  1. Mixing up tons and yards. Always confirm which unit the quote is in, and ask for the supplier's weight per yard for your stone.
  2. Skipping the compaction allowance. Loose stone settles 10–15% once raked and driven on.
  3. Using pea gravel for vehicles. Round stone slides and rutting is constant.
  4. No edging. Gravel migrates into lawns and beds without a border.
  5. Laying it over weeds. Remove vegetation and consider fabric underneath to slow regrowth.

Frequently asked questions

How many tons should I order for one cubic yard of gravel?

A cubic yard of gravel weighs roughly 1.2–1.5 tons, depending on stone type, size and moisture. Using 1.4 tons per yard is a safe estimate for ordering.

How much area will one ton of gravel cover?

At 1.4 tons per cubic yard, one ton covers about 116 sq ft at 2 inches, 77 sq ft at 3 inches or 58 sq ft at 4 inches.

How much gravel do I need for a 10×10 area?

A 100 sq ft area needs about 0.62 cubic yards (0.86 tons) at 2 inches and 0.93 cubic yards (1.3 tons) at 3 inches. Add about 10% extra for compaction.

Do I need landscape fabric under gravel?

Fabric helps keep stone from sinking into soft soil and slows weeds, so it is useful for paths and driveways. It is not required, and it can trap debris over time, so use a quality woven product and a decent depth of stone.

What size gravel is best for a driveway?

Angular crushed stone around 3/4 inch, often with fine particles that bind it, makes a stable surface. Many installers use larger base stone below and a smaller top layer.

Is gravel cheaper than mulch?

Per cubic yard, gravel often costs more upfront than bulk mulch, but it lasts far longer and does not need annual refreshing. Over several years the difference narrows.

The bottom line

Multiply square feet by depth in inches and divide by 324 for cubic yards, then multiply by 1.4 for tons and add 10% for compaction. Use 2–3 inches for paths and 4–6 inches for driveways, and buy in bulk for anything bigger than a small project. For multiple areas and instant unit conversion, try the free topsoil and gravel calculator.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Soil Calculator · Paver Patio Calculator

Sources: Aggregate density ranges from typical supplier guidance and US geological aggregate references; driveway and path base guidance from US university extension services and state transportation department low-volume road guidance. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Prices are illustrative examples; check your local quarry or supplier. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Winter Pruning Guide: What to Prune and What to Leave
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Prune in winter when plants are dormant, but only those that bloom on new growth or need structural cuts. Late winter is best for apple, pear, grape, roses, butterfly bush and most shade trees. Wait until after bloom for lilac, forsythia and azalea, and never remove more than a quarter of a tree's live crown.

Dormant pruning is one of the best garden jobs for a cold, clear day. Without leaves you can see the structure of a tree or shrub, and the cuts heal quickly when growth restarts in spring. But pruning at the wrong time costs you a year of flowers or fruit, so it pays to know which plants belong on the winter list.

This guide gives you a plant-by-plant timing table, the cuts to make, tools to use and the mistakes to avoid. If your cuts leave wood to mulch or compost, the mulch calculator helps you plan what to do with the clippings.

Key takeaways
  • Best window: late winter, a few weeks before buds swell, for most dormant pruning.
  • Prune in winter: apple, pear, grape, blueberry, shade trees, roses, butterfly bush, panicle hydrangea.
  • Wait until after bloom: lilac, forsythia, azalea, rhododendron, bigleaf hydrangea, spring-blooming spirea.
  • Limit: remove no more than about 25% of a tree's live canopy in one year.
  • Cut point: about ¼ inch above a bud, never flush with the trunk or leaving long stubs.

Is winter a good time to prune?

For many plants, yes. Dormant plants are not using energy for leaves and flowers, so pruning wounds are less stressful, insects and many disease spores are inactive, and bare branches reveal crossing or dead limbs. Late winter, just before growth starts, is also when a pruning cut closes fastest.

The exceptions matter. Plants that bloom on last year's wood already carry next summer's flower buds in winter; pruning them now removes the flowers. In very cold regions, pruning stone fruit or tender shrubs in mid-winter can lead to dieback. And a few trees are best pruned at other times for disease reasons, such as oaks (avoid April through July, when beetles spreading oak wilt are active).

What should you prune in winter, and when?

PlantPrune whenNotes
Apple, pearLate winter (Feb–Mar)Remove dead, crossing and crowded branches; open the center to light
Peach, plum, cherryLate winter to early spring, or right after bloomCold-sensitive; avoid cutting during deep freezes
GrapesLate winter, before sap risesFruit forms on one-year-old canes; heavy pruning is normal
BlueberriesLate winterRemove oldest canes and low, weak growth
Shade trees (maple, ash, linden)Winter dormancyMaples may "bleed" sap in spring, which is harmless
Hybrid tea and floribunda rosesLate winter to early spring, as buds swellCut dead and weak canes; wait until the worst cold has passed
Butterfly bush, panicle hydrangea, Japanese spireaLate winterBloom on new wood; can be cut back hard
Crape myrtleLate winter, lightlyRemove crossing limbs and suckers only; avoid topping
Lilac, forsythia, azalea, rhododendronAfter bloom, not winterFlower buds are already set
Bigleaf and oakleaf hydrangeaAfter bloom, minimalMost flower on old wood; remove only dead stems

Exact timing depends on climate. In USDA zones 3–5, late winter may mean March or later; in zones 8–9 it may mean January or February. If you are not sure of your zone, see our guide to planting dates by hardiness zone.

How do you make a proper pruning cut?

Step 1: Start with the three Ds

Remove dead, damaged and diseased wood first. These cuts help the plant at any time of year and often make the rest of the job obvious.

Step 2: Remove crossing and rubbing branches

Where two branches rub, wounds form and invite disease. Keep the stronger or better-placed one.

Step 3: Cut just above a bud

When shortening a branch, cut at a slight angle about ¼ inch above a healthy bud that points the direction you want growth to go, usually outward.

Step 4: Cut large limbs in three steps

For a limb thicker than 2 inches, make an undercut about 12 inches out, then cut from the top a few inches beyond it so the limb falls without tearing the bark. Finally, remove the stub just outside the branch collar, the swollen ring where the branch joins the trunk. Do not cut flush with the trunk, and do not leave a long stub.

Step 5: Skip wound paint

Current extension guidance does not recommend wound dressing for most pruning cuts; trees seal wounds themselves, and a clean cut is better than a coating.

🧮

Chipping the prunings? Use the mulch calculator to see how many cubic yards of chips your beds can absorb at 3 inches deep.

How much can you prune at once?

The International Society of Arboriculture advises that no more than about one quarter of a tree's live crown should be removed in a single season; for mature trees, a lower amount is safer. Removing more triggers a flush of weak, fast-growing shoots called water sprouts.

Shrubs differ. Some tolerate rejuvenation pruning: cutting a third of the oldest stems to the ground each year for three years renews dogwoods, spirea and many other multi-stemmed shrubs without losing all their flowers. Hard cuts to 6–12 inches suit butterfly bush and similar plants that bloom on new growth.

What tools do you need for winter pruning?

ToolCuts up toBest for
Bypass hand prunersAbout ¾ inSmall stems, fruit canes, roses
LoppersAbout 1½–2 inShrub stems, tough canes
Pruning saw2 in and largerTree limbs
Pole prunerUp to about 1–2 in, overheadHigh branches without a ladder

Use bypass tools (blades that slide past each other) rather than anvil tools, which crush stems. Sharp blades make clean cuts that heal faster. If you are cutting out diseased wood, wipe the blades with 70% rubbing alcohol between cuts so you do not spread the problem.

Stay away from power lines and hire a pro for big limbs. Trees with branches near utility lines or limbs thicker than about 4–6 inches overhead are a job for a certified arborist. Falling limbs injure people every year.

6 winter pruning mistakes to avoid

  1. Pruning spring bloomers in winter. You'll cut off this year's flowers.
  2. Topping trees. Cutting main branches to stubs weakens the tree and leads to weak regrowth.
  3. "Volcano" pruning of crape myrtle. Cutting to thick knuckles every year is unnecessary; remove only crossing limbs and small twigs.
  4. Pruning in a deep freeze. Wood is brittle and cuts can split; wait for a mild day.
  5. Leaving stubs or cutting flush. Both slow healing; cut just outside the branch collar.
  6. Using dull or dirty tools. They tear bark and spread disease.

How do you prune an apple tree in winter?

Apple and pear trees are the classic dormant-pruning job. Aim for an open center that lets light reach every branch, because fruit ripens and colors best in sunlight.

  1. Remove dead, broken and diseased wood.
  2. Cut out water sprouts, the fast vertical shoots that grow from branches, and suckers at the base.
  3. Thin one of any two branches that cross or rub.
  4. Shorten branches that hang low enough to touch the ground.
  5. Step back often. You can always take more off next year, but you can't put a branch back.

Young trees need training more than pruning, so remove only what is necessary during the first few years and let the tree build a strong frame.

Frequently asked questions

What month is best for winter pruning?

February to March is best for most dormant pruning, a few weeks before buds swell. In warm climates, January works; in cold climates, wait until the hardest freezes are over.

Can I prune trees when it is below freezing?

You can, but wood is brittle in deep cold and tender plants may suffer dieback. Choose a mild day when temperatures are above about 20°F if you must prune in the cold.

Which shrubs should never be pruned in winter?

Spring-flowering shrubs such as lilac, forsythia, azalea, rhododendron and bigleaf hydrangea have their flower buds formed by winter, so wait until after they bloom.

Should I seal pruning cuts with paint?

No. Extension services generally advise against wound dressings, because trees compartmentalize wounds on their own and the coating can trap moisture.

Is it too late to prune once buds break?

For many trees and shrubs, light pruning after buds open is fine, but heavy pruning at that stage wastes stored energy. Fruit trees do best if pruned before bud break.

Can I prune roses in winter?

Do major pruning of hybrid tea and floribunda roses in late winter to early spring as buds swell. In fall and early winter, trim only long canes that could whip in the wind.

The bottom line

Prune dormant fruit trees, shade trees, grapes, roses and summer-blooming shrubs in late winter, and leave spring bloomers until after they flower. Remove the three Ds first, take no more than a quarter of the crown and make clean cuts. Chip the prunings and use the mulch calculator to plan where they go.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Pruning timing and technique from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and Penn State Extension; the one-quarter crown guideline and cut placement from the International Society of Arboriculture (TreesAreGood.org); oak wilt timing from state forestry and extension guidance. Timing varies by USDA zone. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Winter Houseplant Care: Light, Water and Humidity Fixes
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

In winter, give houseplants more light, less water and no fertilizer. Move plants to the brightest window, water only when the top 1–2 inches of soil are dry, keep them away from heaters and cold glass, and aim for 40–50% humidity and 65–75°F. Growth slows in low light, so most plants need far less care.

Houseplants are tropical or subtropical plants kept in rooms that are dry, drafty and dim in winter. The usual winter problems, such as yellow leaves, leaf drop, crispy brown tips and mushy stems, almost always come from three things: too little light, too much water and dry air.

This guide fixes each one in turn, with simple checks rather than fixed schedules. If you keep plants outdoors in summer, our planting calendar helps with bringing them in before frost.

Key takeaways
  • Light: winter sun is weaker and shorter; move plants closer to a south or west window.
  • Water: check the soil first; most plants need water less often in winter.
  • Humidity: heated homes often drop below 30%; aim for 40–50% for tropical plants.
  • Temperature: 65–75°F days and no colder than about 55–60°F nights for most tropicals.
  • Feeding: pause or cut back fertilizer from late fall to late winter.

Why do houseplants struggle in winter?

Three changes hit at once. Day length shortens to nine or ten hours in the northern US, and the sun sits lower, so light through a window can be much weaker than in summer. Indoor heating dries the air, often to 20–30% relative humidity. And plants grow slowly, which means they use less water and nutrients, but many people keep watering and feeding on the summer schedule.

How much light do houseplants need in winter?

Light drops sharply with distance from the glass. A plant 3 feet from a window can receive far less light than one on the sill. Move plants closer in winter, and rotate pots a quarter turn weekly so growth stays even.

Window direction (Northern Hemisphere)Winter lightGood for
SouthBrightest, longestSucculents, cacti, citrus, jade, herbs
WestBright afternoon sunMost foliage plants; fiddle-leaf fig, rubber plant
EastGentle morning lightPothos, philodendron, peace lily, ferns
NorthDimmestSnake plant, ZZ plant, cast iron plant

If a room is too dark, add a full-spectrum LED grow light 6–12 inches above the plants for roughly 10–14 hours a day on a timer. Low-light tolerant plants such as snake plant and ZZ plant survive on very little; sun lovers do not.

Wipe dust off leaves with a damp cloth every month or two. A film of dust blocks light that is already scarce.

How often should you water houseplants in winter?

Water when the plant needs it, not on a calendar. Slow growth and cooler rooms mean soil stays wet longer, and overwatering is the leading cause of death for houseplants.

The finger test

Push a finger 1–2 inches into the potting mix. For most foliage plants, water when it feels dry at that depth. For succulents and cacti, let the whole pot dry out. For ferns and peace lilies, water when the top inch is dry.

How to water

  1. Use room-temperature water; cold water from a tap can shock roots.
  2. Water slowly until it runs out the drainage holes.
  3. Empty the saucer after 15–30 minutes so roots do not sit in water.
  4. Water in the morning so the pot dries during the day.
Yellow leaves and soft, dark stems usually mean overwatering, not underwatering. If the soil smells sour or the pot feels heavy days after watering, let it dry out, and repot into fresh mix if roots look brown and mushy.

How do you raise humidity for houseplants?

Most common houseplants, such as pothos and spider plants, tolerate average home humidity. Tropicals like calathea, ferns and orchids prefer 40–60%. Brown leaf tips and edges are a classic sign of dry air.

  • Group plants together. Transpiration raises humidity around them slightly.
  • Use a humidifier. It is the only method that raises room humidity measurably. A cheap hygrometer shows the level.
  • Pebble trays (a tray of wet stones under the pot, with the pot above the water line) help a little in the immediate area.
  • Skip misting. It raises humidity for minutes and can promote leaf spots.
  • Move plants out of bathrooms with no windows or kitchens with no light; humidity doesn't replace light.
🧮

Planning to repot or move plants to bigger containers? Use the soil calculator to work out potting-mix volume, and the garden calculator hub for other planning tools.

What temperature do houseplants need in winter?

Most tropical houseplants do well at 65–75°F in the day and cooler at night, but not below about 55–60°F. Cold-sensitive plants such as African violets, orchids and calatheas suffer below 60°F. Cactus and some succulents tolerate cooler rooms of 50–55°F, and a cool winter rest helps Christmas cactus bloom.

  • Keep plants off cold windowsills at night. Glass can be many degrees colder than the room. Pull pots back or slide a sheet of cardboard between pot and glass.
  • Keep away from heat vents, radiators and fireplaces, which dry plants and scorch leaves.
  • Avoid drafts from exterior doors that open repeatedly in winter.

Should you fertilize or repot in winter?

Generally, no. Plants growing slowly in low light cannot use fertilizer, and salts build up in the soil and burn roots. Stop feeding from about late fall (October or November) and restart in spring when new growth appears, at the label rate. Plants under grow lights that are actively growing can be fed at half strength.

Repotting is also better in spring. Do it in winter only if the plant is root-bound and struggling, or if you must replace soggy mix.

How do you prevent pests in winter?

Dry indoor air favors spider mites; overwatering favors fungus gnats and mealybugs.

  • Inspect leaf undersides every couple of weeks for webbing, stippling or small white cottony spots.
  • Isolate infested plants and rinse them in the shower, then use insecticidal soap per the label.
  • For fungus gnats, let the top inch of soil dry and use yellow sticky traps.
  • Quarantine plants that spent summer outdoors for two weeks before putting them with others.

6 winter houseplant mistakes

  1. Watering on a schedule. Check the soil instead.
  2. Leaving plants behind curtains or on cold sills. Cold glass and dim light slow growth.
  3. Placing plants near heaters. They dry quickly and scorch.
  4. Feeding all winter. Salt build-up burns roots.
  5. Moving plants constantly. Frequent moves cause leaf drop.
  6. Misting instead of fixing humidity. The effect disappears in minutes.

Which houseplants are easiest in winter?

Some plants shrug off low light and dry air, which makes them good choices if you want fewer problems.

  • Snake plant and ZZ plant: tolerate dim rooms and very infrequent watering.
  • Pothos and philodendron: forgiving, and quick to recover from a missed watering.
  • Spider plant and cast iron plant: handle average indoor humidity and cooler rooms.
  • Jade and aloe: need bright light but very little water in winter.

The fussiest are calathea, ferns, fiddle-leaf fig and orchids, which dislike drafts, dry air and sudden changes. Give them the best spot you have or accept a few lost leaves until spring.

How do you move plants safely in and out of winter conditions?

If your plants spent summer outdoors, bring them inside before nights fall below about 50°F, rinse the leaves, check for pests and give them a week or two to adjust to lower light. They will likely drop some leaves as they adapt; this is normal. In spring, reverse the process gradually, moving plants to shade first and into brighter light over a week or two to prevent sunburn.

Frequently asked questions

Why are my houseplant leaves turning yellow in winter?

The most common causes are overwatering, low light and cold drafts. Check the soil moisture first, then move the plant to a brighter, warmer spot. A few lower leaves yellowing is normal as plants slow down.

Do houseplants need less water in winter?

Usually yes. Slower growth and cooler, darker rooms mean the soil takes longer to dry. Water only when the top 1–2 inches are dry.

Is it OK to put houseplants outside in winter?

No, not in most of the US. Tropical houseplants are damaged below about 50°F and killed by frost, so keep them indoors until all danger of frost has passed.

Do I need a grow light for houseplants in winter?

Not for low-light plants, but sun-loving species such as succulents, citrus and herbs benefit from an LED grow light on a timer when natural light is weak.

When should I start fertilizing houseplants again?

Restart in spring, around March or April, once you see new leaves and growth and days are longer. Use the label rate or half strength to begin.

The bottom line

Winter houseplant care is about doing less, in the right places: move plants to light, water by checking the soil, add humidity where plants need it and hold the fertilizer until spring. For potting-mix volumes when you repot, use the soil calculator.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Planting Calendar · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Houseplant light, watering, humidity and temperature guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; ranges are general and vary by species. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Spring Garden Checklist: Month-by-Month To-Do List
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Spring garden work follows soil temperature and your last frost date, not the calendar. In early spring, clean up, test soil and sow peas and spinach as soon as soil can be worked. Plant tomatoes and peppers only after the last frost, when nights stay above 50°F, and start crabgrass prevention when soil reaches about 55°F.

Spring arrives at different times across the US, so a checklist tied to dates only works for one region. This one is tied to triggers you can measure: the soil is workable, the last frost has passed, the soil is warm enough for a given crop.

Use it as a template. Find your average last frost with our frost dates by ZIP code tool, and get crop-by-crop sowing windows from the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Soil workable: squeeze a handful; if it crumbles instead of staying in a wet ball, you can dig.
  • Cool-season crops (peas, spinach, lettuce, radish) go in 4–6 weeks before the last frost, when soil is roughly 40°F or above.
  • Warm-season crops (tomato, pepper, cucumber, squash) wait until after the last frost and soil near 60°F or warmer.
  • Crabgrass preventer goes down when soil temperature reaches about 55°F for several days.
  • Mulch after the soil warms, 2–3 inches deep.

What should you do first in early spring (February to April)?

Early spring is cleanup and prep. You are waiting for soil to thaw and dry, so focus on jobs that don't need warm ground.

  1. Clear winter debris from beds, but wait for steady 50°F days before removing leaf litter and stems where beneficial insects may still be sheltering.
  2. Cut back ornamental grasses and last year's perennial stems before new growth appears.
  3. Test your soil (pH and nutrients) before you fertilize or lime. See our guide to calculating soil and amendment volumes.
  4. Prune summer-flowering shrubs and roses; leave lilac and forsythia until they finish blooming.
  5. Sharpen and clean tools, and check hoses and irrigation for winter damage.
  6. Start seeds indoors for tomatoes, peppers and other warm-season crops about 6–8 weeks before the last frost.

When is the soil ready to work?

Digging wet soil in spring creates hard clods that last all season. Use the squeeze test: grab a handful from 4 inches down and squeeze. If it forms a ball that holds together when you poke it, it's too wet. If it crumbles, go ahead. A soil thermometer pushed 2 inches deep in the morning tells you which crops can go in.

CropMinimum soil temp to sowWhen (relative to average last frost)
Peas, spinachAbout 40°F4–6 weeks before
Lettuce, radish, kaleAbout 40–45°F3–5 weeks before
Carrot, beet, potatoAbout 45°F2–4 weeks before
Tomato, pepper transplantsSoil about 60°F; nights above 50°F1–2 weeks after
Beans, cornAbout 60°FAt or 1–2 weeks after
Cucumber, squash, melonAbout 65–70°F1–3 weeks after

These are general ranges from extension sources; variety and local weather matter, so check seed packets.

🧮

Want exact sowing and transplant dates for your area? Use the planting calendar and enter your ZIP code to get dates for each crop.

What should you do in mid spring (March to May)?

Mid spring is the main planting window for most of the country, usually from a few weeks before to about the last frost.

  • Add compost to beds: 1–2 inches, worked into the top few inches or spread on the surface. A 4×8 bed takes 2.7–5.3 cubic feet.
  • Direct-sow cool-season crops and succession-plant lettuce and radish every two weeks.
  • Harden off seedlings over 7–10 days by putting them outdoors for a few hours more each day.
  • Divide perennials such as hostas and daylilies as shoots emerge.
  • Feed the lawn if your grass is cool-season and the soil is above about 55°F; warm-season lawns wait until they have fully greened up.
  • Apply pre-emergent crabgrass control when soil is about 55°F for several days (forsythia bloom is a traditional signal); skip it where you plan to overseed.

What should you do in late spring (April to June)?

After the last frost date, switch to warm-season crops and mulch.

  1. Transplant tomatoes, peppers and eggplant once nights stay above 50°F.
  2. Sow beans, corn, cucumbers, squash and melons when soil reaches 60–70°F depending on the crop.
  3. Mulch with 2–3 inches of straw, shredded leaves or bark once the soil has warmed. Mulching cold soil keeps it cold.
  4. Set up trellises and cages before plants need them, so you don't damage roots later.
  5. Water deeply but less often, about 1 inch of water per week including rain for most vegetable gardens.
  6. Watch for pests such as aphids and cutworms; protect transplants with collars of cardboard or foil around stems.

How much mulch and compost do you need?

BedCompost, 2 inMulch, 3 in
4 × 8 ft raised bed (32 sq ft)5.33 cu ft8 cu ft
100 sq ft vegetable garden16.7 cu ft (0.62 cu yd)25 cu ft (0.93 cu yd)
200 sq ft flower border33.3 cu ft (1.23 cu yd)50 cu ft (1.85 cu yd)

The numbers come from square feet × inches deep ÷ 12 = cubic feet, and cubic feet ÷ 27 = cubic yards. For multiple beds, the mulch calculator does the sums.

Don't plant warm-season crops just because the days feel warm. A single cold night after the last average frost date can still kill tomatoes. Check the 10-day forecast and keep frost cloth ready until nights are reliably above 40–45°F.

Spring lawn and tree checklist

  • Rake matted leaves and dead grass gently; save heavy dethatching for later.
  • Overseed bare patches of cool-season lawn in early spring if soil is above about 50°F, or wait until fall for best results.
  • Mow at the recommended height for your grass; avoid removing more than one-third of the blade at once.
  • Mulch trees in a wide ring, 2–3 inches deep and pulled back from the trunk.
  • Check for winter damage on shrubs and wait for new growth before cutting back dead-looking stems.

Spring gardening mistakes to avoid

  1. Planting by date, not conditions. A warm week in March doesn't change your frost risk.
  2. Working wet soil. It compacts and dries into clods.
  3. Skipping hardening off. Indoor seedlings can sunburn or wilt within hours.
  4. Over-fertilizing. Lush growth attracts pests; use a soil test.
  5. Buying everything at once. Plants for cool-season and warm-season crops need different dates.

When is spring where you live?

Months in the headings above are rough, because spring moves north by about 10–15 miles a day. Use your average last frost date as the anchor and shift the checklist earlier or later.

Region (USDA zones)Typical average last frostFirst big planting window
Southern states (zones 8–10)Late February to early AprilFebruary–April
Mid-Atlantic, lower Midwest (zones 6–7)Mid-April to early MayLate March–May
Northern states (zones 4–5)Mid-May to early JuneLate April–June

Treat these as general ranges and look up the exact date for your area before you buy plants.

How do you keep a spring garden plan simple?

Write your average last frost date at the top of a page, then list each crop with a sow or transplant date counted from it. Add the date you will harden off seedlings and the date you plan to mulch. Keeping the plan on one page makes it easy to adjust when a late cold snap or a warm spell changes the timing, and it gives you something to compare against next year.

Take notes as you go: which varieties did well, what you planted too early and how long the soil took to dry out. A season of notes is worth more than any generic calendar.

Frequently asked questions

What should I do in the garden first in spring?

Start with cleanup, a soil test and sharpening tools while the ground is still cold. Sow peas and spinach as soon as the soil is workable.

How do I know when it is safe to plant outside?

For cool-season crops, the soil must be workable and above about 40°F. For tomatoes and peppers, wait until after your average last frost and until nights stay above 50°F.

When should I put down crabgrass preventer?

Apply it when soil temperature at 2 inches deep reaches about 55°F for several consecutive days, typically before forsythia drops its blooms.

Should I fertilize my garden beds in spring?

Add compost every spring and use a soil test to guide any extra fertilizer. Heavy-feeding crops like tomatoes and squash benefit from a balanced fertilizer at planting.

How often should I water new spring plantings?

Keep seeds evenly moist until they sprout; for transplants, water deeply once or twice a week so roots grow down, adjusting for rain.

The bottom line

Match each job to a trigger: workable soil, the last frost, or a soil temperature. Clean up and test early, sow cool-season crops first, then plant warm-season crops after frost and mulch once the ground has warmed. Check your dates with the planting calendar and plan quantities with the mulch calculator.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Lawn Fertilizer Calculator

Sources: Spring planting, soil temperature and lawn guidance from US university extension services, including Cornell Cooperative Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and Penn State Extension; frost date data from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Volume math: cubic feet = square feet × depth (in) ÷ 12; 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Winterize Raised Garden Beds: A Simple Fall Routine
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To winterize raised beds, clear spent plants, top up with 2 inches of compost, then cover the soil. Use 2–4 inches of shredded leaves or straw, a cover crop, or fall-planted garlic so the surface is never bare. Check the wood frame and drain hoses. A 4×8 bed needs about 5⅓ cubic feet of compost for a 2-inch layer.

Raised beds drain fast and warm early in spring, which also means they lose organic matter and nutrients faster when left bare in winter. Rain compacts exposed soil, weeds sprout in any gap and freeze-thaw cycles break down soil structure. A little work in fall gives you a bed that is ready to plant as soon as the soil thaws.

This routine takes about an hour per bed. If you are not sure how much material to buy, the soil calculator converts bed dimensions to cubic feet, cubic yards and bags in seconds.

Key takeaways
  • Never leave soil bare: cover it with mulch, a cover crop or a crop such as garlic.
  • Top-dress with compost: 2 inches adds 5.33 cu ft to a 4×8 bed, 2.67 cu ft to a 4×4 bed.
  • Mulch depth: 2–4 inches of shredded leaves or straw; 4 inches on a 4×8 bed is 10.67 cu ft.
  • Don't till or dig: turning frozen or wet soil damages structure; add material to the top instead.
  • Check the frame: tighten screws, replace rotted boards and clear gaps before ice forms.

When should you winterize raised garden beds?

Start after your main crops are finished and ideally four to six weeks before the ground freezes. That gives a cover crop time to establish and garlic time to root. In the northern US that means September to October; in zones 7–8, October to November. Use our frost dates by ZIP code tool to find your first fall frost, then count back.

What are the steps to winterize a raised bed?

Step 1: Clear spent plants and debris

Pull annuals and remove fallen fruit. Toss diseased material in the trash rather than a cool compost pile. For beans and peas, cut the tops and leave the roots in the soil to decompose.

Step 2: Pull weeds and harvest what's left

Weeds that set seed in fall create a carpet of seedlings in spring. Remove them now, and pick the last green tomatoes before frost. Root crops such as carrots and parsnips can stay under mulch and be harvested as needed.

Step 3: Check the soil level and top up

Raised-bed soil settles over a season as organic matter breaks down. If the surface has dropped, fill it back up with compost or a bed mix. As a rule, top-dress with 1–2 inches of compost each fall.

Bed sizeCompost, 1 inCompost, 2 inMulch, 4 in
4 × 4 ft (16 sq ft)1.33 cu ft2.67 cu ft5.33 cu ft
3 × 6 ft (18 sq ft)1.5 cu ft3 cu ft6 cu ft
4 × 8 ft (32 sq ft)2.67 cu ft5.33 cu ft10.67 cu ft
Three 4 × 8 ft beds8 cu ft16 cu ft (0.59 cu yd)32 cu ft (1.19 cu yd)

Cubic feet = square feet × depth in inches ÷ 12. A bag of compost is typically 1 or 2 cubic feet, so a 4×8 bed's 5.33 cubic feet means about three 2-cu-ft bags.

🧮

Have several beds or an unusual size? Use the soil calculator to total up compost and soil for every bed, including bags versus bulk.

Step 4: Cover the soil

Choose one of these three options. Bare soil is the one thing to avoid.

  • Mulch: spread 2–4 inches of shredded leaves, straw or other weed-free organic mulch. It insulates, suppresses weeds and feeds worms. Keep it a couple of inches away from any plants that are still growing.
  • Cover crop: sow winter rye, oats or crimson clover in early fall to hold the soil and add organic matter; chop and turn under or cut and leave in spring.
  • Winter crops: garlic, kale and spinach all overwinter in many zones; garlic goes in about 2–4 weeks before the ground freezes.

Step 5: Add protection for tender crops (optional)

Low tunnels with hoops and row cover extend greens and carrots into winter in zones 5 and warmer. A heavier cover or a cold frame adds more protection. For hardy crops, row cover also keeps leaves clean and cuts moisture swings.

How do you care for the wood frame in winter?

Winter moisture, snow and freeze-thaw cycles are tough on frames. A 10-minute inspection avoids spring repairs.

  • Tighten loose screws and corner brackets; swelling wood can pop joints.
  • Replace boards that are soft or crumbly when you press a screwdriver into them.
  • Remove soil or mulch piled against any wood above the soil line, which holds moisture.
  • Leave untreated cedar, redwood and composite beds unsealed; they weather naturally.
  • Check for a gap between the bed and the ground where mice may nest, and fill it with gravel or hardware cloth.
Don't dig or walk on wet or frozen beds. Compaction in winter pushes air out of the soil and takes weeks to recover. Work from the paths and leave the surface to settle.

Should you amend raised bed soil in fall or spring?

Do both, with different materials. In fall add slow-to-break-down organic matter: compost, shredded leaves, aged manure. In spring, add fast-acting nutrients based on a soil test, because nitrogen from fertilizer applied in fall can wash out of a well-drained bed before plants can use it. See our guide to what soil volume each raised bed needs before you order material.

Can you plant in raised beds over winter?

Yes, with the right crops. Garlic is planted in fall and harvested the following summer. Spinach, kale, mâche and some lettuces survive under row cover in cold climates, and carrots and beets sown in late summer can be left in the ground under mulch. In zones 8–10, cool-season vegetables grow all winter.

5 raised-bed winterizing mistakes

  1. Leaving soil bare. Rain compacts it and washes nutrients out.
  2. Tilling or digging deeply. It damages soil structure and brings up weed seeds.
  3. Mulching with whole oak leaves in a thick mat. They can pack together; shred them first.
  4. Using weedy straw or hay. Make sure the mulch is seed-free.
  5. Ignoring the frame. A small repair now saves replacing a board in spring.

What about raised beds in cold-winter regions?

In zones 3–5, soil in raised beds can freeze solid from November until March. That is normal and not a problem for a bed covered in mulch. Snow is a good insulator, so don't shovel it off the beds; pile it on instead. In zones 6–7, soil freezes and thaws repeatedly, so a thick mulch layer helps keep the temperature steady and prevents heaving of shallow-rooted plants and garlic. In zones 8–10, winter is a growing season for greens, peas and brassicas, and the main job is replacing nutrients with compost between crops.

Whatever your climate, the principle is the same: protect the soil surface, add organic matter and leave the soil structure alone.

What should you do with compost and tools at the end of the season?

Fall is also the best time to build your next year's supply. Pile shredded leaves and spent plant material in a bin so it can break down over winter, and you'll have free compost by spring. Empty and clean any watering cans, drain drip lines and bring in trellis netting, plant labels and cages so they do not weather. A quick note on what grew where helps you rotate crop families next year, which reduces disease and pest buildup in the same soil.

Frequently asked questions

Should I cover raised beds in winter?

Yes. A cover of mulch, a cover crop or winter vegetables protects the soil from erosion and compaction, prevents weeds and adds organic matter. A tarp also works but must be removed in spring.

Can I leave dead plants in my raised bed over winter?

Healthy plants can stay as a natural mulch, but remove diseased ones, since they can carry problems into next season. Chop and leave bean and pea roots in the soil.

Is it OK to put leaves in raised beds?

Yes. Shredded leaves are a free source of organic matter. Spread them 2–4 inches thick, or let them break down into the soil over winter.

Do raised beds freeze solid?

Raised beds freeze more deeply than in-ground soil because they are exposed on the sides. Mulch, snow cover and a thick layer of organic matter reduce how fast and how deep the freezing goes.

How much compost should I add to a raised bed in fall?

One to two inches is typical. That is 2.67–5.33 cubic feet for a 4×8 bed.

The bottom line

Clear the bed, top up with 1–2 inches of compost, cover the surface with mulch, a cover crop or garlic and give the frame a quick check. Use the soil calculator to buy the right amount, then let winter do its work.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Planting Calendar · Plant Spacing Calculator

Sources: Raised bed, cover crop and winter mulching guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Oregon State University Extension and Colorado State University Extension; frost date data from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Volume math: cubic feet = square feet × depth (in) ÷ 12. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Test Soil pH at Home (and Fix It)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The most accurate way to test soil pH is a lab test through your state's extension service, which usually costs a modest fee and returns pH plus lime or sulfur recommendations. Home kits and meters give a rough reading. Most vegetables and lawns grow best at a pH of 6.0 to 7.0.

Soil pH controls whether plants can actually take up the nutrients that are already in your soil. If it is too acidic or too alkaline, fertilizer is wasted and plants show yellow leaves and poor growth, even when you water and feed them correctly. Testing is cheap, and it prevents the single most common guess in gardening: adding lime or sulfur you don't need.

This guide compares the ways to test, shows you how to take a sample that gives a true reading and explains how to raise or lower pH. When you're ready to add amendments to a raised bed, the soil calculator shows how much material your bed holds.

Key takeaways
  • Target: pH 6.0–7.0 suits most vegetables, flowers and lawns.
  • The scale is logarithmic: pH 5.5 is 10 times more acidic than pH 6.5, and pH 5.0 is 100 times more acidic than 7.0.
  • Best test: a university or state extension lab, which also gives amendment rates.
  • Sample: mix 5–10 spots, 4–6 inches deep for gardens, per area, and air-dry before sending.
  • Changing pH is slow: lime and sulfur take weeks to months; retest in 3–6 months.

What does soil pH mean?

Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14. A reading of 7.0 is neutral, below 7.0 is acidic and above 7.0 is alkaline. Most garden soils fall between 5.0 and 8.0, and the pH tends to reflect the local rainfall and rock: wetter regions such as the Northeast and Southeast are often acidic, while drier western areas are often alkaline.

The reason pH matters is nutrient availability. In strongly acidic soil, phosphorus and calcium are less available and aluminum can reach toxic levels. In alkaline soil, iron, manganese and zinc are tied up, so plants like blueberries and azaleas show yellow leaves with green veins (iron chlorosis).

What is the ideal soil pH for vegetables, lawns and flowers?

PlantPreferred pH
Most vegetables (tomato, pepper, beans, carrot, lettuce)6.0–7.0
Potatoes5.0–6.0 (more acidic helps limit scab)
Blueberries4.5–5.5
Azalea, rhododendron, camellia5.0–6.0
Cool-season lawn grasses (Kentucky bluegrass, fescue)6.0–7.0
Warm-season lawns (Bermuda, zoysia)5.8–7.0
Lavender, clematis6.5–8.0

Ranges vary slightly by source, so check your extension service for local figures.

How do you test soil pH at home?

Option 1: Send a sample to a lab (best)

State land-grant universities and many county extension offices run soil testing labs, typically for a modest fee. You mail a dry sample and get back pH, buffer pH, nutrient levels and recommendations in pounds of lime or sulfur per 1,000 sq ft for your crop. Commercial labs offer the same service.

Option 2: Color-change test kit

Kits use a chemical indicator and a color chart. They are inexpensive and good for a ballpark check, but colors are subjective, and results can be off by half a pH unit or more. Use distilled water as directed.

Option 3: Digital probe meter

Probe meters are quick but vary in quality and often need frequent calibration. Treat them as a screening tool and confirm unexpected readings with a lab.

The vinegar and baking soda test

Fizzing when vinegar is added suggests alkaline soil, and fizzing with baking soda and water suggests acid soil. This only sorts soil roughly into groups. It gives no number and cannot guide how much to apply.

MethodAccuracyGives amendment rates?Best for
Extension / lab testHighYesNew gardens, problem areas, before liming
Color kitModerateNoQuick check, yearly monitoring
Digital probeVariableNoScreening several beds
Vinegar / baking sodaVery lowNoCuriosity only
🧮

Working out amendments for a raised bed? Use the soil calculator to find your bed volume in cubic feet, then match lab recommendations to your actual area.

How do you take a soil sample for a pH test?

  1. Use clean tools. A stainless steel trowel and a plastic bucket avoid contamination from rust or fertilizer.
  2. Pick 5–10 spots across the area you want to test, such as a vegetable bed or the front lawn. Treat areas that differ (lawn vs vegetable bed) as separate samples.
  3. Dig to the right depth. Take a thin slice 4–6 inches deep in gardens, and 2–4 inches deep in lawns. Remove surface mulch and leaves first.
  4. Mix the cores together in the bucket, breaking up clods.
  5. Dry the sample on a clean sheet of paper at room temperature; don't use heat.
  6. Fill the lab bag or box as instructed, and note the crop you plan to grow.

Avoid sampling right after liming or fertilizing, when soil is very wet, or in the first few weeks after a heavy compost application, since those can skew readings.

How do you raise soil pH?

To make soil less acidic, add ground agricultural limestone (calcium carbonate). If a lab test also shows low magnesium, dolomitic limestone supplies both calcium and magnesium. Wood ash also raises pH but is variable and should be used sparingly.

  • Rate: depends on your soil texture and how far you need to move the pH. Clay and high-organic soils resist change and need more than sandy soils. Follow your lab report, which gives pounds per 1,000 sq ft.
  • Timing: apply in fall or early spring so rain can carry it into the soil, and work it into the top 4–6 inches in a bed.
  • Speed: expect noticeable change in 3–6 months, with full effect in a year; finer powders work faster than pelletized lime.

How do you lower soil pH?

To make soil more acidic, use elemental sulfur. Soil bacteria convert it to sulfuric acid, so it takes weeks to months and works faster in warm, moist soil. Rates are small and depend on soil type; follow the lab recommendation. Aluminum sulfate works faster but can add aluminum and harm plants if overused.

For small changes, adding peat moss, pine needles or acidifying fertilizers like ammonium sulfate helps slightly, but they will not shift a strongly alkaline soil. In very alkaline or chalky soils (common in parts of the Southwest and Midwest), growing acid-loving plants in containers or raised beds with purchased mix is often more practical than trying to rebuild the whole yard.

Don't add lime or sulfur without a test. It is easy to overcorrect, and a pH swing of one unit is a tenfold change in acidity. Overliming is difficult to undo and can lock up iron and zinc.

How often should you test soil pH?

Test every 2–3 years for established beds and annually while you are correcting a problem. Retest 3–6 months after liming or adding sulfur. Test any new site before building beds, and take separate samples if the front and back yards differ.

Common soil pH testing mistakes

  1. Sampling one spot. Soil varies across a yard; mix several.
  2. Using tap water in a kit. Hard water changes the result; use distilled water.
  3. Testing mulch or compost. Sample the soil below.
  4. Adding amendments before testing. You can push pH the wrong way.
  5. Expecting instant results. pH changes take months.

Why does my soil pH matter for fertilizer?

Fertilizer works best inside the right pH range. In soil that is too acidic or alkaline, applied nutrients are locked up in forms roots can't absorb, and the unused fertilizer can wash into drains. A lawn at pH 5.0, for example, may respond poorly to nitrogen until lime brings it up, and an alkaline bed may need iron chelate for acid-loving plants. Fixing pH first often saves money. If you also plan to feed your lawn, our lawn fertilizer calculator works out the amount once your soil is in range.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good pH for a vegetable garden?

A pH of 6.0–7.0 suits most vegetables. Potatoes tolerate and prefer slightly more acidic soil, 5.0–6.0, and blueberries need 4.5–5.5.

Are home soil pH test kits accurate?

They are good for a rough range but can be off by half a unit or more because colors are hard to read. For decisions about lime or sulfur, use a lab test.

Where can I get a soil test near me?

Your state's cooperative extension service or land-grant university usually offers soil testing by mail for a modest fee. Search for your state's name plus "extension soil test."

Do coffee grounds or vinegar change soil pH?

Not significantly. Used coffee grounds are close to neutral and a vinegar solution changes pH only briefly. Use sulfur for lasting acidification.

Can I test soil pH in winter?

Yes, if the ground isn't frozen. A sample taken from thawed soil gives a correct reading, and fall testing leaves time to apply lime before spring planting.

The bottom line

Take a mixed sample, send it to an extension lab, and follow its recommendation instead of guessing. Aim for pH 6.0–7.0 for most plants, change it slowly and retest in a few months. When your plan calls for new soil or amendments, use the soil calculator to size the job.

Related tools: Lawn Fertilizer Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Soil pH, sampling and liming guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension, Oregon State University Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; crop pH ranges are general extension figures and vary slightly by source. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Protect Plants from Frost: Fast Fixes That Work
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To protect plants from frost, cover them before sunset when the forecast is 32°F or lower. Use frost cloth, a sheet or buckets, keep covers touching the ground to trap soil heat, and water the soil first. Remove covers in the morning once the temperature rises above freezing.

A frost warning on a spring evening, or an early cold snap in fall, can wipe out a season's tomatoes and peppers in a single night. The good news is that most frost damage is preventable with covers you already own and about ten minutes of work.

This guide covers the temperatures that actually hurt each type of plant, the covers that work (and the ones that don't), what to do on the night, and how to rescue plants that were hit. To see when your area's frost normally arrives, use our frost dates by ZIP code tool.

Key takeaways
  • Frost vs freeze: frost forms at air temperatures near 32°F, while a hard freeze at 28°F or below kills most tender plants.
  • Timing: cover in the late afternoon, before the soil's stored heat escapes.
  • Gain: a typical row cover adds roughly 2–8°F depending on its weight; a bedsheet adds a few degrees.
  • Never: let plastic touch the leaves, or leave covers on in full sun.
  • Hardy crops such as kale, spinach and garlic can handle temperatures well below 32°F.

What temperature is frost, and when does it damage plants?

Frost happens when air near the ground cools to about 32°F (0°C) and moisture freezes on surfaces. Leaves can freeze even when the weather station reports 34–36°F, because clear, still nights cool the ground faster than the air a few feet up.

The National Weather Service uses three terms:

  • Frost advisory: temperatures roughly 33–36°F with clear, calm conditions.
  • Freeze warning: temperatures expected at 32°F or below, during the growing season.
  • Hard freeze: temperatures at or below about 28°F for several hours, which kills most tender plants.

Which plants need frost protection?

Different plants tolerate different lows. Extension services group vegetables by cold hardiness; temperatures below are the approximate lows at which damage begins.

GroupExamplesDamage begins around
TenderTomato, pepper, basil, cucumber, squash, beans, eggplant32°F or slightly above (cold-sensitive below 50°F)
Semi-hardyLettuce, broccoli, cabbage, potato tops, beetAbout 28–32°F
HardyCarrot, cauliflower, peas, onion, radishAbout 25–28°F
Very hardyKale, spinach, brussels sprouts, garlic, collardsOften below 20–25°F

For flowers and landscape plants, new spring growth and open blossoms are the most exposed. Fruit-tree blossoms, for example, can be damaged by temperatures just below 30°F, though the exact point depends on how far the bloom has progressed.

How do you protect plants from frost tonight?

Here is the sequence that works for most home gardens.

Step 1: Check the forecast low and the wind

Frost risk is highest on clear, calm, dry nights. Cloud cover and wind keep air mixed and warmer. If your forecast low is 34°F or colder and the sky is clear, cover.

Step 2: Water the soil in the afternoon

Moist soil holds more heat than dry soil and releases it overnight. Watering earlier in the day lets the water warm up and avoids leaving the foliage wet at night.

Step 3: Cover before sunset

Put covers on by late afternoon so they trap the heat the soil absorbed during the day. Drape fabric over plants, then lay it to the ground and weigh the edges with bricks, boards or soil. Gaps let warm air escape.

Step 4: Support the cover

Stakes, hoops, tomato cages or lawn chairs keep fabric from crushing leaves. The cover should reach to the ground all around.

Step 5: Uncover in the morning

Remove covers once the air is above freezing and the frost on the ground has melted, usually mid-morning. In full sun, covers can overheat plants quickly.

🧮

Not sure when your last or first frost falls? Check the garden calculator hub for planting and spacing tools, then look up your local dates before you buy plants or seed.

What are the best covers for frost protection?

CoverTypical gainNotes
Floating row cover, light (0.5 oz/sq yd)2–4°FLets in light; leave on for days
Floating row cover, heavy (1.5 oz/sq yd)6–8°FBlocks more light; remove in sun
Bedsheet, blanket, burlap2–5°FFree; remove daily
Cardboard box, bucket, flower pot2–4°FGood for single small plants
Cloche or milk jug with bottom cut off2–5°FRemove cap on warm days
Cold frame or hoop house5–10°FVent on sunny days

The gains in the table are rough ranges: the real number depends on wind, humidity and how well the cover seals to the ground. Row cover is sold by weight, and heavier fabrics give more protection but pass less light.

Plastic against leaves can do more harm than good. Clear plastic conducts cold, and any leaf that touches it can freeze. If you use plastic, keep it propped away from the foliage and vent it by morning, because it also overheats in sun.

Do string lights, water jugs and mulch really help?

  • Incandescent string lights: old-style bulbs give a small amount of heat under a cover. LED lights give almost none.
  • Water jugs: dark-colored gallon jugs filled with water absorb heat by day and release it at night, which can raise the temperature by a degree or two.
  • Mulch: a layer of straw or leaves protects roots of perennials and garlic. It will not protect leaves above the mulch from frost.
  • Sprinklers: commercial growers use water to protect fruit blossoms because freezing water releases heat. This requires continuous watering all night and can cause ice damage in a home garden, so it is not recommended for most gardeners.

What if frost already hit your plants?

  1. Don't prune right away. Frozen leaves can still shelter the lower parts of the plant. Wait until new growth shows where the damage ends.
  2. Check in a few days. Scratch a stem with a fingernail: green tissue underneath means it is alive.
  3. Water gently if the soil is dry; do not fertilize damaged plants until new leaves appear.
  4. Harvest. Pick green tomatoes and peppers before a hard freeze; green tomatoes will ripen indoors.

Mistakes that undo your frost protection

  1. Covering too late. If the evening air has already dropped, the soil heat has escaped.
  2. Leaving gaps at the ground. Warm air rises out of the cover.
  3. Planting out too early. Tender transplants should wait until after your average last frost date.
  4. Using wet covers. A soaked sheet can freeze solid.
  5. Ignoring pots. Roots in containers are more exposed than in-ground roots. Move pots against a wall or indoors.

How do you protect container plants and young trees?

Pots lose heat faster than in-ground plants because cold air surrounds the roots from every side. Move containers against a south-facing wall, under a porch eave or into a garage or unheated shed for the night. If a pot is too heavy to move, cluster it with others and wrap the pots with burlap or bubble wrap, then cover the plants themselves with fabric.

Young fruit trees and tender shrubs can be wrapped from the ground up with frost cloth, tied loosely at the top. Remove the wrap in the morning so the plant is not overheated by midday sun. For blossoms on fruit trees, cover on the nights when the forecast is below about 30°F, since open flowers are more sensitive than dormant buds.

Frequently asked questions

Will a frost kill my tomato plants?

A light frost at 32°F can blacken tomato leaves and kill young plants. Tomatoes are damaged by temperatures near freezing and are also stressed when nights fall below about 50°F, so cover them or wait until after the last frost to plant.

Is it too cold to leave plants uncovered at 40°F?

Usually not for the plants themselves, but clear, calm nights can let leaf temperatures drop below the forecast. If the forecast is 36°F or lower with no wind or clouds, cover tender plants.

Can I use a plastic tarp to cover plants?

You can for a night or two if it is held off the foliage on stakes or hoops and removed in the morning. Fabric is safer because it breathes and does not conduct cold to the leaves.

Do covered plants need watering before a freeze?

Yes. Moist soil stores and releases more heat than dry soil, so water in the afternoon before a frost night.

How long can I leave row cover on?

Light and medium row covers can stay on for days or weeks during cold weather because they let light and rain through. Remove them to allow pollination of crops such as squash, and vent them on sunny days.

The bottom line

Know your plants' limits, cover them before sunset with fabric that reaches the ground, and uncover them in the morning. Plan around your average frost dates and use the garden calculators to plan a layout you can cover easily.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Plant Spacing Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Frost, freeze and hard freeze definitions from the National Weather Service; vegetable cold-tolerance groupings from US university extension services, including Oregon State University Extension and Penn State Extension; frost date data from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Temperature gains from covers are approximate ranges. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: How to Kill Weeds Naturally Without Harming Your Garden
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The most reliable natural ways to kill weeds are pulling them while the soil is damp, smothering them with cardboard and 3 inches of mulch, and spot-treating with boiling water or flame. Household vinegar only burns leaves and rarely kills roots, and salt harms soil. Stopping seeds with mulch matters more than killing every weed.

Most gardeners want a weed-free bed without spraying chemicals near vegetables, pets or kids. The honest answer is that no natural method is as fast as a herbicide, but several are cheap, effective and safe if you use them in the right place and at the right time.

This guide ranks the options by how well they work, shows how to match the method to the weed and flags the popular home remedies that backfire. For mulch quantities, use the mulch calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Best long-term: 2–3 inches of mulch over cardboard or newspaper starves weeds of light.
  • Best for taproots (dandelion, dock): pull after rain with a weeding knife.
  • Boiling water and flame kill top growth on paths and cracks; perennials may regrow.
  • Household 5% vinegar burns leaves of young weeds but seldom kills roots.
  • Avoid salt: it sterilizes soil and washes into nearby beds.

What is the best natural weed killer?

There is no single best method because weeds differ. Annual weeds such as chickweed and crabgrass grow from seed each year and die when pulled or smothered. Perennial weeds such as bindweed, Canada thistle and quackgrass regrow from roots and need repeated effort. Use the table to match the tool to the job.

MethodBest forKills roots?Effort / cost
Hand-pulling or hori-hori knifeAnnuals, dandelion, small bedsYes, if root comes outTime; free
Mulch over cardboardLarge beds, new garden areasSmothers over a seasonModerate; low cost
Boiling waterDriveway cracks, paths, patiosOften not for deep rootsLow; free
Flame weederGravel, paths, young weedsNo (top growth)Tool cost; fire risk
Solarization (clear plastic)Large weedy areas in summerYes in the top few inchesPlastic; 4–8 weeks
Horticultural vinegar (20%)Young annual weeds on hardscapeSeldomHazardous to skin and eyes
Corn gluten mealPreventing seeds from sproutingNo (pre-emergent only)Moderate

How does pulling weeds work best?

Hand-pulling is the most effective natural method in beds, if you do it at the right time.

  1. Pull after rain or watering. Moist soil releases the root.
