  2. Get the whole taproot with a long, narrow knife or fishtail weeder. Broken roots of dandelion and dock regrow.
  3. Pull before seed set. One dandelion or purslane plant can make thousands of seeds.
  4. Pull little and often. Ten minutes twice a week beats a full Saturday every month.
  5. Bag seed heads. Don't compost weeds that are already going to seed.

How do you kill weeds with mulch and cardboard?

Sheet mulching smothers weeds by blocking light. It works well for starting a new bed or reclaiming an overgrown one without digging.

Step 1: Cut or mow the weeds low

Leave the clippings on the ground; they become part of the layer.

Step 2: Lay overlapping cardboard

Use plain brown cardboard with tape and staples removed, or 6–10 sheets of newspaper. Overlap edges by at least 6 inches so no light gets through. Wet it thoroughly.

Step 3: Cover with 3–4 inches of mulch

Use wood chips, shredded bark or compost. For a 100 sq ft bed at 3 inches deep you need 25 cubic feet, or 0.93 cubic yards. Add 10% for settling.

Step 4: Plant through the layer

Cut an X in the cardboard and plant. The cardboard breaks down in about 3–6 months, by which time most weeds beneath it have died.

🧮

Not sure how much mulch your weed-smothering layer needs? Use the mulch calculator to convert bed size and depth into cubic yards and bags.

Does boiling water kill weeds?

Yes, on contact. Pouring boiling water on weeds in sidewalk cracks, gravel paths and patios kills the leaves and the top of the root. Young annuals usually die; deep-rooted perennials often regrow and need repeat treatments. Use a kettle with a spout, pour slowly at the base and keep it away from desirable plants, since it kills whatever it touches. Take care to avoid burns.

Does vinegar kill weeds?

Partly. Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid. It burns leaves of small, young weeds in sunny, dry weather but rarely kills roots, so perennials grow back. Horticultural vinegar at 20% works better but is corrosive and can burn skin and eyes. If you use it, wear goggles and gloves, and follow the label. Extension specialists note that vinegar is non-selective and can damage lawn grass and nearby plants.

Don't use salt. Table salt or rock salt on weeds sterilizes the soil for years, washes into nearby beds and lawns and can kill trees whose roots extend under the treated area. It also harms soil structure.

Can you stop weeds before they sprout?

Preventing seeds from germinating is easier than killing weeds already growing.

  • Mulch 2–3 inches deep in beds. Light is what most weed seeds need.
  • Corn gluten meal is a natural pre-emergent. Iowa State University research found it can reduce germination of crabgrass and other annual weeds if applied at about 20 lb per 1,000 sq ft (0.32 oz per sq ft) before seeds sprout and kept from being washed away. It does nothing to established weeds and prevents grass seed from sprouting too, so don't use it where you are overseeding. For a 200 sq ft area that rate is 4 lb.
  • Dense plantings. Closely spaced plants shade the soil. Use the plant spacing calculator to choose spacing that closes the canopy quickly.
  • Avoid disturbing soil. Every time you dig, you bring buried weed seeds to the surface where they can germinate.
  • Edge beds so lawn grass doesn't creep in.

How do you kill weeds in a lawn naturally?

The strongest natural lawn weed control is a thick, healthy lawn. Mow at the tall end of the recommended height for your grass, water deeply and infrequently, fertilize on schedule and overseed thin patches in the right season. For existing weeds, hand-pull dandelions after rain and spot-treat a few weeds with a flame or boiling water only if you accept some risk to the grass around them. Corn gluten meal in early spring can reduce crabgrass, but results vary and it needs correct timing.

Mistakes that make weeds worse

  1. Tilling weedy ground. Cutting perennial roots into pieces creates more plants.
  2. Letting weeds flower. Seeds persist in soil for years.
  3. Mulching too thin. Less than 2 inches lets light through.
  4. Mulching over live perennials. Perennial weeds can push through; dig or smother them first.
  5. Spraying on windy days. Even natural herbicides burn plants you want.

How does solarization kill weeds?

Soil solarization uses the sun to cook weeds and seeds in the top few inches of soil. It works best in sunny regions with hot summers.

  1. Mow or cut the weeds low, rake the surface smooth and water the soil well.
  2. Cover the area with clear plastic (1–4 mil), burying the edges in a trench to seal in heat.
  3. Leave it in place for 4–8 weeks during the hottest, sunniest part of the year.
  4. Remove the plastic and plant without digging, which would bring up new seeds from below.

Clear plastic works better than black for this purpose because it lets sunlight through to heat the soil. In cool or cloudy climates, results are weaker.

Frequently asked questions

What kills weeds permanently?

For annual weeds, pulling before they seed plus mulch is effective. For perennial weeds, repeated cutting, smothering for a full season or solarizing can exhaust the roots. Nothing is permanent because seeds blow in.

Will vinegar and dish soap kill weeds permanently?

No. A vinegar and soap mix burns top growth but rarely kills roots, so perennial weeds regrow within weeks.

How long does it take to smother weeds with cardboard?

Most annual weeds die in 2–3 months under cardboard and 3 inches of mulch. Tough perennials like bindweed and quackgrass can take a full season or more.

Is it safe to use boiling water near plants?

It's safe in cracks and paths. Keep it away from garden plants and tree roots, because it kills any roots it reaches.

What is the best mulch for weed control?

Wood chips and shredded bark at 2–4 inches work well in beds. Compost is good but grows weeds if it is not fully finished. Under paths, use cardboard under chips.

The bottom line

Pull weeds when the soil is damp, smother large areas with cardboard and 3 inches of mulch, and save boiling water or flame for paths and cracks. Skip salt and don't count on household vinegar. For the right amount of mulch, use the mulch calculator.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Lawn Fertilizer Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator

Sources: Weed control guidance from US university extension services, including Iowa State University Extension (corn gluten meal research), University of California IPM, Washington State University Extension and Penn State Extension; vinegar herbicide cautions from extension publications. Always follow product labels and safety instructions. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Garden Tool Maintenance: Clean, Sharpen and Store for Winter
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To maintain garden tools for winter: clean off soil, remove rust, sharpen cutting edges, oil metal parts and store tools dry and off the floor. Wash and dry tools after use, rub light oil on blades, sand and oil wooden handles once a year, and drain fuel or add stabilizer in power equipment before storing it.

Good tools last for decades if they are cleaned, sharpened and stored dry. Neglected ones rust, dull and crush stems instead of cutting them, and dull blades spread disease from plant to plant. Winter is the time to do all of it in a single afternoon, while the garden is quiet.

This guide gives you a simple routine, tool by tool. Nothing here needs special equipment beyond a wire brush, a file or stone and a can of oil. When spring arrives, the planting calendar helps you plan what to do first.

Key takeaways
  • Clean first: dirt holds moisture and starts rust; wash and dry tools after every use.
  • Sharpen: follow the factory bevel (commonly about 20–30 degrees on pruners and hoes); only one side of bypass blades.
  • Oil: a thin film on blades and pivots, and linseed or tung oil on wooden handles.
  • Power tools: use fuel stabilizer or run the engine dry, and always disconnect the spark plug before touching blades.
  • Store dry, hung up, in a place that doesn't swing between hot and cold.

What basic supplies do you need?

SupplyUse
Stiff brush and bucket of waterRemove caked soil
Wire brush or steel woolScrub surface rust
White vinegarSoak heavily rusted parts
Mill file, diamond file or whetstoneSharpen edges
70% rubbing alcoholDisinfect blades
Light machine oil (or camellia oil)Protect blades and pivots
Boiled linseed oil or tung oilCondition wooden handles
Sandpaper (80 to 120 grit)Smooth splintered handles

How do you clean garden tools?

  1. Knock off dry soil with a stiff brush or putty knife.
  2. Scrub with soapy water and rinse.
  3. Dry completely with a rag. Rust starts on damp metal, so don't skip this step.
  4. Disinfect pruners, loppers and saws used on diseased plants by wiping or soaking blades in 70% rubbing alcohol for about 30 seconds. Household bleach (1 part to 9 parts water) also works but corrodes metal, so rinse and oil afterward.

A bucket filled with sand and a little oil is a popular way to clean and oil shovels and trowels together: plunge the tool into it a few times after use. Keep the sand damp with oil, not soaked.

How do you remove rust from garden tools?

Light surface rust

Scrub with a wire brush or steel wool until you see bare metal, wipe clean and oil.

Heavy rust

Soak the metal part in white vinegar for 30 minutes to a few hours (up to 24 hours for severe rust, checking regularly), then scrub, rinse, dry quickly and oil. Vinegar is acidic and will etch metal if left too long, so don't leave it overnight unless needed. Do not soak wooden handles.

Always dry and oil immediately after de-rusting. Bare metal rusts again in hours. A thin coat of oil seals the surface.

How do you sharpen garden tools?

A sharp tool cuts cleanly, heals faster on plants and takes less effort. Sharpen once a year, or whenever the edge no longer slices cleanly through a stem or paper.

Pruners and loppers (bypass)

  1. Open the blade and clamp it, or hold it steady.
  2. Using a diamond file or whetstone, follow the existing bevel on the outside of the cutting blade only, in one direction from the base toward the tip.
  3. Make 10–20 strokes until a fine burr forms on the flat inside edge.
  4. Remove the burr with a single flat pass on the flat side. Leave the anvil blade alone.
  5. Wipe, close, test and oil the pivot.

Shovels, spades and hoes

Clamp the tool and file the edge with a mill file, stroking away from the edge at the existing bevel. A sharp edge slices through roots and soil; you don't need a razor edge, just clean metal at a consistent angle.

Lawn mower blades

Disconnect the spark plug wire before working on the mower. Remove the blade, sharpen it with a file or grinder, keeping the original angle, and check it for balance on a nail or balancer. An unbalanced blade vibrates and damages the engine. Many people take blades to a shop once a year.

How do you care for wooden handles?

Wooden handles dry out, splinter and crack. Once a year:

  1. Sand the handle lightly with 80–120 grit sandpaper to remove splinters and old finish.
  2. Wipe off dust.
  3. Rub in boiled linseed oil or tung oil with a rag, let it soak in for about 15–30 minutes and wipe off the excess.
  4. Let it cure as the label says. Rags soaked in linseed oil can heat up and ignite; lay them flat to dry outdoors or put them in a sealed metal container filled with water.

How do you winterize power equipment?

  • Gas mowers and trimmers: add fuel stabilizer to a full tank and run the engine for a few minutes, or run the tank dry, following the owner's manual. Gasoline with ethanol degrades in a few months.
  • Change the oil on four-stroke engines and check the air filter.
  • Clean the deck underside to remove packed clippings.
  • Batteries: remove lithium-ion batteries and store them indoors in a cool, dry place at partial charge, as the manufacturer recommends.
  • Hoses and sprinklers: drain, coil and store them where they won't freeze.

Check your manual for specifics; storage steps vary by brand and model.

🧮

While you're planning next season, use the mulch calculator and the soil calculator to work out the materials your beds will need in spring.

Where and how should you store garden tools?

  • Hang tools on hooks or a wall rack so blades don't sit on damp concrete.
  • Store in a dry shed or garage. A fluctuating temperature creates condensation; silica gel packets in a toolbox help.
  • Keep sharp tools covered or in sheaths.
  • Group by use so you can find what you need quickly in spring.

Garden tool maintenance mistakes to avoid

  1. Putting tools away dirty or wet. Rust forms quickly.
  2. Over-sharpening or changing the bevel. Follow the factory angle.
  3. Sharpening both sides of a bypass pruner. Only the outer bevel is sharpened.
  4. Leaving fuel in small engines all winter without stabilizer.
  5. Forgetting to disconnect the spark plug before touching mower blades.

How much does tool maintenance really save?

Tools last longer and work better when cared for. A quality hand pruner or spade can last decades with annual attention, while a neglected one may need replacing in a few seasons. The bigger saving is effort: a sharp blade needs less force, so your hands and wrists tire less, and clean cuts heal faster on plants. A 15-minute wipe-down after each use, plus one annual afternoon of sharpening and oiling, is all it takes.

What is a simple yearly tool maintenance schedule?

  • After every use: knock off soil, wipe blades and hang tools up.
  • Monthly in season: check handles and fasteners, and oil pivots on pruners and loppers.
  • Once a year (late fall or winter): sharpen blades, de-rust, oil wooden handles, service the mower and drain the fuel system.
  • Early spring: test everything, replace worn parts and sharpen again if needed before the busy season begins.

Keeping a small kit in one place, with a file, a rag and a can of oil, makes the habit easy to keep.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I sharpen garden tools?

Sharpen pruners, loppers and hoes once a year, or when the edge starts to crush stems or slice poorly. Mower blades are typically sharpened once a season, or more often in sandy soil.

What is the best oil for garden tools?

Light machine oil, 3-in-1 oil or camellia oil work well on metal blades. Boiled linseed or tung oil is best for wooden handles.

Can I use WD-40 on pruners?

Yes, it works as a cleaner and a short-term rust protector, but it evaporates. Follow it with a light oil for longer protection on blades and pivots.

How do I clean sticky sap from pruners?

Wipe the blades with rubbing alcohol or mineral spirits on a rag, scrub gently with steel wool and then oil. Sap makes blades stick and cut poorly.

Do I need to disinfect garden tools?

Disinfect when cutting diseased plants and between cuts on disease-prone plants such as roses and fruit trees. Otherwise, regular cleaning is enough.

The bottom line

Clean and dry tools, remove rust, sharpen at the factory angle, oil metal and wood, and store everything dry and off the floor. An afternoon now means smoother work in spring. When you're ready to plan next season, start with the mulch calculator and soil calculator.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Planting Calendar · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Tool cleaning, sharpening and storage guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and Oregon State University Extension; equipment storage per manufacturers' owner's manuals; disinfectant guidance from extension plant-disease publications. Follow your tool and engine manuals. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Fall Garden Cleanup Checklist: What to Cut, Leave and Mulch
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Fall garden cleanup is mostly about removing diseased plants and weeds, not tidying everything. Pull spent vegetables, cut back diseased perennial foliage, plant bulbs and garlic, then leave hollow stems and seed heads standing until spring. Add 2–3 inches of shredded leaves or mulch after the ground starts to cool.

A perfectly bare garden looks neat in November but it isn't what plants, soil or wildlife need. The goal of fall cleanup is to break disease cycles, protect the soil and make spring easier, and you can do all of that in a weekend or two without bagging every leaf.

This checklist is ordered the way the work actually flows: vegetables first, then perennials, then leaves and mulch, then tools and water. If you want to know how much mulch your beds will take, the free mulch calculator turns bed sizes into cubic yards and bags.

Key takeaways
  • Always remove: diseased vegetable plants, weeds that have gone to seed and fruit left on the ground.
  • Often leave: hollow perennial stems and seed heads, which shelter native bees and feed birds until spring.
  • Mulch depth: 2–3 inches of shredded leaves or bark; 200 sq ft at 3 inches takes 50 cubic feet, about 12 bags of 30-gallon leaf bags.
  • Timing: plant bulbs and garlic before the ground freezes, and mulch perennials after it has cooled, not while it is still warm.
  • Tools and water: drain hoses and clean tools before the first hard freeze.

What should you do first in fall garden cleanup?

Start where cleanup matters most for plant health: the vegetable garden. Any plant that was sick this summer can carry its problem into next year, so these jobs come before the pretty tidy-up.

  1. Pull spent annual vegetables once frost has ended production, or sooner if the plants are finished.
  2. Bag or trash diseased plants. Tomato and potato foliage with blight, squash leaves with severe powdery mildew and any plant with a known soilborne disease should not go into a cool home compost pile.
  3. Pick up fallen fruit and tomatoes. They harbor rot and attract rodents.
  4. Pull weeds before they set seed, or cut off the seed heads and bag them.
  5. Leave roots of beans and peas in the ground and cut the tops instead; the roots break down and leave nitrogen-rich nodules in the soil.

What should you cut back and what should you leave?

This is the question behind most "fall cleanup" searches. A good rule: cut back what is diseased or mushy, leave what is hollow, sturdy or seed-bearing. The table below is a starting point; plants vary, so check your own.

Plant typeFall actionWhy
Hostas, daylilies, peoniesCut back to 1–2 in after foliage collapsesRemoves slug eggs and fungal spores (peony botrytis, hosta leaf spots)
Bearded irisCut leaves to 4–6 in fans; clear debrisReduces iris borer eggs on old leaves
Coneflower, black-eyed Susan, sedumLeave standing until springSeed heads feed finches; stems protect crowns
Ornamental grassesLeave until late winterWinter structure; cut to 4–6 in before new growth
RosesRemove fallen leaves; light trim onlyBlack spot overwinters on leaves; hard pruning waits until spring
Hydrangea (bigleaf)Do not pruneFlower buds form on old wood in many varieties
Annual flowersPull and compost if healthyPrevents rotting stems; reseeders can stay

Why leave hollow stems for pollinators?

Many native bees nest in hollow or pithy stems, and others overwinter in leaf litter. Extension programs and conservation groups such as the Xerces Society recommend leaving some stems and leaves in place, and cutting the stems you do remove to about 8–24 inches rather than flat to the ground. In spring, wait until daytime temperatures are regularly above about 50°F before cutting them down.

Don't compost diseased material in a cool pile. Home piles rarely stay hot enough to kill blight, mildew or soilborne fungi. Put diseased plants in the trash or yard-waste collection if your city allows it.

What do you do with fallen leaves?

Leaves are free mulch and compost, so the question is how much to keep. Thick whole leaves mat down and smother lawn and low plants, but shredded leaves break down fast and feed worms and soil life.

  • On the lawn: mow over them a few times so the pieces are dime-sized or smaller and fall down between the grass blades. If you can no longer see grass through the layer, rake or bag the excess.
  • In garden beds: shred and spread 2–3 inches between plants. Pull the layer back about 2 inches from stems and crowns.
  • In a compost pile: layer them with green material such as kitchen scraps and grass clippings.
  • As a pile of leaf mold: stack moistened leaves in a wire bin or bag for a year or two to make a soil conditioner.

A standard 30-gallon leaf bag holds about 4 cubic feet. To mulch 200 sq ft of beds at 3 inches you need 200 × 3 ÷ 12 = 50 cubic feet, or about 12 full bags of shredded leaves. Unshredded leaves take far more room, which is one reason shredding pays off.

🧮

Planning to cover your beds with bark or compost instead? Use the mulch calculator to get cubic yards, bags and cost for every bed.

When should you mulch perennials and shrubs?

Apply winter mulch after the soil has cooled and the first hard frosts have passed, not while it is still warm. The goal is to keep soil temperature steady and prevent freeze-thaw heaving, not to keep it warmer. In the coldest zones (3–5) that is often November; in zones 7–8 you may mulch mostly to protect shallow roots and suppress winter weeds.

Bed sizeDepthVolume needed
100 sq ft2 in16.7 cu ft (0.62 cu yd)
100 sq ft3 in25 cu ft (0.93 cu yd)
200 sq ft3 in50 cu ft (1.85 cu yd)
400 sq ft2 in66.7 cu ft (2.47 cu yd)

Keep mulch a few inches away from trunks and stems. Piled-up mulch holds moisture against bark and gives mice a sheltered place to nibble.

What should you plant or divide in fall?

Fall is planting season for many things. Roots keep growing in cool soil even after the top of the plant slows down.

  • Spring bulbs: tulips, daffodils and crocuses go in after soil temperatures drop below about 60°F, and several weeks before the ground freezes.
  • Garlic: plant a few weeks before the ground freezes; our guide to planting dates by ZIP code helps with the timing.
  • Perennials, shrubs and trees: warm soil plus cool air is ideal. Water them well until the ground freezes.
  • Divide crowded perennials such as daylilies and hostas about 4–6 weeks before hard freeze so roots can settle.

How do you prep tools, hoses and irrigation?

Do this before the first hard freeze, which is usually around the average first frost date for your area. You can look up local dates with our frost dates by ZIP code tool.

  1. Drain and coil hoses, and store them out of the sun. Water left inside can freeze and split them.
  2. Disconnect hoses from spigots. A connected hose can trap water in the faucet and cause a pipe to burst.
  3. Blow out or drain in-ground sprinklers or hire someone to do it; check your system manual for the right air pressure.
  4. Clean and oil tools so rust does not set in over winter.
  5. Empty and store pots. Terra-cotta cracks when it freezes with wet soil inside.

5 fall cleanup mistakes to avoid

  1. Cutting everything to the ground. You remove overwintering habitat and seed for birds, and you don't gain much.
  2. Mulching too early. If the soil is still warm, mulch can keep rodents and slugs cozy and hold excess moisture against crowns.
  3. Composting diseased plants. This brings blight and mildew back next summer.
  4. Bagging all your leaves. You then buy mulch in spring that you already had for free.
  5. Tilling the whole garden. Digging in fall breaks soil structure and exposes bare soil to winter rain; cover it with mulch or a cover crop instead.

How long does fall cleanup take?

For an average suburban yard, plan roughly two weekends. Spend the first on vegetables, weeds and diseased foliage, and the second on leaves, mulch, bulbs and tools. Splitting the work this way keeps it from feeling like a chore, and it lets you wait for the right moment to cut back perennials and mulch rather than doing everything in one rush.

  • Weekend one (October): pull spent vegetables, remove diseased plants, plant garlic and bulbs, start a leaf pile.
  • Weekend two (after the first hard frosts): cut back collapsed perennials, mulch beds, drain hoses, clean and store tools.
  • Late winter: cut down the stems you left standing, once insects start to wake.

Where your first frost falls decides the whole schedule, so check the date for your ZIP code and work backward from it.

Frequently asked questions

When should I start fall garden cleanup?

Start after the first hard frost has killed tender annuals and vegetables, which is typically October to early November in much of the US. Do not rush perennials: they need foliage to store energy until it dies back on its own.

Should I cut back perennials in fall or spring?

Cut back plants with diseased or mushy foliage, such as peonies, hostas and bearded iris, in fall. Leave sturdy, hollow or seed-bearing stems such as coneflower and ornamental grasses until early spring.

Is it OK to leave leaves on garden beds over winter?

Yes, a thin layer of shredded leaves is good for beds. Avoid thick mats of whole leaves, especially oak or magnolia, which can smother low plants and shed water.

What vegetables can stay in the garden over winter?

Carrots, parsnips, leeks, kale and spinach tolerate frost and, with mulch, can be harvested well into winter in many areas. Garlic planted in fall also stays in the ground.

Should I water the garden in fall?

Yes, if the weather is dry. Evergreens, new trees and shrubs benefit from a deep soak until the ground freezes, because they continue to lose water through foliage in winter.

The bottom line

Remove what is diseased, leave what helps wildlife, use your leaves as mulch and get bulbs, garlic and tools sorted before the ground freezes. When you know how much cover your beds need, the mulch calculator turns the plan into a shopping list.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator

Sources: Fall garden and perennial care guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and Cornell Cooperative Extension; pollinator habitat recommendations from the Xerces Society; frost date data from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Volume math: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; a 30-gallon bag is about 4 cubic feet. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: Cover Crops for Home Gardens: Easy Winter Soil Builders
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The best cover crop for most home gardens is winter rye, sown 4–6 weeks before your first hard freeze at roughly 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft. Use crimson clover or hairy vetch to add nitrogen, and oats where you want a crop that winterkills. Cut or mow cover crops before they set seed, and wait 2–3 weeks before planting.

Cover crops are plants grown for the soil rather than for the table. Sown in fall on a bare bed, they hold soil in place, crowd out weeds, feed worms and soil microbes and add organic matter when you cut them in spring. They are among the cheapest ways to improve a vegetable garden, with seed costing a few dollars for a typical bed.

This guide helps you choose a cover crop, work out how much seed you need and know when to sow and end it. If you're planning the soil volume for new beds at the same time, the soil calculator makes quick work of that.

Key takeaways
  • Winter rye: the toughest; about 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft (3–4 oz per 100 sq ft), sown until about 4 weeks before the ground freezes.
  • Legumes (crimson clover, hairy vetch, Austrian winter pea) add nitrogen but need earlier sowing.
  • Oats grow fast in fall and usually winterkill in cold zones, leaving easy-to-plant mulch.
  • End the crop before it goes to seed, then wait 2–3 weeks before planting.
  • Seeding rates on the packet may differ; always follow the label.

What is a cover crop and why use one?

A cover crop is a plant sown to protect and improve soil between food crops. Benefits that extension and USDA-NRCS sources describe include:

  • Erosion control: roots and leaves keep rain from carrying soil away.
  • Weed suppression: dense growth crowds out winter and early-spring weeds.
  • Organic matter: the cut crop breaks down into humus that improves structure and water-holding.
  • Nitrogen from legumes: clovers, vetch and peas host bacteria that capture nitrogen from the air; some is released as the plants decompose.
  • Nutrient capture: grasses such as rye hold leftover nutrients that would otherwise leach out.

Which cover crop should you choose?

Cover cropTypeFall sowingWinter hardinessBest for
Winter ryeGrassUp to ~4 weeks before ground freezesVery hardy (zones 3+)Weed control, erosion, biomass
OatsGrass8–10 weeks before hard freezeWinterkills below ~15–20°FEasy spring planting, no-kill hassle
Crimson cloverLegume6–8 weeks before first hard frostHardy to about zone 6–7Nitrogen, pollinator flowers
Hairy vetchLegume6–8 weeks before first hard frostHardy to zone 4–5Heavy nitrogen, mulch; can self-seed
Austrian winter peaLegume6–8 weeks before hard freezeHardy to about zone 6Nitrogen, edible shoots
BuckwheatBroadleaf (summer)Late spring to late summerKilled by first frostFast fill-in between crops, bees

Hardiness limits vary with variety and weather, so check the seed supplier's notes for your zone. Not sure of your zone? Our planting calendar shows your frost dates and zone by ZIP code.

How much cover crop seed do you need?

Seed is sold by the pound and rates are usually given per acre. These are common broadcast ranges converted to home-garden units (1 acre = 43,560 sq ft):

Cover cropPer acre (approx.)Per 1,000 sq ftPer 100 sq ft
Winter rye90–120 lb2.1–2.8 lb3.3–4.4 oz
Oats80–110 lb1.8–2.5 lb2.9–4.0 oz
Crimson clover15–25 lb0.3–0.6 lb0.6–0.9 oz
Hairy vetch25–40 lb0.6–0.9 lb0.9–1.5 oz
Austrian winter pea70–100 lb1.6–2.3 lb2.6–3.7 oz
Buckwheat50–90 lb1.1–2.1 lb1.8–3.3 oz

Example: a 4×8 raised bed (32 sq ft) needs about 1.1–1.4 oz of winter rye. Always follow the rate on your seed packet, since seed size and sowing method (broadcast vs drilled) change the amount.

🧮

Planning the bed you'll plant after the cover crop? Use the soil calculator to work out how much compost to add when you finish the crop.

How do you sow a cover crop?

Step 1: Clear the bed

Remove spent plants and weeds. A cover crop will not outcompete large weeds.

Step 2: Loosen the surface

Rake the top inch or two. No deep digging is needed.

Step 3: Broadcast the seed evenly

Mix small seed with a handful of sand or dry soil to spread it evenly. Walk in two directions so you cover the whole bed.

Step 4: Rake and press

Rake the seed lightly into the soil to a depth of about ½ to 1 inch for large seed like rye and peas, shallower for clover. Tamp or walk over the soil to improve contact.

Step 5: Water and wait

Keep the soil moist until seedlings show, usually within 7–14 days. Legume seed can be dusted with the matching inoculant (sold with the seed) to help nitrogen-fixing bacteria colonize the roots.

When and how do you end a cover crop in spring?

Timing matters more than method. Cut, mow or flatten the crop before it sets seed (for rye, before it heads out; for clover and vetch, at early bloom). If left to seed, rye and vetch can become weeds.

  • Cut and leave on the surface: use a string trimmer, mower or shears, then leave the residue as mulch and plant through it.
  • Cut and cover: lay a tarp or cardboard for 3–6 weeks to smother regrowth, especially for rye.
  • Turn under: if you do dig, incorporate the green material at least 2–3 weeks before planting. Fresh residue ties up nitrogen as it breaks down, and rye can inhibit small-seeded crops like carrots and lettuce for a few weeks.
  • Winterkilled crops such as oats can be raked back and planted into directly.
Rye can be hard to manage in a small bed. If your garden is mostly hand tools and you aren't comfortable cutting and smothering a dense mat, choose oats (winterkills in cold zones) or crimson clover instead of winter rye.

Can you use cover crops in raised beds?

Yes. Raised beds suit cover crops because they are small and easy to cut by hand. Choose oats or crimson clover if you want to plant early. After cutting, add 1–2 inches of compost on top before planting. See our fall routine for winterizing raised beds with the right soil volume.

Common cover crop mistakes

  1. Sowing too late. Seed needs time to establish; late sowing gives thin cover.
  2. Letting it go to seed. Rye and vetch become weeds if allowed to mature.
  3. Planting right after turning under. Wait two to three weeks to avoid nitrogen tie-up and allelopathy.
  4. Using cover crops with the same family as your vegetables. Peas and vetch share some diseases with garden peas and beans.
  5. Skipping the seed rate. Too little leaves gaps for weeds; too much wastes seed.

What cover crops work in summer?

If a bed will sit empty for six weeks or more in summer, a warm-season cover crop keeps weeds down and builds soil. Buckwheat is the usual choice: it sprouts within days, flowers in about four to six weeks, feeds bees and is killed by the first frost. Cut it at the first flowers and before seeds form. Cowpeas and sunn hemp fix nitrogen and suit the South, where summers are long.

Turn the cut residue into a mulch layer or work it lightly into the top inch of soil, then plant a fall crop after a week or two.

Frequently asked questions

What is the easiest cover crop for a beginner?

Oats are the easiest: they germinate quickly, grow fast in fall and winterkill in cold zones, leaving a mulch you can plant through. Winter rye is more effective but harder to remove.

How late can I plant a cover crop in fall?

Winter rye can go in up to about four weeks before the ground freezes. Legumes and oats need six to ten weeks of mild weather to establish.

Do cover crops attract pests?

They can shelter slugs and voles, but they also host beneficial insects. Cutting them before the main crop and keeping mulch back from stems reduces pest problems.

How long before planting vegetables after a cover crop?

Wait two to three weeks after cutting or turning under a cover crop. For rye, waiting three to four weeks helps seed germination in direct-sown crops.

Can I grow a cover crop in summer?

Yes. Buckwheat and cowpeas grow fast in warm weather and can fill a bed that would otherwise sit empty for 6–8 weeks.

The bottom line

Pick winter rye for toughness, oats for ease or crimson clover for nitrogen, sow it at the right rate for your bed and end it before it sets seed. Match your sowing date to your first frost, and plan the spring soil refresh with the soil calculator.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator

Sources: Cover crop selection, timing and management from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and Cornell Cooperative Extension, and from USDA-NRCS and SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) cover crop guidance. Seeding rates are converted from typical per-acre ranges (1 acre = 43,560 sq ft); follow the label on your seed. Last reviewed: November 2026.

items.title: When to Mulch: Best Time in Spring and Fall
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Mulch in mid to late spring, after the soil has warmed to roughly 50–60°F and weeds have been pulled. A second layer in late fall, once the ground starts to cool but before it freezes hard, protects roots over winter. Mulching too early in spring can slow warming, and mulching too late lets weeds get ahead.

Mulch timing is less about the calendar than about soil temperature and what the plants are doing. Put it down too early and you insulate cold soil, delaying growth. Put it down too late and weeds have already taken the bed. Get the timing right and one layer works all season.

This guide gives the best window for spring and fall, how it changes by USDA zone, and the prep work that makes mulch worth the effort. Once you know when, the mulch calculator tells you how much to buy.

Key takeaways
  • Spring: after soil reaches about 50–60°F and perennials are up, typically April to May in most of the US.
  • Fall: late fall, once the first hard frost has passed, to insulate roots and buffer freeze-thaw cycles.
  • Warm climates: mulch before summer heat (March–April in the South) and refresh as needed.
  • Always first: pull weeds, edge the bed and water dry soil.
  • Not in a hurry: a week or two of delay in spring costs little; piling mulch onto cold, wet soil can cost more.

What is the best time of year to mulch?

For most of the US, there are two good windows: mid to late spring and late fall. Spring mulch conserves moisture, suppresses weeds and keeps roots cooler through summer. Fall mulch evens out soil temperature through winter, so roots are less exposed to freeze-thaw cycles.

If you only mulch once a year, make it spring: that is when weed control and moisture savings matter most. In cold climates, check that the layer is still at least 2 inches heading into winter.

Why does soil temperature matter more than the date?

Mulch is an insulator. In spring, an insulating layer over cold soil keeps it cold for longer, which can slow root growth and delay the soil warming that vegetables and warm-season flowers need. Waiting until soil reaches roughly 50–60°F at a 2–4 inch depth (a few days of steady mild weather) lets it warm first. A cheap soil thermometer takes the guesswork out.

In fall, the goal is reversed. You want the soil to cool first, then apply mulch so that it keeps the ground frozen instead of encouraging repeated thaws. Apply after the first hard frost but before the ground freezes solid.

When should you mulch by region?

These are typical windows, not rules. A cold spring or an early fall shifts them by weeks, so check the soil rather than the calendar.

USDA zonesTypical spring windowTypical fall windowNotes
3–4 (northern states)Mid May – early JuneLate October – November, after ground coolsSpring soil warms late; fall mulch protects against freeze-thaw
5–6 (Midwest, Northeast)Late April – MayNovemberWait for perennials to emerge in spring
7 (mid-Atlantic, transition)April – MayNovember – early DecemberMulch before summer heat
8–9 (Southeast, Gulf, Pacific)March – AprilOptional; refresh in October–NovemberSummer heat makes mulch most valuable
10 and warm southern regionsFebruary – AprilRefresh as neededMulch breaks down faster in heat and humidity

To check your own zone, look up your ZIP code in the planting calendar.

🧮

Timing sorted? Use the mulch calculator to turn your bed sizes and your chosen depth into cubic yards, bags and a cost, before the spring rush at the garden center.

What should you do before you mulch?

  1. Pull weeds, roots and all. Mulch suppresses seedlings but perennial weeds grow right through it.
  2. Edge the bed with a spade or an edger so mulch stays in the bed and not the lawn.
  3. Water if the soil is dry. Mulch holds moisture in but does not wet dry soil by itself.
  4. Add fertilizer or compost first, if the bed needs it, because it is harder to work in later.
  5. Rake old mulch to break up any crust, and remove it if it is deeper than about 4 inches in total.
  6. Spread 2–3 inches of fresh mulch and pull it back from stems and trunks.

Can you mulch in summer or winter?

Yes. Summer mulching works well for vegetable gardens and new plantings, because it cuts evaporation and cools the root zone. The only catch is water: make sure the soil is moist before you cover it. Winter mulching is trickier. A layer of straw, shredded leaves or evergreen boughs over tender perennials after the ground freezes helps, but wait for freezing weather so mice do not nest in it before then.

Avoid spreading wet, heavy mulch in a thick layer over frozen ground or waterlogged soil. It will not harm plants outright but it can hold water against crowns and invite rot.

When should you mulch around new plantings?

Right after planting. Newly planted trees, shrubs and perennials benefit from mulch immediately, because it slows evaporation while roots establish. Water the plant in first, then add 2–3 inches, keeping the trunk or crown clear. The same rule applies to fall plantings: mulch after planting, then water through autumn.

When should you not mulch?

  • On saturated, cold spring soil. Wait for it to drain and warm.
  • Over self-seeding annuals you want to return (such as poppies or larkspur). Hold off until seedlings are up.
  • Over ground-nesting bee sites. Many native bees nest in bare soil; leave a few patches of bare ground.
  • Before bulbs have emerged, if you are using very thick layers. A light layer is fine.
Do not mulch too early because of a warm week. A warm spell in March can tempt you, but fresh mulch keeps soil from soaking up daytime warmth that would otherwise radiate back at night, so a late frost can hit tender growth a little harder. If a hard frost is forecast, wait until it has passed.

Does the best time depend on what you are mulching?

AreaBest timingWhy
Perennial bedsAfter new shoots are 2–4 in tallLets the crowns warm and makes it easy to see where to keep mulch off
Vegetable bedsAfter the soil warms and seedlings are established, usually a few weeks after plantingWarm-season crops such as tomatoes and peppers prefer warm soil before it is covered
Trees and shrubsSpring or fall, or any time at plantingRoots benefit year-round; the key is depth and keeping the trunk clear
Strawberries and garlicLate fall or winter, after the ground coolsStraw protects crowns and cloves from freeze-thaw heaving
Roses and tender perennialsLate fall, after hard frostInsulates the crown; remove the extra in spring

The common thread is that the soil should be at the right temperature for the plants before the mulch goes on. Cool-season crops and spring bulbs do not mind early mulch. Heat-lovers do.

How often should you refresh mulch?

Organic mulch decomposes in one to three years, so most beds need a top-up every one or two years rather than a full layer each spring. Measure what is left with a ruler and add only enough to bring it back to 2–3 inches. The mulch calculator lets you enter the depth you already have and calculates the difference for you.

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to mulch in spring or fall?

Spring is better for weed control and moisture retention through summer. Fall mulching mainly helps insulate roots, so many gardeners do both: a main layer in spring and a light top-up in late fall.

Should you mulch before or after the last frost?

After. Mulch slows the soil from warming and can trap cold air near plants, so wait until the last hard frost has passed unless the soil is already warm.

Can you put mulch down in winter?

You can, with straw or leaves over tender perennials after the ground freezes. Wood mulch can go down in late fall, but avoid piling it on very wet soil.

Do you need to remove old mulch before adding new?

Usually no. Rake it to loosen it and add only enough to reach 2–3 inches in total. Remove some if the layer is matted, moldy or already deeper than about 4 inches.

What month is best to mulch?

In most of the US, May is the best single month, with March–April in the South and late May to early June in the far North. Let soil temperature decide.

How long does mulch last before it needs replacing?

Shredded hardwood and bark typically lasts one to two years, coarser wood chips can last two to three, and compost or straw breaks down faster. Gravel and rock do not decompose.

The bottom line

Mulch in mid to late spring after the soil warms, and top up in late fall in cold climates. Pull weeds first, apply 2–3 inches and keep it off stems. Then use the mulch calculator to work out exactly how much to order.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Planting Calendar · Soil Calculator

Sources: Mulching guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map for zone references. Timing windows are typical ranges and vary with weather each year. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Topsoil vs Garden Soil vs Potting Mix: Which to Use Where
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Use topsoil to fill and level the ground, garden soil to improve in-ground and raised beds, and potting mix only in containers. Topsoil is screened native soil with little organic matter; garden soil is topsoil blended with compost; potting mix is soilless, made of peat or coir, bark and perlite. Do not swap them 1-for-1.

The soil aisle looks simple until you stand in it. Topsoil, garden soil, potting soil, raised bed mix, fill dirt: the bags look similar and the prices vary by a factor of five. Buy the wrong one and plants struggle, or you spend more than you needed to.

This guide explains what each product is, where it belongs and how much to buy for common jobs. Once you know which, the soil calculator converts your dimensions into cubic yards and bags.

Key takeaways
  • Topsoil: cheapest, for filling holes, leveling and lawn bases.
  • Garden soil: topsoil plus compost, for in-ground flower and vegetable beds.
  • Potting mix: soilless, light and sterile-ish, only for pots and containers.
  • Raised beds: a blend of topsoil and compost, or a bagged raised-bed mix; never pure topsoil or potting mix.
  • Quantity: square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards for any of them.

What is the difference between topsoil, garden soil and potting mix?

ProductWhat it isOrganic matterBest useTypical cost
Fill dirtSubsoil dug from below the top layerVery lowRaising grade, filling holes (not for plants)Lowest
TopsoilScreened top layer of native soilLow to moderate; variesLeveling lawns, backfilling, base for new lawnsLow
Garden soilTopsoil blended with compost or other organic matterModerate to highIn-ground flower and vegetable beds, top-dressingMedium
Raised-bed mixTopsoil/compost blends, or bagged mix tuned for bedsHighRaised bedsMedium to high
Potting mixSoilless: peat or coir, bark, perlite, vermiculiteHigh (peat/bark)Containers, hanging baskets, seed starting (fine grade)Highest per cubic foot
CompostDecomposed organic matterVery highAmending soil, mulching, ingredient in mixesLow to medium

"Topsoil" has no single legal standard in the US, so quality varies enormously between suppliers. One bag or yard can be dark and crumbly, another pale and full of clay or stones. Always look at a sample before you order a load.

When should you use topsoil?

Topsoil is the budget workhorse. It is right when you need volume more than fertility:

  • Leveling low spots in a lawn with thin layers (up to about 1/2 inch at a time, so grass grows through).
  • Backfilling around a new foundation, patio or retaining wall.
  • Building a base for a new lawn where native soil is poor: roughly 4–6 inches.
  • Ingredient in a raised bed mix (about 60%, with compost and a coarse aggregate).

Do not use plain topsoil as the only fill in a raised bed. It compacts and drains poorly in a confined space, and it is rarely rich enough to feed vegetables.

When is garden soil the right choice?

Garden soil is topsoil that has already been blended with compost. Use it when you are planting in the ground or topping up a bed:

  • Filling a planting hole for shrubs or perennials (mix with native soil, do not replace it).
  • Adding 1–2 inches over a bed and working it into the top few inches.
  • Raising a low bed by a few inches.

Beware of products labeled "garden soil" that are mostly bark fines or composted forest products. Squeeze a handful: it should hold its shape loosely and break apart, not stay soggy or crumble into dust.

Why should potting mix stay in containers?

Potting mix is engineered for pots. It is light, drains fast, and holds air, because roots in a small container would suffocate in heavy soil. That is exactly why it is wrong for beds: it dries out quickly, shrinks as the peat or bark breaks down, and costs several times more per cubic foot than topsoil or garden soil.

Conversely, garden soil in a pot becomes dense and waterlogged. Even "potting soil" sold in bags is normally soilless; read the label's ingredient list. One cubic foot of potting mix fills about 7.5 gallons, so a 2 cubic foot bag fills roughly three 5-gallon pots.

🧮

Know where each product goes? Enter your bed dimensions in the soil calculator to convert depth and area into cubic yards, bags and weight, for topsoil, garden soil or potting mix.

How much topsoil or garden soil do you need?

The formula is the same for all three: square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards. For potting mix in containers, work in cubic feet instead.

JobArea × depthAmount
Level a lawn with a thin top-dressing1,000 sq ft × 1 in3.09 cu yd
Overseeding with a light soil layer1,000 sq ft × 1/4 in0.77 cu yd
New lawn base1,000 sq ft × 4 in12.35 cu yd
Top up a perennial bed100 sq ft × 2 in0.62 cu yd
New in-ground bed100 sq ft × 6 in1.85 cu yd

Add about 10% for settling and uneven ground. Soil is heavy: roughly 1 to 1.4 tons per cubic yard depending on moisture and type, so check your trailer or truck capacity before loading.

How can you tell good topsoil from bad?

  1. Look and feel. Dark, crumbly and slightly moist is good. Pale, sticky clay or sandy and dusty is not.
  2. Check for debris. Rocks, roots, construction waste and weeds mean low-grade fill.
  3. Smell. It should smell earthy. A sour, rotten smell means anaerobic, poorly composted material.
  4. Ask the source. Screened topsoil from a reputable landscape supplier is better than "fill" from a construction site, which can carry weed seed and contamination.
  5. Consider a lab test for pH and nutrients, especially if you plan to grow vegetables on new soil, since urban fill can have contaminants.
Don't use soil from unknown sources for edible gardens. Construction-site topsoil and old industrial or roadside soil can contain lead or other contaminants. If you are unsure, use a certified raised-bed mix or test the soil first through your state extension service.

Should you buy soil in bags or in bulk?

Bags suit small jobs: a 40 lb bag of topsoil or 1 to 2 cubic feet of garden soil is easy to carry and store. Bulk is far cheaper once you pass roughly 1 cubic yard, which is 13.5 bags of 2 cubic feet. For a lawn base or several beds, a delivered load is the practical choice. Put a tarp under the pile and spread it within a few days, because wet soil piled on a lawn kills the grass beneath.

Which should you buy for common jobs?

  • Fixing low spots in the lawn: screened topsoil, or a topsoil-sand-compost blend.
  • Planting trees and shrubs: backfill with the native soil you dug out, amended lightly with compost.
  • New vegetable or flower bed in the ground: garden soil or compost worked into native soil.
  • Raised beds: a mix of topsoil and compost, or bagged raised-bed mix.
  • Pots and hanging baskets: potting mix.
  • Seed starting: a fine seed-starting mix.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use garden soil in pots?

Not ideally. Garden soil is too dense for containers and can drain badly and compact. Use a potting mix, which is formulated to stay light and aerated in pots.

Is potting soil the same as potting mix?

In practice, yes: both are mostly soilless blends of peat or coir, bark and perlite. The term "soil" on the bag does not mean it contains real soil.

Is topsoil good for growing vegetables?

It can be, if it is dark, crumbly and screened, and blended with compost. Straight topsoil is rarely rich enough on its own and can compact in raised beds.

What is the cheapest way to fill a large garden bed?

Buy bulk topsoil and compost by the cubic yard and mix them 2:1, rather than buying bagged garden soil. Bulk costs far less per cubic foot for beds over about 50 sq ft.

Can I put topsoil over grass to level my lawn?

Yes, in layers no deeper than about 1/2 inch, so grass can grow through. Deeper fills smother the grass and are better done by stripping the turf first.

What is fill dirt used for?

Fill dirt is subsoil used to raise grade or fill holes under hardscapes. It has little organic matter and is not suitable for plants without a layer of topsoil on top.

The bottom line

Use topsoil to fill and level, garden soil to feed beds and potting mix only in pots. For any of them, square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 gives the cubic yards. Let the soil calculator work out the amount and bags for your project.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Soil and amendment guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and Oregon State University Extension; contamination guidance from state extension soil-testing programs and the US EPA. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; 1 cubic foot ≈ 7.48 US gallons. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Rubber Mulch vs Wood Mulch: Honest Pros, Cons and Costs
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Wood mulch is cheaper and feeds the soil; rubber mulch lasts many years but costs several times more and adds no nutrients. In the example below, 200 sq ft costs about $74 in wood mulch at 3 inches against about $438 in rubber. Wood is the better choice for plant beds; rubber suits playgrounds and low-maintenance borders away from the house.

Rubber mulch is sold as the permanent option: never fades, never washes away, never needs refreshing. Wood mulch is the traditional choice that rots away and has to be redone. Both claims have a catch, and the better pick depends on the spot.

This comparison covers cost over ten years, effects on plants and soil, fire and heat, and playground use. Use the mulch calculator to price the wood option for your own beds, then compare with a rubber quote.

Key takeaways
  • Upfront cost: rubber is often 4–6 times more per cubic yard than wood in the examples below.
  • Lifespan: rubber does not decompose; wood breaks down over one to three years and needs top-ups.
  • Soil: wood feeds soil as it rots; rubber does not.
  • Safety: rubber burns hot and is hard to extinguish, so keep it away from the house and fire sources.
  • Best uses: rubber for playgrounds and permanent borders; wood for gardens, trees and veggies.

What is the difference between rubber and wood mulch?

Wood mulch is shredded bark, chips or ground wood. It is an organic material: it holds moisture, keeps the soil cooler, then decomposes and improves the soil. Rubber mulch is shredded recycled tires, usually sold in nuggets or chips and often dyed brown, red or black. It is inorganic, so it does not rot, but it also adds nothing to the soil.

Which is cheaper, rubber or wood mulch?

Wood wins on upfront price by a wide margin. Using example prices (not quotes): wood mulch at $40 per cubic yard in bulk, and rubber mulch at $7 for a 0.8 cubic foot bag, which works out to $8.75 per cubic foot or $236 per cubic yard. Prices vary a lot between suppliers and regions, so get local quotes.

200 sq ft bedWood (3 in)Rubber (3 in)Rubber (2 in)
Cubic yards1.851.851.23
Material cost (example)$74$438$292

Over time the gap narrows, because wood has to be topped up. Suppose you refresh the wood each year with 1 inch (0.62 cubic yards for 200 sq ft) for nine years after the first spreading. Total wood is 1.85 + 9 × 0.62 = 7.4 cubic yards, or about $296 at $40 per yard, before delivery and labor. Even after ten years, the wood costs less than the rubber in this example. Rubber mainly saves labor, not money.

🧮

Want to price your own beds? Use the mulch calculator to get the cubic yards, bags and cost for wood at 2, 3 or 4 inches, then multiply by a rubber supplier's per-yard quote to compare.

How long does each type last?

Wood mulch typically needs refreshing every one to two years in most climates, since shredded types break down faster than coarse chips or large bark. Rubber mulch is commonly marketed with a lifespan of ten years or more; since it does not decompose, it stays in place until you remove it. In practice, rubber can slowly thin from wind, foot traffic, mowing and washout, and the dye may fade.

Which is better for plants and soil?

For plant growth, wood wins. As it decomposes, it adds organic matter, feeds soil life and improves structure. Rubber holds heat, does not add nutrients and does nothing for soil structure. Because tires can contain compounds such as zinc, several university extension resources advise against using rubber mulch around vegetables and berries, and some caution against it for trees and shrubs where runoff or buildup could be a concern. Research results vary by plant, so this is a reason to be cautious rather than a verdict.

Weed control is similar when both are laid 2–3 inches deep over a clean bed. Rubber is slightly better at not blowing away; wood is better at being easily removed and replaced.

Is rubber mulch a fire risk?

Both can burn, and wildfire guidance warns that embers ignite any combustible mulch. Rubber is a particular concern because once it is burning it gives off heavy smoke, burns hot and is hard to put out. Fire-safety guidance generally recommends keeping any combustible mulch, rubber included, a few feet from the foundation, vents and wooden decks, and never next to grills, fire pits or places where cigarettes are discarded. Gravel or pavers are the best choice immediately beside a house in wildfire-prone areas.

Keep rubber mulch away from the house and from heat sources. It can reach high surface temperatures in full sun, so avoid it where bare feet or pets play, and think twice about hot, dry climates. Choose a non-combustible ring of gravel or pavers around foundations.

What about playgrounds?

Rubber is common on playgrounds because it cushions falls. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission playground handbook lists loose-fill depths by fall height; for a 10-foot fall height, it lists about 9 inches of wood chips and about 6 inches of shredded rubber, uncompressed. Those depths are far deeper than the 2–3 inches used in garden beds. Playground surfacing needs to meet impact-attenuation standards and be maintained, so for a play area use the CPSC handbook and ASTM F1292 as your guide, or consult a certified playground inspector.

Bonded or poured-in-place rubber surfacing is different from loose rubber mulch and is installed professionally.

Other pros and cons at a glance

FactorWood mulchRubber mulch
Cost per yard (example)About $40About $236
Feeds the soilYesNo
Lifespan1–3 yearsMany years
Blows or floats awayCan float in heavy rainStays put better
Fire behaviorBurns; smoldersBurns hot, hard to extinguish
Vegetable gardenPaths and perennialsNot recommended
RemovalEasy; can be dug into soil or left to rotHard; pieces can persist in soil for years
Heat in summerCoolWarms up in sun

How do you install rubber mulch if you choose it?

  1. Clear and weed the bed completely, because rubber is very hard to separate from soil later.
  2. Lay landscape fabric or a weed barrier if you want a clean removal later, and cut slits for plants.
  3. Spread 2–3 inches (about 1.2 to 1.9 cubic yards per 200 sq ft) and rake it level.
  4. Edge the bed with a firm border so it stays out of the lawn, where it can damage mower blades.

Wind-blown leaves and dust settle on top of any mulch, so rubber still needs the occasional raking and weeding.

Which should you choose?

  1. Vegetable gardens, perennial beds and trees: wood (or straw, leaves, compost).
  2. Playgrounds: follow safety standards; rubber and engineered wood fiber are both used at the proper depth.
  3. Low-maintenance borders away from the house: rubber is an option if you accept the cost and the lack of soil benefit.
  4. Next to the foundation: use gravel or pavers rather than either.
  5. Tight budget or big area: wood chips from a local tree service or landscape yard.

Frequently asked questions

Does rubber mulch attract bugs?

Rubber is not a food source so it does not draw termites or ants the way damp wood can. Insects can still shelter under any mulch, so keep it off the foundation.

Is rubber mulch bad for the soil?

It does not improve soil, and tires can contain zinc and other compounds that some extension sources advise against around edible plants. For soil health, organic mulch is better.

How much rubber mulch do I need?

The same volume as wood at the same depth: square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 gives cubic yards. 200 sq ft at 3 inches needs 1.85 cubic yards.

Can you put rubber mulch over wood mulch?

You can, but it is better to remove the wood first. Wood decomposes underneath, leaves the layer uneven and can make the rubber sink and mix into soil.

Which mulch is better for a sloped yard?

Shredded wood mats together and stays put on slopes. Rubber also resists washing but is harder to rake back into place, so shredded wood is a good default.

Does rubber mulch get hot in summer?

Yes. Dark rubber can become noticeably hotter than wood in direct sun, so avoid it where children play barefoot and in very hot climates.

The bottom line

Choose wood mulch for gardens, trees and vegetable beds, where soil health matters and the lower cost wins. Consider rubber only for playgrounds or permanent borders away from the house, and budget several times more. Price the wood option in seconds with the mulch calculator.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: US Consumer Product Safety Commission, Public Playground Safety Handbook (loose-fill surfacing depths); ASTM F1292 (impact attenuation); mulch guidance from US university extension services including Penn State Extension and the University of Maryland Extension. Prices are illustrative examples; get local quotes. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How to Improve Clay Soil for Gardening
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To improve clay soil, work 2–3 inches of compost into the top 6–8 inches, repeat every year and mulch the surface. Do not add sand, which can turn clay into concrete, and do not dig when the soil is wet. For 100 sq ft, 3 inches of compost is about 0.93 cubic yards. Improvement builds over several seasons.

Clay soil is rich in nutrients and holds water well, yet it can be the hardest soil to garden in: sticky and cloddy when wet, hard as brick when dry, and slow to drain. Roots struggle to push through it and, in wet spells, they can be starved of oxygen.

The good news is that you can fix it without special products. This guide covers how to test your soil, what to add and how much, what to avoid and a year-by-year plan. When you have your numbers, the soil calculator converts them into cubic yards of compost.

Key takeaways
  • Add organic matter: 2–3 inches of finished compost worked into the top 6–8 inches.
  • Never add sand to clay in small amounts; it tends to make soil denser.
  • Do not work wet clay. Wait until a handful crumbles instead of smearing.
  • Mulch and top-dress with 1–2 inches of compost each year; earthworms do the deep work.
  • Be patient: real change takes 2–3 seasons; raised beds give faster results.

How can you tell if you have clay soil?

Clay particles are tiny, packed tightly and sticky when wet. Two quick tests tell you what you have:

  • Ribbon test: squeeze a handful of moist soil between thumb and finger and push it out into a ribbon. A ribbon that holds for more than about 2 inches before breaking indicates a high clay content.
  • Jar test: fill a straight-sided jar one-third with soil, add water to near the top and a teaspoon of dish soap, then shake and let it settle. Sand settles in about a minute, silt in a few hours and clay over a day or more. A clay layer above half of the total is a heavy clay.
  • Drainage test: dig a hole 12 inches deep, fill it with water, let it drain, then fill again. Water that drains slower than about 1 inch per hour is generally considered poor drainage, and water still standing after a day signals a real problem.

For nutrient and pH results, send a sample to your state's extension soil-testing lab. Clay soils are often fertile and near-neutral to alkaline, so what you need is structure, not fertilizer.

What is the best way to improve clay soil?

Add plenty of organic matter: compost, aged leaf mold, well-rotted manure or composted bark fines. As organic matter breaks down it glues clay particles into crumbs. The spaces between the crumbs carry air and water, so the soil drains better and still holds moisture.

  1. Check moisture. Squeeze a handful. If it forms a sticky ball that stays put, wait. If it crumbles when poked, you can work it.
  2. Spread 2–3 inches of compost over the bed.
  3. Loosen the soil with a garden fork, 8–12 inches deep, rather than rototilling. Tilling clay breaks the crumb structure and can create a hard pan below.
  4. Mix the compost into the top 6–8 inches so that it makes up roughly a quarter to a third of the volume.
  5. Rake smooth and plant, or mulch with 2–3 inches of shredded leaves or wood chips.
  6. Repeat each year with 1–2 inches of fresh compost on top.

How much compost do you need?

The formula is square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards. These quantities are before a 10% allowance.

Area2 in3 in4 in
4 × 8 ft bed (32 sq ft)5.3 cu ft · 0.20 yd8 cu ft · 0.30 yd10.7 cu ft · 0.40 yd
100 sq ft0.62 yd0.93 yd1.23 yd
200 sq ft1.23 yd1.85 yd2.47 yd
1,000 sq ft6.17 yd9.26 yd12.35 yd

For a 4 × 8 ft bed at 3 inches, that is 8 cubic feet, or 4 bags of 2 cubic feet.

🧮

Have a bed with odd corners or several areas? Use the soil calculator to convert your dimensions and amendment depth into cubic yards, bags and weight.

Should you add sand or gypsum to clay?

Skip sand. Mixing a small amount of sand into clay produces a dense, brick-like material, like the ingredients of adobe. You would need to add sand to roughly half the volume of the soil to change its texture, which is impractical. Coarse materials like fine bark or compost work better.

Gypsum is often recommended online, but extension guidance generally says it only helps in sodic soils (high sodium, common in arid regions), which a lab test can identify. In most home gardens it makes little difference compared with organic matter.

What else helps clay soil?

  • Mulch. A permanent 2–3 inch layer of shredded leaves or wood chips feeds earthworms and prevents the surface from crusting.
  • Cover crops. Deep-rooted crops such as daikon radish, clover or winter rye open channels in the soil and add organic matter when turned under or chopped.
  • No-dig layers. Instead of tilling, put 3–4 inches of compost on top each year and let worms mix it in.
  • Raised beds. A 10–12 inch raised bed filled with a topsoil-compost mix gives you good soil immediately, while the ground below slowly improves.
  • Mounds and swales. Planting on a gentle mound sheds winter wet from roots of shrubs and perennials.
  • Stay off wet soil. Walking on it compacts it. Use boards or paths.

Which plants grow well in clay soil?

While you improve the soil, choose plants that tolerate it. Many natives and tough perennials do: asters, coneflower (Echinacea), black-eyed Susan, bee balm, daylilies and hostas, as well as shrubs such as viburnum and dogwood. In vegetable gardens, brassicas (cabbage, broccoli), lettuce, beans and squash cope better than carrots and potatoes, which need loose soil unless you use raised beds. Check your local extension for a list for your region.

What mistakes make clay soil worse?

  1. Digging when wet. Wet clay smears into clods that dry as hard as pottery. If a handful holds a tight, shiny ball, wait a few days.
  2. Walking on beds. Foot traffic squeezes out the air spaces you are trying to build. Set up permanent paths and keep beds narrow enough to reach across, about 4 feet.
  3. Adding too little. A thin sprinkle of compost does nothing. Plan on a real layer, 2–3 inches, the first year.
  4. Digging a planting hole and backfilling with all-new soil. The hole becomes a clay-walled bathtub that holds water around the roots. Mix some compost with the native soil and make the hole wide rather than deep.
  5. Overwatering. Clay holds moisture longer than sandy soil, so check a few inches down before watering again.

A simple yearly plan for clay

WhenTask
FallSpread 2–3 inches of compost or shredded leaves; sow a cover crop; stay off wet soil
Early springWait for soil to crumble, fork it loose and rake in any remaining cover crop
Planting timeAdd 1–2 inches of compost around transplants, mulch 2–3 inches
SummerWater deeply and infrequently; clay holds moisture longer than you think
Next yearRepeat; expect noticeably better structure by year 2–3

Frequently asked questions

Will adding compost really fix clay soil?

It will not turn clay into loam overnight, but yearly compost makes it crumbly and well drained over two to three seasons. It is the single most effective amendment.

Can I grow vegetables in clay soil?

Yes. Many crops, including tomatoes, beans, brassicas and squash, do well once the soil has been amended. For carrots and potatoes, a raised bed is easier.

Should I till clay soil?

Avoid rototilling, especially when wet. It destroys soil structure and can create a hard layer below. Loosen with a garden fork and add organic matter on the surface instead.

Why does my clay soil crack in summer?

Clay shrinks as it dries, opening cracks that can tear roots. Mulch, organic matter and deep, infrequent watering reduce the swings between wet and dry.

How long does it take to improve clay soil?

Most gardeners see better structure after the first season of compost and clear improvement after two to three. Continued yearly additions keep the benefit.

Is coffee grounds or mulch good for clay soil?

Both are fine in moderation. Mulch feeds soil life as it decomposes, while coffee grounds should be composted or applied in thin layers to avoid forming a crust.

The bottom line

Improve clay by working 2–3 inches of compost into the top 6–8 inches, repeating yearly and mulching, while avoiding sand and wet digging. A 100 sq ft bed needs about 0.93 cubic yards at 3 inches. Use the soil calculator to work out your own amount.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Clay soil improvement and amendment guidance from US university extension services, including Colorado State University Extension, Penn State Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; soil texture methods from USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. Volume conversion: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How to Calculate Cubic Yards for Soil, Mulch and Gravel
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Cubic yards = length (ft) × width (ft) × depth (ft) ÷ 27. If depth is in inches, use square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324. For example, a 10 × 12 ft area covered 4 inches deep is 120 × 4 ÷ 324 = 1.48 cubic yards. A cubic yard of soil, mulch or gravel is 27 cubic feet.

Bulk soil, mulch, sand and gravel are all sold by the cubic yard, yet we measure garden space in feet and depth in inches. That mismatch is where orders go wrong. One conversion, 27, and one shortcut, 324, solve it.

This page walks through the formulas with worked examples for rectangles, circles, triangles and trenches, then gives a quick-reference chart and the conversion to tons for gravel. For fast answers on any project, use the topsoil and gravel calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Feet formula: length × width × depth (all in feet) ÷ 27 = cubic yards.
  • Inches shortcut: square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards.
  • One cubic yard: 27 cubic feet, which covers 324 sq ft at 1 inch deep or 108 sq ft at 3 inches.
  • Gravel and stone: about 1.4 tons per cubic yard, but check with your supplier.
  • Order 5–10% extra for settling and uneven ground; round up to the next half yard.

What is a cubic yard?

A cubic yard is a cube that measures 3 feet on each side: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic feet. In visual terms, it is about the size of a washing machine or a small fridge lying down. It is also roughly 4.5 wheelbarrow loads (a 6 cu ft barrow) or 6.75 loads in a 4 cu ft barrow.

Cubic yards are the standard unit for bulk landscape materials in the US, including topsoil, compost, mulch, sand and gravel. Bagged products are sold in cubic feet, so you need to convert between the two.

How do you calculate cubic yards step by step?

  1. Measure length and width of the area in feet. For irregular shapes, see below.
  2. Choose a depth and convert to feet by dividing inches by 12 (3 inches = 0.25 ft; 4 inches = 0.33 ft).
  3. Multiply length × width × depth to get cubic feet.
  4. Divide by 27 to get cubic yards.
  5. Add 5–10% and round up.

Example: a 10 × 12 ft area at 4 inches deep. 10 × 12 × 0.333 = 40 cubic feet. 40 ÷ 27 = 1.48 cubic yards. With 10% extra, 1.63, so order 1.75 or 2 cubic yards, depending on the supplier's increments.

What is the quick formula using square feet and inches?

Because 12 inches per foot × 27 cubic feet per yard = 324, you can skip the depth conversion: square feet × inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards. The same 10 × 12 ft area at 4 inches: 120 × 4 ÷ 324 = 1.48. The same answer, one fewer step.

🧮

Skip the arithmetic. Enter your dimensions in the topsoil and gravel calculator and get cubic yards, tons and bags in one step, with an allowance for settling.

Cubic yard chart: how much do you need by area and depth?

Area1 in2 in3 in4 in6 in
50 sq ft0.150.310.460.620.93
100 sq ft0.310.620.931.231.85
200 sq ft0.621.231.852.473.70
500 sq ft1.543.094.636.179.26
1,000 sq ft3.096.179.2612.3518.52

All values are cubic yards. For double the area, double the number; for double the depth, double the number.

How do you measure irregular shapes?

  • Circle: area = 3.14 × radius × radius. A circle 12 ft across has a 6 ft radius: 3.14 × 36 = 113 sq ft. At 3 inches deep: 113 × 3 ÷ 324 = 1.05 cubic yards.
  • Triangle: area = base × height ÷ 2.
  • L-shape or complex layout: split into rectangles and add. A 12 × 10 ft section plus an 8 × 6 ft section = 120 + 48 = 168 sq ft.
  • Curved bed: take three or four widths along its length, average them and multiply by the length.
  • Trench or footing: length × width × depth. A 30 ft trench 1 ft wide and 1 ft deep is 30 cubic feet = 1.11 cubic yards.
  • Sloped or uneven ground: measure the depth at several points and use the average.

How do you convert cubic yards to tons?

Gravel, crushed stone and sand are often sold by the ton, so you need weight. A common rule of thumb is about 1.4 tons per cubic yard for crushed stone and gravel, which is where you get the 1 ton ≈ 0.71 cubic yards figure. Actual density varies with stone size, moisture and type (roughly 1.2–1.5 tons per cubic yard), so always ask the supplier for their conversion.

Example: a gravel path 20 ft long, 3 ft wide and 3 inches deep: 60 sq ft × 3 ÷ 324 = 0.56 cubic yards. × 1.4 = 0.78 tons. In practice, round up to 1 ton.

Cubic yards of gravelApproximate tons (at 1.4 t/yd)
11.4
22.8
34.2
57.0

Soil and compost are lighter per yard: topsoil is about 1 to 1.4 tons per cubic yard depending on moisture, and wood mulch roughly 0.2 to 0.4 tons.

How many bags equal a cubic yard?

  • 1 cubic foot bags: 27 bags
  • 1.5 cubic foot bags: 18 bags
  • 2 cubic foot bags: 13.5 bags
  • 3 cubic foot bags: 9 bags

Bags of gravel or sand are often sold by weight (40 or 50 lb) rather than volume, so use tons instead: a ton is 2,000 lb, or 40–50 of those bags.

Worked examples for common projects

ProjectMathResult
Mulch a 20 × 4 ft bed, 3 in deep80 × 3 ÷ 3240.74 cu yd
Gravel base for a 12 × 14 ft patio, 4 in deep168 × 4 ÷ 3242.07 cu yd (about 2.9 tons)
Top-dress 1,000 sq ft of lawn, 1/2 in1,000 × 0.5 ÷ 3241.54 cu yd
Fill a 4 × 8 ft raised bed, 12 in deep32 cu ft ÷ 271.19 cu yd

In each case, add 5–10% before you order, then round to the supplier's increments (many sell by the half yard).

Common mistakes when calculating cubic yards

The most expensive mistake is the depth unit. Mixing feet and inches turns a 4 inch layer into a 4 foot one, a 12-fold error. Convert inches to feet (divide by 12) or use the 324 shortcut, and never mix the two.
  1. Forgetting 27. Dividing cubic feet by 3 (feet in a yard) instead of 27 gives a result 9 times too high.
  2. Rounding down. Always round up; running short means a second delivery fee.
  3. Ignoring compaction. Gravel and road base compact 10–20% when tamped, soil settles, and mulch fluffs.
  4. Measuring the wrong depth. Use the finished depth, not the depth of a layer that is already there.
  5. Ignoring obstacles. Subtract areas you will not fill, like a tree trunk circle or a paved patch.

Frequently asked questions

How many cubic feet are in a cubic yard?

There are 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard, because a cubic yard is 3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft. Divide cubic feet by 27 to convert to cubic yards.

How do I convert square feet to cubic yards?

Multiply the square footage by the depth in inches, then divide by 324. For 500 sq ft at 3 inches deep: 500 × 3 ÷ 324 = 4.63 cubic yards.

How many wheelbarrows are in a cubic yard?

A standard 6 cubic foot wheelbarrow holds about 0.22 cubic yards, so a yard takes 4.5 full loads. A 4 cubic foot barrow needs nearly 7.

How much does a cubic yard of gravel weigh?

Roughly 1.4 tons, or about 2,800 pounds, for typical crushed stone or gravel. It varies with stone size and moisture, so confirm with your supplier.

How many square feet does a cubic yard cover?

A cubic yard covers 324 sq ft at 1 inch deep, 162 at 2 inches, 108 at 3 inches and 81 at 4 inches.

How much does a pickup truck hold in cubic yards?

A full-size pickup with a 6.5 ft bed holds about 2 cubic yards of light material like mulch, but far less of heavy material. A yard of gravel can approach the payload of a half-ton truck.

The bottom line

To calculate cubic yards, multiply length by width by depth in feet and divide by 27, or use square feet × inches ÷ 324. Add 5–10%, round up, and convert to tons for gravel. For any project, the topsoil and gravel calculator gives the answer instantly.

Related tools: Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; material densities from US university extension and state transportation aggregate guidance (approximate, vary by product); mulching and soil-volume guidance from US university extension services including Penn State Extension and University of Maryland Extension. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Much Soil for a Raised Bed? Charts for Every Size
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Multiply length × width × depth in feet to get cubic feet of soil. A 4 × 8 ft raised bed filled 12 inches deep needs 32 cubic feet, or 1.19 cubic yards. Divide cubic feet by 27 for yards, or by the bag size (usually 1.5–2 cu ft) for bags. Add about 10% because fresh soil settles.

Filling a raised bed is the biggest single cost of getting started, and the most common place to miscalculate. Order too little and you are stuck with a half-filled bed and a second trip. Order too much and you are paying for soil you do not need. Both are avoidable with one multiplication.
