Below are the formula, charts for common sizes in cubic feet, cubic yards and bags, and tips for cutting the cost. For beds that are not rectangles, or to compare bagged and bulk soil, use the soil calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: length (ft) × width (ft) × depth (ft) = cubic feet. Depth in inches ÷ 12.
  • 4 × 8 ft at 12 in: 32 cu ft = 1.19 cu yd = 16 bags of 2 cu ft (22 bags of 1.5 cu ft).
  • Settling: add about 10%, because fresh soil and compost compact.
  • Depth: 6–8 in works for greens; 10–12 in suits most vegetables; 18 in or more helps root crops and poor native soil.
  • Cost trick: bulk soil is far cheaper per cubic foot than bags once you need over about 1 cubic yard.

How do you calculate soil for a raised bed?

Raised-bed volume is a box: length × width × depth. Use feet for all three, so a depth of 12 inches is 1 foot.

  1. Measure the inside of the bed (not the outside of the frame).
  2. Convert depth to feet by dividing inches by 12. Eight inches is 0.67 ft.
  3. Multiply length × width × depth for cubic feet.
  4. Convert if needed. Cubic feet ÷ 27 = cubic yards. Cubic feet ÷ bag size = bags.
  5. Add 10% for settling and round up.

Example: a 4 × 8 ft bed filled 12 inches: 4 × 8 × 1 = 32 cubic feet. ÷ 27 = 1.19 cubic yards. With 10% extra, 35.2 cubic feet, which is 17.6 bags of 2 cu ft, so buy 18.

How much soil does each raised bed size need?

Volumes are inside dimensions, filled to the stated depth, before any settling allowance.

Bed size6 in deep8 in deep12 in deep
2 × 4 ft4 cu ft · 0.15 yd5.3 cu ft · 0.20 yd8 cu ft · 0.30 yd
4 × 4 ft8 cu ft · 0.30 yd10.7 cu ft · 0.40 yd16 cu ft · 0.59 yd
3 × 6 ft9 cu ft · 0.33 yd12 cu ft · 0.44 yd18 cu ft · 0.67 yd
4 × 8 ft16 cu ft · 0.59 yd21.3 cu ft · 0.79 yd32 cu ft · 1.19 yd
4 × 12 ft24 cu ft · 0.89 yd32 cu ft · 1.19 yd48 cu ft · 1.78 yd

For taller beds, soil volume scales directly with depth. An 18-inch-deep 4 × 8 ft bed holds 48 cubic feet (1.78 cubic yards), and a 4 × 12 ft bed at 18 inches holds 72 cubic feet (2.67 cubic yards).

How many bags of soil do I need?

This table assumes 2 cubic foot bags and includes the 10% settling allowance, rounded up. For 1.5 cubic foot bags, multiply by 1.33 and round up; for 3 cubic foot bags, multiply by 0.67.

Bed size6 in8 in12 in
2 × 4 ft335
4 × 4 ft569
3 × 6 ft5710
4 × 8 ft91218
4 × 12 ft141827
🧮

Planning several beds, or a bed with an L shape or curve? Use the soil calculator. Enter length, width and depth, and it returns cubic feet, cubic yards, bags and weight.

How deep should the soil be?

Depth drives both cost and results. Roots can grow into the ground below if the bed sits on bare soil, so the fill only needs to be as deep as the roots will use.

  • 6–8 inches: lettuce, spinach, radishes, herbs and other shallow roots. Good for budget beds set directly on loosened ground.
  • 10–12 inches: most vegetables, including tomatoes, peppers, beans, cucumbers and carrots (short types).
  • 18 inches or more: deep-rooted or long crops, beds over concrete or compacted soil, and accessible tall beds.

If the bed sits on soil, loosen the ground under it with a fork first, and roots will reach well below the frame.

How much does it cost to fill a raised bed?

The same 32 cubic feet costs very different amounts depending on how you buy it. Using example prices: bagged raised-bed mix at $6 for 1.5 cubic feet works out to $4 per cubic foot, and bulk garden soil or blended mix at $45 per cubic yard is about $1.67 per cubic foot.

Source (example prices)For 32 cu ft
Bagged mix, $6 per 1.5 cu ft22 bags = $132
Bulk mix, $45 per cubic yard (1.19 yd)$53 plus delivery

Delivery fees can erase the bulk savings for one small bed, but for two or more beds, bulk is usually the cheaper route. Local prices vary widely, so get quotes.

How can you use less soil?

For tall beds, you can fill the bottom with wood or other bulky organic material instead of all soil. This is the idea behind "hugelkultur" and lasagna filling. If the bottom third of a 4 × 8 ft bed at 12 inches is branches and logs, soil need drops from 32 to about 21 cubic feet (0.79 cubic yards). The trade-off is that the organic fill breaks down and the bed settles over several years, so top it up with compost. Use only untreated wood, and avoid black walnut.

Do not use all topsoil or all compost. Straight topsoil compacts and drains poorly in a bed, while pure compost can be too rich and too fluffy and shrink quickly. See our raised bed soil mix guide for blends that work.

5 mistakes to avoid when ordering raised bed soil

  1. Using outside dimensions. Frames are 1.5 inches thick, which on a 4 × 8 ft bed overstates volume by roughly 10%.
  2. Forgetting settling. Fresh mixes with lots of compost shrink 10–20% in the first season.
  3. Mixing up cubic feet and bags. Bags labeled in quarts or liters are smaller than they sound: a 40-quart bag is only about 1.5 cubic feet, since 1 cubic foot is roughly 26 dry quarts.
  4. Buying "fill dirt". It is subsoil with little organic matter; use topsoil, garden soil or a raised-bed mix.
  5. Overfilling. Leave an inch or two below the rim so water does not wash soil out.

Frequently asked questions

How many cubic feet of soil are in a 4×8 raised bed?

A 4 × 8 ft raised bed filled to 12 inches holds 32 cubic feet. At 8 inches it holds 21.3 cubic feet and at 6 inches 16 cubic feet.

How many bags of soil for a 4x4 raised bed?

A 4 × 4 ft bed filled 12 inches deep needs 16 cubic feet, which is 8 bags of 2 cu ft or 11 bags of 1.5 cu ft, rounded up. Add a bag or two for settling.

How many cubic yards of soil do I need for a 3×6 raised bed?

A 3 × 6 ft bed at 12 inches deep needs 18 cubic feet, which is 0.67 cubic yards. At 8 inches deep it needs 12 cubic feet, or 0.44 cubic yards.

How do I convert cubic feet to cubic yards for soil?

Divide cubic feet by 27, because a cubic yard is 3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft = 27 cubic feet. For example, 54 cubic feet is 2 cubic yards.

Is it cheaper to buy soil in bags or bulk for raised beds?

Bulk is usually cheaper per cubic foot once you need around a cubic yard or more, but delivery fees matter. Bags win for one small bed or a top-up.

Can I put cardboard or landscape fabric under a raised bed?

Cardboard under the soil suppresses grass and rots away within a season. Avoid plastic sheets, which block drainage, and fabric that restricts roots from reaching deeper soil.

The bottom line

Multiply length × width × depth in feet, convert to cubic yards or bags, then add 10% for settling. A 4 × 8 ft bed at 12 inches needs 32 cubic feet (1.19 cubic yards). For several beds or odd shapes, the soil calculator gives you the totals in seconds.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Raised-bed guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Oregon State University Extension and Colorado State University Extension. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; 1 cubic foot ≈ 28.3 liters. Prices are illustrative examples. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Deep Should Mulch Be? Depth Guide by Mulch Type
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Mulch should be 2–3 inches deep for fine, shredded mulch and 3–4 inches deep for coarse wood chips or bark nuggets. Compost and leaf mold need only 1–2 inches. Never exceed 4 inches, and keep mulch 3–6 inches away from trunks and stems. Add a new layer only when the old one has thinned to about 1 inch.

Mulch depth is the one setting that decides whether mulch helps or hurts. Too little and weeds sail through. Too much and the layer sheds rain, holds the soil soggy and starves roots of oxygen. Most gardeners get this wrong in the same direction: they pile it on, then top it up every spring.

This guide gives the right depth for each mulch type, shows what a cubic yard covers at every depth, and explains how to check what you already have before buying more. If you want exact quantities, the mulch calculator converts your bed size and depth into cubic yards and bags.

Key takeaways
  • Most beds: 2–3 inches of shredded or fine-textured mulch.
  • Coarse mulch: 3–4 inches for wood chips and bark nuggets, which have air gaps.
  • Soil builders: 1–2 inches of compost or leaf mold, topped with something coarser if you want weed control.
  • Hard limit: never more than 4 inches, and never against a trunk or stem.
  • Topping up: measure what is left and add only the difference, to reach your target.

What is the right depth for mulch?

University extension services in different regions land on a similar range: roughly 2 to 4 inches of organic mulch, with the exact figure set by how coarse the material is. Fine mulches knit into a dense mat, so a thinner layer blocks light. Coarse pieces leave gaps, so you need more depth to get the same weed control.

The aim is a layer thick enough to block light and slow evaporation, but thin enough that air and water still reach the soil. Water needs to soak through rather than run off the top.

How deep should each type of mulch be?

Mulch typeDepthNotes
Shredded hardwood or dyed mulch2–3 inMats together; thicker layers can crust and shed water
Wood chips (arborist chips)3–4 inCoarse; best for trees, paths and shrub borders
Bark nuggets3–4 inBig gaps, so go deeper; they can float and wash in heavy rain
Pine straw3–4 in looseSettles to about 2 in within weeks
Straw (vegetable beds)3–4 in looseThinner layers let weeds through; see the vegetable mulch guide for details
Shredded leaves2–3 inMats if left whole; shred first
Compost or leaf mold1–2 inFeeds the soil; weed control is weaker
Pea gravel or river rock2–3 inDoes not break down; use fabric or a separate base layer

Pine straw and straw look deep when you spread them but compress as they get wet, which is why the table lists loose depth. Measure after the first rain and top up if it has dropped well below 2 inches.

How much mulch does each depth need?

Depth is a multiplier on volume, so every extra inch adds real cost. One cubic yard covers 324 square feet at 1 inch, and the coverage divides as you go deeper.

Depth1 cubic yard coversCubic yards for 100 sq ft2 cu ft bags for 100 sq ft
1 in324 sq ft0.315 (4.2 exactly)
2 in162 sq ft0.629 (8.3 exactly)
3 in108 sq ft0.9313 (12.5 exactly)
4 in81 sq ft1.2317 (16.7 exactly)
6 in54 sq ft1.8525

The formula behind the table is square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 = cubic yards. Going from 3 to 4 inches adds a third more mulch for little extra benefit, and going to 6 inches doubles the cost of a 3-inch layer.

🧮

Not sure how much your beds will take at your chosen depth? Enter your bed sizes in the mulch calculator and it will return cubic yards, bags and weight for 2, 3 or 4 inches.

How do you measure the mulch you already have?

Do not guess. Push a ruler or the tip of a trowel straight down through the mulch until you hit soil, then read the depth. Check three or four spots, because mulch is rarely even: it is thicker where you dumped it and thinner near edges and slopes.

  1. Measure in at least four places across the bed.
  2. Rake the surface to break any crust and loosen matted areas.
  3. Subtract the average depth from your target. If you have 1 inch and want 3, you need 2 inches of new mulch.
  4. Calculate the volume for the difference, not the full depth.

This one habit saves most people money. Refreshing a 200 sq ft bed from 1 inch to 3 inches needs 2 inches of new mulch, which is 1.23 cubic yards. Treating it as a fresh bed at 3 inches would have you buying 1.85 cubic yards, half again too much.

What happens if mulch is too deep?

Very deep mulch is the most common landscape mulch mistake. Layers beyond about 4 inches can cause several problems:

  • Water runs off or stays on top. Thick, matted mulch can shed light rain, so the soil underneath stays dry while the surface looks wet.
  • Roots grow upward into the mulch. Shallow roots in mulch dry out quickly and are exposed to cold.
  • Oxygen drops in the soil beneath, especially in heavy clay.
  • Pests and rot. Deep mulch against bark stays damp, which favors rot and gives rodents cover.
Keep a clear collar around every trunk and stem. Pull mulch back 3–6 inches so the root flare and bark stay dry. A cone of mulch against a tree (a "mulch volcano") is far worse than thin mulch.

What happens if mulch is too thin?

Under about 2 inches, light still gets through, and weed seeds in the soil germinate. Thin mulch also dries and breaks down fast, so you end up re-mulching more often. If weeds appear through a thin layer, add mulch to reach the target depth rather than starting over. Pull perennial weeds first, because they will push through any depth.

Do slopes, trees and vegetable beds need different depths?

  • Trees: 2–4 inches of wood chips over as wide an area as practical, ideally out toward the drip line, with the trunk collar clear.
  • Slopes: shredded mulch locks together and stays put better than nuggets, which roll in heavy rain. Stay near 2–3 inches.
  • Vegetable beds: straw, shredded leaves or compost, at 2–3 inches, pulled back from the stems of seedlings.
  • Perennial beds: 2 inches is enough, and keep it off the crowns of plants.
  • Paths: 3–4 inches of wood chips on landscape fabric or cardboard lasts longer and stays drier.

How often should mulch be topped up?

Organic mulch breaks down over one to three years depending on the material and climate. Rather than adding a fixed amount every spring, use the ruler test and refresh only when the layer has thinned to about 1 inch. In many beds that is every second year, and an annual light raking is enough in between.

Frequently asked questions

Is 4 inches of mulch too much?

Four inches is the upper limit and only suits coarse wood chips or bark nuggets. For shredded hardwood, 4 inches can mat and shed water, so stay at 2–3 inches.

Can you put new mulch on top of old mulch?

Yes, if the old layer is thin. Measure it first and add only enough to reach 2–3 inches in total, and rake or fluff matted old mulch before topping up.

How deep should mulch be around a tree?

Use 2–4 inches of wood chips spread as wide as practical, keeping the trunk collar clear by 3–6 inches. The wider the ring, the more the roots benefit.

How deep should mulch be to stop weeds?

About 3 inches of shredded mulch, or 3–4 inches of coarse chips, blocks light well enough to suppress most annual weeds. Perennial weeds need pulling first.

How much deeper does mulch settle after it rains?

Fresh, fluffy mulch commonly compacts by 10–20% in the first weeks, and pine straw can settle by about a third. Start slightly deeper than your target or plan a light top-up.

Does mulch depth differ for flower beds and shrub borders?

Slightly. Perennial beds do well at about 2 inches kept off the plant crowns, while shrub borders and tree rings can take 3–4 inches of coarse mulch.

The bottom line

Aim for 2–3 inches of shredded mulch or 3–4 inches of coarse chips, keep it clear of stems, and check the depth with a ruler before adding more. Multiply square feet by depth in inches, divide by 324, and you have cubic yards. The free mulch calculator does it for any number of beds.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Soil Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Mulching guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; tree-mulching practice from the International Society of Arboriculture. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet = 324 sq ft at 1 inch. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: The Best Soil Mix for Raised Beds (Simple Recipe)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A simple, proven raised bed soil mix is about 60% topsoil, 30% compost and 10% coarse aggregate like perlite or pumice, by volume. A 4 × 8 ft bed 12 inches deep (32 cu ft) needs about 19 cu ft topsoil, 10 cu ft compost and 3 cu ft perlite. Mix on a tarp, fill the bed and water to settle it.

Raised beds are only as good as what is in them. The wrong blend dries out in a week, turns to concrete after rain, or sinks by half by midsummer. The right blend holds moisture, drains freely and feeds plants for the season.

Below are three common recipes, the ratios converted into cubic feet for common beds, and what to avoid. The soil calculator tells you how much total volume to buy first.

Key takeaways
  • Budget mix: 60% topsoil, 30% compost, 10% perlite or pumice by volume.
  • Lightweight mix: equal parts compost, peat or coir, and vermiculite (the "Mel's Mix" style).
  • Compost limit: keep compost at roughly 30–50% of the mix; more shrinks fast and can be too rich.
  • For a 4 × 8 ft bed at 12 in: 32 cu ft total; add 10% for settling.
  • Avoid: fill dirt, pure potting mix, sand mixed into clay and untreated manure.

What should you put in a raised bed?

A good raised bed mix does three jobs: hold water, drain, and supply nutrients. Mineral soil (topsoil) gives body and holds nutrients. Compost feeds microbes and plants. A coarse, light ingredient adds air space so roots can breathe. Everything else is a variation on those three.

The blends below follow the general advice of US university extension services, which commonly recommend mixing topsoil with a generous proportion of finished compost rather than using either alone.

What is the best soil mix ratio for raised beds?

MixRecipe by volumeBest forCost
A: Classic budget mix60% topsoil, 30% compost, 10% perlite or pumiceMost vegetable beds, especially large onesLowest
B: Lightweight "equal parts"1/3 compost, 1/3 peat moss or coconut coir, 1/3 vermiculiteSmall beds, containers, patio gardensHighest
C: Heavy native topsoil50% topsoil, 30% compost, 20% coarse material (perlite, pumice or small bark fines)Clay-heavy topsoil that drains slowlyMedium

Mix A is the one most gardeners should start with. Mix B is light and fluffy, but expensive to fill a large bed, and the peat in it is a non-renewable resource, which is why many gardeners prefer coir. Mix C gives heavy soils more air.

How much of each ingredient do you need?

Take the total volume of the bed, then split it by percent. These amounts are for a bed filled to 12 inches; add 10% for settling.

BedTotalMix A: topsoil / compost / perliteMix B: each of 3 parts
4 × 4 ft16 cu ft9.6 / 4.8 / 1.6 cu ft5.3 cu ft each
3 × 6 ft18 cu ft10.8 / 5.4 / 1.8 cu ft6 cu ft each
4 × 8 ft32 cu ft19.2 / 9.6 / 3.2 cu ft10.7 cu ft each
4 × 12 ft48 cu ft28.8 / 14.4 / 4.8 cu ft16 cu ft each

For a 4 × 8 ft bed, that is 19.2 ÷ 27 = 0.71 cubic yards of topsoil, 0.36 cubic yards of compost and about 1.6 bags of 2 cu ft perlite, rounded up to 2.

🧮

First, work out your total volume. Enter your bed dimensions in the soil calculator to see cubic feet, cubic yards and bags, then split the total with the percentages above.

How much does each mix cost to make?

Using example prices (not quotes) of $35 per cubic yard for bulk topsoil, $40 per cubic yard for bulk compost and $15 for a 2 cu ft bag of perlite, Mix A for a 4 × 8 ft bed at 12 inches costs about:

  • Topsoil: 0.71 yd × $35 = $25
  • Compost: 0.36 yd × $40 = $14
  • Perlite: 2 bags × $15 = $30
  • Total: about $69 before delivery, against roughly $132 for 22 bags of ready-made mix at $6 per 1.5 cu ft.

Perlite is the surprise cost. You can cut the bill by using less aggregate (down to 5%), or by skipping it if your topsoil is already sandy and drains well. Delivery fees apply to bulk loads, so it makes sense for two or more beds.

How do you mix and fill a raised bed?

  1. Loosen the ground under the bed with a garden fork so roots and water can move down.
  2. Lay the ingredients on a tarp in the right ratio. A 5-gallon bucket (0.67 cu ft) is a handy unit: Mix A for a 32 cu ft bed is about 29 buckets of topsoil, 14 of compost and 5 of perlite.
  3. Mix with a shovel until it looks uniform, with no pockets of pure compost.
  4. Fill in layers of 4–6 inches and water each lightly to settle.
  5. Leave 1–2 inches below the rim.
  6. Top up with compost after the first month if the bed has sunk.

Which ingredients are worth the money?

  • Topsoil: a screened, weed-free product from a landscape supplier is much better than bags of cheap "fill". Ask for a sample and feel it: it should crumble, not form a hard ball or stay powdery.
  • Compost: use finished, dark, earthy-smelling compost. A mix of sources (yard waste, composted manure, mushroom compost) gives broader nutrients. Salt-heavy compost can hurt seedlings, so check the supplier.
  • Perlite or pumice: improves drainage and air. Coarse sand is a poor substitute, since sand mixed into clay can set like concrete; if used, it must be coarse and a large share.
  • Peat or coir: hold water and keep the mix light. Coir is more sustainable; peat is acidic, so a mix with a lot of peat may need lime.
  • Vermiculite: holds water and nutrients; mostly used in the lightweight mix.
Don't fill with cheap fill dirt or pure potting soil. Fill dirt is subsoil with almost no organic matter. Potting mix is designed for pots and can shrink and dry fast in a large bed. Avoid raw manure and any compost with unknown herbicide residue.

How do you check and adjust your mix?

Most vegetables grow best at a soil pH of about 6.0–7.0. A simple lab test from your state extension service or a commercial lab checks pH, nutrient levels and organic matter. Test before adding lime or sulfur, which can do harm if applied blindly. Also do a water check: after a good soaking, the bed should drain within a few hours without standing water, and the soil should stay moist about an inch down.

Each spring, add 1–2 inches of fresh compost on top and rake it in lightly. Over the years the soil level drops as organic matter breaks down; topping up restores both volume and fertility.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use only compost in a raised bed?

Pure compost is usually too rich and fluffy, and it shrinks quickly. Most guidance recommends keeping compost at roughly 30–50% of the mix and blending it with topsoil.

Can I use potting soil in a raised bed?

You can, but it is expensive in bulk and dries out and shrinks quickly. It works better as an amendment for part of the mix or for containers than as the whole fill.

Should I add sand to my raised bed soil?

Generally no. Fine sand mixed with clay can make a dense, concrete-like soil. Perlite or pumice improve drainage more safely.

What is Mel's Mix?

Mel's Mix is a popular lightweight recipe from the Square Foot Gardening method: equal parts compost, peat moss (or coconut coir) and vermiculite. It is light and holds water but costs more than a topsoil-based blend.

How often should I replace raised bed soil?

You rarely need to replace it. Add 1–2 inches of compost each year and rotate crops. Replace only if the soil has disease problems, is contaminated or has broken down to almost nothing.

Do I need to fill the bottom of the bed with branches or rocks?

No. Rocks at the bottom do not improve drainage. A layer of logs or branches can reduce the amount of soil you need but they break down and the bed will settle.

The bottom line

A mix of about 60% topsoil, 30% compost and 10% perlite suits most raised vegetable beds, and a 4 × 8 ft bed at 12 inches needs 32 cubic feet in total. Add 10% for settling, top up with compost each spring, and use the soil calculator to get your totals.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Raised-bed and soil-mix guidance from US university extension services, including Oregon State University Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and Penn State Extension. Soil pH ranges from state extension soil-testing guidance. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; 1 US gallon = 0.134 cubic feet. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Best Mulch for Vegetable Gardens (and What to Avoid)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The best mulches for vegetable gardens are straw, shredded leaves, compost and thin layers of untreated grass clippings. Spread 2–3 inches once the soil has warmed and seedlings are established, leaving a gap around each stem. Avoid hay with seeds, dyed mulch and clippings from lawns treated with herbicide.

Mulch in a vegetable garden has to do more than in a flower bed. It must cut weeds and watering, keep soil off the fruit, and then break down into something your crops can use, because the bed gets replanted every year. Wood chips that are ideal around shrubs are often the wrong choice between tomato plants.

This guide ranks the best options, shows how deep to go for each, flags the materials to avoid and gives quantities for common raised-bed sizes. When you are ready to buy, the mulch calculator handles the math.

Key takeaways
  • Best all-round: clean straw (not hay) at 3–4 inches loose, shredded leaves at 2–3 inches.
  • Soil feeders: compost at 1–2 inches, ideally under a coarser mulch for weed control.
  • Grass clippings: only untreated, in thin 1-inch layers that dry between additions.
  • Avoid: hay full of seed, dyed or treated mulch, fresh wood chips worked into the soil, and anything from lawns treated with persistent herbicide.
  • Timing: after soil warms and seedlings are established, usually 2–4 weeks after planting warm-season crops.

What is the best mulch for a vegetable garden?

There is no single winner, because the best mulch depends on the crop and what you have available. The choices below all break down within a season or two, which suits beds that are dug or planted every year.

MulchDepthProsWatch out for
Straw3–4 in looseCheap, light, easy to move; keeps fruit clean; breaks down by next seasonMust be straw, not hay; ask if the grower sprayed herbicide
Shredded leaves2–3 inFree, feeds soil life, good for tomatoes and brassicasWhole leaves mat; shred with a mower first
Compost1–2 inFeeds plants; helps hold moistureWeed control is weak; seeds can sprout in it
Untreated grass clippingsAbout 1 in at a timeFree; nitrogen-richMats and smells if thick; avoid after herbicide use
Cardboard or newspaperSingle layer plus a top mulchSmothers weeds in new beds and pathsRemove tape and glossy ink; cover with 2–3 in of other mulch
Wood chips (paths only)3–4 inLong lasting, great between bedsNot for working into soil; can tie up nitrogen at the surface
Black plasticSheetWarms soil for heat-loving crops like melons and peppersNo organic matter; needs drip or soaker beneath

Straw or hay: which one should you use?

Straw is the dry stalk left after grain is harvested, so it carries few seeds. Hay is cut grass or legumes made for animal feed, and is full of seed heads that sprout in your beds. If you can only get hay, choose a bale described as weed-free or seed-free, and treat it as a compost ingredient rather than a mulch.

There is another issue with both, especially hay: some herbicides used on pastures and grain fields persist through animal digestion and composting, and can stunt tomatoes, beans and potatoes. Ask the seller whether the field was treated, and if you are unsure, test with a few bean seedlings in a pot before mulching the whole garden. University extension services have warned about this repeatedly.

How deep should vegetable garden mulch be?

Use less than you would in a shrub bed: 2–3 inches for most materials, 3–4 inches for loose straw, which settles. Pull mulch 1–2 inches back from stems so the stem stays dry. Very deep mulch keeps soil cold and wet early in the season, which suits lettuce and peas but slows tomatoes, peppers and squash.

🧮

Not sure how many bags or bales your beds need? Enter your bed sizes in the mulch calculator and choose 2, 3 or 4 inches to see cubic feet, bags and cost.

How much mulch does a raised vegetable bed need?

Volume is square feet × depth in inches ÷ 12, giving cubic feet. These quantities assume 2 cu ft bags and no extra for settling; add about 10%.

Bed sizeAreaAt 2 inAt 3 in
4 × 4 ft16 sq ft2.7 cu ft · 2 bags4 cu ft · 2 bags
4 × 8 ft32 sq ft5.3 cu ft · 3 bags8 cu ft · 4 bags
3 × 6 ft18 sq ft3 cu ft · 2 bags4.5 cu ft · 3 bags
4 × 12 ft48 sq ft8 cu ft · 4 bags12 cu ft · 6 bags
100 sq ft in-ground100 sq ft16.7 cu ft · 9 bags25 cu ft · 13 bags

When should you mulch vegetables?

  1. Prepare the bed. Weed it, water it and add compost or fertilizer.
  2. Plant first and wait for transplants to establish or seedlings to reach 3–4 inches.
  3. Check soil temperature. For tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, melons and squash, wait until soil is warm (roughly 60–65°F and up) so mulch does not hold cold in.
  4. Spread the mulch evenly, leaving a clear ring around every stem.
  5. Water deeply after mulching so the soil beneath is moist.
  6. Top up in midsummer if straw has settled below 2 inches.

Cool-season crops such as lettuce, spinach, kale and peas are the exception. They like cool soil, so they can be mulched earlier.

Which mulch works best for specific crops?

  • Tomatoes, peppers and eggplant: straw or shredded leaves once soil is warm. Mulch also reduces the soil splash that spreads leaf diseases.
  • Potatoes: straw or leaves, added as you hill them. Keep tubers covered so they do not turn green.
  • Strawberries: clean straw, which keeps berries off the soil.
  • Garlic and onions: a thin layer of shredded leaves or straw; garlic gets a heavier winter blanket.
  • Squash and cucumbers: straw or plastic; keep vines and fruit off damp soil.
  • Leafy greens and root crops: light compost or fine shredded leaves, since heavy mulch can hide slugs and hinder tiny seedlings.

What mulch should you avoid in a vegetable garden?

Skip these in food beds: dyed or colorized mulch (the colorants are not tested for edible gardens), rubber mulch, and wood from treated lumber or pallets. Do not use black walnut leaves or chips around tomatoes, which are sensitive to the juglone they contain. Avoid grass clippings from lawns recently treated with weed killer, and never use hay of unknown origin.

Fresh wood chips are fine on paths and as a top-dressing around berry bushes and fruit trees. They are not ideal worked into vegetable soil, because soil microbes use nitrogen to break them down.

What about slugs, pests and disease?

Damp mulch gives slugs and snails cover. In wet climates, pull it back from the stems of lettuce and strawberries, and water in the morning so the surface dries by night. On the plus side, a layer under tomatoes limits the splashing of soil-borne spores onto lower leaves, which is a common route for early blight and other leaf spot diseases. Rake mulch back in early spring to let soil warm, and put it back after.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use wood chips in my vegetable garden?

Yes, on paths and around perennial crops like berries, but avoid working fresh chips into the soil. Around annual vegetables, straw or shredded leaves break down faster and are easier to dig in.

Is hay or straw better for mulching a vegetable garden?

Straw is better because it contains few seeds. Hay sprouts weeds and may carry herbicide residue, so use only weed-free hay and ask the seller about herbicide use.

Are grass clippings safe to use as vegetable mulch?

They are safe if the lawn was not treated with herbicide in recent weeks (check the label). Spread them in layers about an inch thick and let each dry before adding more.

Should I remove mulch at the end of the season?

You can leave straw and leaves to break down and dig or rake them into the bed, which adds organic matter. Remove any diseased plant material and mulch that touched it.

Do I need mulch if I already have drip irrigation?

Drip saves water, but mulch still suppresses weeds and moderates temperature. Lay the drip line first, then mulch over or beside it.

Does mulch keep tomatoes from getting blight?

It helps by reducing soil splash on lower leaves, but it does not prevent blight on its own. Combine it with spacing, watering at the base and removing infected leaves.

The bottom line

Use clean straw or shredded leaves at 2–4 inches once the soil has warmed, keep a gap around stems and avoid hay, dyed mulch and herbicide-treated clippings. A 4 × 8 ft bed takes about 4 bags at 3 inches. For your exact beds, the mulch calculator does the math.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Vegetable-garden mulching guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; persistent-herbicide guidance from state extension and agriculture departments. Volumes: cubic feet = square feet × depth in inches ÷ 12. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Bagged vs Bulk Mulch: Cost, Quality and When Each Wins
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Bulk mulch is usually cheaper once you need more than about 2.5 to 3 cubic yards; below that, delivery fees make bagged mulch the better deal. One cubic yard equals 13.5 bags of 2 cu ft. With example prices of $4.50 per bag and $40 per yard plus $50 delivery, the break-even is 2.4 cubic yards.

Standing in the garden center aisle with 30 bags on a cart, it is easy to wonder whether a delivered pile would have been cheaper. Sometimes it would. Sometimes the delivery fee, the tarp and the shoveling make bags the smarter buy. The answer depends on the volume, the local prices and how you will move it.

Below is the break-even math with every number shown, a quality comparison, and a checklist for ordering bulk. For your own prices, the mulch calculator runs the bag-versus-bulk comparison automatically.

Key takeaways
  • Conversion: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet = 13.5 bags of 2 cu ft or 9 bags of 3 cu ft.
  • Break-even: about 2.4–3.3 cubic yards in the examples below, depending on delivery fee and prices.
  • Small jobs: under about 1.5 cubic yards, bags are almost always cheaper once delivery is added.
  • Quality: bags are consistent; bulk varies by supplier, so ask what it is made from.
  • Always: compare cost per cubic foot, not per bag.

How do you compare bagged and bulk mulch prices?

Bags are priced per bag and bulk per cubic yard, so convert both to the same unit first. The simplest is cost per cubic yard. A 2 cu ft bag holds 2/27 of a yard, so you need 13.5 bags per cubic yard. A 3 cu ft bag needs 9 bags per yard, and a 1.5 cu ft bag needs 18.

Many bags show a volume that is nominal. If the label says 2 cu ft, trust it, but compare against the same volume on the competing brand. A bag labeled 1.5 cu ft at a lower price can cost more per cubic foot.

Formula: bag price × (27 ÷ bag size in cu ft) = price per cubic yard. At $4.50 for 2 cu ft: 4.50 × 13.5 = $60.75 per cubic yard.

At what size does bulk mulch become cheaper?

Break-even depends on the delivery fee. Divide the delivery fee by the savings per cubic yard (bag cost per yard minus bulk price per yard). The three example scenarios below use made-up but typical-looking prices, so replace them with your local quotes.

Scenario (example prices)Bags per yard costBulk per yardDeliveryBreak-even
Low bulk price$3.50 bag → $47.25$35$403.3 yd (about 44 bags)
Mid$4.50 bag → $60.75$40$502.4 yd (about 33 bags)
High delivery$5.50 bag → $74.25$45$752.6 yd (about 35 bags)

In the mid scenario, the total costs by project size are:

Mulch neededBags (13.5 per yd × $4.50)Bulk ($40/yd + $50 delivery)Cheaper
1 cubic yard$60.75$90.00Bags
3 cubic yards$182.25$170.00Bulk
5 cubic yards$303.75$250.00Bulk
10 cubic yards$607.50$450.00Bulk

Big jobs widen the gap quickly. At 10 yards, the example saves $157.50, and that is before counting that bags are plastic you have to dispose of.

🧮

Have your own bag price and a quote from a landscape supplier? Enter both in the mulch calculator and it will show your exact break-even and the cheaper option for your beds.

What if you pick up bulk mulch yourself?

Many landscape suppliers let you load a truck or trailer yourself and charge only for the material. With no delivery fee, bulk wins from the first yard in our example: 1 yard at $40 against $60.75 in bags. The catch is hauling. A full-size pickup with a 6.5 ft bed holds about 2 cubic yards, and wood mulch weighs roughly 400–800 lb per cubic yard depending on moisture. Check your truck's payload rating, and never overload a small trailer.

Is bulk mulch lower quality than bagged mulch?

Not by definition, but the range is wider. Bagged mulch from major brands is screened and consistent, so you know the color and texture. Bulk mulch can be better or worse:

  • Good bulk: aged, screened hardwood or bark from a landscape supply yard. It is often darker and fresher than bags that sat on a pallet all winter.
  • Cheap bulk: mixed ground wood waste that can include pieces of treated lumber, pallets or construction debris. Ask what is in it, and avoid mulch from demolition sources.
  • Fresh unaged piles: can have a sour, vinegar or ammonia smell if they heated or went anaerobic. Extension guidance suggests spreading it thin and letting it air for a few days before it goes around plants.
  • Free arborist chips: excellent for paths, tree rings and large beds, but irregular in size and unlikely to be dyed or uniform.

Dyed mulch is available both ways. Bags list the colorant; for bulk, ask the supplier if it is dyed and with what.

Which is easier to spread: bags or a pile?

Bags are tidy and carry well, a bag at a time. Bulk dumps one big pile, then you shovel it into a wheelbarrow. A 3-yard pile is 81 cubic feet, which is about 14 loads in a 6 cu ft wheelbarrow or 20 loads in a 4 cu ft one. Either way, put a tarp under the pile to protect your driveway and to make it easy to scoop up the last of it.

How do you order bulk mulch step by step?

  1. Measure and calculate. Use square feet × depth in inches ÷ 324 for cubic yards, then add 10% for settling.
  2. Call two or three suppliers. Ask for the price per yard, delivery fee, minimum order and what the mulch is made from.
  3. Ask about the yard. Delivery trucks measure a "yard" loosely; confirm the stated quantity.
  4. Choose the drop spot. Close to the beds, on a tarp, off a street, and where the truck's weight will not crack the pavement.
  5. Spread within a few days. A big pile can heat up and the surface can crust.
Don't pay for yards you can't use. Large piles left sitting get weeds, can compact and kill the grass underneath. If an exact amount is hard to guess, order slightly under and top up with a few bags at the end.

What about waste, storage and timing?

Bags create plastic waste: a 10-yard job is 135 empty bags. Some garden centers have no take-back, so factor in the trash. Bags also stay clean and dry in the garage for weeks, while a pile outdoors should be spread within a few days, and quickly if rain is forecast. If a project will run over several weekends, bags let you work at your own pace, and bulk lets you finish in one push.

Seasonality matters too. Demand peaks in spring, when everyone mulches at once, so delivery slots book up. Ordering a week or two ahead, or buying in late fall or summer, can avoid the rush.

What is the best choice for your project?

  • Under about 1.5 cubic yards, no truck: bags.
  • A few beds, with a pickup: self-load bulk, if a yard is close by.
  • Over 3 cubic yards: delivered bulk is usually cheaper.
  • Lots of small, hard-to-reach beds: bags, because a pile has to be wheeled in anyway.
  • You want a specific color: compare directly; bags make color easy, bulk needs a sample.

Frequently asked questions

How many bags of mulch are in a cubic yard?

A cubic yard holds 27 cubic feet, so it equals 13.5 bags of 2 cu ft, 9 bags of 3 cu ft or 18 bags of 1.5 cu ft. Always round up when buying.

Is it cheaper to buy mulch in bags or bulk?

It depends on volume. With typical delivery fees, bulk tends to be cheaper above roughly 2.5–3.5 cubic yards, and bags are cheaper below that.

How much does a delivery of bulk mulch usually cost?

Delivery fees commonly run from about $40 to $100 depending on distance, and some suppliers waive them above a minimum order. Ask for the fee before you compare prices.

How much mulch fits in a pickup truck?

A full-size pickup with a 6.5 ft bed holds about 2 cubic yards level with the sides, but check the payload because wet mulch is heavy.

Can I get free mulch?

Many towns offer free wood chips or compost, and tree services sometimes drop chips for free. Quality varies, so check for weeds, plastic and treated wood.

Do mulch bags actually contain the volume on the label?

Reputable brands list a nominal volume, and settling can make a bag feel smaller. Compare cost per cubic foot across brands rather than per bag.

The bottom line

Convert everything to cubic yards, add 10% for settling, and compare. In most examples, bags win under about 2.5 cubic yards and delivered bulk wins above it. For your prices and bed sizes, the mulch calculator shows the break-even in seconds.

Related tools: Mulch Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Mulching guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. All prices and delivery fees are illustrative examples; get local quotes. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: When to Start Seeds Indoors: Calendar by Last Frost Date
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Start seeds indoors by counting back from your average last frost date: 8 to 10 weeks before for peppers and eggplant, 6 to 8 for tomatoes, 4 to 6 for broccoli, cabbage and lettuce, and 3 to 4 for cucumbers and squash. If your last frost is May 1, that means starting tomatoes around March 13.

The most common seed-starting mistake isn't a bad light or the wrong mix. It's starting too early. Seedlings that stay in pots for 12 weeks get leggy, root-bound and stressed, and they often do worse than younger plants set out on time. Counting back from a reliable date solves it.

This guide gives you the date to count back from, a crop-by-crop weeks chart, a zone-by-zone calendar and tips for hardening off. To find your own frost dates, look them up by ZIP code with the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Count back from your average last spring frost date, not from the calendar month.
  • Peppers and eggplant: 8–10 weeks. Tomatoes: 6–8 weeks. Broccoli, cabbage, lettuce: 4–6 weeks.
  • Squash, cucumbers and melons: only 3–4 weeks; they dislike root disturbance.
  • Carrots, beans, peas, corn and radishes: sow directly outdoors, not indoors.
  • Harden off for 7–10 days before transplanting.

How do you find the right date to start seeds indoors?

You need one number: your average last spring frost date, the day after which a freeze is unlikely. It is an average, so there is still about a 50 percent chance of a frost after it. You can look yours up for free using frost dates by ZIP code, which uses NOAA 1991–2020 climate normals.

  1. Find your last frost date.
  2. Look up the weeks for each crop in the chart below.
  3. Subtract the weeks from your last frost date. That is the day to sow.
  4. Mark the transplant date too, since cool crops go out before the last frost and warm crops after it.

Example: last frost May 5, tomatoes 7 weeks before, so sow on March 17 (May 5 minus 49 days).

🧮

Want exact dates for your garden? Use the planting calendar. Enter your ZIP code to see seed-starting and transplant dates for each crop.

How many weeks before the last frost should you start each crop?

CropWeeks before last frostTransplant outGermination soil temp
Onions (from seed)10–122–4 weeks before last frost65–75°F
Peppers8–101–2 weeks after last frost75–85°F
Eggplant8–101–2 weeks after last frost75–85°F
Tomatoes6–81–2 weeks after last frost70–80°F
Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower4–62–4 weeks before last frost65–75°F
Lettuce, kale4–62–4 weeks before last frost60–70°F
Basil4–61–2 weeks after last frost70–75°F
Marigolds, zinnias4–6After last frost70–75°F
Cucumbers, squash, melons3–41–2 weeks after last frost75–85°F
Petunias, snapdragons10–12After last frost70–75°F

Weeks are typical extension ranges. Use the longer end for slower varieties or if you're short on light, and the shorter end if your seedlings tend to get leggy.

When should you start seeds indoors in your USDA zone?

Last frost dates vary a lot inside any zone, but the table below uses typical dates to show the pattern. Dates are computed by subtracting the weeks above from the typical last frost date. Always shift them to match your own frost date.

USDA zoneTypical last frostPeppers (9 wk)Tomatoes (7 wk)Broccoli (5 wk)Cucumbers (3 wk)
3May 25Mar 23Apr 6Apr 20May 4
4May 15Mar 13Mar 27Apr 10Apr 24
5May 5Mar 3Mar 17Mar 31Apr 14
6Apr 25Feb 21Mar 7Mar 21Apr 4
7Apr 15Feb 11Feb 25Mar 11Mar 25
8Mar 25Jan 21Feb 4Feb 18Mar 4

In zones 9 and 10, frost is rare or absent, and the main limit is summer heat. Start tomatoes and peppers indoors from December to January so they can set fruit before the hottest weather, and plant a second crop in late summer for fall harvest. Broccoli and lettuce are fall-to-winter crops in the South.

What do you need to start seeds indoors?

  • Containers with drainage: cell trays, small pots or recycled containers with holes.
  • Seed-starting mix: a light, sterile, peat- or coir-based mix. Garden soil is too heavy and can carry disease.
  • Light: a south-facing window rarely provides enough. Use a full-spectrum LED or fluorescent shop light 2 to 4 inches above the seedlings, run for 14 to 16 hours a day.
  • Warmth: a heat mat helps peppers, eggplant and tomatoes germinate, which they need at 70 to 85°F.
  • Gentle airflow: a small fan on low strengthens stems and reduces damping-off.

How do you start seeds step by step?

  1. Moisten the mix until it feels like a wrung-out sponge.
  2. Fill cells and sow 2 to 3 seeds per cell at the depth on the packet, usually 2 to 3 times the seed's width.
  3. Cover loosely with a humidity dome or plastic wrap, and keep warm until sprouts appear.
  4. Remove the cover and add light as soon as you see green. Without strong light, seedlings stretch.
  5. Thin to one strong seedling per cell by snipping extras at the soil line.
  6. Water from the bottom and let the surface dry between waterings.
  7. Pot up tomatoes and peppers into 3 to 4 inch pots when they have 2 to 3 sets of true leaves.

How do you harden off seedlings?

Seedlings raised indoors can't take full sun and wind right away. Over 7 to 10 days, give them a gradual outdoor introduction:

  • Days 1–2: 1 to 2 hours in shade, out of the wind.
  • Days 3–4: 3 to 4 hours, with morning sun.
  • Days 5–7: most of the day in sun, bring in at night if it drops below 45°F.
  • Days 8–10: leave out day and night if temperatures stay above 50°F.

Transplant on a cloudy day or in the evening, and water well. Warm-season crops should not go out until nights stay above about 50°F and the soil is at least 60°F.

Don't rush warm-season crops outside. Tomatoes and peppers stall or die in cold soil, and a single night near 32°F kills them. If a late frost is forecast after you've planted, cover plants with row cover, buckets or blankets (not plastic touching the leaves).

What mistakes make seedlings fail?

  1. Starting too early. Old seedlings are leggy and root-bound by transplant day.
  2. Too little light. Tall, pale, floppy seedlings mean they need stronger light placed closer.
  3. Overwatering. Constantly wet mix invites damping-off, a fungus that makes stems collapse at the soil line.
  4. Skipping hardening off. Sunscald and wind burn set plants back by weeks.
  5. Starting direct-sow crops indoors. Carrots, beans, peas and corn resent transplanting and do better sown outside.

Frequently asked questions

Is it too early to start seeds indoors in January?

For most crops, yes. January is right only for slow starters like onions, leeks, and flowers such as petunias, or for gardeners in zones 8 to 10. Tomatoes and peppers started in January are usually leggy by transplant time in colder zones.

Do I need a grow light to start seeds?

Usually yes. Even a bright south window delivers less light than seedlings need, and they stretch. A basic LED shop light 2 to 4 inches above the plants for 14 to 16 hours a day works well.

What is the last frost date and how do I find mine?

It's the average date of the last spring freeze (32°F) in your area. Look it up by ZIP code using NOAA climate normals, and treat it as a guide, not a guarantee.

Which vegetables should be sown directly outdoors?

Carrots, radishes, beets, peas, beans, corn, spinach and turnips grow best from seed sown outside, as they dislike having their roots disturbed.

How long does it take seeds to germinate indoors?

Lettuce and broccoli can sprout in 3 to 7 days, tomatoes in 5 to 10, and peppers in 7 to 14 days at proper temperatures. Check the packet, since old seed or cool conditions can double those times.

Can I start seeds indoors in late spring?

Yes. Heat-loving crops like basil, cucumbers and squash only need 3 to 4 weeks indoors, and in short-summer climates, a late start of fast varieties can still work.

The bottom line

Count back from your average last frost date: 8 to 10 weeks for peppers and eggplant, 6 to 8 for tomatoes, 4 to 6 for cool-season greens and 3 to 4 for squash and cucumbers. Provide strong light, keep seedlings warm, and harden off for a week before planting. For dates tailored to your ZIP code, open the planting calendar.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Seed-starting timing, light and hardening-off guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and Oregon State University Extension; frost data from NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Dates are calculated by subtracting weeks from typical last frost dates and will vary by location. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Vegetable Garden Layout for Beginners: 3 Plans to Copy
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A good beginner vegetable garden layout uses beds 3 to 4 feet wide, 2 to 3 feet apart, in a spot with at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and a water source nearby. Start with 32 to 100 square feet (one 4×8 bed up to two 4×10 beds), put tall crops on the north side and group plants by water needs.

The first year of a vegetable garden usually goes wrong for the same reasons: too much space in too much shade, rows so far apart you spend half your time weeding, and a bed so wide you can't reach the middle. A layout fixes these before you buy a single seed.

This guide walks through choosing a site, deciding bed size and path width, and three complete layouts you can copy, from a single 4 × 8 bed to a 10 × 10 plot. When you're ready to fill your plan, the plant spacing calculator tells you how many plants each bed holds.

Key takeaways
  • Sun: 6–8 hours of direct light; 8+ for tomatoes, peppers and squash.
  • Bed width: 3–4 ft so you can reach the middle from either side.
  • Path width: at least 18 in between beds, 3 ft where a wheelbarrow must pass.
  • Start small: 32–100 sq ft is plenty for a first season.
  • North side for tall crops, so tomatoes and trellises don't shade shorter plants.

Where should you put a vegetable garden?

Site matters more than any other layout decision. Walk your yard at 9 a.m., noon and 4 p.m. and note where the sun lands. Then check these four things:

  • Sun: most vegetables need 6 to 8 hours of direct sun. Leafy greens, peas and herbs tolerate 4 to 6 hours of sun, while fruiting crops like tomatoes, peppers and squash want 8.
  • Water: put the garden within hose reach. If you have to carry water, you will water less often.
  • Drainage: avoid low spots where water pools after rain. Soil should drain within a few hours of a heavy rain.
  • Distance from trees: tree roots steal water and nutrients, and shade ruins yields. Stay at least as far as the tree's drip line, and further from black walnuts.

Also think about convenience. A garden you pass on the way to the car gets visited every day, which means more weeds pulled and more ripe tomatoes picked.

Should you use raised beds, in-ground rows or containers?

OptionBest forProsCons
Raised bedsBeginners, poor or compacted soilBetter drainage, warms earlier, tidy pathsCost of lumber and soil
In-ground bedsGood native soil, larger plotsCheapest, deep rootsNeeds soil testing and amending
RowsLarge gardens, machine tillingSimple, good for corn and potatoesMore path space than plants
ContainersPatios, rentersPortable, good for herbs and tomatoesDries out fast, limited root space

For most beginners, raised or in-ground beds 3 to 4 feet wide beat traditional rows. You walk only on the paths, so the planted soil stays loose, and you can plant closer together because there's no wasted aisle between every row.

How wide should beds and paths be?

Beds should be narrow enough to reach the middle without stepping in, which is usually half the width of your arm span plus a little. That works out to 3 feet for most people and 4 feet if you're tall or have long arms. Length is flexible, but 8 to 12 feet is easy to manage.

Path widths depend on what has to fit:

  • 18 to 24 inches: walking and kneeling in a small garden.
  • 30 to 36 inches: wheelbarrow and comfortable access, the best width for main paths.
  • 4 feet: wheelchair access or space for a garden cart.

Mulch paths with wood chips, straw or gravel over cardboard. They suppress weeds and prevent mud, and the mulch calculator shows how much to buy for a path of any length.

What does a beginner vegetable garden layout look like? Three plans

All three plans keep the tall crops on the north side and group plants by size. Planting areas are calculated from the bed sizes.

Plan 1: One bed, 32 sq ft (4 × 8 ft)

This is the right size for a first year. Put two staked tomatoes at the north end, a block of peppers beside them, bush beans and lettuce in the middle, and carrots and radishes in the south end. Add a row of marigolds or herbs along the edge. The plant spacing calculator gives exact plant counts for each crop.

Plan 2: Two beds, 64 sq ft (two 4 × 8 ft beds)

Place two beds side by side with a 3-foot path between them. The footprint is 4 + 3 + 4 = 11 feet wide by 8 feet long, or 88 sq ft in total, with 64 sq ft (73%) planted. Put warm-season crops (tomatoes, peppers, squash) in one bed and cool-season crops (lettuce, peas, broccoli) in the other. The second bed makes crop rotation easy next year.

Plan 3: 10 × 10 ft plot, 80 sq ft planted

Divide a 10 × 10 square into two 4 × 10 beds with a 2-foot center path: 4 + 2 + 4 = 10 feet. Planted area is 2 × 40 = 80 sq ft, or 80% of the plot. Put a trellis along the north edge for cucumbers or pole beans, a compost bin just outside the plot and a hose bib on the south end.

PlanFootprintPlanted areaShare plantedGood for
1 bed (4 × 8)32 sq ft32 sq ft100%First-year trial, 1–2 people
2 beds (two 4 × 8, 3 ft path)88 sq ft64 sq ft73%2–3 people, crop rotation
10 × 10 plot (two 4 × 10, 2 ft path)100 sq ft80 sq ft80%Family of 4, salads plus tomatoes
🧮

Know your bed size but not your plant count? Open the plant spacing calculator, enter each bed and crop, and get the number of plants and seeds to buy.

How do you decide what goes where?

  1. Put tall crops north. Tomatoes, pole beans, corn and trellised cucumbers throw shade; keep them on the north side (south in the Southern Hemisphere).
  2. Group by water needs. Lettuce and cucumbers like steady moisture; tomatoes and peppers prefer even but less frequent watering; herbs like rosemary and thyme prefer it dry.
  3. Plant fast and slow crops together. Radishes (about 25 days) fill the gaps around slow crops like peppers (about 70+ days from transplant).
  4. Keep perennials separate. Asparagus, rhubarb and berries live for years; give them their own corner so you don't till them up.
  5. Leave room for succession. Save a space for a second planting of beans, lettuce or fall carrots. Check dates in the planting calendar.

What should a beginner grow first?

Pick crops you actually eat that are forgiving to grow: lettuce, radishes, bush beans, zucchini, cherry tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, carrots and herbs such as basil, chives and parsley. Skip the fussy ones (cauliflower, celery, melons in short-season areas) until you've had a good season or two.

A good beginner rule is to plant two or three vegetables you love for every one you're curious about. Also, favor varieties labeled for your region, since they are bred for local pests, disease and day length.

What mistakes should you avoid in the first season?

  1. Starting too big. A 20 × 30 plot that you can't keep weeded is worse than a 4 × 8 bed that thrives. Add a bed next year.
  2. Planting in shade. Fewer than 6 hours of sun means small harvests, whatever else you do right.
  3. Making beds too wide. Stepping on the soil compacts it and harms roots.
  4. Forgetting water access. Install a hose, soaker line or drip irrigation from day one.
  5. Overcrowding. Plant to mature size, not seedling size, or plants shade and crowd each other.
  6. Skipping labels. Mark each variety and sowing date. You'll forget by July.
Test the soil before you plant. If your garden is on a former lawn, near an older house or beside a busy road, a soil test checks nutrients and lead. A state extension service can run one for a small fee, and results come with fertilizer recommendations.

Frequently asked questions

How big should my first vegetable garden be?

A first garden of 32 to 100 square feet (one 4 × 8 bed up to a 10 × 10 plot) is plenty. It grows a surprising amount and takes only a few hours a week to maintain.

Is it better to plant vegetables in rows or beds?

Beds are better for most home gardens. They allow closer spacing, cut the walking area and keep soil loose because you never step on it. Rows suit very large gardens or crops like corn and potatoes.

Which direction should a vegetable garden face?

Choose a site that gets full sun from the south, and run beds north to south if you can so both sides get equal light. Put tall crops on the north end so they don't shade shorter ones.

How far apart should raised beds be?

Allow 2 to 3 feet between beds. Two feet works for walking, while 3 feet leaves room for a wheelbarrow and kneeling.

How many hours a week does a vegetable garden take?

A 4 × 8 bed typically takes 1 to 3 hours a week once it is established, mostly for watering, weeding and harvesting. Planting weeks and mid-summer harvest weeks take longer.

Should I plant in the same spot every year?

Rotate crop families to a different bed or area every year if you can. Tomatoes, peppers and potatoes shouldn't follow each other, because they share soil-borne diseases.

The bottom line

A beginner-friendly vegetable garden layout is simple: a sunny, level site near water, beds 3 to 4 feet wide, paths of 2 to 3 feet and tall crops on the north side. Start with one or two 4 × 8 beds, and add more once you know what you will actually eat. Use the plant spacing calculator to turn your plan into a shopping list.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator · Planting Calendar

Sources: Site selection, bed width and layout guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and University of Maryland Extension. Footprints and planted areas are calculated from the bed and path dimensions shown. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: USDA Hardiness Zones Explained (and Why They Matter)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

USDA hardiness zones divide North America into 13 zones based on the average coldest winter temperature, each 10°F wide and split into 5°F "a" and "b" halves. Zone 6 means winter lows of −10°F to 0°F. A plant "hardy to zone 5" should survive a typical winter low of −20°F to −10°F.

If you've ever read a plant tag that said "Zones 4–8," you've met the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. It's the standard US reference for choosing trees, shrubs and perennials that will survive your winters. It's also one of the most misunderstood numbers in gardening, because many people assume it predicts frost dates, summer heat or growing season length. It doesn't.

This guide explains how the zones work, how to find yours, how to read plant tags and what the map leaves out. For when to actually plant, pair your zone with the dates in the planting calendar.

Key takeaways
  • Zones are based on one thing: the average annual lowest winter temperature (1991–2020 data in the 2023 map).
  • Each zone is 10°F wide; each half zone ("a" or "b") is 5°F.
  • Lower numbers mean colder winters. Zone 3 gets to −40°F to −30°F; zone 9 only 20°F to 30°F.
  • Zones don't predict frost dates, heat, rainfall or snow cover.
  • Pick plants rated for your zone or a lower number (a zone 4 plant is fine in zone 6).

What are USDA hardiness zones?

The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, produced by the USDA Agricultural Research Service with Oregon State University's PRISM Climate Group, divides the US into zones by the average annual extreme minimum winter temperature, the single coldest night of each winter averaged over 30 years. Each zone is a 10°F band, and each band is split into two 5°F half zones, labeled "a" for the colder half and "b" for the warmer half.

The current map was released in November 2023 and uses weather data from 1991 to 2020. The USDA reports that about half of the country moved into a warmer half zone compared with the 2012 map, and the other half stayed the same. If your zone changed, your plants didn't, but the average lowest temperatures in your area did.

USDA hardiness zone chart: temperature range by zone

ZoneAverage coldest winter night (°F)Approx. °CWhat it means for gardening
3−40 to −30−40 to −34Only very hardy perennials, trees and shrubs
4−30 to −20−34 to −29Cold-hardy plants; short growing season
5−20 to −10−29 to −23Many popular perennials thrive
6−10 to 0−23 to −18Wide choice; some tender shrubs need shelter
70 to 10−18 to −12Crape myrtle, camellias and many broadleaf evergreens
810 to 20−12 to −7Figs, lavender, many evergreens
920 to 30−7 to −1Citrus in protected sites; frost possible
1030 to 40−1 to 4Frost-free most years; tropicals and many palms
11–1340 to 704 to 21Essentially frost-free; Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the Florida Keys

The map also includes zones 1 and 2 (down to −60°F) for Alaska. A half zone sits 5°F between: zone 6a is −10°F to −5°F, and 6b is −5°F to 0°F.

How do I find my hardiness zone?

  1. Use the official USDA map. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map website lets you enter a ZIP code and shows your zone and temperature range.
  2. Check the half zone, not just the number. Zone 7a and 7b can differ in what survives.
  3. Note your frost dates separately using frost dates by ZIP code, because your zone doesn't give them.
🧮

Know your zone and want to know when to plant? Open the planting calendar. Enter your ZIP code to get sowing, transplanting and harvest dates for each vegetable.

How do you read a plant tag with zone numbers?

A tag that says "Zones 4–9" tells you the plant's hardy range. The first number is the coldest winter it can survive on average. The second is usually the hottest area where it still does well, or the warm limit before it struggles from lack of winter chill or from heat.

  • Your zone should fall inside the range. If you're in zone 6, a plant labeled 4–8 is a good match.
  • Choose margin for borderline plants. If you're at the cold edge of the range, plant in a sheltered spot and mulch heavily.
  • Container plants are less hardy. Roots in pots are exposed to cold from all sides. A common extension rule of thumb is to treat a pot as one to two zones colder than the ground.
  • Annual vegetables don't use zones. Tomatoes and beans are killed by frost in every zone, so frost dates matter, not hardiness.

What do hardiness zones not tell you?

Zones are a single measurement, which means several things that affect plants are missing:

  • Frost dates and growing season length. Two places in the same zone can have last-frost dates a month apart.
  • Summer heat. The American Horticultural Society publishes a separate Heat Zone Map (zones 1–12), based on the number of days per year above 86°F. A plant can survive a Georgia winter and still fail in a Georgia summer.
  • Rainfall and humidity. A plant that thrives in dry Colorado may rot in wet Florida at the same zone.
  • Snow cover. Snow insulates roots. A zone 4 yard with reliable snow may be gentler than a zone 6 yard with bare, windy winters.
  • Soil drainage, wind and exposure. Wet winter soil kills many plants that tolerate cold when dry.
  • Sharp, unusual cold snaps. The map is an average of annual lows, not a record. Any given year can be colder than your zone.

What is a microclimate and how can it change your zone?

A microclimate is a small area that is warmer or colder than your general zone. A sunny spot against a south-facing wall, a courtyard or a paved area can be a half zone to a full zone warmer, so you can sometimes grow a plant rated for a milder zone. A low hollow where cold air settles, or an exposed hilltop, can be a half zone to a full zone colder.

Use microclimates deliberately: put marginal plants in your warmest, most sheltered spot, and put hardy plants in the exposed areas. Watch your yard on a frosty morning to see where the frost melts first.

Don't "push" the zone with expensive plants. Buying a plant rated one or two zones too tender is a gamble. If you want to try, choose a smaller, cheaper plant, plant it in your warmest microclimate, mulch the roots in late fall, and accept that it may not return.

Why do hardiness zones matter for vegetable gardeners?

Strictly, hardiness zones matter most for perennials, trees, shrubs and overwintering crops such as garlic, asparagus and rhubarb. For annual vegetables, your last and first frost dates and your summer heat matter more. Your zone is still a handy shorthand: cooler zones (3–5) have short seasons and favor quick, cold-tolerant crops, while hot zones (9–10) shift cool-season crops like lettuce and broccoli to fall and winter.

Plan your season with the planting calendar, which uses frost dates for your ZIP code rather than a zone alone.

Frequently asked questions

What hardiness zone am I in?

Enter your ZIP code on the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map website. It returns your zone, half zone and the temperature range for your area.

Did the USDA zones change in 2023?

Yes. The 2023 map, based on 1991–2020 weather data, moved about half the country into a warmer half zone compared with the 2012 map. Your plants don't change, but the average winter low in your area did.

Can I grow a plant that is rated for a warmer zone?

Sometimes, in a warm microclimate with good mulch and drainage. The plant might survive mild winters but die in a harsh one, so treat it as a risk, not a sure thing.

Is a lower zone number colder or warmer?

A lower number means colder winters. Zone 3 averages winter lows of −40°F to −30°F, while zone 10 averages 30°F to 40°F.

What is the difference between hardiness zones and frost dates?

Hardiness zones describe how cold winters get. Frost dates describe when the last spring and first fall freezes usually happen. Two areas in the same zone can have very different frost dates.

Do hardiness zones apply outside the United States?

The USDA map covers the US and Puerto Rico. Canada publishes its own plant hardiness zones and Europe uses separate systems, so use the map made for your region.

The bottom line

USDA hardiness zones tell you how cold winters usually get, in 10°F bands, so you can pick perennials, shrubs and trees that survive. They don't tell you frost dates, heat or rainfall, so use them together with a local frost date and your own microclimate. When you're ready to plan the season, the planting calendar turns your location into a schedule.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator

Sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University PRISM Climate Group, USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map (2023, based on 1991–2020 data); American Horticultural Society Heat Zone Map; US university extension services including Penn State Extension and University of Minnesota Extension; NOAA NCEI 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. Celsius values are converted from the Fahrenheit ranges. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Tomato Plant Spacing: How Far Apart to Plant Tomatoes
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Space tomato plants 24 to 36 inches apart for most home gardens, with rows 3 to 4 feet apart. Tight spacing of 18 to 24 inches works for staked, pruned plants. Caged plants need 24 to 36 inches, and unsupported sprawling plants need 36 to 48 inches. Bush (determinate) types can go closer than vining (indeterminate) types.

Tomatoes are generous plants. A seedling that fits in your hand in April can be a 5-foot, 3-foot-wide tangle by August. Gardeners who plant too close see fewer tomatoes, more blight and fruit that never ripens in the shade. Those who plant too far apart waste bed space and mulch.

This guide covers the right spacing for each way of growing tomatoes, how it changes in raised beds and containers, and how many plants fit in a given area. For your own bed dimensions, the plant spacing calculator gives an exact plant count.

Key takeaways
  • Staked and pruned: 18–24 in apart, rows 3–4 ft apart.
  • Caged: 24–36 in apart, rows 4 ft apart.
  • Sprawling on the ground: 36–48 in apart, rows 4–5 ft apart.
  • Containers: one plant per pot of at least 5 gallons; bigger pots are better for vining types.
  • Plant deep: bury two-thirds of the stem so roots form along it.

How far apart should you plant tomatoes?

The right gap depends on the plant's growth habit and how you support it. Indeterminate (vining) tomatoes keep growing and flowering until frost, so they need more room than determinate (bush) tomatoes, which grow to a set height and ripen most fruit within a few weeks. Extension guidance varies slightly by state, but the ranges below are consistent.

Growing methodSpace between plantsSpace between rowsBest for
Staked and pruned to 1–2 stems18–24 in3–4 ftIndeterminate types, small gardens
Caged (round wire cage)24–36 in4 ftDeterminate and compact indeterminate types
Trellis or string (Florida weave)18–24 in4 ftLong rows, many plants
Sprawling, no support36–48 in4–5 ftLarge gardens, hot dry climates
Dwarf / patio varieties12–18 in2 ftContainers and edges

If the label gives a different number, trust the label: a few heirloom varieties grow 7 feet tall and as wide as 4 feet, while "micro" tomatoes stay under a foot.

Why does tomato spacing matter so much?

Spacing affects three things that decide your harvest.

  • Airflow and disease. Fungal diseases such as early blight, late blight and septoria leaf spot spread when leaves stay wet. Open spacing lets foliage dry after rain and watering.
  • Light. Tomatoes need 6 to 8 hours of direct sun. Crowded plants shade each other, which lowers fruit set and delays ripening.
  • Roots. Neighboring plants compete for water and nutrients. Tightly packed plants wilt faster in heat and show more blossom-end rot when watering is uneven.
🧮

Planning a bed or a row? Use the plant spacing calculator to see how many tomato plants fit in your space at the spacing you choose.

How many tomato plants fit in a given area?

Each plant needs its spacing multiplied by its row width. The table shows plants per 100 square feet at common combinations, computed as 100 ÷ (spacing × row spacing in feet).

Plant × row spacingArea per plantPlants per 100 sq ft
18 in × 3 ft4.5 sq ft22
24 in × 3 ft6 sq ft16
24 in × 4 ft8 sq ft12
36 in × 4 ft12 sq ft8

As a rule, a family of four needs somewhere between 3 and 6 healthy plants for fresh eating, depending on variety, and about 8 to 12 if you also want to can or freeze sauce. Those numbers are a gardener's rule of thumb, not an exact yield figure, so adjust to what you actually use.

How should you space tomatoes in a raised bed?

Raised beds warm early and drain well, which tomatoes love, but the narrow width limits layout. In a 4-foot-wide bed:

  • Plant one row down the center at 24 to 30 inches apart on stakes or a trellis, or
  • Plant two staggered rows, 24 inches apart in the row and 24 inches between the rows, for bush or caged types, and
  • Keep plants at least 6 to 12 inches from the board so you can reach the leaves and the fruit doesn't rest on the wood.

A 4 × 8 bed fits 4 to 6 tomatoes comfortably. Tomatoes can follow a cool-season crop in the same bed, so check dates in the planting calendar.

How far apart should tomatoes be in containers?

Grow one tomato per pot. The common guideline is a minimum of 5 gallons for determinate and dwarf types and 10 to 20 gallons for vigorous indeterminate varieties, which need more root room and are less likely to dry out. Space pots 18 to 24 inches apart (edge to edge) so leaves don't touch. A 24-inch pot works for one large plant plus a few basil seedlings around the edge.

How do you plant tomatoes step by step?

  1. Wait for warm soil. Transplant after your last frost date, when nights stay above 50°F and soil is at least 60°F. Find your date with the frost dates by ZIP code tool.
  2. Mark the spots. Use stakes or a tape measure so spacing is exact.
  3. Dig deep. Make a hole deep enough to bury two-thirds of the stem, or lay a leggy plant sideways in a shallow trench. Tomatoes root along buried stems, which gives a sturdier plant.
  4. Strip the lower leaves that would be buried or touch the soil.
  5. Install support now, before the roots grow. Pushing a stake or cage in later damages them.
  6. Water well and mulch with 2 to 3 inches of straw or shredded leaves to reduce soil splash, a major cause of leaf disease.

How do determinate and indeterminate tomatoes differ in spacing?

Determinate (bush) varieties such as many paste and early slicing tomatoes grow to about 3 to 4 feet, set fruit over a few weeks and stop. They need less support and tolerate closer spacing, but should not be pruned heavily because the suckers carry fruit. Indeterminate (vining) varieties, including most heirlooms and cherry types, keep growing to 6 feet or more until frost.

For vining types, pruning to one or two main stems and tying them to a stake lets you plant at the tight end of the range. Without pruning, they fill the space quickly and need the wider end. Check the plant tag or seed packet for "determinate" or "indeterminate", often abbreviated "det" or "indet".

What mistakes cause tomato spacing problems?

  1. Planting by seedling size. A 6-inch transplant will be 3 feet wide by midsummer.
  2. Mixing sprawling and staked plants in the same row. Sprawlers shade and smother staked neighbors.
  3. Crowding to fit more plants. Eight crowded plants often yield less than five spaced ones.
  4. Ignoring the support's footprint. A round cage is 18 to 24 inches wide before the plant adds foliage.
  5. Planting where tomatoes grew last year. Rotate to a new spot (or a different bed) to reduce soil-borne diseases.
Plant tomatoes away from black walnut trees. Walnut roots release juglone, a compound that wilts tomatoes within the root zone, and walnut roots often reach well beyond the tree's drip line. Use a raised bed or containers with fresh soil if you have a walnut nearby.

Frequently asked questions

Can you plant tomatoes 12 inches apart?

Only dwarf or patio varieties do well at 12 inches. Standard determinate and indeterminate tomatoes need at least 18 to 24 inches, or they will compete for light and water and develop more leaf disease.

How far apart should determinate tomatoes be?

Plant determinate (bush) tomatoes 18 to 24 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. They stay smaller than indeterminate types and ripen most of their fruit over a few weeks.

How far apart should indeterminate tomatoes be?

Indeterminate (vining) tomatoes need 24 to 36 inches between plants when trained on a stake, trellis or cage, and up to 48 inches if left to sprawl.

Can you plant two tomato plants in one hole?

It is not recommended. Two plants in one hole compete for the same roots, nutrients and water, and the dense foliage holds moisture and disease. Space them at least 18 to 24 inches apart instead.

How far apart should cherry tomatoes be planted?

Most indeterminate cherry tomatoes get large and vigorous, so give them 24 to 36 inches. Compact "patio" cherry types can be spaced 12 to 18 inches in pots or beds.

How far apart should tomato rows be?

Leave 3 to 4 feet between rows of staked or caged tomatoes, and 4 to 5 feet for sprawling plants. That gives you room to walk, prune and harvest without breaking stems.

The bottom line

Plant tomatoes 24 to 36 inches apart in rows 3 to 4 feet apart as a safe default, closer (18 to 24 inches) for staked and pruned plants, and farther (36 to 48 inches) if they'll sprawl. Bury the stem, support early and mulch. To fit the right number of plants in your bed, run your dimensions through the plant spacing calculator.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Soil Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Tomato spacing, support and container guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and University of Maryland Extension; frost date data from NOAA NCEI. Plants per area are calculated from spacing. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Square Foot Gardening Spacing Chart (Plants per Square)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

In square foot gardening, each 12 × 12 in square holds 1, 4, 9 or 16 plants, depending on the crop's mature spread. Large plants such as cabbage or broccoli get one square, leaf lettuce and chard get 4, bush beans and spinach get 9, and carrots and radishes get 16. To space any crop, divide 12 by its spacing in inches and square the result.

Square foot gardening (SFG) turns a raised bed into a grid of one-foot squares and plants each square at a fixed density. The appeal is simple: no row math, no wasted paths, and a plan you can sketch on the back of an envelope. The catch is that the "right" number of plants per square depends on the crop, and most charts only cover a handful of vegetables.

This spacing chart covers the common crops, shows the formula so you can work out any vegetable that isn't listed, and includes a ready-made plan for a 4 × 8 bed. If you'd rather skip the arithmetic, the plant spacing calculator gives plant counts for any bed size and crop.

Key takeaways
  • Four densities: 1, 4, 9 or 16 plants per square foot, based on 12 in, 6 in, 4 in or 3 in spacing.
  • Formula: (12 ÷ spacing in inches) squared = plants per square foot, rounded down.
  • Big plants take more than one square: peppers and broccoli at 18 in need about 4 squares each in standard extension spacing.
  • A 4 × 8 bed has 32 squares, enough for a mixed plan of roughly 8 to 12 different crops.
  • Grids need a trellis plan: put tall or climbing crops on the north side so they don't shade shorter ones.

How do you calculate plants per square foot?
