Every square foot is 12 inches by 12 inches. If a crop wants plants spaced s inches apart in every direction, you can fit 12 ÷ s plants along each side of the square. Multiply that number by itself and you have the plants per square, rounded down because you can't plant half a seedling.

  1. Find the recommended spacing on the seed packet or plant tag (use the in-row spacing for the thinned plants).
  2. Divide 12 by that spacing. For 4 in spacing: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
  3. Square the result. 3 × 3 = 9 plants per square foot.
  4. If the spacing is larger than 12 in, work out how many squares one plant needs: (spacing ÷ 12) squared, rounded up. For 18 in: 1.5 squared = 2.25, so allow 4 squares (a 2 × 2 block) or one plant per 2.25 sq ft if you're mixing neighbors.

The method comes from Mel Bartholomew's book Square Foot Gardening. His original chart uses the same four densities. Extension spacing for some crops (tomatoes and peppers especially) is wider than the one-plant-per-square shortcut, so the chart below follows mainstream extension spacing and tells you when a plant needs more room.

🧮

Not sure how many plants your bed holds? Use the plant spacing calculator. Enter your bed size and crop to get plant counts, row spacing and seed quantities.

Square foot gardening spacing chart: how many plants per square?

These plant counts are calculated from typical spacing for each crop. Use them as a starting point and check your seed packet if your variety is unusually large or compact.

Plants per squareSpacingCrops
163 inRadishes, carrots, scallions, garlic chives
94 inBush beans, bulbing onions, beets, spinach, turnips, bush peas
46 inLeaf lettuce, Swiss chard, garlic, parsley, arugula, dwarf marigolds
112 inKale, bok choy, head lettuce, collards, trellised cucumbers, basil
1 per 4 squares18 inPeppers, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, eggplant
1 per 4 squares or more24 inStaked tomatoes, determinate tomatoes
1 per 9 squares36 inZucchini and summer squash, winter squash (trellised), sprawling indeterminate tomatoes

Pole beans and peas are special cases. Plant a row of 6 to 8 seeds along the base of a trellis in one square (spacing about 3 to 4 in along the trellis) rather than filling the whole square, so the vines can climb rather than crowd.

How do you space big plants like tomatoes and peppers in a grid?

Here the SFG shortcut and extension advice part ways. A single square gives a pepper plant only 12 inches in each direction, while extension services typically recommend 18 inches between pepper plants and 18 to 36 inches between tomatoes depending on how they're trained. Crowded plants have less airflow, more disease and smaller harvests.

The practical fix is to give big plants a 2 × 2 block of four squares. Plant the tomato or pepper in the middle of the block and use the corners for something low and quick, such as radishes, basil or lettuce, that will be harvested before the main plant fills in. In a 4 × 8 bed, this fits 8 staked tomatoes at 24 in if the whole bed is given over to them, but a mixed bed is usually better.

Mind the shade. Tomatoes on a 6-foot stake or trellis throw shade over their neighbors. Put them on the north side of the bed (the south side if you're in the Southern Hemisphere) so sun-loving crops to the south keep getting light.

What is a good square foot garden layout for a 4×8 bed?

A 4 × 8 ft bed has 32 squares. This plan mixes tall crops on the north edge with quick, low crops in front. The plant counts are computed from the formula above.

CropSquaresPlantsNotes
Tomatoes, staked (north row)8 (two 2×2 blocks)2At 24 in; fill block corners with basil or radishes
Peppers4 (one 2×2 block)1Use 2 blocks for 2 plants
Bush beans2189 per square
Carrots23216 per square
Radishes116Replant every 2 to 3 weeks
Leaf lettuce4164 per square, stagger sowings
Swiss chard14Cut-and-come-again
Kale221 per square
Bulbing onions2189 per square
Marigolds or herbs6variesEdge squares, flowers for pollinators

How do you set up a square foot garden grid?

  1. Build or choose a bed no wider than 4 feet, so you can reach the middle from either side without stepping on the soil.
  2. Fill it with loose, rich soil. Square foot gardening depends on good soil because plants are close together. Work out how much you need with the soil calculator.
  3. Mark the grid permanently. Wood lath, thin strips of lumber or heavy string stapled to the bed edge all work. Marked squares prevent the slow drift to uneven spacing.
  4. Plant by square, not by row. Press seeds to the right depth (usually 2 to 3 times the seed's width), then thin to the target number once seedlings have two sets of true leaves.
  5. Water and feed more often than a row garden. Densely planted squares use water and nutrients faster. Top up with 1 inch of compost between crops.

When should you replant a square?

One of the best features of the grid is succession planting. When you pull a spent crop, the square is ready for something new in minutes. Loosen the top 2 inches, rake in a handful of compost, and replant.

  • Quick crops (30 to 45 days): radishes, baby lettuce and spinach are ready in 3 to 6 weeks, so a single square can produce several harvests in a season.
  • Season-long crops: tomatoes, peppers and kale hold their squares until frost.
  • Cool-season swaps: after summer beans finish, sow carrots, beets or fall lettuce in the same squares. Check your timing with the planting calendar.

What mistakes make square foot gardens fail?

  1. Treating every plant as a one-square crop. Peppers, broccoli and tomatoes need a full block in standard extension spacing.
  2. Overcrowding without thinning. Sowing 16 carrot seeds is fine; leaving 16 untouched when 10 germinate is not. Thin to the target number early.
  3. Shading the south side. Tall crops belong on the north edge.
  4. Skimping on soil. Dense planting needs fertile, loose soil at least 6 to 12 inches deep.
  5. Forgetting airflow. In humid climates, give tomatoes and squash extra room so leaves dry quickly after rain.

Frequently asked questions

How many carrots can you plant in one square foot?

Sixteen carrot seeds fit in a square foot at 3 inch spacing. Sow a few extra and thin to 16 once seedlings are 2 inches tall.

Can you grow tomatoes in square foot gardening?

Yes, but give each plant at least a 2 × 2 foot block of four squares, which equals 24 inch spacing, and grow it up a stake or cage. One plant in a single square is too crowded for most varieties.

How many squares does a 4×8 raised bed have?

A 4 × 8 foot bed has 32 squares, because 4 × 8 = 32 square feet. A 4 × 4 bed has 16 squares and a 3 × 6 bed has 18.

Is square foot gardening worth it?

It works best for small spaces and beginners because the grid makes spacing simple and keeps beds compact and easy to weed. The trade-off is that dense planting needs richer soil and more frequent watering than wide rows.

How do you thin seedlings in a square foot garden?

Snip the extra seedlings at soil level with scissors, rather than pulling them, so you don't disturb the roots of the plants you're keeping. Thin when seedlings have two sets of true leaves and keep the strongest ones.

What is the best spacing for lettuce in a square?

Four leaf lettuce plants per square (6 inch spacing) is standard. Heading types like romaine and butterhead do best at one plant per square if you want full-size heads.

The bottom line

For any crop, divide 12 by its spacing in inches and square the answer: that is how many plants fit in a square foot. Most vegetables land on 1, 4, 9 or 16, and big plants like tomatoes and peppers need a 2 × 2 block of squares. Sketch your grid, put the tallest crops on the north side, and use the plant spacing calculator for exact counts in any bed size.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator

Sources: Spacing for individual vegetables from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension and Oregon State University Extension; the 1, 4, 9, 16 grid system from Mel Bartholomew, Square Foot Gardening. Plant counts are calculated from the spacing formula shown above. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How to Build a Raised Garden Bed: Materials, Cost, Steps
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To build a 4×8 raised garden bed, screw three 8-foot 2×12 boards into a rectangle (two long sides, and two ends cut from the third board) with 4×4 corner posts and 3-inch exterior screws. It takes 1 to 2 hours, holds about 1 cubic yard of soil and costs roughly $140 to $290 with example prices, depending on the lumber.

A raised bed is one of the easiest woodworking projects you can do. It needs only four cuts, a drill and a tape measure, and a basic design lasts for years. The harder decisions come before you pick up a saw: where to put it, what wood to use, and how much soil to buy.

This guide gives you a complete cut list for a 4 × 8 bed, example costs, step-by-step assembly and tips to avoid common mistakes. When your frame is done, the soil calculator tells you how much soil to order for your bed's exact size and depth.

Key takeaways
  • Size: 4 ft wide (you can reach the middle) by 8 ft long is the standard.
  • Materials for one bed: three 8-ft 2×12s, one 8-ft 4×4, about 24 exterior screws.
  • Soil needed: about 27 cubic feet (1 cubic yard) for a bed filled 11¼ in deep.
  • Example cost: about $140–$190 with pine or fir, $240–$290 with cedar (including soil).
  • Check for square by measuring both diagonals; they should match.

What size should a raised garden bed be?

The standard raised bed is 4 feet wide, which lets you reach the middle from either side without stepping in. Length is flexible, but 8 feet is the easiest to build from standard lumber without waste. Narrower, 3-foot beds suit shorter gardeners or children.

For height, a single 2×12 board gives about 11¼ inches (a 2×12 is actually 1½ × 11¼ inches), which is deep enough for most vegetables. If you want deeper soil or an easier-to-reach bed, stack two boards for about 22½ inches. See the soil calculator for volumes at any height. Leave at least 2 to 3 feet between beds for paths.

What wood is best for a raised bed?

MaterialTypical lifespanExample costNotes
Untreated pine or firAbout 3–7 years$Cheapest; rots fastest in wet climates
Cedar or redwood10+ years$$$Naturally rot resistant; can be hard to find in some regions
Modern pressure-treated lumber10+ years$$Generally considered safe for vegetable beds by many extension services; use a liner if you prefer
Composite or metal20+ years$$$$No rot; metal can get hot in summer
Concrete blockDecades$$Heavy; holes can hold herbs; may raise pH slightly

Lifespans are typical ranges and depend on climate, soil moisture and how well the wood drains. Avoid railroad ties and old treated lumber from before 2004. Railroad ties are treated with creosote, and older residential lumber was treated with chromated copper arsenate (CCA), both of which are best kept away from edible plants.

What materials and tools do you need for a 4×8 raised bed?

Here is the shopping list for a single 4 × 8 ft bed, one board high.

ItemQuantityPurpose
2×12 × 8 ft boards3Two long sides, plus one cut in half for the 2 ends
4×4 × 8 ft post1Cut into four 12-inch corner posts (with spare)
3-inch exterior deck screwsAbout 24Three per board end, plus extras
Cardboard or landscape fabric1 rollWeed barrier under the bed
Hardware cloth (optional)4 × 8 ftUnder the bed if gophers or moles are a problem

Tools: a saw (handsaw or circular saw), a cordless drill with a bit and driver, a tape measure, a pencil, a speed square or framing square and a level.

🧮

Planning a different size or depth? Use the soil calculator to get cubic feet, cubic yards and bags of soil for any bed, and the garden calculator for the rest of your project.

How much does it cost to build a raised bed?

Prices vary by region and change often, so treat the numbers below as examples only. They use $22 for an untreated 2×12×8, $55 for a cedar 2×12×8, $15 for a 4×4×8 post and $12 for screws, plus soil.

Cost itemPine / firCedar
3 boards (2×12×8)$66$165
Corner post and screws$27$27
Frame subtotal$93$192
Soil, bulk (≈1.0 cu yd at $45)$45$45
Soil, bagged (14 bags × $7)$98$98
Total, with bulk soil$138$237
Total, with bagged soil$191$290

The soil is often the biggest cost, which is why bulk delivery usually wins for beds that are larger than 4 × 4 ft.

How do you build a raised bed step by step?

  1. Choose and level the site. Pick a spot with 6 to 8 hours of sun, close to water. Mow or remove tall grass, and level the ground with a shovel.
  2. Cut the boards. Leave two 8-foot boards uncut. Cut the third in half to make two 48-inch pieces, then trim 3 inches off each so the ends fit between the long sides (45 inches).
  3. Cut the corner posts. Cut the 4×4 into four 12-inch pieces (or 11¼ inches to match the board height).
  4. Assemble the frame upside down on flat ground. Stand a post in each corner, pre-drill, then drive three 3-inch screws through each board into the post.
  5. Check that it is square. Measure the diagonals from corner to corner; they should be equal (about 107⅜ inches on the outside of a 4 × 8 frame). Adjust until they match.
  6. Move it into place and make sure it's level, using a level on the board edges. Shim low corners with soil, not wood.
  7. Line the bottom. Lay overlapping cardboard (remove tape) or landscape fabric inside the bed to smother grass. Add hardware cloth first if you have gophers.
  8. Fill with soil to within an inch of the top, water it thoroughly and let it settle before planting.

How much soil does a raised bed need?

A 4 × 8 bed built from 2×12s measures 45 × 93 inches on the inside. At an 11¼-inch fill, that is 45 × 93 × 11.25 ÷ 1,728 = 27.2 cubic feet, or about 1.0 cubic yard. That works out to 14 bags of 2 cubic feet. Allow another 10 percent for settling.

One common blend is roughly 60 percent topsoil, 30 percent compost and 10 percent aeration material such as perlite, though blends vary. Don't fill with plain topsoil; it compacts. The soil calculator converts any bed size into cubic yards and bags.

What mistakes should you avoid when building a raised bed?

  1. Making it too wide. Beds wider than 4 feet force you to step in and compact the soil.
  2. Skipping corner posts. Screws alone can pull out in wet soil, and the long sides can bow outward, especially when full.
  3. Using the wrong lumber. Avoid railroad ties and pre-2004 treated wood.
  4. Building on a slope without leveling. Soil and water slump to the low side.
  5. Forgetting the path. Allow 2 to 3 feet between beds and mulch with wood chips or gravel.
  6. Placing in shade. Fewer than 6 hours of sun means small harvests.
Bow-out warning: a long, deep bed full of wet soil pushes outward. If your bed is longer than 8 feet or taller than one board, add a cross-brace (a 2×4 or a length of cable) across the middle so the sides don't bow.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to build a raised bed?

A 4 × 8 raised bed takes about 1 to 2 hours to cut and assemble. Allow another hour or two to level the site, line the bottom and fill it with soil.

Is pressure-treated wood safe for a vegetable garden bed?

Modern pressure-treated lumber (made since 2004) uses copper-based preservatives, not arsenic, and many extension services consider it acceptable. If you'd rather avoid it, choose cedar or redwood instead.

Do raised beds need a bottom?

No. An open bottom lets roots and drainage reach the ground below. Line it with cardboard to smother grass, or hardware cloth if burrowing animals are a problem.

Can I put a raised bed on grass?

Yes. Mow the grass short, lay overlapping cardboard on top, build the frame on it and fill with soil. The grass dies from lack of light and decomposes.

How do I stop a raised bed from rotting?

Choose rot-resistant lumber like cedar, keep the bottom edge out of standing water and leave the soil side unsealed. Good drainage matters more than any sealant.

Is it cheaper to build or buy a raised bed?

Building is usually cheaper per bed, especially with standard lumber, and gives you any size you want. Kits can save time and cut boards for you but often cost more and use thinner wood.

The bottom line

A 4 × 8 raised garden bed needs three 8-foot 2×12 boards, a 4×4 post and some screws, takes an afternoon and holds about 1 cubic yard of soil. Keep it 4 feet wide, level, in full sun and lined with cardboard, then fill with a quality mix. Use the soil calculator to order the right amount for your size and depth.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Raised bed construction, lumber safety and soil guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension, Oregon State University Extension and Clemson Cooperative Extension; treated lumber information from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Volumes and costs are calculated from the dimensions and example prices shown; local prices will differ. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Many Plants Fit in a 4x8 Raised Bed? Crop-by-Crop Chart
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A 4×8 raised bed (32 sq ft) holds about 8 tomatoes, 10 peppers, 32 cucumbers or kale plants, or 288 bush beans if you fill the whole bed with one crop. Most gardeners mix crops instead. To find your own number, divide each bed side in inches by the plant spacing, drop the decimals and multiply the two results.

The most common raised bed in US backyards is 4 feet wide and 8 feet long, and the most common question is what to put in it. Plant too many and you get small harvests and disease; plant too few and you waste soil you paid for. The right number depends on the crop's mature size, not on how big the seedlings look in the pot.

This guide gives plant counts for a full 4 × 8 bed, quick numbers for other bed sizes and three mixed-bed plans that add up. To work out any other crop or bed shape, the plant spacing calculator does the arithmetic for you.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: (bed width in inches ÷ spacing) × (bed length in inches ÷ spacing), rounded down on each side.
  • Full 4 × 8 bed, one crop: 8 tomatoes at 24 in, 10 peppers at 18 in, 32 kale at 12 in, 128 garlic at 6 in.
  • Large crops first: plan tomatoes, peppers and squash, then fill gaps with fast greens and roots.
  • Vertical crops save space: a trellised cucumber or pole bean row uses a strip 6 inches wide.
  • Leave edge room: keep the first row 6 to 12 inches from the board so mature plants don't flop over the edge.

How many plants fit in a 4×8 raised bed?

A 4 × 8 bed measures 48 in × 96 in. With plants set on a square grid at a given spacing, the maximum number is the width divided by the spacing times the length divided by the spacing, each rounded down. The table shows the maximum for a bed planted entirely with one crop. Real beds hold fewer plants per crop because you'll grow several things at once.

CropSpacingMax plants in a 4×8 bed
Zucchini / summer squash36 in2
Tomatoes (staked)24 in8
Peppers, eggplant18 in10
Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower18 in10
Kale, collards, bok choy12 in32
Cucumbers (on a trellis), potatoes12 in32
Head lettuce8 in72
Garlic, leaf lettuce, chard6 in128
Bush beans, onions, beets, spinach4 in288
Carrots, radishes3 in512

These counts treat the whole bed as plantable. In practice, trim a few plants off the large-crop numbers to leave a 3 to 6 inch buffer at the edge. Tomatoes at 24 in spacing, for example, fit in two rows of four, but a 4-foot-wide bed gives each row only a 12-inch margin, which is plenty.

How many plants per square foot for each size of raised bed?

For a quick estimate when you only know the bed size, use this table. It shows how many plants fit at four common spacings. Notice how quickly the numbers fall as spacing grows: doubling the spacing divides the count by four.

Bed sizeAreaAt 6 inAt 12 inAt 18 inAt 24 in
3 × 3 ft9 sq ft36941
4 × 4 ft16 sq ft641644
3 × 6 ft18 sq ft721883
4 × 8 ft32 sq ft12832108
4 × 12 ft48 sq ft192481612
🧮

Have an L-shaped bed or a mix of crops? Try the plant spacing calculator. Enter bed size and crop to get plant counts and seed quantities without doing the division yourself.

What does a full 4×8 mixed-bed plan look like?

Few gardeners want 512 carrots. A mixed bed mixes tall and small crops, early and late ones, and usually yields something fresh every week. Here are three plans for a 4 × 8 bed, with plant counts that fit the spacing in the chart above.

Plan 1: Salsa bed

  • 2 tomatoes at 24 in (north end, staked)
  • 4 peppers at 18 in (middle)
  • 2 jalapeño or hot pepper plants (south of the peppers)
  • 1 square foot of cilantro, sown every 3 weeks
  • Onions at 4 in along the south edge: 12 plants

Plan 2: Salad and snack bed

  • One 4-ft trellis of cucumbers, 4 plants at 12 in
  • 16 leaf lettuce plants at 6 in
  • 32 carrots at 3 in
  • 16 radishes at 3 in, re-sown every 2 weeks
  • 6 basil plants at 12 in

Plan 3: Cool-season greens bed

  • 8 broccoli or cabbage at 18 in
  • 6 kale or collards at 12 in
  • 20 spinach at 4 in
  • 16 beets at 4 in

Match each plan to your season using the planting calendar, which gives sow and transplant dates for your ZIP code.

Should you plant the same number of plants every year?

Not always. Three factors can push you above or below the chart numbers:

  • Variety size. Determinate (bush) tomatoes can go as close as 18 inches; big indeterminate types do better at 24 to 36 inches. Check the tag.
  • Climate. In hot, humid areas, wider spacing improves airflow and cuts fungal disease. In dry, cool climates, slightly tighter spacing is fine.
  • Soil and feeding. Dense planting needs rich soil. If your bed is only 6 inches deep or you don't feed regularly, plant at the wider end of the range.

How do you avoid overcrowding a raised bed?

  1. Draw the mature size, not the seedling. A 6-inch tomato transplant becomes a 3-foot plant. Sketch circles at mature width on paper before you plant.
  2. Plant tall crops on the north side so they don't cast shade on shorter ones.
  3. Grow up where you can. Cucumbers, pole beans, peas and small squash on a trellis use a fraction of the floor space.
  4. Fill gaps with fast crops. Radishes and baby lettuce finish in 3 to 6 weeks, before the big plants need the room.
  5. Thin early. Crowded seedlings produce fewer and smaller vegetables, and root crops can fail entirely.
Don't pack tomatoes shoulder to shoulder. Crowded tomato plants stay wet after rain or watering, which favors early blight, septoria leaf spot and other fungal diseases. If your bed is small, grow fewer plants and prune lower leaves to improve airflow.

How much soil does a 4×8 raised bed need for all those plants?

A 4 × 8 bed filled 12 inches deep holds 32 cubic feet, or about 1.19 cubic yards of soil. At 8 inches deep it is 21.3 cubic feet (0.79 cubic yards). Plants at the dense end of the range rely on that soil for water and nutrients, so don't skimp. The soil calculator gives exact volumes for your depth and bag size.

Frequently asked questions

How many tomato plants can I put in a 4x8 raised bed?

Eight staked tomatoes fit at 24 inch spacing, but 4 to 6 plants give better airflow and are easier to prune and pick. Two rows of three or four plants, running the length of the bed, work well.

How many pepper plants can I grow in a 4x8 bed?

Up to 10 pepper plants fit at 18 inch spacing. Most people plant 6 to 8 and use the remaining space for herbs or onions.

Can I plant different vegetables right next to each other in a raised bed?

Yes. Mixing crops is normal in a raised bed. Just keep each plant at its own spacing and put tall crops on the north side so they don't shade short ones.

How far from the edge should I plant?

Leave 3 to 6 inches for small crops and 6 to 12 inches for large ones like tomatoes and squash. That keeps stems and leaves from draping over the board.

How many plants fit in a 4x4 raised bed?

A 4 × 4 bed holds 4 tomatoes or peppers at 24 inch spacing, 16 kale plants at 12 inches, or 64 lettuce at 6 inches.

Does a bigger raised bed mean more yield?

Only if you fertilize and water enough. A bigger bed gives more room, but yield depends on sun, soil and spacing, not bed size alone.

The bottom line

A 4 × 8 raised bed holds 8 staked tomatoes, 10 peppers, 32 kale plants or hundreds of small roots, but you'll get better harvests from a mixed plan that gives each crop its full spacing. Divide each side of your bed by the spacing, multiply, and trim a few plants for edge room. Use the plant spacing calculator to check any combination.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Planting Calendar · Garden Calculator

Sources: Vegetable spacing from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and Oregon State University Extension. Plant counts are calculated from bed dimensions (48 × 96 in) and the spacings shown. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Deep Should a Raised Bed Be? Depth by Crop
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

A raised bed should hold at least 6 to 8 inches of soil for greens and herbs and 12 inches for most vegetables, and 18 inches is better for tomatoes, carrots and potatoes. If the bed sits on loosened native soil, roots can grow deeper than the frame. On concrete or hard clay, build the full depth you need.

Depth is the decision that most affects both your harvest and your budget. A taller bed holds more soil, which costs more, but it also drains better, reduces bending and gives roots room. A shallow bed is cheap and quick to fill, but it dries faster and limits some crops.

This guide shows how deep to build for each vegetable, how much soil each depth needs, and when a deeper bed is worth it. The soil calculator converts any depth into cubic yards and bags.

Key takeaways
  • Minimum depth: 6 in for lettuce, radishes and herbs; 12 in for most vegetables.
  • Best depth for tomatoes, carrots, potatoes and squash: 12–18 in or more.
  • Native soil counts: on loosened ground, roots go below the frame; on concrete or compacted fill, they can't.
  • Soil volume doubles when depth doubles. A 4×8 bed needs 16 cu ft at 6 in and 32 cu ft at 12 in.
  • Height and soil depth differ: a bed can be built taller than the soil it holds.

How deep does a raised bed need to be for vegetables?

Most vegetable roots do their feeding in the top 6 to 12 inches of soil, so a bed with 12 inches of good soil grows nearly every common crop. Deeper soil helps in hot or dry weather because it holds more water and keeps roots cooler. The minimums below assume the bed sits on ground that has been loosened, so roots can also reach beyond the frame.

CropMinimum soil depthBetter depthNotes
Lettuce, spinach, arugula, radishes6 in8 inShallow roots; bolt less in deeper, cooler soil
Herbs (basil, parsley, chives)6 in8–12 inRosemary and perennial herbs prefer 12 in
Onions, garlic, scallions6 in8–10 inBulbs need loose soil
Bush beans, peas, kale8 in12 inFine roots reach deeper if allowed
Beets, turnips10 in12 inRoots swell 2–3 in
Peppers, eggplant, cucumbers12 in12–18 inEven moisture matters most
Carrots (long varieties), parsnips12 in12–18 inStones or compaction cause forked roots
Tomatoes12 in18+ inRoots can grow 2–3 ft deep given the chance
Potatoes, squash, melons12 in18+ inPotatoes can be hilled with more soil as they grow

Choose short carrot varieties such as Chantenay or round Parisian types, if your bed is only 8 to 10 inches deep.

How much soil does each depth need?

Soil volume is bed area × depth. The table shows a 4 × 8 ft bed (32 sq ft) at each depth, with bags of 2 cubic feet rounded up. Add 10 percent for settling.

Soil depthCubic feetCubic yards2 cu ft bags
6 inches160.598
8 inches21.30.7911
10 inches26.70.9914
12 inches321.1916
18 inches481.7824
24 inches642.3732
🧮

Have a different bed size? Use the soil calculator. Enter length, width and depth to get cubic feet, cubic yards and the number of bags to buy.

Does it matter what is under the bed?

Yes. This is the factor that changes the answer the most.

On loosened native soil

If the bed sits on lawn or garden soil and you remove the grass (or smother it with cardboard), roots of tomatoes, peppers and other crops will grow into the ground below. A 6- to 12-inch bed can then perform like a much deeper one. Loosen the top few inches with a fork before placing the frame for best results.

On concrete, pavers or compacted subsoil

If the bottom is hard, roots stop at the bottom of your soil. Build at least 12 inches deep, and 18 or more for tomatoes, squash and root crops. A bed on a patio also dries out faster and gets hot, so deeper soil is more helpful there. Make sure it can drain through holes or gaps at the base.

Over landscape fabric or a weed barrier

Plastic or woven landscape fabric stops roots and slows drainage. Use plain cardboard, which breaks down within a season, or no barrier at all, if you want roots to reach the ground.

Is a deeper raised bed always better?

Not always. Deeper beds drain better, stay cooler and hold more water, but they cost more soil and lumber, and the extra depth at the bottom is rarely used by shallow roots.

  • Worth it: for tomatoes and root crops, on concrete, for gardeners who want a bed at waist height, or in hot, dry regions.
  • Not needed: for lettuce and herbs, or on good native soil.
  • Accessibility: a 24- to 30-inch bed can be reached from a chair or without bending. A bed this tall needs sturdy construction and a lot of soil; see the volumes above.

How can you fill a deep raised bed without buying so much soil?

A 24-inch bed needs 64 cubic feet in a 4 × 8 footprint, which is the most expensive part of the project. Some ways to reduce cost without hurting plants:

  1. Put coarse organic material in the bottom. Logs, branches and leaves (the idea behind hugelkultur) fill space and slowly decompose. Use well-seasoned wood, because fresh wood ties up nitrogen as it rots.
  2. Use native soil. If your yard soil is decent, dig and mix 1 part into 2 parts compost-rich mix for the lower layer.
  3. Buy bulk. Bagged soil costs more per cubic foot than bulk soil delivered by the yard.
  4. Put the best mix on top. Fill the top 8 to 12 inches with quality raised bed mix where roots are active.

Whatever you use, expect the fill to settle by 15 to 25 percent over a season, and top up with 1 to 2 inches of compost each spring.

Don't fill with fresh wood chips or sawdust alone. Fresh wood pulls nitrogen from the soil as it decomposes and starves plants. Keep wood in the lower layers, well below the root zone, or use it only as mulch on top.

What mistakes do gardeners make with raised bed depth?

  1. Building 6 inches on concrete and expecting tomatoes to thrive.
  2. Mixing up board height and soil depth. A 12-inch board filled to 8 inches holds only 8 inches of soil.
  3. Using fabric under the bed that prevents roots and water from moving down.
  4. Not allowing for settling. New fill sinks by 15 to 25 percent. Fill to the top and refill next spring.
  5. Skipping drainage on a hard surface. Without it, roots sit in water and rot.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 6-inch deep raised bed enough?

It is enough for lettuce, spinach, radishes, herbs and green onions, especially over loosened ground. Tomatoes, carrots and potatoes will do better with 12 inches or more.

Is 12 inches deep enough for tomatoes?

Yes, if the bed sits on loosened native soil so roots can go deeper. In a bed on concrete, aim for 18 inches or more to avoid drying and stress.

How tall should a raised bed be for easy access?

For an easy reach, 24 to 30 inches puts the soil at a comfortable height without bending. For wheelchair access, 24 to 30 inches with a narrow width works well.

Do I need to dig out the ground under a raised bed?

No. Just remove or smother the grass and loosen the top few inches of soil so roots and water can move down. Digging out a deep hole is rarely worth it.

How deep should the soil be for carrots in a raised bed?

For long varieties, plan on 12 inches of loose, stone-free soil. For shorter types like Chantenay or round Parisian, 8 to 10 inches is enough.

Can a raised bed be too deep?

It can't harm plants, but it can waste soil and money. Beyond 18 to 24 inches, most vegetable roots don't use the extra depth unless the bed is on concrete.

The bottom line

Build a raised bed 6 to 8 inches deep for greens and herbs, 12 inches for most vegetables and 18 inches or more for tomatoes, carrots and potatoes, and go deeper if it sits on concrete or compacted soil. A 4 × 8 bed needs 32 cubic feet at 12 inches and 48 cubic feet at 18. Work out the exact amount with the soil calculator before you order.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Raised bed depth and root-depth guidance from US university extension services, including University of Minnesota Extension, Oregon State University Extension, Penn State Extension and Clemson Cooperative Extension. Soil volumes are calculated as area in square feet × depth in inches ÷ 12 for cubic feet. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Composting for Beginners: A Simple Backyard Method
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To start composting, build a pile or bin at least 3 × 3 × 3 feet and layer about 3 parts "browns" (dry leaves, cardboard) to 1 part "greens" (food scraps, grass clippings) by volume. Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge, turn it every week or two, and you'll have finished compost in roughly 2 to 6 months.

Composting turns kitchen scraps and yard waste into dark, crumbly material that feeds your soil. It cuts what you send to the curb, saves money on soil amendments and improves almost every kind of garden soil. It also looks more complicated than it is. The recipe comes down to three things: the right mix of ingredients, moisture and air.

This guide covers a simple backyard method, what to compost and what to leave out, how to fix common problems and how to use the finished compost. To work out how much compost your beds need, use the garden calculator or the soil calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Ratio: about 3 parts browns to 1 part greens by volume (a gardener's rule of thumb, around a 25–30:1 carbon-to-nitrogen balance).
  • Size: at least 3 × 3 × 3 ft (27 cubic feet) to heat up and break down efficiently.
  • Moisture: like a wrung-out sponge, with a drop or two when squeezed.
  • Air: turn every 1–2 weeks for hot compost, or monthly for slower compost.
  • Time: about 2–6 months actively managed, 6–12+ months if left alone.

What is compost and how does composting work?

Compost is organic matter that has been broken down by bacteria, fungi and small creatures such as worms and beetles into a stable, soil-like material. The microbes need four things: carbon (food and energy from browns), nitrogen (protein from greens), water and oxygen. Get the balance right and the pile warms to 130°F to 160°F as microbes work, which speeds decomposition and kills most weed seeds and disease organisms. Get it wrong and you get a soggy, smelly or dry, inactive pile.

What can you compost? Browns and greens

"Greens" are wet, nitrogen-rich materials. "Browns" are dry, carbon-rich materials. The color is a guide, not a rule.

Browns (carbon)Greens (nitrogen)
Dry fall leavesFruit and vegetable scraps
Shredded cardboard and paper (no glossy)Coffee grounds and tea bags
Straw (not hay with seeds)Fresh grass clippings (untreated)
Small twigs, pine needlesFresh garden trimmings and spent plants
Sawdust from untreated wood (small amounts)Manure from plant-eaters (cows, horses, chickens, rabbits)
Paper towels and napkins (unbleached, no chemicals)Eggshells (crushed; technically neutral)

What should you not compost?

  • Meat, fish, bones, dairy and greasy food: they attract rodents and flies and can smell.
  • Pet waste from cats and dogs: it can carry parasites and pathogens.
  • Diseased plants: unless your pile reliably hits hot temperatures, leave them out.
  • Weeds with mature seeds or aggressive roots such as bindweed or Bermuda grass.
  • Treated wood, coal or charcoal ash, and glossy paper.
  • Grass clippings, hay or manure treated with persistent herbicides. Some weed killers survive composting and damage tomatoes, beans and other garden plants. If you aren't sure where it came from, don't use it.

How do you start a compost pile step by step?

  1. Pick a spot. Choose a level, well-drained place in partial shade, close enough to the kitchen and garden that you'll actually use it. Keep it a few feet from fences and buildings.
  2. Choose a bin or go free-form. A bin made from pallets, wire mesh or a store-bought tumbler works. A simple pile is fine too. Aim for at least 3 × 3 × 3 feet (27 cubic feet).
  3. Start with a coarse base of twigs or straw, 4 to 6 inches deep, for airflow at the bottom.
  4. Layer browns and greens. Add about 3 buckets of browns for every 1 bucket of greens, in layers 2 to 4 inches thick. Mix as you go if you can.
  5. Moisten each layer until it feels like a wrung-out sponge.
  6. Cover with a lid, tarp or layer of browns to keep out flies and excess rain.
  7. Turn it with a fork every 1 to 2 weeks to add oxygen. Move the outside material to the center.
  8. Check moisture and temperature now and then. A compost thermometer is helpful but not required.
🧮

Wondering how much finished compost your beds need? Use the soil calculator to get cubic feet and cubic yards for any bed and depth, or the garden calculator for the whole project.

What size should a compost bin be?

A pile smaller than 3 feet on a side loses heat quickly and breaks down slowly. A pile larger than about 5 feet is hard to turn and can go without oxygen in the center. The sweet spot is 3 to 4 feet on each side.

Bin sizeVolumeNotes
3 × 3 × 3 ft27 cu ft (1 cu yd)Minimum for hot composting
3 × 3 × 4 ft36 cu ftGood for a family yard
4 × 4 × 3 ft48 cu ftRoom for yard waste in fall
Tumbler, 10–18 cu ft10–18 cu ftEasy to turn; slower to heat if half full

Finished compost is much smaller than the raw pile. A 27 cubic foot pile often shrinks to about half that volume or less, so a single bin makes only a few cubic feet of compost per batch. Two or three bins let you add to one while another matures.

How do you know when compost is finished?

Finished compost is dark brown, crumbly and smells like a forest floor. You shouldn't be able to recognize the original ingredients, except for a few woody bits. Other signs:

  • The pile no longer heats up after turning.
  • The volume has dropped to about half or less.
  • A handful kept in a closed bag for a few days doesn't smell sour or like ammonia.

With hot, frequent turning, compost can be ready in 2 to 3 months. A slower, "cold" pile that you only add to occasionally takes 6 to 12 months or longer.

How do you use finished compost?

Compost is a soil amendment and a mulch, not a replacement for soil. Typical uses:

  • Vegetable beds: spread 1 to 2 inches over the surface and work it into the top 4 to 6 inches before planting.
  • Mulch: a 1 to 2 inch layer around plants feeds the soil and holds moisture.
  • Lawns: top-dress with a 1/4 to 1/2 inch layer.
  • Potting mix: use up to about 25 percent compost in a container mix.
AreaDepthCompost needed
100 sq ft (a 10 × 10 bed)1 inch8.3 cu ft (0.31 cu yd)
100 sq ft2 inches16.7 cu ft (0.62 cu yd)
400 sq ft2 inches66.7 cu ft (2.47 cu yd)
1,000 sq ft lawn1/4 inch20.8 cu ft (0.77 cu yd)

How do you fix common composting problems?

ProblemLikely causeFix
Bad smell (rotten egg or ammonia)Too wet or too many greensMix in dry browns and turn to add air
Pile is dry and nothing happensToo dry or too many brownsAdd water while turning; mix in fresh greens
Damp but coldNot enough nitrogen or the pile is too smallAdd greens, such as coffee grounds or grass clippings; make the pile bigger
Flies or rodentsExposed food scraps or meat and dairyBury scraps under browns; leave out meat and dairy; use a closed bin
Matted, slimy layersGrass clippings packed in thick layersMix clippings with browns in thin layers
Wash your hands and wear gloves when handling compost, and don't breathe the dust of dry, finished compost. If you have a weakened immune system or lung condition, wear a mask when turning a pile, since compost can release mold spores.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to turn my compost pile?

No, but turning makes it faster. A pile turned every 1 to 2 weeks can finish in 2 to 3 months; one that is never turned can take a year or more.

Can I compost in winter?

Yes, but the pile cools and slows in cold weather. Keep adding scraps buried in the center, insulate with leaves or straw, and expect the pile to speed up again in spring.

Will a compost pile attract rats?

It can if you add meat, dairy or oily food, or leave scraps uncovered. Compost only plant scraps, bury them under browns and use a bin with a lid or fine mesh to keep rodents out.

Are coffee grounds and eggshells good for compost?

Coffee grounds are a green material rich in nitrogen, so mix them with browns. Eggshells are fine in small amounts but break down slowly unless crushed.

How long does compost take to be ready?

With the right mix, moisture and regular turning, compost is ready in about 2 to 6 months. A neglected cold pile takes 6 to 12 months or longer.

Can I use finished compost as potting soil?

Not by itself. Straight compost is too dense and rich for containers. Mix it into potting mix at up to about 25 percent.

The bottom line

Composting for beginners comes down to a pile of at least 3 × 3 × 3 feet, about 3 parts browns to 1 part greens, damp like a wrung-out sponge and turned every week or two. In 2 to 6 months you'll have dark, crumbly compost to spread 1 to 2 inches deep over your beds. Use the soil calculator to work out how much your garden can use.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Soil Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Composting ratios, temperatures, troubleshooting and safety from the US Environmental Protection Agency and US university extension services, including Cornell Cooperative Extension, University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension and Oregon State University Extension. Application volumes are calculated as area × depth in inches ÷ 12 (cubic feet) ÷ 27 (cubic yards). Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Companion Planting Chart: Good and Bad Vegetable Neighbors
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Companion planting works best when the pairing has a clear reason: flowers that feed beneficial insects, plants that share space without competing, or crops that shouldn't share diseases. Good bets include tomatoes with basil and marigolds, carrots with onions, and corn with beans and squash. Bad neighbors include fennel, black walnut trees and potatoes next to tomatoes.

Most companion planting charts read as fact when much of the advice is garden folklore. Some pairings have solid science behind them, some have a plausible mechanism but little testing, and some are simply habit. Knowing which is which saves you from rearranging a bed for no benefit.

This chart rates each pairing by how strong the evidence is, explains the reasoning in plain English, and shows which combinations to avoid. When you're ready to place plants, the plant spacing calculator will tell you how many of each fit in your bed.

Key takeaways
  • Strongest evidence: flowers that attract beneficial insects, three sisters planting and keeping tomatoes away from black walnut.
  • Mixed evidence: carrot and onion pairs, nasturtium as an aphid trap, marigolds against nematodes (works best as a full-season cover crop).
  • Mostly folklore: many "tomatoes taste better beside basil" style claims.
  • Always safe: space plants to their mature size, and rotate crop families each year.

What is companion planting and does it really work?

Companion planting is growing different plants close together so they help each other. The help can take several forms: attracting predators and pollinators, masking or confusing pests, shading soil, supporting climbers, or taking different nutrients from different soil depths. A few of these mechanisms are well documented. Many specific pairs have never been tested in controlled trials.

University extension services generally give a measured answer: diverse plantings tend to have fewer pest outbreaks than a single crop, and flowers that feed beneficial insects help. But no pairing replaces good spacing, watering, rotation and scouting. Treat companion planting as a bonus, not a pest-control plan.

Companion planting chart: good vegetable neighbors

The last column rates the evidence: Strong means the mechanism is well supported, Some means there is plausible research but results vary, and Folklore means widely repeated but little tested.

CropGood neighborsWhy it might helpEvidence
TomatoesBasil, marigolds, carrots, onionsAromatic plants may confuse pests; low crops fill the soil surfaceFolklore to some
CornPole beans, squashCorn supports beans; squash shades soil (the "three sisters")Strong (traditional)
CarrotsOnions, leeks, chivesStrong onion smell may disrupt carrot rust flySome
Cabbage familyDill, thyme, nasturtiumsDill feeds wasps that attack cabbage worms; nasturtium may act as an aphid trapSome
CucumbersDill, nasturtium, radishesFlowering herbs feed predators and pollinatorsSome
LettuceTall crops, radishes, carrotsShade from taller plants delays bolting in summerSome
BeansCarrots, cucumbers, corn, marigoldsDifferent root depths; beans add some nitrogen to soil over timeSome
PeppersBasil, onions, marigoldsCompact crops share space without crowdingFolklore
SquashNasturtiums, marigolds, cornFlowers draw pollinators and predatorsSome
Most vegetablesSweet alyssum, calendula, dill, yarrowSmall-flowered plants feed hoverflies and parasitic wasps that eat aphids and caterpillarsStrong

Which vegetables should not be planted together?

Bad neighbors are usually those that compete for the same resources, share diseases, or release chemicals that slow other plants. This table lists the pairings most worth avoiding.

Avoid plantingNext toReasonEvidence
Tomatoes, peppers, potatoesBlack walnut treesJuglone from walnut roots can wilt and kill sensitive plantsStrong
PotatoesTomatoes (same bed or next season)Both are nightshades and share early and late blightStrong
FennelMost vegetablesGardeners widely advise giving fennel its own spot because it appears to slow neighborsSome
Beans and peasOnions, garlic, chivesTraditional advice says alliums stunt legumesFolklore
Cabbage familyStrawberriesTraditional advice cites competition for nutrientsFolklore
CarrotsDill (when dill goes to seed)Both are in the carrot family; gardeners often advise separating mature dill from carrotsFolklore
Heavy feeders (corn, squash, tomatoes)Each other in cramped spacingCompetition for water and nutrientsStrong
Juglone is real. Black walnut roots, and to a lesser extent butternut and hickory, release juglone into the soil, and tomatoes, peppers, potatoes and eggplant are among the most sensitive plants. If you have a walnut, grow these crops in raised beds with imported soil or in containers well away from the root zone.
🧮

Planning which companions fit your bed? Use the plant spacing calculator to see how many plants of each crop fit before you fill gaps with flowers and herbs.

What are the three sisters and how do you plant them?

The most famous companion planting system is the three sisters of corn, climbing beans and squash, developed by Native American peoples and still grown today. Corn gives the beans something to climb, beans add nitrogen to the soil through their root nodules over time, and big squash leaves shade the soil and reduce weeds.

  1. Prepare a mound about 12 inches across and 6 inches high, spaced 3 to 4 feet from the next mound, after soil reaches 60°F or higher.
  2. Plant 4 to 6 corn seeds in the mound and let them grow to about 6 inches tall.
  3. Add 4 pole bean seeds around the corn once the stalks are 6 inches tall.
  4. Add 2 squash seeds at the edge of the mound a week or two later, letting the vines spread outward.

The system needs space and doesn't fit a small raised bed. In small gardens, use a trellis for climbing beans or cucumbers and let compact squash sprawl at the base.

Do marigolds really keep pests away?

This is one of the most repeated claims in gardening, and the truth is narrower than the folklore. Research on French marigolds (Tagetes patula) shows they can reduce root-knot nematodes in soil when grown as a dense cover crop for a full season and then tilled in. A few marigolds at the end of a tomato row don't do the same job. Marigolds do attract pollinators and some predators, which is a useful, if more modest, benefit.

What really helps pest control in a garden?

If you want the results people claim from companion planting, these practices are better supported than most plant pairings:

  • Grow a patch of small flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, cilantro, yarrow, calendula) so beneficial insects have nectar all season.
  • Rotate crop families each year, which interrupts disease and pest cycles.
  • Space plants properly for airflow and light.
  • Use row cover over brassicas and squash early in the season to block egg-laying insects.
  • Scout regularly and remove pests by hand when numbers are low.

How do you use companion planting in a small bed?

Start with a main crop, then fit companions into the gaps rather than crowding the main plant. In a 4 × 8 bed, you might plant staked tomatoes on the north side with basil at their feet, onions or carrots in the next row and a border of alyssum and marigolds around the outside. Use the same spacing you would for each crop on its own, because companions do not make plants immune to crowding.

Keep a simple garden map each year. It makes crop rotation easy and shows which combinations did well in your conditions. Match planting dates with the planting calendar so companions are ready at the same time.

Frequently asked questions

What should not be planted next to tomatoes?

Keep tomatoes away from potatoes, which share blight, and from black walnut trees, whose roots release juglone. Fennel and brassicas such as cabbage and broccoli are also commonly advised against as neighbors.

Does basil really improve tomatoes?

There is little scientific evidence that basil improves tomato flavor. Basil is a good neighbor mainly because it is compact, enjoys the same sun and watering, and its flowers attract pollinators.

What are the best companion plants for vegetables in general?

Small-flowered plants like sweet alyssum, dill, cilantro, calendula and yarrow are the best all-round companions because they feed hoverflies and parasitic wasps, which eat aphids and caterpillar pests.

Can you plant cucumbers and tomatoes together?

You can, as long as each has enough space and support. Tomatoes and cucumbers like similar sun and water, but cucumbers sprawl, so grow them on a trellis to keep them from shading the tomatoes.

Do onions repel carrot flies?

Some trials suggest that interplanting onions or leeks with carrots can reduce carrot rust fly damage, but results are mixed. Floating row cover is a more reliable control.

Is companion planting an organic pest control method?

It is one organic tool, best used together with crop rotation, row covers and healthy soil. It rarely controls a heavy infestation on its own.

The bottom line

The best companion plants are the ones with a clear job: flowers for beneficial insects, climbers that use their neighbors for support, and crops kept apart from disease and black walnut roots. Skip complicated charts and focus on spacing, rotation and a few flowering plants. To plan how many of each plant fit, open the plant spacing calculator.

Related tools: Planting Calendar · Soil Calculator · Garden Calculator

Sources: Companion planting and beneficial-insect guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension, Oregon State University Extension and University of Minnesota Extension; juglone sensitivity information from extension horticulture publications; three sisters planting from Native American agricultural tradition. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: When to Plant Garlic: Fall Planting Dates by USDA Zone
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick Answer

Plant garlic in the fall, starting around your average first frost date to roughly 4 weeks later, and at least 2–4 weeks before the ground freezes solid. For USDA Zones 3–5, plant from mid-September to early October. For Zones 6–7, plant from October to mid-November. For Zones 8–10, plant from November to January. Plant cloves 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart.

Garlic is the ultimate "plant it and forget it" crop, and it's the one vegetable most gardeners put in the ground just as the rest of the garden is winding down. Cloves planted in autumn establish strong root systems, sit dormant through the freezing winter, and explode with vigorous green growth in the spring for a mid-summer harvest.

Timing is everything: plant too early, and the cloves send up tall green tops that will be destroyed by winter freezes. Plant too late, and the roots won't have time to anchor before the ground turns to ice.

Key Takeaways for Growing Garlic

  • Growth Cycle: Plant in fall; harvest the following summer (approx. 8–9 months).
  • Temperature Trigger: Plant after the soil cools to roughly 60°F or below.
  • Depth and Spacing: 2 inches deep, 6 inches apart, pointed end facing up.
  • Variety by Zone: Hardneck thrives in cold-winter zones (3–7); softneck excels in mild-winter zones (6–10).
  • Winter Protection: Apply 4–6 inches of straw or shredded leaf mulch in cold-winter regions.

When is the best time to plant garlic?

Garlic requires a sustained period of cold weather—a process called vernalization—to split from a single clove into a fully formed bulb with multiple cloves. Fall planting provides this natural chilling period.

The optimal goal is for the cloves to grow healthy roots in cool soil without pushing much green growth above ground. Extension services from leading agricultural universities advise planting 4 to 6 weeks before the ground freezes solid. A reliable trigger for gardeners is soil temperature: begin planting when your soil temperature at a 4-inch depth drops consistently below 60°F. Garlic is incredibly frost-tolerant; a few inches of green growth before winter will usually survive the snow.

What are the garlic planting dates by USDA zone?

Use this chart as your baseline. These planting windows are calculated based on typical average first fall frost dates. Always adjust for your specific microclimate or elevation.

USDA Zone Typical First Frost Planting Window Best Garlic Type
Zone 3Mid-SeptemberSep 15 – Oct 6Hardneck
Zone 4Late SeptemberSep 30 – Oct 21Hardneck
Zone 5Early OctoberOct 10 – Oct 31Hardneck
Zone 6Mid-OctoberOct 20 – Nov 17Hardneck / Softneck
Zone 7Early NovemberNov 1 – Nov 29Hardneck / Softneck
Zone 8Mid-NovemberNov 15 – Dec 13Softneck
Zone 9Early DecemberDec 1 – Mid-Jan*Softneck
Zone 10Late Dec (if any)Dec 20 – Late Jan*Softneck

*Note: Zones 9 & 10 require pre-chilling (see below).

🧮 Want exact dates? Don't guess. Use our free Planting Calendar, enter your ZIP code, and get a customized garlic planting window based on your local first-frost date.

Can you plant garlic in warm climates?

Yes, but there is a catch. In Zones 9 and 10, winters are often too mild to vernalize the cloves naturally. Without cold exposure, your garlic will grow into a single, onion-like round rather than a bulb with distinct cloves.

The Pro Fix: Pre-chill your seed garlic. Place the unbroken bulbs in a paper bag in your refrigerator crisper drawer for 4 to 8 weeks before planting. Keep them far away from ripening fruits (like apples), which emit ethylene gas and cause premature sprouting. Always choose softneck varieties adapted to southern heat.

Should you plant Hardneck or Softneck garlic?

Selecting the right variety for your climate is half the battle. Here is how they compare:

Feature Hardneck Garlic Softneck Garlic
Cold ToleranceExcellent; demands cold wintersGood; prefers moderate winters
Cloves per Bulb4–12 (Large, easy to peel)10–20 (Smaller, layered tightly)
Culinary BonusProduces edible garlic scapesDoes not produce scapes
Storage Life4–6 months8–12 months (can be braided)
Best ZonesZones 3–7Zones 6–10

How do you plant garlic step-by-step?

  1. Source certified seed garlic. Avoid grocery store garlic. Supermarket garlic is often treated with sprout inhibitors and is usually a softneck variety unsuited for northern winters. Buy from a reputable seed catalog or local nursery.
  2. Prep the soil. Garlic hates soggy feet. Choose a full-sun location with loose, well-draining soil. Work in 2–3 inches of rich compost to boost fertility and drainage.
  3. Crack the bulbs. Gently separate the bulbs into individual cloves 1 to 2 days before planting. Keep the papery skin (the tunic) intact to prevent rot. Plant only the largest, plumpest cloves (save the small inner cloves for cooking).
  4. Plant pointed end up. This is crucial. Plant cloves 2 inches deep (3 inches in frigid Zones 3–5), spaced 6 inches apart, in rows roughly 12 inches apart.
  5. Water deeply. Water the bed to settle the soil around the cloves and trigger root growth.
  6. Apply Mulch. Insulate the bed with 4–6 inches of clean straw, shredded leaves, or weed-free hay. This prevents freeze-thaw cycles from heaving the cloves out of the soil.

Common garlic planting mistakes to avoid

⚠️ Pro Warning: Don't plant in heavy, wet clay. Garlic sitting in winter puddles will rot, and fungal diseases will ruin the crop. If you have heavy clay, build raised beds or mound the soil into ridges.
  • Planting upside down: If you plant the blunt (root) end facing up, the shoot will expend massive energy trying to perform a U-turn underground, resulting in deformed, small bulbs.
  • Planting too early: Unseasonably warm soil triggers rapid top growth, which will be killed off by hard freezes, wasting the plant's energy reserves.
  • Ignoring crop rotation: Planting garlic in the same spot year after year invites nematodes and fungal diseases (like white rot). Wait 3 to 4 years before planting alliums (onions, leeks, garlic) in the same soil again.
  • Late spring nitrogen: Fertilizing heavily in late spring delays the bulbing process and prioritizes leaf growth. Feed garlic early in spring, then stop fertilizing once the scapes form.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you plant garlic in the spring?

Yes, you can plant in spring as soon as the soil can be worked. However, because the garlic lacks a full overwintering cold period (vernalization), the harvested bulbs will be significantly smaller. Fall planting always yields the largest bulbs.

Is it too late to plant garlic in November?

Not in Zones 6–9, where November is actually prime planting time. In Zones 3–5, the ground may already be frozen solid. If you can still dig the soil, plant it and mulch heavily. If the ground is impenetrable, you must wait until spring.

Do you need to soak garlic cloves before planting?

It is optional. Some expert growers soak cloves in a mix of water, liquid kelp, and a splash of rubbing alcohol or hydrogen peroxide to kill fungal spores and jumpstart growth. However, healthy seed garlic planted in rich soil will perform perfectly well unsoaked.

When do I harvest garlic planted in the fall?

Fall-planted garlic is typically harvested the following summer, between June and August. The visual cue to harvest is when the lower third to half of the leaves turn brown and die back, while 5 to 6 upper leaves remain green.

Related Gardening Tools: Plant Spacing Calculator · Soil Volume Calculator · Mulch Coverage Calculator

Sources & Methodology: Garlic planting timelines and cultural guidance are synthesized from US university agricultural extension data, including Cornell Cooperative Extension, the University of Minnesota Extension, Oregon State University Extension, and Clemson Cooperative Extension. Dates utilize the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. Last reviewed for accuracy: October 2026.

items.title: When to Overseed Your Lawn (and How to Do It Right)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Overseed cool-season lawns from late August to mid October, ideally about 45 days before your first fall frost. Overseed warm-season lawns in late spring to early summer, once soil stays above about 65–70°F. Fall is the best season because warm soil and cool air help seedlings root without heat stress or weed competition.

Overseeding means spreading new grass seed over an existing lawn without tearing it up. It fills thin spots, adds fresh and tougher varieties, and crowds out weeds. Done at the right time, one weekend of work can turn a patchy lawn thick by spring. Done at the wrong time, the seed gets baked, flooded or smothered by weeds.

This guide gives the best dates for each grass type, the steps in order, and the common mistakes to avoid. To work out how many pounds you need, use the garden calculator for the area and the rates below.

Key takeaways
  • Cool-season grass: late August–mid October (best), early spring (second choice).
  • Warm-season grass: late spring to early summer, when soil is 65–70°F or warmer.
  • Soil temperature: cool-season seed germinates best between about 50°F and 65°F.
  • Rate: about half the new-lawn rate; for example, 3–4 lb tall fescue per 1,000 sq ft.
  • Moisture: keep the seedbed damp until the seed sprouts, which takes 5–30 days by species.

What is the best time of year to overseed a lawn?

For the cool-season grasses that dominate the northern US, early fall is the best time. Soil is still warm from summer, which speeds germination, while air temperatures are mild so seedlings don't dry out. Weed pressure drops as summer annuals die, and seedlings get several months of cool growth before winter. Penn State and Michigan State Extension both emphasize fall as the best window.

Spring is a second choice. Spring-seeded grass has to establish before summer heat arrives, and crabgrass is germinating at the same time, so you can't use a normal crabgrass preventer.

When should you overseed by grass type and region?

Region / grassBest windowSoil target
Northern US (Kentucky bluegrass, fescue, ryegrass), zones 3–5Mid August – mid SeptemberSoil 50–65°F
Transition zone (tall fescue), zones 6–7September – mid OctoberSoil 50–65°F
Bermudagrass, zones 7–10Late spring – early summer (May–June)Soil 65–70°F+
Zoysiagrass, zones 6–9Late spring – early summerSoil 65–70°F+
Winter color on dormant Bermuda (annual or perennial ryegrass)Fall, when nighttime lows are in the 50sSoil about 65–70°F and falling

The simplest approach: count back about 45 days from your average first fall frost. A first frost around October 20 makes September 1 a good date. Use a soil thermometer pushed 2 inches into the ground if you want precision.

How do you know if your lawn needs overseeding?

Overseed when bare spots total more than about 10–15% of the lawn, grass thins visibly under trees or on slopes, or weeds are taking space that grass used to hold. A lawn more than about 8–10 years old often benefits from newer disease-resistant varieties. If more than half the lawn is dead or weeds, starting over with a full renovation may be better.

🧮

First get your area right. Use the garden calculator to work out the square footage, then multiply by the overseeding rate for your grass.

How do you overseed a lawn step by step?

  1. Mow low. Cut to about 1.5–2 inches and bag the clippings so seed can reach soil.
  2. Remove thatch and debris. Dethatch or rake hard where thatch exceeds about 1/2 inch. Seed must touch soil.
  3. Aerate if the soil is hard. Core aeration leaves holes where seed can settle and improves rooting.
  4. Pick a good seed. Match the grass already growing, or choose newer improved cultivars for your region and shade level.
  5. Spread seed in two directions. Use a broadcast spreader at about half the new-lawn rate: roughly 3–4 lb per 1,000 sq ft for tall fescue or ryegrass, 1–2 lb for Kentucky bluegrass.
  6. Apply a starter fertilizer. A product with more phosphorus helps roots, unless a soil test or local rule says otherwise.
  7. Water lightly and often. Keep the top inch moist, usually 5–10 minutes two or three times a day, until seedlings emerge.
  8. Mow when new grass reaches about 3–4 inches, using a sharp blade and never removing more than a third of the height.

How long does overseeded grass take to sprout?

Germination speed depends on species and soil temperature. Perennial ryegrass is fastest; Kentucky bluegrass is slowest and can look like nothing is happening for weeks.

GrassTypical days to germinate
Perennial ryegrass5–10
Tall fescue7–14
Bermudagrass (seed)7–14 (in warm soil)
Fine fescue7–21
Zoysiagrass (seed)14–21 or longer
Kentucky bluegrass14–30

What should you do about weed killer and crabgrass preventer?

Most pre-emergent herbicides block grass seed too. Do not apply crabgrass preventer within about 6–12 weeks of seeding unless the label says it is safe for new grass. Many broadleaf weed killers also harm seedlings; wait until new grass has been mowed at least three or four times.

What overseeding mistakes should you avoid?

  1. Seeding on top of thatch. Seed that doesn't touch soil dries out.
  2. Letting the seedbed dry out. A few hot, dry days can kill sprouts.
  3. Too much seed. Crowded seedlings are weak and prone to disease.
  4. Mowing too soon or with a dull blade, which pulls out seedlings.
  5. Waiting too late. Seed that sprouts just before a hard freeze may not survive winter.

What seed should you choose for overseeding?

Match the species already in your lawn, or pick improved varieties of a grass that suits your sun and region. Look for the label's variety names and the National Turfgrass Evaluation Program (NTEP) performance ratings, which universities publish. Avoid cheap mixes heavy in annual ryegrass; they green up fast but die out.

SiteGood overseeding choice (cool-season)
Full sun, high trafficPerennial ryegrass or Kentucky bluegrass blends
Hot, dry, low-maintenanceTurf-type tall fescue
Shade under treesFine fescue mixes (creeping red, chewings, hard fescue)
Mixed conditionsTall fescue / bluegrass / ryegrass blend

Kentucky bluegrass spreads by rhizomes and can repair itself, but it is slow to germinate. Pairing it with a little perennial ryegrass gives quick cover while the bluegrass establishes.

What does the first month after overseeding look like?

  • Week 1: keep the top inch of soil damp with short, frequent watering. Do not mow.
  • Weeks 2–3: the first ryegrass and fescue sprouts appear. Keep watering; bluegrass has not started.
  • Weeks 3–5: first mowing at 3–4 inches. Start to water less often but deeper.
  • Weeks 6–8: apply a normal fall feeding once the new grass has been mowed about four times.

Keep pets and kids off the area where you can. Thin spots that did not take can be reseeded in the same season if there are still 4–6 weeks before hard frost.

Should you overseed in spring instead?

You can, if you missed the fall window or need to repair winter damage. Seed cool-season grass as soon as the soil is workable and above about 50°F, typically March to May depending on region. Expect more watering, because spring seedlings have only a few weeks of mild weather before heat arrives, and expect weed competition from crabgrass. If you plan to use a crabgrass preventer, skip spring seeding or use a seed-safe product, and mow new grass at 3 inches or higher all summer to help it survive.

Frequently asked questions

Is it too late to overseed my lawn in October?

In the northern US it is getting late, but it often still works if soil temperatures are above about 50°F and seed has a month or more to establish. In colder zones, consider a dormant seeding after the ground cools.

Can I overseed without aerating or raking?

You can, but results are usually poor. Seed needs soil contact, so at minimum mow low and rake the surface; slit seeding or core aeration gives much better germination.

Should I overseed before or after fertilizing?

Do both at the same time. A starter fertilizer applied at overseeding feeds seedlings, and a regular feeding can follow once the new grass has been mowed a few times.

What is dormant seeding?

It is spreading seed in late fall or winter after the soil is too cold for germination, so seed sprouts in spring. It works best in cold climates and is less reliable than early fall seeding.

Does overseeding really work?

Yes, when timed correctly and kept moist. Over time it thickens turf and reduces weeds, though it won't fix problems like heavy shade, compaction or poor drainage on its own.

The bottom line

Overseed cool-season lawns in late summer to early fall and warm-season lawns in late spring to early summer. Mow low, expose the soil, spread about half the new-lawn rate in two directions and keep it moist until it sprouts. Use the garden calculator to size the job.

Related tools: Lawn Fertilizer Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Planting Calendar

Sources: Overseeding guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, Michigan State University Extension, the University of Maryland Extension and Clemson Cooperative Extension. Dates are typical; adjust to your local frost dates. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: When to Fertilize Your Lawn: Schedule by Grass Type
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Fertilize cool-season lawns (Kentucky bluegrass, fescue, ryegrass) mainly in early fall and again in late fall. Fertilize warm-season lawns (Bermuda, zoysia, St. Augustine) from late spring through summer, once the grass is fully green. Skip both types during drought, dormancy and the heat of midsummer for cool-season grass.

The right month to fertilize your lawn depends on one thing: which type of grass you have. Feed a cool-season lawn in July and you feed weeds and fungus. Feed a Bermuda lawn in October and you push growth right before frost. Timing it to the grass's growth cycle gives you thicker turf for less product.

This guide gives a month-by-month schedule for both grass types, how much to apply, and the mistakes that burn lawns. Once you know your dates, the lawn fertilizer calculator turns your lawn size and bag label into exact pounds of product.

Key takeaways
  • Cool-season grass: main feeding in September, a second in late October to November, and an optional light feeding in late spring.
  • Warm-season grass: first feeding after full spring green-up, then every 6–8 weeks until about 6 weeks before first frost.
  • Rate: 0.5–1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per application, never more than 1 lb of quick-release nitrogen at once.
  • Yearly total: roughly 2–4 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft, depending on grass type and your state's extension advice.
  • Soil test first: it tells you whether phosphorus or potassium are needed at all.

How do you know if you have cool-season or warm-season grass?

Cool-season grasses grow fastest when air temperatures are 60–75°F. They dominate the northern two-thirds of the US and stay green through winter in mild areas. Warm-season grasses grow fastest at 80–95°F, are common across the South, and turn tan after the first hard frost.

If your lawn greens up early in spring and looks its best in fall, you have cool-season grass. If it greens up late (after soil warms in April or May) and browns in winter, you have warm-season grass. In the transition zone (roughly from Virginia and Kentucky to Kansas and north Texas) both types are grown, so check what your neighbors' lawns do.

When is the best time to fertilize a cool-season lawn?

Cool-season grass puts its energy into roots and thickening in fall, which is why extension services such as Penn State and the University of Minnesota build the program around September and November. Spring feeding is lighter because heavy nitrogen in April pushes leaf growth just before summer stress.

MonthWhat to doTypical nitrogen
Late April–MayLight feeding, optional; slow-release is best0.5–1 lb per 1,000 sq ft
June–AugustUsually none; stressed lawns can go dormant0–0.5 lb (slow-release only, if irrigated)
Early to mid SeptemberMain feeding; pair with overseeding1 lb per 1,000 sq ft
Late October–November"Winterizer" feeding while grass is still green, before the ground freezes1 lb per 1,000 sq ft

A good rule for the second fall feeding: apply it after the last mowing is a few weeks away but before the ground freezes. Grass keeps absorbing nitrogen at soil temperatures above freezing, long after top growth slows.

When is the best time to fertilize a warm-season lawn?

Warm-season grass grows when soil is warm, so feed it when it is actively growing, not when it first wakes up. Wait until the lawn is mostly green and you have mowed it two or three times, usually late April to May in the upper South and March to April in the Gulf states.

Month (upper South)What to doTypical nitrogen
April–MayFirst feeding after full green-up0.5–1 lb per 1,000 sq ft
JuneSecond feeding0.5–1 lb per 1,000 sq ft
July–AugustThird feeding for Bermuda and zoysia; skip if drought-stressed0.5–1 lb per 1,000 sq ft
September (at most)Last feeding, no later than about 6 weeks before first frost0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft
October onwardNone; late nitrogen can reduce winter hardiness0

In frost-free areas of Florida, Texas and the Gulf Coast, the growing season is longer, so the schedule can stretch. Local extension offices publish exact dates.

🧮

Know the month but not the amount? Use the lawn fertilizer NPK calculator. Enter your lawn size and the numbers on your bag to get pounds of product per application.

How much nitrogen does each grass need per year?

Total yearly nitrogen varies a lot by species. These are typical ranges per 1,000 sq ft per year for a home lawn, drawn from the general pattern in state extension guides. Your state's recommendation takes priority if it differs.

GrassTypeTypical lb N per 1,000 sq ft per year
Kentucky bluegrassCool2–4
Tall fescueCool2–4
Fine fescueCool1–2
Perennial ryegrassCool2–4
BermudagrassWarm3–5
ZoysiagrassWarm2–3
St. AugustinegrassWarm2–4
CentipedegrassWarmLow; follow your state extension rate

The lower end suits shady, clipped-and-returned (mulched) lawns and homeowners who want a low-maintenance yard. The upper end suits full-sun, high-traffic turf.

How do you fertilize a lawn step by step?

  1. Test your soil. A lab test from your county extension office costs little and tells you whether you need phosphorus, potassium or lime.
  2. Pick the product. Check the three numbers (N-P-K) on the bag. A bag that is 20% nitrogen contains 10 lb of nitrogen per 50 lb, which treats 10,000 sq ft at 1 lb per 1,000 sq ft.
  3. Mow first and apply to dry grass. Granules stick to wet blades and can burn them.
  4. Calibrate your spreader. Use the setting printed on the bag as a start, then check the output on a driveway tarp.
  5. Apply in two directions. Half the product going north to south, half east to west, avoids streaks.
  6. Sweep granules off hard surfaces back onto the lawn, and water in about 0.25–0.5 inch unless the label says otherwise.

Should you use slow-release or quick-release fertilizer?

Quick-release (water-soluble) nitrogen greens the lawn within days but wears off in 2–4 weeks and carries the highest burn risk. Slow-release nitrogen, such as polymer-coated urea or sulfur-coated urea, feeds for 6–12 weeks, allows a heavier single application and is far more forgiving if your spreader is not perfectly calibrated.

For most homeowners, a product that is at least 30–50% slow-release nitrogen is the safest choice for spring and summer feedings. Save the quick-release products for the fall feedings of cool-season grass, when you want a fast response and temperatures are mild. The bag lists the sources of nitrogen in the guaranteed analysis, so look for "slow-release" or "controlled-release" there.

What mistakes make fertilizing burn or weaken a lawn?

Never fertilize drought-stressed, dormant or frozen lawns. Quick-release nitrogen applied to stressed grass can burn the leaves, and fertilizer on frozen ground runs off into storm drains. Always follow the product label, and check whether your city or state restricts fertilizer dates or phosphorus.
  1. Applying more than the label allows. More nitrogen does not mean greener grass; it means leaf burn and runoff.
  2. Feeding cool-season grass in summer heat. It encourages disease such as brown patch.
  3. Feeding warm-season grass too early. If roots are still waking up, weeds take the nitrogen.
  4. Mixing up weed-and-feed timing. Herbicide in the product needs to be applied when weeds are growing, which may not be the best fertilizing date.
  5. Skipping the soil test. Adding phosphorus to soil that already has plenty can be illegal in some states and harms waterways.

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to fertilize your lawn in spring or fall?

For cool-season grass, fall is better because the plant builds roots and stores energy for the next year. For warm-season grass, spring and summer are better, because that is when it grows.

Should I fertilize before or after rain?

Apply just before light rain or water it in afterward. Avoid applying before heavy rain, which can wash fertilizer into storm drains.

Can you fertilize a lawn too often?

Yes. Frequent heavy applications cause fast, weak growth, burn, thatch buildup and nutrient runoff. Stay at or below 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per feeding.

What temperature is too cold to fertilize a lawn?

Do not apply to frozen ground. Cool-season grass can still take up nitrogen while soil is above freezing, but warm-season grass is dormant below about 55–60°F soil temperature and gets no benefit.

Do I need to fertilize a newly seeded lawn?

Yes. Use a starter fertilizer at seeding, then wait until the new grass has been mowed about four times before the first regular feeding.

The bottom line

Cool-season lawns want fertilizer in September and November; warm-season lawns want it from late spring through summer, ending about six weeks before frost. Keep each feeding to 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft or less, and let a soil test guide the rest. To turn your lawn size and bag label into pounds of product, use the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Related tools: Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Garden Calculator · Planting Calendar

Sources: Lawn fertilization guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, the University of Minnesota Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and the University of Florida IFAS Extension. Always confirm dates and rates with your state's extension office. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: When to Aerate Your Lawn: Timing, Tools and Steps
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Aerate cool-season lawns in early fall (or spring), and warm-season lawns in late spring to early summer, when the grass is growing fast.
