Core aeration pulls plugs about 2–3 inches deep to relieve compacted soil. Most lawns need it once a year or every other year; clay soils and heavy-traffic lawns benefit most.

Lawn aeration punches holes in the soil so air, water and nutrients can get down to the roots. If your lawn is thin, puddles after rain or feels hard when you push a screwdriver into it, compaction is a likely cause, and aerating is often the single most effective fix.

This guide explains when to aerate by grass type, how to tell whether you need to, how to do it, and what to do right after. Plan the follow-up feeding with the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Cool-season grass: aerate in early fall (best) or early spring.
  • Warm-season grass: aerate in late spring to early summer, when actively growing.
  • Plug size: core tines pull plugs about 1/2–3/4 inch wide and 2–3 inches deep, spaced about 2–4 inches apart.
  • Frequency: once a year for compacted or clay soil; every 1–3 years for healthy lawns.
  • Best combo: aerate, then overseed and fertilize the same day.

What does lawn aeration do?

Foot traffic, mowing and rain compress soil over time. Compacted soil has fewer air pockets, so water runs off, roots stay shallow and fertilizer sits on the surface. Core aeration removes small plugs of soil, creating channels that let air and water reach the root zone and giving roots room to grow. It also helps break down thatch, as microbes in the soil plugs mix back into the lawn surface.

When is the best time to aerate your lawn?

The rule: aerate when the grass is actively growing, so it can recover and fill holes quickly. This also lines up with the best time to overseed.

Grass typeBest timeSecond choiceAvoid
Kentucky bluegrass, ryegrass, fescue (cool-season)Late August – OctoberEarly spring (March–May)Midsummer heat, drought, dormancy
Bermudagrass, zoysiagrass (warm-season)Late spring – early summer (May–June)Midsummer if wateredFall and winter dormancy
St. Augustinegrass, centipedegrassLate spring – early summer, if needed—Dormancy; usually needs less often

Aerate when the soil is moist but not soggy, ideally a day or two after rain or watering. Dry soil resists the tines; saturated soil clumps and clogs the machine.

How do you know if your lawn needs aerating?

  • Water puddles or runs off instead of soaking in.
  • The screwdriver test: if a screwdriver won't push 4–6 inches into moist soil, it's compacted.
  • The lawn is thin in high-traffic paths, near the driveway or where kids play.
  • Thatch is over 1/2 inch. Cut a wedge of turf and measure the brown spongy layer between green grass and soil.
  • The soil is heavy clay, or the lawn was built on subsoil after construction.
  • Grass struggles even with correct water and fertilizer.
🧮

Planning to feed right after aerating? Use the lawn fertilizer calculator to work out pounds of product for your lawn size.

What is the difference between core and spike aeration?

TypeHow it worksEffectiveness
Core (plug) aerationHollow tines remove plugs of soilBest: relieves compaction
Spike aerationSolid tines poke holesLimited: can increase compaction around holes
Liquid aerationSoil-loosening products sprayed onLittle independent evidence; not a replacement for cores
Slit seederCuts grooves and drops seedGood for overseeding; not a full aerator

University extension services recommend core aeration over spikes. Rent a gas-powered core aerator for a medium or large lawn; hand tools suit small spots.

How do you aerate a lawn step by step?

  1. Mark hidden hazards. Flag sprinkler heads, shallow lines and invisible dog fence wires.
  2. Water the day before if the soil is dry, so tines penetrate 2–3 inches.
  3. Make two passes in different directions. For compacted areas, a second pass at right angles gives better coverage (holes about 2–3 inches apart).
  4. Leave the plugs. They break down within 1–2 weeks and return nutrients and microbes to the lawn.
  5. Overseed and fertilize immediately. Seed falls into the holes and has excellent soil contact.
  6. Water lightly and often for new seed; otherwise resume normal deep watering.

How often should you aerate?

For most home lawns, once every 1–3 years is enough. Aerate every year if you have clay soil, a lot of traffic, or thatch above 1/2 inch. Sandy soil that drains well may only need it every few years. Lawns that were built on fill soil after construction often benefit most from the first treatment.

What aeration mistakes should you avoid?

Don't aerate right after applying a pre-emergent herbicide. Breaking the soil surface can disturb the chemical barrier that stops crabgrass seeds. Aerate before applying, or wait until the label says it's safe.
  1. Aerating a drought-stressed or dormant lawn, which can't recover quickly.
  2. Aerating wet clay, which smears and seals the holes instead of opening them.
  3. Raking up the plugs. They are free topdressing.
  4. Using spikes and expecting results on hard-packed soil.
  5. Skipping the overseed/fertilize step, when holes are the best opportunity of the year.

What is the difference between aerating, dethatching and topdressing?

JobWhat it doesWhen you need it
Core aerationRemoves plugs to relieve compaction and improve water and air flowHard soil, clay, heavy traffic, thin turf
DethatchingRemoves the layer of dead stems and roots above the soilThatch deeper than about 1/2 inch
TopdressingSpreads a thin layer (about 1/4 inch) of compost or soilImproving soil, leveling small dips; often after aeration
OverseedingAdds seed to thicken turfThin lawn; combines well with aeration

These jobs work well together in early fall for a cool-season lawn: aerate, overseed, spread a thin layer of compost, and feed. Dethatching, if needed, goes first. Most healthy lawns do not need all four every year.

Should you rent a core aerator or hire a pro?

Renting a gas-powered core aerator is worthwhile for lawns over about 2,000–3,000 sq ft. The machines are heavy (often over 200 lb) and are usually easier with a trailer or a friend to help load. Hiring a lawn service is simpler for large or sloped lawns. For small yards and spot repairs, a manual step-on core aerator is enough, but it is slow work. Whichever route you pick, price it as an example: ask for a quote based on lot size and check what the price includes.

What should you do in the weeks after aerating?

  • Days 1–7: water normally; if you overseeded, keep the top inch moist with short, frequent sessions.
  • Weeks 2–3: soil plugs break down; run the mower over any stubborn ones.
  • Weeks 3–6: new grass fills the holes. Keep traffic light.
  • Following spring or fall: repeat only if the lawn is still compacted; check with the screwdriver test.

Does aeration help with thatch and clay soil?

Yes, in both cases, though the effect builds over time. In clay, repeated yearly core aeration slowly opens the top few inches and improves drainage. For thatch, aeration brings soil microbes to the surface, which speeds decomposition, but thatch deeper than an inch usually needs a power rake or dethatcher first. Healthy lawns that are mowed at the right height and not overfertilized build thatch more slowly, so correcting those habits matters too.

Is aeration worth it for a healthy lawn?

If the lawn is thick, drains well and passes the screwdriver test, you can skip a year with no harm. Aeration pays off most on new-construction lawns, clay soil, heavily used lawns and any lawn that you plan to overseed. When in doubt, test a small patch first: aerate one corner, and compare how that area looks and drains over the next month.

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to aerate in spring or fall?

For cool-season grass, fall is better because it also lets you overseed and avoids spring crabgrass. For warm-season grass, late spring to early summer is better because that is when it grows.

Should I aerate before or after mowing?

Mow before you aerate so tines work cleanly and you can see sprinkler heads. Wait a few days after aerating before mowing again.

Do you need to water after aerating?

If you overseeded, keep the surface moist until seedlings emerge. If not, normal deep watering is enough, since the holes help water soak in.

Can you aerate a lawn too much?

Yes. Doing it too often or when the lawn is stressed can damage turf. Once a year in the right season is the most that most lawns need.

What should I do with the soil plugs?

Leave them on the lawn. They break down in a couple of weeks. You can break them up by running a mower over them or raking lightly.

The bottom line

Aerate when your grass is growing: early fall for cool-season lawns, late spring for warm-season lawns. Use a core aerator on moist soil, leave the plugs, then overseed and feed the same day. Use the lawn fertilizer calculator to plan the follow-up feeding.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Core aeration guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, Michigan State University Extension, the University of Minnesota Extension and Clemson Cooperative Extension. Timing varies by region; check with your local office. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How to Measure Your Lawn's Square Footage (Any Shape)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

To measure lawn square footage, multiply length by width (in feet) for each rectangular section, then add the sections together. For triangles, use base × height ÷ 2; for circles, 3.14 × radius². Subtract the house, driveway, patio and planting beds. A 30 × 40 ft lawn is 1,200 sq ft.

Almost every lawn job starts with the same number: square feet. Fertilizer, grass seed, weed treatments, sod and even lawn-service quotes are all priced or dosed by the area. Guess it wrong by 20% and you buy too much or too little, or under- or over-apply a product.

The good news is that you don't need surveying tools. This guide shows five ways to measure your lawn, with worked examples for odd shapes, and how to handle the parts that aren't grass. Once you have the number, plug it into the garden calculator or the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Rectangle: length × width. A 30 × 40 ft area is 1,200 sq ft.
  • Triangle: base × height ÷ 2. Circle: 3.14 × radius × radius.
  • Subtract the house, driveway, walks, patios and beds from the lot to get only grass.
  • One acre is 43,560 sq ft; a typical suburban lawn is 5,000–10,000 sq ft.
  • Round up slightly for seed or fertilizer, but never guess the area by eye.

How do you calculate the area of a lawn?

All lawns, however curvy, are made of a few simple shapes. Sketch your lawn on paper, divide it into rectangles, triangles and circles, measure each one in feet, and add up the areas. This table shows the formulas.

ShapeFormulaExampleArea
Rectanglelength × width40 × 60 ft2,400 sq ft
Trianglebase × height ÷ 230 × 12 ft180 sq ft
Circle3.14 × radius²radius 15 ft707 sq ft
Trapezoid(side A + side B) ÷ 2 × height(50 + 30) ÷ 2 × 40 ft1,600 sq ft
Circle with a hole (ring)3.14 × (outer radius² − inner radius²)outer 8 ft, inner 2 ft188 sq ft

Measure in feet. If you only have inches, divide by 12. Always measure the grass itself, not the property line.

How do you measure an irregularly shaped lawn?

Real yards have curves, corners and islands. Here are three reliable methods.

Method 1: Split it into shapes

Draw the lawn, then divide it with straight lines into rectangles and triangles. An L-shaped lawn with one 60 × 40 ft rectangle and one 20 × 30 ft rectangle is 2,400 + 600 = 3,000 sq ft.

Method 2: Average the widths

For a curved or kidney-shaped lawn, measure the length, then measure the width at 3 or 4 points. A 40 ft long lawn with widths of 8, 10, 12 and 9 ft averages 9.75 ft wide, so about 40 × 9.75 = 390 sq ft. This is accurate to within about 10%, which is good enough for seed and fertilizer.

Method 3: Start from the lot and subtract

Take the lot area, subtract everything that isn't grass. Example: an 80 × 120 ft lot is 9,600 sq ft. Subtract a 40 × 30 ft house (1,200), a 12 × 40 ft driveway (480), a 3 × 30 ft walk (90) and 150 sq ft of beds. That leaves 7,680 sq ft of lawn, which is about 0.18 acre.

🧮

Have the area and need quantities? Use the garden calculator for areas and volumes, or the lawn fertilizer calculator to turn square feet into pounds of product.

What tools can you use to measure a lawn?

ToolBest forAccuracyNotes
25–100 ft tape measureSmall and medium yardsHighEasier with a helper; stakes help
Measuring wheelLong edges and big lawnsGoodInexpensive; roll along the edge
Online map measuring toolQuick estimatesFair to goodUse the area tool on a satellite view; trees may hide edges
County GIS or parcel mapLot sizeGoodGives lot area, not lawn area
PacingRough estimateFairCalibrate your step first

How do you pace a lawn accurately?

Measure out 30 ft with a tape and walk it normally, counting steps. If it takes 12 steps, your step is 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 ft. A lawn edge of 48 steps is then 48 × 2.5 = 120 ft. Do this on level ground and average a few walks.

What should you subtract from your lawn area?

Only subtract things that won't get the product or seed. These are the usual ones:

  • Buildings, including porches and sheds.
  • Hard surfaces: driveways, sidewalks, patios, decks.
  • Planting beds, trees and mulched areas with no grass.
  • Pools, ponds and play areas without turf.

Don't subtract small areas like individual tree bases or the strip along a sidewalk; the amounts are tiny and fertilizer and seed need an edge.

What measuring mistakes should you avoid?

Don't use the lot size from your listing or deed as your lawn size. The house, driveway and beds usually take a third or more of a suburban lot, so using the lot number overstates your lawn and can lead to over-application of fertilizer or herbicide.
  1. Mixing units. Make sure everything is in feet before multiplying.
  2. Measuring along a slope. A tape laid along a slope reads slightly long; for home lawns the error is small, so ignore it.
  3. Forgetting the front, side and back yards if you're treating the whole property.
  4. Double-counting overlapping shapes when you split the lawn.
  5. Using a radius instead of a diameter for circles. Radius is half of the distance across.

How big are common lawn sizes?

This reference helps you sanity-check your own measurement:

DimensionsSquare feetRough size
25 × 40 ft1,000Small townhouse yard
40 × 50 ft2,000Small yard
50 × 60 ft3,000Small suburban lawn
50 × 100 ft5,000Average suburban lawn
100 × 100 ft10,000Large suburban lawn
Quarter acre10,890Lot, before subtracting the house
Half acre21,780Large lot

What does your square footage tell you to buy?

Once you have the number, the shopping math is short. At 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft, a 7,680 sq ft lawn needs 7.68 lb of nitrogen, which is about 32 lb of a 24% product. Overseeding the same lawn with tall fescue at 3–4 lb per 1,000 sq ft takes roughly 23–31 lb of seed. Sod is sold by the square foot or by the pallet, usually covering around 450–500 sq ft, so always round up and add about 5–10% for cuts on curved edges.

Keep your number written down with the date. You will use it every year for fertilizer, seed, weed control and watering run times.

How do you account for slopes and tight corners?

For fertilizer and seed, measuring along a gentle slope as if it were flat is fine, since the difference is only a few percent. On a steep bank, measure along the ground surface with a tape, because the true area is larger than the flat map view. In tight corners, treat the corner as a small triangle or rectangle and add it to the total instead of rounding the whole shape up.

How often should you re-measure?

Measure once and keep the number unless the yard changes. Re-measure after you add a patio, expand a bed, remove a tree or install a shed, since each one changes how much grass you actually have. A quick sketch with the dimensions on it, stored with your fertilizer receipts or in a phone note, saves you from repeating the whole job next spring and keeps every product amount consistent from year to year.

Frequently asked questions

How big is the average lawn in square feet?

It varies widely, but many suburban lawns fall between about 5,000 and 10,000 sq ft. A quarter-acre lot is 10,890 sq ft before subtracting the house and driveway.

How many square feet are in an acre?

One acre is 43,560 sq ft. Half an acre is 21,780 sq ft and a quarter acre is 10,890 sq ft.

How do I convert square yards to square feet?

Multiply square yards by 9. A sod order of 100 square yards covers 900 sq ft.

How do I measure a lawn with a smartphone?

Use the area-measuring tool in a satellite map app: tap around the lawn's edges, and it displays the square footage. Check for tree shadows and compare to a tape measurement of one edge.

Why does lawn size matter for fertilizer and seed?

Rates are given per 1,000 sq ft, so an error in area leads directly to an error in how much you apply. Too much can burn the lawn; too little wastes the effort.

The bottom line

Break your lawn into rectangles, triangles and circles, measure each in feet, add the areas and subtract anything that isn't grass. Ten minutes with a tape measure saves money on every product you buy afterward. Take your number to the garden calculator and the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Related tools: Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Mulch Calculator

Sources: Standard geometric area formulas; 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft (US customary units, NIST); lawn product rates per 1,000 sq ft from US university extension services such as Penn State Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Much Grass Seed Do I Need? Rates by Grass Type
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Most cool-season lawns need 2–3 lb of Kentucky bluegrass seed or 6–8 lb of tall fescue or ryegrass per 1,000 sq ft for a new lawn, and about half that to overseed. Warm-season lawns need less: roughly 1–2 lb of Bermuda or zoysia per 1,000 sq ft. Always check the bag label, then multiply by your lawn size.

Grass seed is sold by the pound, but lawns are measured in square feet, and seeding rates differ by a factor of ten between species. Kentucky bluegrass seed is tiny, so a pound has millions of seeds; tall fescue seed is much larger. That's why one rate can't fit every lawn.

This guide gives seeding rates for common grass types, shows how to convert them to pounds for your lawn, and covers the difference between starting from scratch and overseeding. To get the area right first, the garden calculator helps you work out square footage.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: pounds of seed = lawn area (sq ft) ÷ 1,000 × the rate per 1,000 sq ft.
  • New lawn rates: Kentucky bluegrass 2–3 lb, fine fescue 4–5 lb, tall fescue and ryegrass 6–8 lb per 1,000 sq ft.
  • Overseeding: use about half the new-lawn rate.
  • Warm-season grasses: Bermuda and zoysia about 1–2 lb; centipede only 0.25–0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft.
  • Mixes: follow the bag; the label rate is built for that mix.

How much grass seed do you need per 1,000 square feet?

Seeding rates are per 1,000 sq ft and depend mostly on seed size and how quickly the grass fills in. These figures reflect typical extension recommendations. If your bag gives a different rate, the bag wins, since coated seed and blends change the math.

GrassTypeNew lawn (lb per 1,000 sq ft)Overseeding (lb per 1,000 sq ft)
Kentucky bluegrassCool2–31–2
Perennial ryegrassCool6–83–4
Tall fescueCool6–83–4
Fine fescueCool4–52–3
BermudagrassWarm1–2Varies; follow bag
ZoysiagrassWarm1–2Varies; follow bag
CentipedegrassWarm0.25–0.5Rarely overseeded
BahiagrassWarm3–4Varies; follow bag

St. Augustinegrass is not grown from seed in most home lawns; it is planted as sod, plugs or sprigs. If your yard is shady, look for a shade mix, but expect the rate to be at the higher end.

How many pounds of seed do you need for your lawn size?

Multiply your lawn's area by the rate. Here are the amounts for typical lawn sizes, using the new-lawn rates above. For overseeding, use the lower number in the overseeding column instead.

Lawn sizeKentucky bluegrass (2–3 lb)Fine fescue (4–5 lb)Tall fescue / ryegrass (6–8 lb)
1,000 sq ft2–3 lb4–5 lb6–8 lb
2,500 sq ft5–7.5 lb10–12.5 lb15–20 lb
5,000 sq ft10–15 lb20–25 lb30–40 lb
10,000 sq ft20–30 lb40–50 lb60–80 lb

Example: a 5,000 sq ft tall fescue lawn being overseeded needs 5 × 3–4 lb = 15–20 lb. The same lawn started from bare soil needs 5 × 6–8 = 30–40 lb.

🧮

Not sure of your lawn's square footage? Use the garden calculator for areas, then multiply by the rate for your grass.

What is the difference between a new lawn and overseeding?

A new lawn starts from bare, prepared soil, so seed has to produce 100% of the turf. Use the full rate. Overseeding adds seed into an existing lawn to thicken it or fix thin patches. The existing grass fills in part of the area, so about half the rate is plenty. Going heavier just causes seedlings to compete and die off.

For small bare spots, a good starting point is the new-lawn rate, since there is no grass there to help.

How do you spread grass seed evenly?

  1. Prepare the soil. For a new lawn, loosen the top 4–6 inches, remove rocks and rake smooth. For overseeding, mow low and rake out dead grass so seed touches soil.
  2. Measure and weigh. Calculate your pounds and set aside half for the first pass. A cheap kitchen or luggage scale works.
  3. Set the spreader. Use the setting on the bag, then spread half the seed walking one direction.
  4. Spread the second half crosswise. A perpendicular pass fills gaps.
  5. Rake in lightly so seed is about 1/4 inch deep. Most grass seed needs light and soil contact to germinate.
  6. Roll or press, then mulch. A thin layer of straw (about 1 bale per 1,000 sq ft, with seed still visible) holds moisture. Water lightly several times a day until seedlings are up.

What do the numbers on a grass seed bag mean?

Look at the label's "analysis" panel. It lists the percentage of each variety, pure seed, inert matter, weed seed and germination, plus a test date. Good seed has at least 85% germination, under 0.5% weed seed and a test date within the last year. Cheap mixes often contain a high percentage of annual ryegrass or "other crop," which is a fast cover but not a lasting lawn.

If the bag is coated seed, its weight includes the coating, so you may need to apply more by weight than the uncoated figure. Check the bag's coverage statement.

What seeding mistakes waste seed and money?

Don't put down crabgrass preventer at the same time as seed. Most pre-emergent herbicides stop grass seed from sprouting too. Wait until after the new grass has been mowed several times, or use a product labeled safe for new seedlings.
  1. Seeding at the wrong time. Seed sprouts best when soil temperatures are right: for cool-season grass, early fall; for warm-season grass, late spring.
  2. Using too much seed. Overcrowded seedlings are thin and prone to disease.
  3. Burying seed too deep. More than 1/4 to 1/2 inch of soil on top keeps many seeds from emerging.
  4. Letting it dry out. Seed that begins to germinate and then dries dies. Keep the top inch moist.
  5. Buying by price, not label. A $20 bag with 50% filler covers less than a $30 bag of pure seed.

Should you use seed, sod or plugs?

Seed is the cheapest way to start a lawn, but it needs the most patience and the most watering. Sod gives an instant lawn but costs several times more per square foot. Plugs and sprigs are common for warm-season grasses that spread by runners, such as Bermuda, zoysia and St. Augustine.

MethodSpeedBest forMain drawback
SeedWeeks to a full lawn; best in the right seasonLarge areas, cool-season grasses, overseedingNeeds consistent moisture and weed control
SodImmediate; roots in about 2 weeksSlopes, erosion, quick resultsHigher cost; must be laid and watered right away
Plugs / sprigsMonths to fill inWarm-season spreadersSlow; weeds fill gaps

How do you care for new grass seedlings?

The first six weeks decide the lawn. Keep the seedbed moist but not soggy, then taper as roots deepen.

  • Days 1–14: water lightly two or three times a day to keep the top inch damp. Do not let it dry out.
  • Weeks 3–4: cut back to once a day or every other day with longer sessions as seedlings appear.
  • First mowing: when grass reaches about 3–4 inches, with a sharp blade, removing no more than one third of the height.
  • After four mowings: switch to normal deep, infrequent watering and apply a regular fertilizer if the schedule calls for it.
  • Foot traffic: keep it off the area as much as possible until the lawn has been mowed several times.

Unused grass seed stays viable for roughly a year or two if kept cool and dry. Check the test date on the label and avoid seed that has been stored in a hot garage.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a 50 lb bag of grass seed cover?

At 6–8 lb per 1,000 sq ft (tall fescue or ryegrass), a 50 lb bag seeds about 6,000–8,000 sq ft of new lawn, or roughly 12,500–16,500 sq ft when overseeding at 3–4 lb.

Can I put too much grass seed down?

Yes. Excess seed crowds seedlings, producing weak, shallow-rooted grass that is prone to fungus. Stay within the rate on the bag.

How many grass seeds are in a pound?

It varies widely: roughly 2 million for Kentucky bluegrass, about 250,000 for tall fescue and around 230,000 for perennial ryegrass. This is why the pounds-per-1,000-sq-ft rates differ so much.

Should I cover grass seed with topsoil or straw?

A thin layer of straw or peat holds moisture and helps seed stay in place. If you use topsoil, keep it to 1/8–1/4 inch so seed isn't buried.

Will grass seed grow if I just throw it on the lawn?

Rarely well. Seed that lands on thatch or dense grass doesn't touch soil. Mow low, rake the surface and press seed in for much better results.

The bottom line

Pick your grass, find its rate per 1,000 sq ft, and multiply by your lawn area. For a new lawn, use the full rate; for overseeding, use about half. Measure carefully, split the seed into two passes and keep it moist until it comes up. The garden calculator helps with the area step.

Related tools: Lawn Fertilizer Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator

Sources: Seeding-rate guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and the University of Georgia Extension, and seed label standards from state seed-labeling programs. Seeds-per-pound figures are approximate; check your product label. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Much Fertilizer per 1,000 Sq Ft? Pounds of Nitrogen
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Most lawn feedings call for 0.5 to 1 pound of actual nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft. To find pounds of product, divide 100 by the nitrogen percentage on the bag: a 20% nitrogen fertilizer takes 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft to deliver 1 lb of nitrogen, and a 30% product takes about 3.3 lb.

The most common fertilizer mistake isn't picking the wrong product; it's putting down the wrong amount. The bag's rate is written for that specific bag, but if you switch brands, buy a different grade or treat an odd-shaped yard, you need to work it out yourself. The math is simpler than it looks, and getting it right protects both your lawn and local waterways.

This guide gives the one formula you need, a chart of product amounts by nitrogen percentage, and worked examples for common lawn sizes. For instant answers, use the lawn fertilizer NPK calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: pounds of product per 1,000 sq ft = pounds of N wanted × 100 ÷ nitrogen % on the bag.
  • Standard dose: 0.5–1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per feeding.
  • Upper limit: no more than 1 lb of quick-release nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft at a time.
  • Bag coverage: a 50 lb bag of 20% nitrogen covers 10,000 sq ft at 1 lb N per 1,000.
  • Measure first: wrong square footage causes most over- and under-application.

How do you calculate fertilizer per 1,000 square feet?

Fertilizer rates for lawns are set in pounds of nitrogen, not pounds of product, because nitrogen is what drives growth and what can burn grass. The product is only a carrier for that nitrogen. So the calculation has three steps.

Step 1: Choose pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft

For most feedings, pick 1 lb (or 0.5 lb for slow-release light feedings and for warm-season grasses in summer). Your extension service's schedule for your grass type gives the exact number; the calculator uses the same inputs.

Step 2: Divide by the nitrogen percentage

Take pounds of nitrogen wanted, multiply by 100, and divide by the first number on the bag.

Example: bag is 24-0-6, wanted 1 lb N: 1 × 100 ÷ 24 = 4.17 lb of product per 1,000 sq ft.

Step 3: Multiply by your lawn size in thousands

A 5,000 sq ft lawn is five "thousands." So 4.17 × 5 = 20.8 lb of 24-0-6, about 21 lb for the whole lawn.

How much product do you need per 1,000 sq ft?

This chart does Step 2 for you for common bag grades. Find the bag's nitrogen percentage in the first column.

Nitrogen % on bagProduct for 1 lb N per 1,000 sq ftProduct for 0.5 lb N per 1,000 sq ftArea one 50 lb bag covers at 1 lb N
10%10.0 lb5.0 lb5,000 sq ft
16%6.25 lb3.1 lb8,000 sq ft
20%5.0 lb2.5 lb10,000 sq ft
24%4.2 lb2.1 lb12,000 sq ft
28%3.6 lb1.8 lb14,000 sq ft
32%3.1 lb1.6 lb16,000 sq ft
46% (urea)2.2 lb1.1 lb23,000 sq ft

Values are rounded. The coverage column shows why a high-nitrogen bag costs less per treatment even when the price tag is higher.

🧮

Skip the table. Use the lawn fertilizer NPK calculator: enter your lawn size, the bag's three numbers and the nitrogen rate, and get pounds of product and bags needed.

How much fertilizer does a whole lawn need?

Here are example totals for a 1 lb N per 1,000 sq ft feeding with a 24-0-6 fertilizer, which takes 4.17 lb of product per 1,000 sq ft.

Lawn sizePounds of 24-0-6Pounds of nitrogen applied
2,000 sq ft8.3 lb2 lb
5,000 sq ft20.8 lb5 lb
7,500 sq ft31.3 lb7.5 lb
10,000 sq ft41.7 lb10 lb

If a result falls between bag sizes, buy the next size up and save the remainder, since fertilizer stores well when kept dry. Don't spread the extra "to use it up."

How do you measure the lawn area to get this right?

Don't use the lot size from the listing; it includes the house, driveway and beds. Measure only the grass. Pace off or tape each section, multiply length × width for rectangles, and add them. Subtract the house, driveway, patios and planting beds. If you're unsure, an online map measuring tool or your county's GIS parcel map is close enough. The garden calculator can also help with area.

How do you apply fertilizer evenly?

  1. Weigh the product. Weigh out the pounds you calculated rather than relying on the spreader dial alone.
  2. Set the spreader. Start with the dial setting printed on the bag, which is built for that product.
  3. Apply half, then the other half. Split the product, spread the first half in one direction and the second half crosswise.
  4. Close the hopper at turns, and shut it off before stopping. Spreaders drop a pile where they sit still.
  5. Sweep strays off driveways, sidewalks and into the lawn so product doesn't wash into storm drains.
  6. Water it in lightly if the label directs.

What are the most common fertilizer-rate mistakes?

The bag's label rate is a maximum, not a goal. Never apply more than the label directs. Excess nitrogen burns grass and runs off into streams and groundwater.
  • Confusing pounds of product with pounds of nitrogen. 5 lb of 20% fertilizer is 1 lb of nitrogen, not 5.
  • Using the wrong square footage, especially measuring the whole lot.
  • Doubling up on areas where passes overlap, leaving dark green stripes and burned tracks.
  • Applying quick-release at the slow-release rate. Slow-release products tolerate heavier doses; quick-release does not.
  • Treating a larger area than the bag covers, which leaves the lawn underfed.

How many bags should you buy?

Work it through for a real lawn. Say you measured 7,680 sq ft of grass, and you want 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft with a 24-0-6 fertilizer.

  1. Thousands of square feet: 7,680 ÷ 1,000 = 7.68.
  2. Pounds of product per 1,000 sq ft: 100 ÷ 24 = 4.17 lb.
  3. Total product: 7.68 × 4.17 = 32 lb.

A 40 lb bag covers this lawn with 8 lb left over, which keeps for the next feeding. If the bag is sold only in 15 lb sizes, buy three (45 lb) and save the rest. Always buy to the next full bag rather than stretching the product thin.

What does a yearly plan look like in pounds?

For a 5,000 sq ft cool-season lawn that gets 3 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft over a year in three feedings of 1 lb, using a 24% nitrogen product, you apply about 20.8 lb of product each time, or roughly 62.5 lb across the year. Using a 10% product would need 150 lb. Your state extension service sets the right annual total for your grass; the schedule is in our guide to when to fertilize your lawn.

Feedings per yearLb of N per feeding (per 1,000 sq ft)Annual N (per 1,000 sq ft)
21.02.0
31.03.0
40.753.0
41.04.0

Frequently asked questions

How many pounds of fertilizer do I need for 5,000 square feet?

With a 20% nitrogen fertilizer at 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft, you need 25 lb of product. With a 30% product, you need about 16.7 lb.

How much fertilizer for 1 acre?

An acre is 43,560 sq ft, so at 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft you need 43.6 lb of nitrogen, which is about 218 lb of a 20% fertilizer.

Is 1 pound of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet too much?

No, it is the standard maximum for quick-release products. Slow-release products can be applied at higher rates per application, but follow the label.

How do I fertilize a small lawn with a hand spreader?

Divide the lawn into 1,000 sq ft sections, measure the amount for one section, and apply that to each. This keeps the rate even on small or irregular yards.

What happens if I put on twice the recommended fertilizer?

You risk leaf burn, brown or yellow streaks, and excessive growth. If it happens, water the lawn deeply to dilute the fertilizer and stay off the area until the grass recovers.

The bottom line

Decide how many pounds of nitrogen your lawn needs (usually 0.5–1 lb per 1,000 sq ft), divide 100 by the bag's nitrogen percentage, and multiply by the number of thousands of square feet. Spread half in each direction and keep fertilizer off hard surfaces. For quick results, try the lawn fertilizer NPK calculator.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Soil Calculator

Sources: Fertilizer-rate guidance from US university extension services, including the University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension and Clemson Cooperative Extension. An acre is 43,560 sq ft. Always follow the rate and directions on your product label. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: How Long to Water Your Lawn: Sprinkler Run Times
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Most lawns need 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week, including rain. With rotor sprinklers (about 0.5 in/hr) that is 2–3 hours per week; with spray heads (about 1.5 in/hr) it is 40–60 minutes. Split it into two or three deep waterings, early in the morning, rather than a little every day.

How long to water your lawn is really two questions: how much water the grass needs, and how fast your sprinklers deliver it. Run time is just the first number divided by the second. Guess it, and you end up with either a soggy lawn full of fungus or brown patches by July.

This guide shows how to measure your own sprinkler output with a simple can test, gives run times for common sprinkler types and soils, and explains cycle-and-soak watering for slopes and clay. If you'd rather skip the arithmetic, the irrigation run time calculator does it from your numbers.

Key takeaways
  • Target: 1–1.5 in per week for cool-season grass, about 1 in for warm-season grass, rain included.
  • Formula: run time (minutes) = inches needed ÷ sprinkler output (in/hr) × 60.
  • Output varies: rotors apply about 0.4–0.6 in/hr, standard spray heads 1.5–2 in/hr.
  • Frequency: 2–3 deep waterings a week beat daily light watering.
  • Timing: between about 4 and 9 a.m., when wind and heat are lowest.

How much water does a lawn need per week?

The widely used guideline from university extension services is 1 to 1.5 inches per week during the growing season for cool-season grasses, and about 1 inch for warm-season grasses, which use less water. That total includes rainfall. A half-inch rain on Tuesday means you only need to supply the other half inch.

Hot, windy weather in July can push needs above 1.5 inches, especially in sandy soil. Cool spring and fall weeks may need only half an inch. The grass tells you: when it takes on a dull blue-gray tint, or footprints stay pressed into it, it is thirsty.

How do you measure how fast your sprinkler waters?

Do the "tuna can test." It takes about 30 minutes and turns guesswork into a real run time.

  1. Set 5–6 straight-sided, flat-bottomed cans (tuna or cat food cans work) at different spots in one watering zone.
  2. Run that zone for exactly 15 minutes.
  3. Measure the depth of water in each can with a ruler and add up the readings.
  4. Divide the total by the number of cans to get the average depth, then multiply by 4 to get inches per hour.

Example: six cans average 0.25 inch after 15 minutes. That is 0.25 × 4 = 1.0 in/hr. If the cans vary a lot (some at 0.1, some at 0.4), you have uneven coverage; look for clogged or misaligned heads.

How long should you run each type of sprinkler?

Here are typical outputs (precipitation rates) and the run times they imply. Your real number from the can test beats any average in this table.

Sprinkler typeTypical outputTime for 1 inTime for 1.5 in
Multi-stream rotator (MP rotator)0.4 in/hr150 min225 min
Gear-drive rotor0.5 in/hr120 min180 min
Oscillating or impact sprinkler1.0 in/hr60 min90 min
Fixed spray head1.5 in/hr40 min60 min
Fixed spray head (older, high-flow)2.0 in/hr30 min45 min

These are the weekly totals. Divide them across two or three days. A rotor system needing 120 minutes per week would run, for example, 60 minutes on Monday and 60 minutes on Thursday.

🧮

Have the output from your can test? Open the irrigation run time calculator, enter your sprinkler rate and the inches you want, and get run minutes per zone.

How often should you water: daily or a few times a week?

Water deeply and infrequently. Frequent shallow watering keeps roots near the surface where heat and drought hit them first, and it keeps the leaf blades wet, which encourages disease. Deep watering, 0.5 to 0.75 inch per session, trains roots to reach down.

A practical pattern for most lawns is two sessions a week in cool weather and three in midsummer. Water new seed or sod differently: new seed needs light watering once or twice a day until it germinates.

How does soil type change your watering time?

Soil decides how much water the ground can take before it runs off. Sand drinks quickly but holds little; clay holds plenty but takes it in slowly.

Soil typeApprox. water intakeBest approach
Sandy1–2 in/hr or moreSmaller, more frequent sessions (about 0.5 in, 3 times a week)
Loam0.3–1 in/hrStandard: 0.5–0.75 in, 2 times a week
Clay0.1–0.3 in/hrCycle and soak (below), watch for runoff

If water pools or runs onto the sidewalk before your cycle is done, the soil can't absorb it that fast. That is when to use cycle and soak.

What is cycle and soak watering?

Instead of one long run, split the time into two or three short cycles with 30–60 minutes between them. A zone that needs 30 minutes might run 10 minutes, rest, then repeat twice. Most modern controllers have a setting for it. It is especially helpful on slopes and clay soil.

What is the best time of day to water a lawn?

Early morning, roughly 4 to 9 a.m., is best. Wind is low, the sun is not yet evaporating water, and the grass dries by midday, which cuts disease. Evening watering leaves grass wet through the night, which raises the risk of fungal problems. Midday watering works but wastes water to evaporation.

What watering mistakes should you avoid?

Watch for local rules. Many cities and water districts restrict lawn watering days or hours, especially in drought. Check yours before you set the timer.
  1. Setting every zone to the same time. Sun, shade, slopes and different head types mean zones need different minutes.
  2. Ignoring rain. A rain sensor or a skipped cycle after a good storm saves water and money.
  3. Watering daily for 10 minutes. It feels responsible but encourages shallow roots.
  4. Never checking heads. Broken, tilted or clogged heads create dry spots that homeowners fix by overwatering the rest.
  5. Watering dormant grass on a schedule. A brown, dormant lawn needs only about 0.25–0.5 inch every 2–4 weeks to stay alive, not the regular weekly amount.

How should watering change through the year?

The 1–1.5 inch target applies to the growing season. Grass needs far less in cool weather and a bit more at the peak of summer, so adjust the controller every month or two instead of leaving it on one program all year.

SeasonCool-season lawnWarm-season lawn
Spring0.5–1 in per week, often met by rainWater as grass greens up; about 0.5–1 in
Summer1–1.5 in per week; dormancy is possible in droughtAbout 1 in per week, up to 1.5 in in extreme heat
Fall1 in per week for new seed; ease off as it coolsReduce steadily as growth slows
WinterUsually none; water only in dry, thawed spellsLittle to none while dormant

How can you tell when the lawn needs water?

You do not have to wait for brown. Three simple checks show thirst early:

  • Footprint test: walk across the lawn. If the blades spring back, it is fine. If footprints linger for several minutes, the grass has lost turgor and needs water.
  • Color: a blue-gray or dull tint is the first sign of drought stress, usually a day or two before wilting.
  • Soil probe: push a long screwdriver or soil probe into the ground. If it slides in easily to 6 inches, there is moisture; if it stops at 2–3 inches, the soil is dry.

Water as soon as you see the first sign. Grass recovers quickly from mild stress but struggles after it has gone fully brown.

Frequently asked questions

How many minutes should I water my lawn each day?

There is no single daily number. Work out the weekly inches (1–1.5) and divide by your sprinkler's output; for spray heads that is about 20–30 minutes, two to three times a week.

How do I know if I am overwatering my lawn?

Signs include spongy soil, mushrooms, yellowing grass, a heavy moss or algae layer and water running off the lawn. Probe the soil with a screwdriver: if it goes in with no effort 6 inches down a day after watering, you are likely giving too much.

Should I water my lawn after it rains?

Not until you have measured the rain. If a rain gauge shows about 0.5 inch or more, skip the next watering. Count rain toward the weekly 1–1.5 inch target.

Is it okay to water the lawn at night?

It is not ideal. Water sitting on the blades overnight can promote lawn diseases, so early morning is the better habit.

How long should I water new grass seed?

Keep the top inch of soil moist with brief watering, about 5–10 minutes once or twice a day, until germination. Then taper to less frequent, deeper watering over the next several weeks.

The bottom line

Give the lawn about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, in two or three early-morning sessions. Measure your sprinkler output with the can test, then divide inches needed by inches per hour. For quick answers by zone, use the irrigation run time calculator.

Related tools: Lawn Fertilizer Calculator · Garden Calculator · Planting Calendar

Sources: Lawn irrigation guidance from US university extension services, including Colorado State University Extension, the University of Minnesota Extension and the University of Florida IFAS Extension, and the EPA WaterSense program. Output figures are typical ranges; measure your own system. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: What Do Fertilizer Numbers Mean? NPK Explained Simply
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are the percentages, by weight, of nitrogen (N), phosphate (P₂O₅) and potash (K₂O). A 50 lb bag of 20-5-10 contains 10 lb of nitrogen, 2.5 lb of phosphate and 5 lb of potash. Nitrogen drives leaf growth, phosphorus supports roots and flowers, and potassium builds stress tolerance.

Walk down the fertilizer aisle and every bag has three numbers on the front: 10-10-10, 24-0-6, 5-10-5. The numbers look like a secret code, but they follow a simple rule, and knowing it lets you compare bags properly and stop paying for nutrients you don't need.

This guide explains what N, P and K each do, how to turn the numbers into actual pounds of nutrient, and how to choose the right ratio. When you are ready to turn a bag's numbers into pounds per application, the lawn fertilizer NPK calculator does the arithmetic.

Key takeaways
  • The code: N-P-K = percent nitrogen, phosphate and potash by weight, always in that order.
  • Pounds of nutrient: bag weight × percent. A 50 lb bag of 20-5-10 holds 10 lb N.
  • Ratio matters: 20-5-10 is a 4-1-2 ratio, typical for lawns.
  • A zero is meaningful: 24-0-6 has no phosphorus, which many lawns do not need.
  • Test before you buy: a soil test shows which nutrients are actually low.

What do the three fertilizer numbers stand for?

Every fertilizer sold in the US carries a "fertilizer grade" made of three numbers. They are always listed in the same order and always mean the same thing:

PositionNutrientChemical form on the labelWhat it does for plants
FirstNitrogen (N)Elemental NLeafy growth, deep green color, protein
SecondPhosphorus (P)Phosphate (P₂O₅)Root development, flowering, seed and fruit set
ThirdPotassium (K)Potash (K₂O)Disease resistance, drought and cold tolerance

A grade of 20-5-10 means 20% of the bag's weight is nitrogen, 5% is phosphate and 10% is potash. The rest is filler or carrier material, plus any secondary nutrients such as sulfur or iron.

How do you calculate pounds of nutrient in a bag?

Multiply the bag weight by each percentage. This is the single most useful trick in fertilizing, because it lets you compare a cheap bag to an expensive one fairly.

Bag (50 lb)Lb of NLb of P₂O₅Lb of K₂O
20-5-1010.02.55.0
10-10-105.05.05.0
24-0-612.003.0
32-0-416.002.0

Example: a 50 lb bag of 24-0-6 contains 50 × 0.24 = 12 lb of nitrogen. Priced at $30, that is $2.50 per pound of nitrogen. A 50 lb bag of 10-10-10 at $25 gives only 5 lb of nitrogen, which is $5 per pound, so the "cheaper" bag costs twice as much for the nutrient lawns use most. (Prices are examples only.)

🧮

Want the pounds of product for your own lawn? Open the lawn fertilizer calculator, enter the three numbers from your bag and your lawn size.

What does nitrogen do, and how do you tell if a lawn needs more?

Nitrogen is the nutrient plants use in the largest amounts, and it is the one that makes grass green. A nitrogen-hungry lawn turns pale yellow-green, grows slowly and thins out, often with older leaves yellowing first. Too much nitrogen has the opposite effect: lush, fast growth that needs mowing constantly, more disease and thatch, and runoff into waterways.

Nitrogen leaches easily and doesn't stay in soil like phosphorus does, so lawns need it repeatedly. That's why the first number on lawn fertilizers is usually the biggest.

Why does lawn fertilizer often have no phosphorus?

Many established lawns already have enough phosphorus in the soil. Extra phosphorus washes into lakes and streams, where it feeds algae blooms. For this reason a number of states and municipalities restrict phosphorus on established lawns unless a soil test shows a need, which is why you see so many "0" bags. New lawns, and soils that test low, are the exception.

Check your state and local rules, and use a soil test from your county extension office or a state lab to decide.

What does potassium do?

Potassium helps plants regulate water, resist disease and survive heat, drought and cold. It doesn't cause the visible green-up nitrogen does, so it is easy to overlook. Lawns on sandy soil and heavily irrigated lawns are the most likely to run short. Again, a soil test is the way to know.

What are the other numbers and words on the bag?

  • Slow-release or controlled-release nitrogen: the label lists the percentage of nitrogen that is slow-release. This feeds over weeks rather than days and burns less.
  • Secondary nutrients: sulfur, calcium, magnesium. Listed if included.
  • Micronutrients: iron, manganese and others, often added to lawn products for a darker green.
  • Organic grade: organic products such as feather meal or composted manure commonly have lower numbers (for example 5-2-0) but feed slowly and add organic matter.
  • Added herbicide or insecticide: "weed and feed" products mix fertilizer with a pesticide; follow the label closely.

How do you choose the right ratio for your plants?

The ratio (the relationship between the three numbers) matters more than the size of the numbers. Here are typical choices:

UseTypical gradeWhy
Established lawnHigh N, low P, some K (e.g. 24-0-6 or 20-5-10)Grass uses mostly nitrogen
New lawn or seedingStarter (e.g. 18-24-12)Extra phosphorus for young roots
Vegetable gardenBalanced (e.g. 10-10-10) or compostFruiting crops need all three
Flowering plantsHigher P (e.g. 5-10-5)Supports blooms
"More" is not better. Fertilizer salts can burn roots and leaves, and excess nutrients wash into storm drains and groundwater. Stay within the rate on the label, and never apply fertilizer to frozen or saturated ground.

How do you compare fertilizer prices fairly?

Compare the cost per pound of nitrogen, not the cost per bag. Divide the price by the pounds of nitrogen in the bag (bag weight × nitrogen percentage). These are example prices only:

BagExample priceLb of NCost per lb of N
50 lb of 10-10-10$255.0$5.00
50 lb of 20-5-10$3510.0$3.50
40 lb of 24-0-6$309.6$3.13
40 lb of 32-0-4$4012.8$3.13

The table shows why the largest numbers are not automatically the best value, and why the smallest-numbered bag is rarely a bargain. Quality of nitrogen source (slow-release versus quick-release) also affects price and performance.

What do nutrient deficiencies look like?

Symptoms can mimic each other, so confirm with a soil or tissue test before adding a nutrient.

NutrientTypical symptomWhere it shows first
NitrogenPale green to yellow, slow growthOlder, lower leaves
PhosphorusStunted plants, purplish tintYoung plants, cold soil
PotassiumYellow or brown leaf edges, weak stemsOlder leaves

Cold, wet soil and wrong pH can also lock up nutrients, so a yellow lawn is not always a hungry lawn.

Why do soil tests beat guessing?

A soil test costs far less than a season of the wrong fertilizer. State university labs and many county extension offices report your soil pH, phosphorus and potassium levels and recommend pounds of nutrient per 1,000 sq ft for your crop or lawn. The pH result matters as much as the nutrients: when soil is too acidic or too alkaline, plants cannot take up nutrients that are present. Take a sample of 8–10 spots in the area, 3–4 inches deep for lawns, mix them in a clean bucket and send about a cup of the mix to the lab.

Frequently asked questions

What does 10-10-10 fertilizer mean?

It means the product is 10% nitrogen, 10% phosphate and 10% potash by weight, so 100 lb of it contains 10 lb of each nutrient. It's a balanced, general-purpose grade, often used for vegetable gardens.

Are higher fertilizer numbers better?

Not necessarily. Higher numbers mean a more concentrated product, so you apply less by weight, but you must still match the nutrient to the plant and follow the rate on the label.

Why are there three numbers and what order are they in?

The law requires them in the order N-P-K: nitrogen, phosphate (P₂O₅) and potash (K₂O). The percentages are of the product's total weight.

What fertilizer number is best for grass?

Lawns generally need mostly nitrogen, so look for a high first number and a low or zero middle number, such as 24-0-6, unless a soil test shows low phosphorus.

Is organic fertilizer different on the label?

It uses the same N-P-K system, but the numbers are usually lower because the nutrients come from natural materials. They release more slowly and improve the soil.

The bottom line

N-P-K is the percentage of nitrogen, phosphate and potash in the bag. Multiply bag weight by each percentage to see the pounds of nutrient, compare price per pound of nitrogen, and use a soil test to decide whether you need phosphorus or potassium at all. To convert the numbers into pounds of product for your yard, use the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Soil Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator

Sources: Fertilizer-label and nutrient information from US university extension services, including the University of Minnesota Extension, Penn State Extension and Purdue Extension, and state fertilizer regulations. Prices are illustrative examples. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: Cool-Season vs Warm-Season Grass: What Grows Where
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

Cool-season grasses (Kentucky bluegrass, fescue, ryegrass) grow best at 60–75°F and suit the northern two-thirds of the US. Warm-season grasses (Bermuda, zoysia, St. Augustine, centipede) grow best at 80–95°F and suit the South. Cool types stay green through winter; warm types go tan after frost. The transition zone can grow either.

Choosing between cool-season and warm-season grass is the single biggest decision in lawn care, because everything else follows from it: when you seed, when you fertilize, how low you mow and how much water you use. Choose the wrong type for your climate and you fight the lawn every summer or every winter.

This guide compares the two groups, lists the main grasses in each, and shows how to pick one for your yard. Once you know your type, plan feeding with the lawn fertilizer calculator.

Key takeaways
  • Temperature: cool-season grows best at 60–75°F air temperature; warm-season at 80–95°F.
  • Seasonal color: cool-season stays green in winter in mild areas; warm-season goes dormant and tan after frost.
  • Where: cool-season across the North, warm-season across the South, either in the transition zone.
  • Seeding time: cool-season in early fall; warm-season in late spring.
  • Mixing them in one lawn is a recipe for patchwork; pick one and stick with it.

What is the difference between cool-season and warm-season grass?

The difference is how each group photosynthesizes. Cool-season grasses use a pathway that is efficient in mild temperatures and slows down in heat. Warm-season grasses use a different pathway that thrives in heat and strong sun but shuts down when it gets cold. That one fact explains the differences in climate range, growth cycle, water use and color.

TraitCool-season grassWarm-season grass
Best growth temperatures60–75°F80–95°F
Peak growthSpring and fallSummer
WinterGreen in mild areas; dormant in hard freezesDormant and tan after frost
Summer heatCan go dormant or thinThrives
RegionNorth, Upper Midwest, Pacific NorthwestSoutheast, Gulf Coast, Southwest
Best seeding timeLate summer to early fallLate spring to early summer
Main fertilizer windowFall (September, November)Late spring through summer

Which grasses are cool-season and warm-season?

Here are the common home-lawn grasses, with typical mowing heights from university extension guidance. Heights vary by cultivar; your local extension office may publish a narrower range.

GrassTypeMowing heightShade toleranceBest known for
Kentucky bluegrassCool2.5–3.5 inLow–mediumDense, self-repairing, rich color
Tall fescueCool3–4 inMediumHeat and drought tolerance among cool grasses
Perennial ryegrassCool2–3 inLowFast germination, good wear tolerance
Fine fescuesCool2.5–4 inHighShade and low-fertility soils
BermudagrassWarm1–2 inVery lowHeat, drought and traffic tolerance
ZoysiagrassWarm1–2.5 inMediumDense turf, some cold tolerance
St. AugustinegrassWarm2.5–4 inMedium–highCoastal and shady Southern lawns
CentipedegrassWarm1–2 inLow–mediumLow maintenance on acidic soils
🧮

Once you know your grass type, plan its feeding. Open the lawn fertilizer calculator and enter your lawn size and bag numbers.

Where does each grass type grow in the US?

As a rough guide, cool-season grasses suit USDA hardiness zones 3–6, warm-season grasses suit zones 8–10, and zone 7 is the border. The practical band where either may be grown is called the transition zone, a wavy belt stretching from roughly the Mid-Atlantic coast through Virginia, Kentucky, Missouri and Kansas to northern Texas and parts of the Southwest.

RegionCommon choiceNotes
Northeast, Upper Midwest, mountain statesKentucky bluegrass, fescue, ryegrass blendsCold winters favor cool-season
Pacific NorthwestFine fescue, ryegrass, bluegrassMild, moist climate suits cool-season
Transition zoneTall fescue (cool) or zoysia / Bermuda (warm)Each has weak seasons: summer for fescue, winter for warm types
Southeast and Gulf CoastSt. Augustine, Bermuda, centipede, zoysiaHot summers favor warm-season
Desert SouthwestBermudaNeeds irrigation; cool-season can be overseeded for winter color

Your local extension office can tell you which grasses do best in your county. Soil, shade and irrigation matter as much as the map.

How do the two types differ in care?

Mowing and water

Cool-season grasses are generally mowed higher (about 2.5–4 inches), which shades the soil and keeps roots cool. Warm-season grasses tolerate close mowing, but need regular cutting during summer. Both need about 1 inch of water per week or more in summer; deep rooted tall fescue and Bermuda handle drought best.

Fertilizing

Cool-season lawns get their main feeding in fall; warm-season lawns get theirs in late spring and summer. Feeding at the wrong time wastes product and feeds weeds. A schedule by month is in our guide on when to fertilize your lawn, and the nitrogen rates are in the calculator.

Weeds and winter

Warm-season lawns go dormant and tan, which is normal but leaves bare-looking ground where winter weeds can sprout. Cool-season lawns face summer crabgrass instead. Neither is "better"; they simply have different weak seasons.

Can you mix cool-season and warm-season grasses?

You can, but you generally shouldn't. In a mixed lawn each type grows in its own season, so the lawn looks green in some areas and brown in others, and the two types need different mowing heights and fertilizer dates. The exception is overseeding dormant warm-season turf with ryegrass in the far South to keep it green through winter, a common practice that requires a deliberate plan.

What mistakes do homeowners make when choosing?

Don't pick grass by looks alone. A lush cool-season lawn in a Florida yard will struggle through every summer. Match the grass to your climate, sun, soil and how much work you want to do.
  1. Choosing by neighbor's lawn color in winter, not by how it performs over the year.
  2. Planting Bermuda in shade. It needs full sun.
  3. Seeding at the wrong time. Seed each type in its own growing season.
  4. Ignoring shade. Under heavy trees, fine fescues or St. Augustine beat Bermuda or bluegrass.
  5. Expecting winter green from warm-season grass. Dormancy is normal.

How do you pick the right grass for your yard?

Run through these five questions before buying seed or sod:

  1. What is your climate? Check your USDA zone and your county extension office's lawn recommendations.
  2. How much sun does the lawn get? Under 4 hours of direct sun needs shade-tolerant fine fescue or St. Augustine; Bermuda needs 6–8 hours or more.
  3. How much traffic? Kids and pets favor Bermuda, zoysia, perennial ryegrass and Kentucky bluegrass, which recover well.
  4. How much water and mowing will you accept? Tall fescue and Bermuda are drought tolerant; fine fescue needs little feed.
  5. Do you mind a tan winter? If not, warm-season grass in the South is the natural choice.

Which type stays greener in a drought?

Both groups can go dormant in a drought and recover when it rains, but warm-season grasses such as Bermuda and zoysia generally survive hot, dry spells with less water than cool-season grasses. Among cool-season grasses, tall fescue has deep roots and handles summer stress best, while Kentucky bluegrass and perennial ryegrass usually need more irrigation to stay green.

What about the transition zone?

Gardeners between zones 6 and 7 face the hardest choice. Cool-season grasses suffer in humid summer heat, with disease and thinning in July and August. Warm-season grasses turn brown for four to five months of winter and may be damaged by hard freezes. Tall fescue, zoysia and Bermuda are the most common choices, and extension offices in states like Virginia, Kentucky, Missouri and Arkansas publish specific recommendations by county.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell what type of grass I have?

Look at when it greens up and when it browns. If it is green in cool weather and struggles in July heat, it is cool-season. If it turns tan after the first frost and wakes up in late spring, it is warm-season. Your county extension office can identify a sample.

What grass is best for the transition zone?

Tall fescue is the most common choice for low-maintenance lawns, while zoysia and Bermuda suit sunny, heat-tolerant lawns. Each fails in a different season, so choose by what you can live with.

Is warm-season grass lower maintenance than cool-season grass?

Not always. Warm-season grass often needs less water in summer but requires more frequent mowing and special care in winter. Cool-season grass may need more water in summer.

Which grass type stays green all year?

Cool-season grass stays green longest, especially in mild-winter areas. In the far South, warm-season lawns can be overseeded with ryegrass for green winter color.

Can I switch from cool-season to warm-season grass?

It's possible but requires removing the old turf and planting the new grass in its growing season. Check with your local extension service first, since the new grass must survive your winters.

The bottom line

Match your grass to your climate: cool-season grasses in the North and Northwest, warm-season grasses in the South, and a careful choice in the transition zone. Once you know the type, the calendar for seeding, feeding and mowing falls into place. Start with the lawn fertilizer calculator to plan your first feeding.

Related tools: Garden Calculator · Irrigation Runtime Calculator · Planting Calendar

Sources: Grass-type and mowing-height guidance from US university extension services, including Penn State Extension, North Carolina State Extension, Clemson Cooperative Extension and the University of Florida IFAS Extension; USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map. Ranges vary by cultivar and state. Last reviewed: October 2026.

items.title: The Renter's Guide to Peel & Stick Wallpaper (Install & Removal)
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
🏠 Renter's Guide

How to Install & Remove Peel-and-Stick Wallpaper

Zero damage. Zero anxiety. The complete guide to prepping, hanging, and safely removing temporary wallpaper to protect your security deposit.

Peel-and-stick wallpaper seems like a renter's dream: a way to add a bold accent wall or cover up "landlord beige" with zero long-term commitment. But one question holds everyone back: will it actually come off without damaging the wall and costing you your security deposit?

The answer is a definitive yes-but only if you follow the correct process for preparation, installation, and removal. Many guides gloss over the hard parts, making it seem as easy as applying a sticker. This leads to frustrating bubbles, crooked patterns, and potential paint damage. This is the complete, anxiety-free tutorial.

{getToc} $title={Table of Contents} $count={Boolean} $expanded={Boolean}

When installed and removed correctly, high-quality peel-and-stick wallpaper will not damage your drywall or paint.

Will It Really Spare Your Deposit?

Think of it as a giant, high-quality decal. Unlike traditional wallpaper that requires a messy, water-activated paste, peel-and-stick has a self-adhesive backing. The adhesive is formulated to be strong enough to stay up for years but low-tack enough to release cleanly.

✅ Ideal Surfaces

Smooth, semi-gloss, or satin-finish painted walls. These finishes are non-porous and "slick," allowing the adhesive to bond but release cleanly later.

❌ Risky Surfaces

Matte or flat-finish paint. These paints are chalky and porous; the adhesive can bond too strongly, potentially peeling the paint off.

⛔ Do Not Apply To

Unprimed drywall, highly textured walls (like heavy "orange peel"), or delicate, peeling vintage plaster. The paper will either fall off or ruin the wall.

📢 Safety First: The 30-Day Rule

If you've just painted your walls, you must wait at least 30 days for the paint to fully cure. Applying wallpaper to fresh paint (even if it feels dry to the touch) is a guaranteed way to peel that paint off when it's time for removal.

🛠️ Your Complete Tools & Materials List

Gathering these items before you start is the difference between a fun afternoon project and a day of total frustration.

You don't need heavy machinery, just precision tools: a sharp blade and a smoothing squeegee are your best friends.

  • ✔ Peel-and-Stick Wallpaper: Buy 15-20% more than your square footage to account for pattern matching.
  • ✔ Plastic Squeegee / Smoothing Tool: Essential for pushing out air bubbles.
  • ✔ Utility Knife: With extra sharp, snap-off blades. A dull blade will tear the vinyl.
  • ✔ Tape Measure & 2-Foot Level: For drawing your plumb line.
  • ✔ Isopropyl Alcohol & Water: For prepping and cleaning the wall.

Phase 1: The Critical Prep Work

You cannot get a flawless finish with a dirty, untested wall. This phase is 90% of the job.

The 48-Hour Patch Test

Before you commit, order a small sample. Cut a 1-foot square and apply it to a hidden spot on your wall. Leave it on for at least 48 hours, then try to remove it. If it comes off easily without pulling the paint, you are good to go. Do not skip this test.

Clean the Wall Surface

Dust, oils, and grime will prevent the adhesive from sticking. Remove all outlet covers. Wipe down the entire wall with a 50/50 mix of isopropyl alcohol and water. Let the wall dry 100%.

Phase 2: Installation Step-by-Step

Draw Your Plumb Line

Do not trust your ceiling or corners to be perfectly straight. Measure out from the corner a distance 1 inch less than the width of your wallpaper roll. Use your level to draw a faint, perfectly vertical pencil line from ceiling to floor. You will align your first panel against this line.

The "Center Out" Smoothing Method

Peel back only the first 12 inches of the backing. Align the top edge with the ceiling (leaving 2 inches of extra "bleed") and your side edge with the plumb line. Press the top section onto the wall. Using your squeegee, smooth the paper working from the center out to the edges to push all air out. Slowly pull the backing down a foot at a time and repeat.

Match and Overlap

Take your second panel and slide it up or down against the first until the pattern clicks into place perfectly. Check your brand's instructions: some require a 1/2-inch overlap, while others are designed to be "butted" edge-to-edge.

💡 Pro-Fix: Crooked Panels & Air Bubbles

If you hang a panel and it's crooked, don't panic. Gently peel it back and reposition it. If you find a small air bubble after smoothing, do not try to press it flat (it will crease). Instead, poke a tiny hole in the bubble with a pin and squeegee the air out through the hole.

Phase 3: The Zero-Damage Removal Guide

The time has come to move out. Follow this method to save your security deposit.

Using low heat softens the adhesive, allowing the vinyl to release from the paint without tearing it.

🔥 Step 1: Apply Low Heat

Set a hairdryer to its lowest, warmest setting. Hold it 6 inches from the top corner to soften the adhesive.

📐 Step 2: The 45-Degree Pull

Do not rip it off like a bandage. Pull the paper slowly, steadily, and downwards at a 45-degree angle. Keep the hairdryer aimed at the seam as you pull.

🧽 Step 3: Clean Residue

If any sticky residue remains on the wall, wipe it down with a citrus-based cleaner (like Goo Gone) or your alcohol/water mix.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use peel-and-stick wallpaper in a bathroom? ＋
Yes, but with caution. It is not recommended for inside a shower enclosure. For a powder room or a well-ventilated bathroom, it works great. Choose a high-quality, vinyl-based paper, as it will be water-resistant. Be aware that constant high humidity can eventually loosen the adhesive at the seams.
What if I have cheap "landlord paint" on my walls? ＋
"Landlord paint" is often a cheap, flat, or matte finish, which is the riskiest surface for adhesive. This is exactly why the 48-hour patch test is mandatory. If you do the patch test and the sample pulls off any paint or feels like it's ripping the drywall paper, do not proceed.
How much extra wallpaper should I buy for a pattern? ＋
The non-negotiable rule is to buy 15-20% more than your wall's total square footage. This "waste" is what you use to cut your panels to ensure the pattern matches up perfectly from one panel to the next. It is always better to have extra than to run out and risk buying a second batch with slightly different dye lots.

items.title: How Much Mulch Do I Need? Coverage Chart, Formula & Bag Guide
items.author: Fadzilla
items.content:
Quick answer

One cubic yard of mulch covers 108 square feet at 3 inches deep, the depth most garden beds need. To work out your own amount, multiply the bed's length × width in feet to get square feet, multiply by the depth in inches, then divide by 324. The answer is in cubic yards. For bags, multiply cubic yards by 13.5 to get the number of 2 cu ft bags.

Buying mulch is one of those jobs where guessing costs you twice. Buy too little and you're back at the garden center mid-project. Buy too much and you're left with half a yard of wood chips slowly composting in the driveway. The fix is a two-minute measurement and one simple formula.

This guide covers that formula, a ready-made coverage chart, how many bags common bed sizes need, the right depth for each type of mulch, and when bulk delivery beats bags. If you'd rather skip the math, the free mulch calculator does all of it, including odd shapes, tree rings and a bag-vs-bulk price comparison.

Key takeaways
  • Formula: square feet × depth (in) ÷ 324 = cubic yards.
  • Coverage: 1 cubic yard = 324 sq ft at 1 in, 162 at 2 in, 108 at 3 in, 81 at 4 in.
  • Bags: 1 cubic yard = 13.5 bags of 2 cu ft, or 9 bags of 3 cu ft.
  • Depth: 2–3 in for most wood mulches; never more than 4 in, and never piled against trunks.
  • Buy 10% extra: fresh mulch settles, and edges always take more than you expect.

How do you calculate how much mulch you need?

Every mulch calculation comes down to volume: area × depth. The only complication is that beds are measured in feet, depth in inches and bulk mulch is sold in cubic yards. Here's the whole process in four steps.

Step 1: Measure the area in square feet

For a rectangle, multiply length × width. A bed 20 ft long and 4 ft wide is 80 sq ft. Measure the inside of any edging, and subtract large areas you won't mulch, such as a patio or a big shrub base.

Step 2: Choose your depth in inches

Most beds need 3 inches of new mulch, or 2 inches if you're topping up an existing layer. See the depth chart below for each mulch type.

Step 3: Convert to cubic yards

Multiply square feet by depth in inches, then divide by 324. The 324 comes from 12 inches per foot × 27 cubic feet per cubic yard.

Example: 80 sq ft × 3 in ÷ 324 = 0.74 cubic yards.

Step 4: Convert to bags (if buying bagged mulch)

Multiply cubic yards by 27 to get cubic feet, then divide by your bag size and round up.

Example: 0.74 × 27 = 20 cu ft ÷ 2 cu ft bags = 10 bags. Add 10% for settling and buy 11.

🧮

Have several beds, a circle or a ring around a tree? Use the mulch calculator. Add every bed, pick your mulch type and get cubic yards, bags, weight and cost in one go.

Mulch coverage chart: how much does a cubic yard cover?

Use this chart when ordering bulk mulch, which is sold by the cubic yard in the US.

Mulch depth1 cubic yard covers1 cubic foot covers
1 inch324 sq ft12 sq ft
2 inches162 sq ft6 sq ft
3 inches108 sq ft4 sq ft
4 inches81 sq ft3 sq ft

How many bags of mulch do I need?

Bagged mulch in the US is usually sold in 2 cubic foot bags, sometimes 1.5 or 3 cu ft. This table shows how much common bed sizes need, before the 10% settling allowance.

AreaAt 2 in deepAt 3 in deep
4 × 8 ft raised bed (32 sq ft)0.2 cu yd · 3 bags0.3 cu yd · 4 bags
10 × 10 ft (100 sq ft)0.62 cu yd · 9 bags0.93 cu yd · 13 bags
10 × 20 ft (200 sq ft)1.23 cu yd · 17 bags1.85 cu yd · 25 bags
20 × 20 ft (400 sq ft)2.47 cu yd · 34 bags3.70 cu yd · 50 bags
500 sq ft3.09 cu yd · 42 bags4.63 cu yd · 63 bags
1,000 sq ft6.17 cu yd · 84 bags9.26 cu yd · 125 bags

Bag counts are for 2 cu ft bags. For 3 cu ft bags, multiply by 0.67. For 1.5 cu ft bags, multiply by 1.33.

How deep should mulch be?

Depth matters as much as quantity. Too thin and weeds push straight through. Too thick and the layer sheds water and starves shallow roots of oxygen. University extension services consistently recommend 2–4 inches, depending on how coarse the mulch is.

Mulch typeRecommended depthWhy
Shredded hardwood / dyed mulch2–3 inKnits together into a dense mat that blocks weeds
Wood chips / large bark nuggets3–4 inCoarse pieces leave gaps that let light through
Cedar or cypress2–3 inLight and slow to break down
Pine straw3–4 in looseSettles to about 2 in within weeks
Compost or leaf mold1–2 inFeeds the soil; thicker layers stay soggy
Pea gravel / river rock2–3 inUse landscape fabric underneath
Don't build "mulch volcanoes." Piling mulch against tree trunks or shrub stems keeps the bark constantly wet, which invites rot, disease and gnawing rodents. Pull mulch back so there's a 3–6 inch bare ring around every trunk.

How to measure odd-shaped beds

Few beds are perfect rectangles. These shortcuts are accurate enough for buying mulch:

  • Circle: area = 3.14 × radius². A round bed 8 ft across has a 4 ft radius, so 3.14 × 16 = 50 sq ft.
  • Triangle or corner bed: area = base × height ÷ 2.
  • Ring around a tree: work out the area of the full circle, then subtract the small bare circle at the trunk.
  • Curvy or kidney-shaped bed: measure the length, then take three or four widths along it and average them. Length × average width gets you within about 10%.
  • Complicated layout: split it into rectangles and circles, work out each one, and add them together. The calculator lets you add as many beds as you need.

Topping up old mulch: how much to add

You rarely start from bare soil. Organic mulch breaks down over one to two years, so most beds only need a refresh. Push a trowel into the existing layer and measure how much is left, then add only the difference. If 1 inch remains and you want 3, add 2 inches.

Before topping up, rake the old layer to break up any crust that sheds water. If old mulch is matted, moldy or already deeper than 4 inches, remove some of it first.

Bagged vs bulk mulch: which is cheaper?

Bulk mulch is almost always cheaper per cubic yard, but the delivery fee changes the math for small jobs. Using example prices of $4.50 for a 2 cu ft bag, $40 per cubic yard in bulk and a $50 delivery fee:

  • One cubic yard in bags: 13.5 bags × $4.50 = $60.75
  • One cubic yard in bulk: $40 + $50 delivery = $90
  • Break-even: bulk becomes cheaper at about 2.4 cubic yards (roughly 33 bags).

Your local prices will differ, so plug them into the mulch calculator, which shows which option is cheaper for your exact project. Bulk has two other advantages for big jobs: no plastic bags to dispose of, and one delivery instead of several car trips.

Will it fit in my truck?

A full-size pickup with a 6.5 ft bed holds about 2 cubic yards of mulch level with the sides. Wood mulch weighs roughly 400–800 lb per cubic yard depending on moisture, so it's well within most half-ton trucks' payload. Rock and gravel are a different story: at roughly 1.4 tons per cubic yard, one yard can max out a light pickup.

5 mulching mistakes that waste money

  1. Measuring the outside of the edging. On narrow beds, a few inches of edging adds up to a lot of mulch you don't need.
  2. Forgetting settling. Fresh, fluffy mulch compacts 10–20%. Buy about 10% extra.
  3. Going too deep. More than 4 inches doesn't stop more weeds; it just costs more and can suffocate roots.
  4. Mulching over weeds. Pull or smother existing weeds first, or perennial weeds will come straight through.
  5. Mulching too early in spring. Wait until the soil has warmed, usually mid to late spring. Mulch insulates, and cold soil under mulch stays cold longer.

Frequently asked questions

How much mulch do I need for a 4×8 raised bed?

A 4 × 8 ft raised bed (32 sq ft) needs 8 cubic feet of mulch at 3 inches deep, which is 4 bags of 2 cu ft. At 2 inches it needs 5.3 cubic feet, or 3 bags. In vegetable beds, use straw, shredded leaves or compost instead of wood mulch.

How many yards of mulch do I need for 1,000 square feet?

At 3 inches deep, 1,000 sq ft needs 9.26 cubic yards; at 2 inches it needs 6.17 cubic yards. With 10% extra for settling, order about 10 yards or 7 yards respectively.

Is 2 inches of mulch enough?

Two inches is enough for fine mulches like shredded hardwood, and when topping up an existing layer. For new beds or coarse wood chips, 3 inches gives better weed control and moisture retention.

How much area does a bag of mulch cover?

A 2 cu ft bag covers 12 sq ft at 2 inches deep or 8 sq ft at 3 inches. A 3 cu ft bag covers 18 sq ft at 2 inches or 12 sq ft at 3 inches.

How much mulch do I need around a tree?

A mulch ring 6 ft across at 3 inches deep, with a 1 ft bare circle at the trunk, needs about 7 cubic feet, or 4 bags of 2 cu ft. Wider rings are better for trees, ideally out to the drip line, but keep the depth at 2–3 inches.

When is the best time to put down mulch?

Mid to late spring, after the soil has warmed and spring weeds have been pulled, is ideal. A second application in fall helps insulate perennials and shrub roots through winter.

The bottom line

Measure your beds, multiply square feet by depth in inches and divide by 324. That's your cubic yards. Aim for 2–3 inches of most wood mulches, add 10% for settling, and compare bag and bulk prices before you buy. For multiple beds, odd shapes or a quick cost comparison, the free mulch calculator does the work in seconds.

Related tools: Soil Calculator · Topsoil & Gravel Calculator · Plant Spacing Calculator

Sources: Mulching guidance from US university extension services, including University of Maryland Extension, Penn State Extension and the University of Minnesota Extension; tree-mulching recommendations from the International Society of Arboriculture. Volume conversions: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Prices are illustrative examples; check your local garden center. Last reviewed: October 2026.
